note: Latin ab, Greek ἀπό and English of/off all go back to one Indo-European word. Classical ab did not survive in Romance on its own; Italian da is usually explained as dē + ab.

ex.en: from the founding of the City (of Rome)

note: Church Latin, from Aramaic abbā 'father' via Greek. English abbey comes from the derivative abbātia.

ex.en: He has gone, departed, escaped, broken out. (Cicero on Catiline)

note: Literally 'to bristle away from' (horreō 'bristle, shudder'). Portuguese aborrecer has drifted from 'loathe' to 'annoy, bore'.
The participle abiectus 'thrown down, cast off' gave English abject.
A rare literary verb in Latin that became the everyday word for 'hide' in Spanish, Portuguese, Romanian and (with an extra prefix) Italian.
The participle absolūtus 'loosened, finished, complete' is the source of absolute.
The participle absēns, absentis is the source of absent; Spanish and Portuguese ausente show b turning into u.

ex.en: may the omen be absent (i.e. touch wood)

note: Related to surdus 'deaf, muffled': the original sense was 'jarring, out of tune'.
From unda 'wave': literally 'to flow over the edge', like redundant (re- + unda) 'overflowing'.

ex.t: Quō ūsque tandem abūtēre, Catilīna, patientiā nostrā?
ex.en: How long, Catiline, will you go on abusing our patience? (Cicero)

note: Greek ἄβυσσος 'bottomless'. Spanish abismo and French abîme come from a Late Latin superlative *abyssimus 'the very deepest'.

cite: ac, short form of atque, used before consonants
forms: short form of atque, used before consonants

note: Italian accendere is the everyday word for switching on a light or an engine. Romanian aprinde 'kindle' comes from apprehendere 'seize'.
ad + cantus 'song added (to speech)': a word-for-word calque of Greek προσῳδία, from which English prosody comes.
From ad + cadō 'fall': an accident is something that 'falls to' you. Impersonal accidit, ut… 'it happens that…'.
The Romance verbs continue the frequentative acceptāre; Portuguese aceitar shows the popular change -pt- to -it-, as in conceptum > conceito.
From ad + causa 'lawsuit': to call someone to account in court. The grammatical term accusative is a mistranslation of Greek αἰτιατική 'the case of what is caused'.
In Romance the word narrowed to 'sour'. French aigre gave vinaigre 'sour wine', and via Old French also English eager, originally 'keen, sharp'.
In Spanish and Portuguese acervo now names the holdings of a library or museum. The ancient 'heap' paradox (when does a pile of grain stop being a heap?) is the sorītēs.
Italian keeps the Latin word, while the west says 'sour wine' (vinaigre, from vīnum ācre). Romanian oțet came back via Slavonic, which had borrowed it from Latin.

en: Achilles (Greek hero of the Trojan War)

note: The basic meaning is 'sharp edge'; an army drawn up for battle is a cutting edge. Late Latin aciārium 'edge-metal' is the Romance word for steel.
ad + quaerō 'seek': the long ae becomes ī in compounds, as in inquīrō and requīrō.
Italian and Romanian keep the short word; the west prefers the diminutive acucula 'little needle'.
Spanish agudo and French aigu show the popular voicing of -c- to -g- (lost altogether in French). The acute accent is the 'sharp' one.
As the case endings wore away, ad took over the job of the dative: Latin dat librum Petrō became Italian dà il libro a Pietro, Spanish da el libro a Pedro.

ex.en: for the greater glory of God (motto of the Jesuits)

note: Greek ἀδάμας means 'unconquerable'. Late Latin reshaped it as *diamas, perhaps under the influence of words in dia-, which is how adamant and diamond became two words.
Spanish añadir continues the verb with an extra prefix (in + addere). Elsewhere the everyday word comes from other compounds.
Spanish aún 'still, even' comes from adhūc; Italian ancora and French encore instead go back to hanc hōram 'this hour'.
An adjective (nōmen adiectīvum) is a word 'thrown to' or added to a noun, translating Greek ἐπίθετον, whence epithet.
Alchemists called a master adeptus, 'one who has attained' the secret; hence adept.
Italian aggiungere is the everyday word for 'add', with the regular change of -di- to -gg- (compare hodiē > oggi).
Every Romance language says 'help' with the frequentative adiūtāre, built on the supine adiūtum; French aider gave English aid.
Built on minister 'servant'; to administer was originally to serve.
The Latin verb mostly means 'be amazed at'; Spanish admirar can still mean 'to astonish'.
ad + optō 'choose': to adopt is to choose someone as one's own. Augustus was Caesar's adopted son.
From ōrō 'speak, pray'. Everyday 'love, adore' is a later weakening of 'worship'.
Also spelled assum, affuī. Adsum! is the answer candidates give when their names are called at a Catholic ordination.
Present participle of adolēscō 'grow up': 'growing'. Its past participle adultus 'grown' gave adult. A Roman adulēscēns could be up to about thirty.
Related to adulterō 'falsify, corrupt' (English adulterate), from ad + alter 'other', not to adultus 'grown up'.
Adventūra 'things about to arrive' became Old French aventure, the source of adventure. Italian l'avvenire is 'the future'.
Participle of advertō 'turn towards': what faces you head-on, hence what opposes you. Rēs adversae is 'misfortune', rēs secundae 'prosperity'.
Literally 'one called to (one's side)': in Rome a friend who supported you in court. The word became the general Romance term for a lawyer.
The original sense is 'hearth' (compare Greek αἴθω 'burn'), so a single aedēs is a temple and plural aedēs a house with many rooms.
aedēs + faciō 'make a house'. English edify keeps the Christian metaphor of 'building up' a person morally.

en: aedile (magistrate in charge of public buildings, markets and games)

note: None of the Romance languages kept aeger. Italian malato and French malade go back to male habitus 'in bad condition'.

ex.en: to take (something) badly, be annoyed at

rel.g: sick note excusing a student from an exam

note: From aeger 'sick'. In British universities an aegrotat ('he is ill') was a degree awarded to a student too ill to sit the exams.
Feminine, like most names of countries in -us. English gypsy is a clipped 'Egyptian', from a mistaken belief about the Roma's origin.

en: Aeneas (Trojan hero, ancestor of the Romans)
note: A Greek first-declension masculine: accusative Aenēān, vocative Aenēā. The epithet that defines him in the Aeneid is pius.

ex.t: Vidēmus nunc per speculum in aenigmate.
ex.en: For now we see through a glass, darkly. (1 Corinthians 13:12)

note: Spanish and Portuguese igual show ae > e > i and -qu- > -gu-. French égal is a learned remake of Old French ivel.
aequē ac (atque) 'just as': aequē ac tū 'just as much as you'.
aequus + nox: the day when night is equal to day.
Literally 'the level (expanse)', from aequus. A favourite poetic word for the sea in Vergil and Ovid.

ex.t: Aequam mementō rēbus in arduīs servāre mentem.
ex.en: Remember to keep a level head when times are hard. (Horace)

note: Borrowed from Greek; the Romance words come from the Greek-style accusative āera. Italian aria also came to mean 'tune', which English borrowed as aria.
From aes 'bronze, money'. The Roman treasury was kept in the temple of Saturn in the Forum.
The derivative aerāmen 'bronze-work' survives everywhere: copper in Italian and Romanian, wire in Spanish and Portuguese. English ore (Old English ār 'brass') is a native cognate.
Italian estate and French été continue aestās, but Spanish verano, Portuguese verão and Romanian vară come from vēr 'spring': the 'early summer' took over the whole season.
The same word covers 'heat' and 'tide': both are a seething or boiling. An aestuārium is where the tide surges in.
French âge (Old French eage) comes from a derived form *aetāticum, which also gave English age. Aetās itself is contracted from *aevitās, from aevum.

ex.en: Grant them eternal rest, O Lord.

note: Greek αἰθήρ is the bright, burning upper air (αἴθω 'burn'), above the misty āēr. The accusative is usually Greek aethera.
Medium aevum 'the middle age' is the source of medieval and Italian Medioevo. Aeternus and aetās are both built on it.
Like ferō, it takes its perfect and supine from other roots: at-tulī (tollō) and al-lātum (from *tlātum).
A typical idiom: afficere aliquem poenā 'to punish someone', literally 'to affect someone with punishment'.
From firmus 'firm': to affirm is to make something solid.

en: the Roman province of Africa (modern Tunisia)
note: For the Romans Africa was first the territory of Carthage; only gradually did the name spread to the whole continent.
English acre and Greek ἀγρός are cognates. In Romance, campus 'open plain' replaced ager everywhere; ager lives on only in learned words like agrarian and agriculture.
ad + gerō 'carry to': earth carried to one place and piled up.
ad + gradior 'step': literally 'step towards', hence 'attack'.
Frequentative of agō: 'keep driving'.
From agō 'drive': a body of men being driven forward. Prīmum agmen is the vanguard, novissimum agmen the rearguard.
Note the supine agnitum (like cognitum), not *agnōtum. The root is the same as in English know and Greek γιγνώσκω.
The diminutive agnellus won in Italian, French and Romanian (miel); Spanish and Portuguese say 'the late-born one'.

ex.t: Agnus Deī, quī tollis peccāta mundī
ex.en: Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world

note: One of the busiest Latin verbs: vītam agere 'live a life', grātiās agere 'give thanks', agenda 'things to be done'. Greek ἄγω 'lead' is the same root.

ex.en: Whatever you are doing, do it (properly).

note: ager + colō 'till the field'. A masculine noun of the first declension, like nauta and poēta.
A defective verb used mainly in a few forms, above all ait 'he says' and āiunt 'they say'. It is the positive counterpart of negō 'say no'.
English aisle is the 'wing' of a church, from Old French ele; its spelling was later confused with isle.
A spoken-Latin variant *alecrus became the Romance word for 'cheerful'; Italian allegro is also the musical 'lively'.
A Gaulish word. Caesar called his legion of Gaulish recruits the Alaudae, 'the Larks', perhaps for the crests on their helmets.

en: Alba Longa, ancient Latin city in the Alban Hills, mother-city of Rome
note: Longa 'the Long' is an adjective agreeing with it (Alba Longa, abl. Albā Longā). Legend makes it the city of Aeneas' son Ascanius and the birthplace of Romulus and Remus.
The Alban Hills (Colli Albani) and Lake Albano south-east of Rome still carry the name.
Only Romanian kept albus as the ordinary colour word (alb). In the west Germanic *blank 'shining' took over, and albus survived as the dawn: alba, aube.

ex.en: The die is cast. (Caesar crossing the Rubicon)

note: A legal alibi is the plea that the accused was 'elsewhere'.
Spanish ajeno and Portuguese alheio are inherited, with -li- becoming j and lh.

ex.t: Homō sum: hūmānī nihil ā mē aliēnum putō.
ex.en: I am human: I consider nothing human foreign to me. (Terence)

note: From alō 'nourish'; alimony (alimōnia) is the same root.

cite: aliquantum, abl. aliquantō 'by a good deal' (with comparatives)
forms: abl. aliquantō 'by a good deal' (with comparatives)

note: French aucun originally meant 'some' but, constantly paired with ne, came to mean 'none'. Spanish and Portuguese algo 'something' is aliquod.
cite: aliquis, aliqua, aliquid; adj. aliquī, aliqua, aliquod
forms: aliqua, aliquid; adj. aliquī, aliqua, aliquod

note: Also spelled allium. A textbook case of Latin -li- in the west: Italian gl, Spanish j, French il, Portuguese lh (compare folium > foglia, hoja, feuille, folha).
Repeated, alius means 'one … another': aliī … aliī 'some … others'. Romance replaced it with alter, originally 'the other of two'.
cite: alius, alia, aliud (gen. alterīus, dat. aliī)

note: Hebrew hallelū-yāh 'praise Yah(weh)', passed through Greek into the Latin liturgy.
Also spelled adloquor. Catullus at his brother's grave: 'to speak in vain to your silent ashes' (mūtam nēquīquam alloquerer cinerem).
From alō 'nourish'. Spanish alma 'soul' is unrelated: it comes from anima.
Its participle altus 'grown, raised up' became the adjective 'high'; adolēscō 'grow up' (adolescent, adult) and alumnus 'nursling' are from the same root.
French autel shows the popular change al > au before a consonant, as in alter > autre.
Alter was 'the other of two' (alter … alter 'the one … the other'); in all the Romance languages it ousted alius as the ordinary word for 'other'.
cite: alter, altera, alterum (gen. alterīus, dat. alterī)

note: Altus measures from the observer, so it means both 'high' and 'deep'. French haut owes its h- to Frankish *hōh 'high'.
From alō 'nourish': 'one who is being fed and raised'. In Spanish and Portuguese it is the ordinary word for a school pupil.
Romanian albie and French auge are its worn-down heirs. The diminutive alveolus 'little hollow' names the air sacs of the lungs and the sockets of the teeth.
Inherited everywhere. Italian amaro is also a bitter herbal liqueur, and amaretto a 'little bitter' almond biscuit or liqueur.
From ambigō 'drive both ways, waver' (amb- 'around, both' + agō).
A compound of eō 'go', but conjugated mostly like a fourth-conjugation verb; perfect also ambīvī.
Literally 'going around' the Forum to solicit votes; from there, the craving for office and honour.
Declined like duo. English both and Greek ἄμφω share the same ancient root.
French aller is probably a worn-down ambulāre; its other forms come from vādere (je vais) and īre (j'irai). An ambulance was first a hôpital ambulant, a 'walking' field hospital.
Hebrew 'truly, so be it'. Romanian amin reflects the Byzantine Greek pronunciation of η as i.
ā 'away from' + mēns 'mind'; compare dēmēns, whence dementia.
The inherited Romance words come from a spoken-Latin *amīcitās, -ātis, with the same suffix as cīvitās > città, ciudad, cité.

ex.t: Amīcitia nisi inter bonōs esse nōn potest.
ex.en: Friendship can exist only between good people. (Cicero)

note: Built on amō. Its opposite inimīcus 'personal enemy' (in- + amīcus) gave enemy, nemico, enemigo, ennemi, inimigo.

ex.t: Amīcus certus in rē incertā cernitur.
ex.en: A sure friend is seen in an unsure situation. (Ennius)

note: Old French ante < amita gave English aunt; modern French tante is a nursery form 'ta ante'. Latin distinguished amita (father's sister) from mātertera (mother's sister).
The classical word for 'lose' left no descendants; every Romance language uses perdere, which in Latin meant 'destroy, waste'.
A grander, mostly poetic word beside flūmen and fluvius. It is an i-stem (abl. amne or amnī, gen. pl. amnium).
The model verb of the first conjugation. French aimer comes from forms like amat > aime, where the stressed a became ai before the nasal; an amateur is one who does something for love.
The locus amoenus, a 'pleasant place' with shade, grass and running water, is a stock setting of ancient and medieval poetry.
French amour is not the regular French outcome (which would be *ameur): it was taken from Occitan, the language of the troubadours' love poetry.
'A theatre on both sides': two semicircular theatres joined into an oval, like the Colosseum (Amphitheātrum Flāvium).

en: amphora (also a unit of liquid measure)
note: Greek ἀμφορεύς, contracted from ἀμφιφορεύς 'carried on both sides', i.e. by two handles.
The neuter comparative of amplus. With numbers it needs no quam: amplius mīlle hominēs 'more than a thousand men'.
Spanish ancho 'wide' shows -mpl- > -nch-; compare implēre > henchir. Italian ampio shows -pl- > -pi-, as in plēnus > pieno.
A round-bellied flask; French ampoule now means both a light bulb and a blister. Horace uses ampullae for 'bombastic words', swollen like bottles.

en: Amulius, king of Alba Longa who seized the throne from his brother Numitor

note: Spoken Latin reshaped the Greek word as *amandula, the source of the Romance forms and English almond. Anatomists later named the almond-shaped amygdala of the brain after it.
Introduces the second half of a double question: utrum … an … 'whether … or …'; haud sciō an 'I am inclined to think that'.

ex.en: Behold the handmaid of the Lord. (Luke 1:38)

note: Also spelled anchora. Italian àncora 'anchor' is stressed on the first syllable, unlike ancóra 'still, again', which comes from hanc hōram.

en: Androclus, runaway slave spared in the arena by the lion he had once helped
note: Aulus Gellius tells the story (Attic Nights 5.14); English knows him as Androcles, from Shaw's play Androcles and the Lion.
Greek ἄγγελος 'messenger'. Romanian înger shows the regular change an- > în-, as in campus > câmp.
The root of narrowness and distress: angustus 'narrow', anxius 'anxious', angor 'anguish', and Greek ἄγχω 'strangle'.

ex.en: A snake lurks in the grass. (Vergil)

note: Romanian unghi shows an- > un- and -gl- > -ghi-, as in ungula > unghie 'nail'.
From physical narrowness to mental distress: anguish is a tightness in the chest. German Angst and English anxious come from the same root.
The basic idea is breath, like Greek ἄνεμος 'wind'. Spanish alma comes from the contracted *anma; Romanian inimă now means 'heart'.
animum advertere 'turn the mind towards'. With in aliquem it means 'take action against someone, punish'.
From anima: 'a breathing thing'. A neuter i-stem: abl. animālī, pl. animālia.
Animus is the thinking, feeling, willing mind; anima is the breath of life. Italian Animo! and Spanish ¡Ánimo! still mean 'Courage!'.

ex.en: I have in mind, I intend

note: Inherited everywhere. Spanish ñ is the regular outcome of Latin -nn-, and the tilde itself began as a small n written above the line.

ex.en: in the year of the Lord (AD)

note: Spanish and Portuguese asa lost the n before s, just as mēnsa became mesa.
Latin ānser lost an initial h- (*hanser), which is why it looks so unlike its cognates goose, German Gans and Greek χήν. The sacred geese of Juno saved the Capitol from the Gauls.
Spoken Latin strengthened ante to ab ante 'from before', whence Italian avanti and French avant (English vanguard, advance).
Old French ancestre, from the nominative antecessor, gave English ancestor; 'one who has gone before' you.

en: sail-yard (the spar a sail hangs from)
note: Also spelled antemna. Renaissance translators of Aristotle used it for insects' feelers, and in the age of radio it became the aerial.
Often split: ante … quam. Takes the subjunctive when the action is anticipated or prevented.
French antique is learned; the everyday French ancien comes from *anteānus, also from ante.
Also spelled annulus. A diminutive of ānus 'ring'; the Romance words all continue a different diminutive, ānellus.
Fourth declension and feminine. Unrelated to ānus (long ā, 2nd decl.) 'ring'.
From angō 'squeeze, choke', like angustus 'narrow' and angor 'anguish'.
Italian cinghiale and French sanglier come from singulāris porcus 'the solitary pig', since old boars live alone.
French ouvrir was reshaped by the opposite verb couvrir (from cooperīre).
Western Romance prefers the diminutive apicula. Native Old French had ef, too short to survive; abeille was borrowed from Occitan.
Greek ἀπόστολος 'one sent out'. French apôtre is the popular development, with l becoming r as in epistola > épître.
One Greek word, many disguises: Italian bottega, Spanish bodega, Portuguese adega, French boutique (via Occitan) and, through learned Latin, English apothecary.
French appeler is the everyday 'call': je m'appelle 'I call myself, my name is'. Not to be confused with appellō, appellere 'drive towards, land'.
ad + petō 'make for': appetītus is the 'reaching out' of desire.
Sailors 'brought the ship to' the shore (nāvem applicāre); hence Spanish llegar and Portuguese chegar 'arrive', with pl- > ll-/ch-. Compare arrivare, arriver from *adrīpāre 'reach the bank'.
To 'grasp' with the mind became 'learn' in the west, while Romanian aprinde means 'set alight' (fire 'catches'). English apprehend keeps both senses: 'arrest' and 'understand'.

en: approach, draw near (+ dat. or ad)
note: Built on propinquus 'near' (prope). The shorter Late Latin appropiāre gave French approcher and English approach.
Short for mēnsis Aprīlis. The Romans linked it with aperīre 'open' (the opening buds), but the name may well be Etruscan.
apud Caesarem 'at Caesar's (house)', apud Platōnem 'in Plato'. French chez does the same job but comes from casa 'house'.
French eau (Old French eve, eaue) shows how far sound change can go. Romanian apă shows its typical qu > p, as in equa > iapă 'mare'.
Often written as two words, aquae ductus 'conveying of water'.
Each legion marched behind a silver eagle; to lose it was the ultimate disgrace.
The cold, stormy north-north-east wind, the Greek Boreas.

en: the Aquitani, people of south-western Gaul
Aquitania, south-western Gaul between the Garonne and the Pyrenees
note: French Aquitaine is a learned form; the name's popular development was Guyenne, via Occitan Guiana.

ex.en: the Altar of Augustan Peace (in Rome)

en: Arachne, Lydian weaver turned into a spider by Minerva
note: Her name is simply Greek ἀράχνη 'spider', the source of English arachnid. A Greek first-declension noun: gen. Arachnēs, acc. Arachnēn.
French araignée first meant the web (*arāneāta); the spider itself was Old French aragne.
In the Romance languages the arbiter is now, above all, the football referee.
Spanish albedrío, as in libre albedrío 'free will', is the popular form, with r > l dissimilation.
Feminine in Latin despite -or, like most tree names; only Portuguese árvore keeps the feminine. Italian albero and Spanish árbol avoid the double r by dissimilation.
Noah's ark is arca Nōē, a great 'chest'. Arcānus 'secret' is literally 'shut in a chest'.
Greek ἀρχι- 'chief' + τέκτων 'builder, carpenter'.
The rainbow is a bow in Romance too: Italian arcobaleno, Spanish arco iris, French arc-en-ciel 'bow in the sky'.
Romanian arde is still the everyday word for 'burn'. English arson comes via Old French from the supine arsum.

ex.en: Through hardships to the stars. (motto of the RAF)

note: The popular descendants keep the farmyard sense 'threshing floor' (Spanish era, Portuguese eira, Romanian arie); the learned area, área is the abstract 'area'.
French argent means both 'silver' and 'money', exactly like Spanish plata. Argentina is named after the Río de la Plata, the 'silver river'.
The root means 'bright, clear' (as in argentum 'silver'): to argue was originally to make something plain.
The siege engine was named for its iron ram's head. The farm animal is usually called by other words today, e.g. Romanian berbec from vervēx.
From the stiff bristle on an ear of wheat came the fishbone and the sharp edge or mountain ridge: French arête.
The neuter plural arma was reinterpreted as a feminine singular 'weapon' in all the Romance languages. English alarm is Italian all'arme! 'to arms!'.

ex.en: Arms and the man I sing (first words of the Aeneid)

note: Originally a place to keep arma 'tools, gear'; now the everyday wardrobe of Italy, Spain, France and Portugal.
The feminine armāta 'armed (force)' became French armée 'army' (English army) and Spanish armada 'fleet, navy'.
French labourer 'plough' comes from labōrāre 'toil', whose sense narrowed to the farmer's main labour.
From arrogō 'claim for oneself' (ad + rogō 'ask').
Ars covers any skill, from carpentry to rhetoric (ars poētica, ars amātōria). Genitive plural artium.

ex.en: Art is long, life is short.

note: A diminutive of artus 'joint'. The learned word gave 'article' everywhere, while the popular forms became Italian artiglio 'claw' and French orteil 'toe'.
ars + faciō 'skill-maker'.

ex.en: What an artist dies in me! (Nero's last words, in Suetonius)

note: Almost always plural, with dative and ablative artubus (not *artibus, which belongs to ars). Greek ἄρθρον 'joint' (whence arthritis) is a cognate.
From arō 'plough'. A favourite word of Vergil's Georgics and of poetry generally.
The arx of Rome stood on the northern summit of the Capitoline hill. Genitive plural arcium.

en: as, a copper coin of small value
a whole unit (divided into twelve unciae)
note: The as was the 'one' of Roman money, and so the one on a die or card became the ace. Catullus values old men's gossip at ūnius assis, 'a single penny'.
ad + scandō 'climb' (compare descendō). Everyday 'go up' is French monter, Italian salire, Spanish subir.

en: Asia Minor; the Roman province of Asia
note: For the Romans Asia usually meant the rich province in western Asia Minor, around Ephesus and Pergamum.
The circumflex of French âne marks a lost s (Old French asne). English ass was borrowed from Latin very early, probably through Celtic.
ad + speciō 'look'; the same root gives spectāre, speculum and English spectacle, inspect, respect.
ad + sentiō 'feel, think': to share someone's opinion.
From assideō 'sit beside': someone who is always sitting at the task.
Borrowed from Greek; the native Latin words are stēlla and sīdus. A disaster (Italian disastro) is an event under an evil star.

ex.en: This is the way to the stars. (Vergil)

note: Greek ἄσυλον 'not to be plundered'. Legend says Romulus opened an asylum on the Capitol to people his new city; in Italian asilo is also a kindergarten.
A stronger 'but' than sed, often introducing an objection: at, inquit … 'but, he says, …'.
Latin had two blacks: āter, matt and gloomy, and niger, glossy. Only niger survived into Romance.

ex.en: Behind the horseman sits black care. (Horace)

note: Plural in form, as in Greek. 'At Athens' is the locative Athēnīs.
Greek ἄτομος 'uncuttable', the Epicurean building block. Cicero uses atomus; Lucretius preferred native words like prīmōrdia 'first beginnings'.
Weightier than et. After words of likeness or difference it means 'as' or 'than': īdem atque 'the same as', aliter ac 'otherwise than'.

en: atrium, entrance hall (of a Roman house)

note: ad + tendō 'stretch towards'. Stretching one's mind towards something became 'wait for it' in French and Italian: a classic false friend.
ad + tangō 'touch'. French atteindre 'reach' gave English attain.
Participle of attonō 'strike with thunder'. French étonner and English astonish, astound come from the related *extonāre.
From augeō 'increase': the auctor makes something grow or stands behind it. The th of English author is a false Greek-style spelling.
Personal weight and prestige, as opposed to potestās, legal power. Augustus claimed to surpass all others in auctōritās, though not in potestās.
Semi-deponent: active present, passive-looking perfect ausus sum 'I dared'. The Romance verbs are built on that participle ausus.

ex.en: Dare to be wise. (Horace; Kant's motto of the Enlightenment)

note: The model fourth-conjugation verb. French ouïr survives only in fixed phrases (par ouï-dire 'by hearsay'); everyday 'hear' is entendre, from intendere.

ex.en: Let the other side be heard as well.

note: ab + ferō, with the prefix in the form au-. Its supine ablātum named the ablative, the case of 'taking away' (separation).
An auction (auctiō) is a sale by 'increasing' bids. The same root gives auctor, auctōritās, auxilium and Augustus.
French bonheur 'happiness' is literally 'good omen': heur goes back via Old French eür to *agūrium. Italians wish each other Auguri!

en: Augustus (title of Octavian and later emperors)
note: Octavian took the title 'the Revered One' in 27 BC, and the month Sextīlis was renamed after him. French août, now often pronounced just 'oot', shows how much a word can shrink.
Greek αὐλή 'courtyard'. In Spanish and Italian an aula is now a classroom or lecture hall; in Portuguese also the lesson itself.
A spoken-Latin derivative *aurāticum 'windy weather' became French orage 'thunderstorm'.
Spoken Latin preferred this diminutive (pronounced oricla) to auris; it is the source of the word for 'ear' in every Romance language.
English ear, German Ohr and Greek οὖς are all cognates; Latin auris has r from earlier s (rhotacism).

ex.en: They have ears, but they will not hear. (Psalm 115)

note: From the same root as Greek ἠώς 'dawn' and English east: the direction of sunrise.
A neat picture of the diphthong au: kept in Romanian aur, ou in Portuguese ouro, o in Italian, Spanish and French. The chemical symbol Au is from aurum.
A rather colloquial Latin verb, rare in literature, which became the ordinary word for 'listen' in every Romance language. Doctors still auscultate the chest.

en: right to take the auspices; command
note: avis 'bird' + speciō 'watch': the magistrate watched the birds before any public act. Hence 'under the auspices of'.
Australia is the terra austrālis 'southern land'. Austria is unrelated: it latinises German Österreich 'eastern realm'.
Aut marks a sharp alternative, vel a free choice. It is the source of the Romance word for 'or'.

ex.en: Either Caesar or nothing. (motto of Cesare Borgia)

note: Postpositive: it never stands first in its clause (ego autem … 'but I …').
Also spelled auctumnus. Romanian toamnă has lost its first syllable; Spanish otoño shows -mn- > -ñ-, as in damnum > daño.
From augeō 'increase': help adds strength. The auxilia were non-citizen units supporting the legions.
Molière's comedy L'Avare (The Miser) is modelled on Plautus' Aululāria.
Imperative of aveō 'be well'. The Angel's greeting Avē Marīa made it a prayer word throughout Europe.

ex.en: Hail, Emperor, those who are about to die salute you. (Suetonius)

note: Italian uccello and French oiseau come from a diminutive *aucellus 'little bird'. Spanish keeps ave for larger birds, but small birds are pájaros, from passer 'sparrow'.

en: Avitus, Roman family name (cognomen); a friend addressed by Martial

note: Literally 'little grandfather' (diminutive of avus). Latin distinguished the mother's brother (avunculus) from the father's (patruus); French oncle and Romanian unchi generalised it, and English took uncle from French.
Spanish eje and Portuguese eixo show the popular development of x (as in laxāre > dejar, deixar).

en: (in Horace) astrological, of the Chaldean star-readers
note: Horace's Babylōniī numerī are horoscope calculations: Babylon was the home of astrology.
Also spelled bacca. Any small round fruit, including the olive. Medieval scholars punned baccalārius 'bachelor' into baccalaureus, as if from bāca laurī 'laurel berry'.
Italians still swear Per Bacco! 'By Bacchus!'.
Italian bacchetta 'little stick' was borrowed by French as baguette, which came to mean the long loaf. The diminutive bacillum 'little rod' named the rod-shaped bacteria.
The bearer of burdens rose in the world: the feminine bāiula became the Italian wet nurse (balia), and the verb bāiulāre 'carry, take charge of' gave the French bailli and English bailiff.
Borrowed from Greek φάλαινα, with b for φ. English baleen, the whale's filter plates, comes via French baleine.
Spanish and Portuguese bobo 'fool' come from balbus: the stammerer was taken for a simpleton.

en: ballista (siege engine for hurling stones or bolts)
note: Built on Greek βάλλω 'throw'. Medieval (arcu)ballista, the 'bow-ballista', became the crossbow: Italian balestra, Spanish ballesta.
Greek βαλανεῖον, shortened in Latin (also balineum). Its descendants show the four western outcomes of -ni-: Italian gn, Spanish ñ, French -in, Portuguese nh.
Greek βαπτίζω 'dip, immerse'. Romanian boteza belongs to the old Christian vocabulary inherited directly from Latin.
English beard is a native cognate; barber, via French, is the 'beard man'.

ex.en: A beard does not make a philosopher.

note: Greek βάρβαρος mimics the 'bar-bar' of incomprehensible speech. The Romans, once barbarians to the Greeks, applied it to everyone else.
A Late Latin word (first in Isidore of Seville). To embark is to go 'into the barca'.

en: basilica, public hall (for courts and business)
note: Greek 'royal (hall)'. Early churches copied its plan, and Romanian biserică 'church' descends from it, while the west took ecclēsia (chiesa, iglesia, église).
French baiser has become vulgar as a verb; for 'kiss' French now says embrasser. Romanian kisses with săruta, originally 'greet' (salūtāre).
Greek βάσις 'step, that on which one stands', from βαίνω 'go'. Greek-style accusative basim or basin.
A colloquial word made literary by Catullus. It displaced the classical ōsculum ('little mouth') and suāvium in all of western Romance.
Classical Latin knew it only as a surname, Bassus 'Stout'; in late popular speech it became the ordinary word for 'low' in the west. The musical bass is Italian basso.
Also spelled batuō. A low-register verb (it appears in Plautus) that became the ordinary Romance 'beat'; battuālia 'fencing practice' turned into French bataille and English battle.
Coined by Cicero, who apologised for the new word. The Beatitudes are the sayings beginning Beātī … 'Blessed are …'.
Italian beato te! 'lucky you!' keeps the classical sense; French béat has soured into 'smug'.

ex.en: Happy the man who, far from business … (Horace)
Of all these the bravest are the Belgae. (Caesar)

note: A rebel is someone who 'makes war again' (rebellāre) after being defeated.
Germanic *werra 'confusion, strife' (English war) replaced bellum everywhere, perhaps partly because bellum sounded like bellus 'pretty'. Old Latin had duellum, whence duel.

ex.en: If you want peace, prepare for war. (after Vegetius)

note: A colloquial diminutive related to bonus (Old Latin duenos). It became the everyday 'beautiful' in Italian and French, displacing pulcher and formōsus.
Used of huge or monstrous animals such as elephants and sea-creatures, and of brutish people.
Inherited everywhere. Bene- is the first half of many compounds: benefit, benevolent, benign; its opposite is male (malediction, malevolent).

ex.t: Sī valēs, bene est; ego valeō.
ex.en: If you are well, good; I am well. (standard letter opening)

rel.g: bless; make the sign of the cross

note: A calque of Greek εὐλογέω 'speak well of'. French bénir has shrunk to two syllables; the name Benedict means 'blessed'.
Portuguese bênção is the much-worn popular form of benedictiōnem.
bene + faciō 'doing good'. In French and Romanian it now usually means 'profit'.

ex.en: To accept a favour is to sell your freedom. (Publilius Syrus)

note: 'Well-born, of good nature' (bene + the root of gignō). Its opposite malīgnus gave malignant.
The circumflex of French bête marks a lost s (Old French beste), and English borrowed beast before the s was lost.

ex.en: to the beasts (condemned to the wild animals in the arena)

note: English beet was borrowed from Latin in Old English times.

en: Bethlehem, town in Judaea, city of David and birthplace of Jesus
note: Hebrew 'house of bread'. Spanish belén also means a Christmas crib, and Belém at the mouth of the Amazon is named after it.
Greek βιβλίον 'book' + θήκη 'repository' (as in apothēca). Beware: Spanish librería and French librairie are bookshops, not libraries.
A reduplicated present (bi-bō) from the same root as Greek πίνω. Italian bere is shortened from older bevere (compare bevo 'I drink'). The supine is supplied by pōtum (pōtō).
bi- + diēs. Likewise triduum 'three days' and biennium 'two years'.
bi- + lanx 'dish, scale-pan'. A pair of scales (lībra bilanx) gave the Romance words for scales and English balance.
Ātra bīlis 'black bile' translates Greek μελαγχολία, the humour blamed for melancholy.

en: two each, two at a time
note: A distributive numeral: bīna castra 'two camps', bīnōs dēnāriōs 'two denarii each'. An Italian binario is a railway track, laid in pairs of rails.
A biscuit is bis coctum 'twice baked'. Italian and French audiences shout Bis! for an encore.

ex.en: He gives twice who gives quickly.

note: From blandus 'smooth-talking, coaxing'.
Spanish blando and Portuguese brando simply mean 'soft'; English bland keeps the idea of smooth mildness.
Italian bestemmia is the popular form. Blame and blaspheme are doublets: spoken Latin *blastēmāre gave Old French blasmer, English blame.
The neuter plural of bonus used as a noun: 'good things'. English goods makes exactly the same move.
A model of the abstract suffix -tās, -tātis: Italian -tà, Spanish -dad, French -té, Portuguese -dade, Romanian -tate, English -ty.

en: (n. as noun) a good thing, advantage
note: Stressed short o diphthongised in Italian buono and Spanish bueno, but not in French bon. The irregular comparison survives too: migliore, mejor, meilleur < melior.
A Greek loan, used in poetry beside the native aquilō.

The animal in the English field kept its native name cow (a cognate of bōs), while its meat on the Norman table became beef, from French bœuf. Latin bōs itself is a dialect form, perhaps from Oscan-Umbrian.
forms: gen. pl. boum, dat./abl. pl. bōbus or būbus

note: A Gaulish word for a Gaulish garment, despised by toga-wearing Romans: southern Gaul was called Gallia Brācāta, 'Trousered Gaul'.
Also spelled brachium, an early loan from Greek βραχίων. To embrace is to take 'into one's arms'; a bracelet is an 'arm ornament'.
English brief comes via French bref; abbreviate and abridge are doublets from Late Latin abbreviāre.

ex.en: I struggle to be brief, and become obscure. (Horace)

note: French Bretagne is Brittany, settled by Britons fleeing the Anglo-Saxons; the island is Grande-Bretagne, 'Great Britain'.
Contracted from *brevima (diēs) 'the shortest day'. In Romance midwinter turned into winter weather: mist in the west, hoarfrost in Romanian.
Italian brutto has gone from 'dull, coarse' to plain 'ugly'. French brut 'raw' is the 'gross' of gross weight and of dry champagne.
Colloquial bucca 'cheek' ousted classical ōs as the word for 'mouth' in the west. Romanian kept the old sense 'cheek', now mostly 'buttock'.

en: signal horn (of herdsmen and the army)
note: The legion's curved signal horn survives in Spanish and Portuguese as the horn of a car.
A Gaulish word. Dante's Malebolge are the 'evil pouches' of hell, and the Chancellor's budget was once a little leather bag (Old French bougette).
Anything round and swelling. The lead seal on a document named the papal bull and, through Anglo-Norman, the English bill.
A late borrowing from Germanic *burgs (cognate with English borough). Its townsfolk, the burgenses, became the French bourgeois.
Greek βύρσα 'hide' became the leather purse, then the stock exchange and the student grant (French bourse, Romanian bursă).
Greek βούτυρον, perhaps 'cow-cheese'. Oil-using Greeks and Romans thought of butter as a barbarian food, used mainly as medicine.
Feminine, like most tree names. Small containers turned from boxwood were called pyxis (Greek πυξίς), the source of English box 'container'.
A slangy word for a working nag that ousted the classical equus everywhere; equus survives only in the feminine 'mare': Spanish yegua, Portuguese égua, Romanian iapă.
Vulgar Latin *cadentia 'the way things fall (out)' became French chance; the participle cāsus gave grammar its 'cases', each a 'fall' away from the nominative.

ex.en: Many soldiers fell in the battle.

note: The caecum is the 'blind' gut, a pouch closed at one end.
In compounds ae weakens to ī: occīdō 'cut down, kill' (Italian uccidere, Romanian ucide), dēcīdō 'cut off' — to decide is to cut the question short — and -cīda 'killer' in homicide.
Latin c was always /k/; before e (here from ae) it palatalised in every Romance language — Italian and Romanian /tʃ/, Spanish /θ/, French and Portuguese /s/.

ex.t: Caelum, nōn animum mūtant quī trāns mare currunt.
ex.en: Those who rush across the sea change their sky, not their mind. (Horace)

note: From caedō 'cut': the chips left by the stone-cutter. Mixed with lime mortar they made Roman concrete, opus caementicium.

en: Caesar (family name of Gaius Julius Caesar)
note: Caesar himself said Kaisar, with a hard K — German Kaiser borrowed it early enough to keep it; Slavonic tsar is the same name worn down.

ex.en: Hail, Caesar, those who are about to die salute you.

note: Squid are calamari in Italian because their ink recalled the calamārium, the scribe's case for reed pens and ink.
From calx 'heel'. To inculcate a lesson is to 'tread it in'; Romanian a călca means both 'to step on' and 'to iron'.
A diminutive of calx 'limestone': Romans reckoned with pebbles on a counting board, and doctors still call kidney stones calculi.
Spanish caliente and Portuguese quente are its present participle calentem; nonchalant is French for 'not being warm (about something)', i.e. not caring.
Speech syncopated it to caldus, the source of Italian caldo and French chaud; Spanish and Portuguese keep caldo only as 'broth' and say caliente, quente for 'hot'.
From calleō 'be thick-skinned, be experienced', from callum 'hard skin': an old hand.
Latin -or nouns were masculine; French made nearly all of them feminine (la chaleur, la couleur), while Italian, Spanish and Portuguese kept them masculine.
English challenge is the same word, worn down in Old French from 'false accusation' to 'claim, defiance'.
Italian calls football calcio, 'kick'; recalcitrant first described a mule 'kicking back' (recalcitrāre).

en: chalk line, finishing line (in the circus)
note: Borrowed into Germanic so early that its c became ch, like cheese from cāseus; the element calcium was named from it in 1808.

ex.t: Facilius est camēlum per forāmen acūs trānsīre, quam dīvitem intrāre in rēgnum Deī.
ex.en: It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. (Vulgate)

note: A photographic camera is short for camera obscūra 'dark room'; the same word came to English much earlier through French as chamber.
Not to be confused with Spanish camino 'road', which is a Celtic word.
A late word of Celtic or Germanic origin that reached every Romance language; French ch- from ca- is the same change as in cheval and chambre.

en: the Campus Martius (exercise ground in Rome)
note: French champ shows ca- > cha-; Champagne is Campānia 'the open country', and a champion fought on the field.

ex.en: The boys are playing on the field.

note: To cancel was to strike out writing with lattice-like crossing lines; the cancellārius was the clerk who sat at the court's railings — the first chancellor.
Greek doctors named the disease 'crab' (καρκίνος) from the swollen veins radiating around a tumour; Latin simply translated it.
A candidātus canvassed for office in a toga whitened with chalk, the toga candida.
An exception among -is nouns: genitive plural canum, not -ium. The Canary Islands are 'dog islands' (Canāriae īnsulae).

ex.en: Beware of the dog! (floor mosaic, Pompeii)

note: Italian cannone 'big tube' gave English cannon, and Spanish cañón 'tube, gorge' gave canyon — Spanish ñ from Latin nn is regular (annus > año).
Canvas was originally hemp cloth. English hemp is the same old migratory word, reshaped by Germanic sound laws (k > h).
The simple verb died out and Romance kept its frequentative cantāre. Germanic *hanan- 'cock', 'the singer', is a cognate — hence English hen.

ex.en: I sing of arms and the man… (Vergil, Aeneid 1.1)
Birds are singing in the wood.

note: Spanish and Portuguese b from Latin p between vowels (capillum > cabello) is regular Western Romance voicing; Italian keeps the p.
Italian capire 'understand' is 'grasp' (compare English 'I get it'); Spanish caber kept the sense 'hold, contain'. Compounds weaken a to i: accipiō, incipiō, recipiō.

en: the Capitol (hill and temple of Jupiter in Rome)

note: To capitulate is to surrender on agreed 'headings', i.e. terms; a monastic chapter met to hear a chapter of the Rule read.
The he-goat is caper. French chèvre shows two typical changes at once: ca- > che- and p > v between vowels.
English case 'box' and cash (first the money box, then its contents) both come from capsa; case 'instance' is a different word, from cāsus.
From Christian captīvus diabolī 'prisoner of the devil', Italian cattivo came to mean 'bad' and French chétif 'wretched, puny'.

ex.en: The prisoners are led into the camp.

note: English catch (Norman French cachier) and chase (Parisian French chacier) are one and the same Vulgar Latin *captiāre.
In Spanish and French slangy words took over the body part (capitia > cabeza, testa 'pot' > tête), leaving the old word for 'chief, end, cape'; Romanian cap still means 'head'.
A cardinal is a 'hinge' on which the Church turns; cardinal numbers, virtues and points are the pivotal ones. Spanish cardenal is also a bruise, from the colour of the robes.
The proofreader's caret (‸) is the Latin verb 'it is lacking', marking where something must be inserted.

ex.en: A good man is free from blame.

note: From cārus 'dear'. Jerome chose it to render Greek ἀγάπη, so the 'charity' of fidēs, spēs, cāritās is love.
A carmen was any solemn chant — hymn, legal formula or magic spell; French charme kept the 'spell', which English borrowed as charm.

ex.en: The poet sings a beautiful song.

note: Romance was built on the oblique stem carn-, not the nominative carō. Carnival is the feast before Lent, when meat is 'put away' (Italian carnevale, from carne levāre).

ex.en: And the Word was made flesh. (John 1:14, Vulgate)

note: English harvest and Greek καρπός 'fruit' share its root 'pluck, gather'. English carp 'find fault' is Norse, not from carpō, despite the sense.

ex.t: Carpe diem, quam minimum crēdula posterō.
ex.en: Seize the day, trusting as little as possible in tomorrow. (Horace)

note: A Gaulish word Caesar met on campaign; car, carry, charge, cargo and career all roll out of it.

ex.en: Carthage must be destroyed. (Cato the Elder)

ex.t: Patria mihi cārior est quam vīta.
ex.en: My country is dearer to me than life.

note: A humble word for a hut that displaced domus as 'house' almost everywhere; in French it survives only as the preposition chez 'at the house of'.
Cheese pressed in a forma 'mould' (cāseus formāticus) gave French fromage and Italian formaggio; the bare cāseus lives on in queso, queijo, cacio and English cheese.
The singular castrum is 'fort', the plural 'camp'. Old English ceaster 'Roman town' survives in Chester, Lancaster, Worcester, Gloucester.
English caste is Portuguese casta 'pure lineage', the word the Portuguese applied to the social classes of India.
From cadō. Grammarians translated Greek πτῶσις 'fall': each case 'falls' away from the upright nominative.
Western Romance voiced the t (cadena) and French dropped it altogether: Old French chaeine contracted to chaîne, the circumflex marking the lost syllable.
French split it into chaire 'pulpit, chair (of a professor)' and the dialect form chaise 'chair'. A cathedral holds the bishop's cathedra; the Pope speaks ex cathedrā, 'from the chair'.

en: Catiline (L. Sergius Catilina, conspirator of 63 BC)

ex.t: Quō ūsque tandem abūtēre, Catilīna, patientiā nostrā?
ex.en: How long, Catiline, will you go on abusing our patience? (Cicero, In Catilinam 1)

note: The house cat reached Rome late; classical fēlēs meant any small hunter such as a polecat. Italian, Spanish and Portuguese voiced the initial c (gatto, gato).
Popular speech said cōda (au > ō, as in plaudō ~ plōdō), the source of Italian coda, Romanian coadă and French queue. A musical coda is the 'tail' of a piece.
In late Latin causa 'legal matter' replaced rēs as the everyday word for 'thing' — Italian cosa, French chose — while learned causa, cause keep the old meaning.

rel.n: via Old French jaiole, from caveola

note: From cavus 'hollow'. Cage and jail are the same word — the plain cavea and its diminutive caveola.
Its compounds fill English: proceed, succeed, exceed, recede, concede — and an ancestor is an antecessor, 'one who went before'.

ex.en: Let arms yield to the toga. (Cicero)

note: Spoken Latin preferred vēlōx (Italian veloce) and rapidus (Romanian repede, French rapide); celer survives only in learned words.

ex.en: The swift horse runs across the plain.

note: A cellārium was a set of storerooms, English cellar; biology's cell dates from Robert Hooke (1665), whose cork pores looked like monks' rooms.
Hell is 'the hidden place' and hall 'the covered place': both share cēlō's root *kel- 'cover', as does Latin occultus.

en: the Celts; in Caesar, the Gauls of central Gaul
note: Caesar says they call themselves Celtae in their own language and Gallī in Latin.

en: dinner (the main Roman meal, in the afternoon)
note: As mealtimes moved later the Roman dinner became 'supper': Leonardo's Last Supper is L'Ultima Cena.

ex.en: After dinner we go for a walk.
Moreover, I propose that Carthage must be destroyed. (Cato the Elder)

en: censor (magistrate who took the census and oversaw morals)
census, register of citizens and property
fixed point of a pair of compasses
note: Greek κέντρον was a 'goad', then the sharp leg of the compasses that stays put while the circle is drawn.
Pronounced kentum: its k matches Greek ἑ-κατόν and, by Grimm's law (k > h), English hundred. Indo-Europeanists call the western branch the 'centum languages' after it.

en: centurion (commander of a century, about 80–100 men)

note: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese continue the diminutive cēpulla; Romanian ceapă is the plain word, and French went its own way with ūniō.
The popular story that sincere means sine cērā 'without wax' is a folk etymology; sincērus is of uncertain origin.
All the Romance words come from a spoken form *ceresia; English cherry dropped the -s of Norman cherise in the belief that it was a plural.

The basic sense 'sift, separate' survives in Spanish cerner and Romanian cerne; certus 'decided, certain' and sēcrētus 'set apart, secret' are old participles of it. The perfect crēvī is identical to that of crēscō.
Originally the participle of cernō, 'sifted, decided'. Caesar's idiom certiōrem facere, 'make (someone) more certain', means 'inform'.

ex.t: Amīcus certus in rē incertā cernitur.
ex.en: A sure friend is discerned in an unsure situation. (Ennius, quoted by Cicero)

note: A Gaulish word recorded by Pliny; Spanish cerveza and Portuguese cerveja kept it, while Italian and Romanian adopted German Bier.
Probably 'the horned one', from the root of cornū and English horn; hart is its Germanic cognate.

en: the other, the rest (usually pl. cēterī, -ae, -a)
note: The plural cēterī 'all the others' is far commoner than the singular; et cētera is 'and the other things'. The neuter cēterum is also an adverb, 'for the rest, moreover'.

en: chaos, the formless void before creation

rel.n: coined from chaos by van Helmont

note: The Flemish chemist van Helmont coined gas from chaos in the 1600s — Dutch g is pronounced like Greek χ.

ex.t: quem dīxēre chaos: rudis indīgestaque mōlēs
ex.en: which they called Chaos: a raw and unordered mass (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.7)

note: Each language kept a different piece of paper: Italian carta 'paper', Spanish carta 'letter', French carte 'card, map', Romanian carte 'book'.
Greek χειρουργός is 'one who works with his hands'; English surgeon is the same word worn down in Anglo-Norman (cirurgien > surgien).
Spanish cuerda shows the diphthong ue from stressed short o; English has both cord (through French) and chord (respelled after the Greek).
Greek χριστός 'anointed' (from χρίω 'anoint') translates Hebrew māšīaḥ, Messiah. Orthodox Romanian took the Greek form directly: Hristos.
Italian cibo keeps the Latin i and so is a learned word; the popular outcome, with short i > e, is Spanish cebo 'bait, feed'.
Cicero's family name means 'chickpea' — Plutarch says an ancestor had a cleft like one on the tip of his nose.

en: Cicero (M. Tullius Cicero, 106–43 BC, orator and statesman)
note: Italian cicerone 'guide' jokingly compares talkative tour guides with the great orator.
A neat sound-change set: -ōnia gives Italian -ogna, Spanish -üeña, French -ogne and Portuguese -onha, all with a palatal n.

en: shepherd's pipe (made from its hollow stem)

note: Classical cilium was the eyelid; Romance moved it to the lashes and brows. Supercilium 'eyebrow' gave Italian sopracciglio and English supercilious.
French cendre shows a glide d between n and r (cin'rem > cendre), as gendre does from generum.

en: Cinna, Roman family name (cognomen); a poetaster mocked by Martial

note: Spanish and Portuguese cerca 'near' continue circā; the c. before a date is circā 'about'.

ex.en: about five miles (a typical phrase in Caesar)

note: Italian cerchio shows -cul- > -chi-, exactly as in occhio from oculus.

ex.en: The soldiers keep watch around the camp.

note: Like its parent dō it has a short a throughout (circumdare, circumdatum), unlike other first-conjugation verbs.
Latin circumferentia 'a carrying round' translated Greek περιφέρεια, the line that runs round a circle.
Gallia Cisalpīna, 'Gaul this side of the Alps', was northern Italy — seen, of course, from Rome.
The Greek lyre travelled through Arabic qītāra into Spanish and came back to Europe as the guitar; German Zither is the same word by a different road.
A frequentative of cieō 'set moving': to cite a witness was to 'call him forth', to excite is to 'call out, stir up'.
The word itself died out; every Romance language rebuilt 'citizen' from its word for 'city', itself from cīvitās.

ex.en: I am a Roman citizen. (Cicero, Against Verres)

note: In late Latin the 'citizen body' became the town itself and replaced urbs; Romanian cetate kept an older 'fortified town' sense.

ex.en: The disaster at Cannae terrified the Romans.

note: A showcase for initial cl-: Italian chi-, Spanish ll-, Portuguese ch-, Romanian ch- (chiamare, llamar, chamar, chema), while French kept cl-. Compare clāvis > chiave, llave, chave, cheie, clé.

ex.en: The girl shouts, but nobody hears.
The soldiers' shout rises to the sky.

note: Romanian chiar has moved from 'clear' to 'even, exactly' (chiar acum 'right now'); Italian chiaro shows the regular cl- > chi-.

ex.en: Cicero was a very famous orator.

note: Aulus Gellius contrasted a scrīptor classicus, a 'first-class' author, with a proletārius one — the source of every 'classic'.
First a 'levy' of citizens: hence both the property classes of the Servian constitution and a 'fleet' of ships.
Italian kept the verb; Spanish (cerrar < serāre 'bolt') and French (fermer < firmāre 'make fast') replaced it with words for securing a door. Compounds weaken au to ū: inclūdō, exclūdō, conclūdō.
The model set for initial cl-: chiave, llave, chave, cheie — and French clé, which keeps cl- as French always does.
Cloves are named for their nail shape: French clou de girofle 'nail of the clove tree', Spanish clavo, Portuguese cravo (where cl- became cr-).
A Roman cliēns owed his patrōnus political support and morning greetings (the salūtātiō) in return for protection.
Greek κλίμα 'slope' meant the tilt of the earth toward the pole — which decides how warm a region is.
From cochlea 'snail': the Roman spoon had a pointed handle for winkling snails and shellfish out of their shells.
From coquō 'cook': Babylon's walls were of baked brick.
A 'block of wood' became wooden tablets bound together, then any bound book, then Justinian's Cōdex of laws — the ancestor of every 'code'.
Greek for 'dormitory': for Christians the dead were only asleep.
co- + eō 'go together'. Conjugated like eō: coit, coīmus, coībant, coīssent.
Defective: only perfect-system forms exist (coepī, coeperam, coeperō); for the present Latin uses incipiō. With a passive infinitive it is itself passive: urbs aedificārī coepta est.
From co- + agitō, 'turn over in the mind'. Spanish and Portuguese cuidar 'take care of' grew out of 'think about'; for plain 'think' Romance chose pēnsāre 'weigh' (pensare, pensar, penser).
From 'blood relative' the word narrowed to 'brother-in-law' independently in Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian.

en: surname, family name (the third name, e.g. Cicerō)
note: A Roman citizen's names: praenōmen (Mārcus), nōmen (Tullius), cognōmen (Cicerō). Italian cognome is still the ordinary word for 'surname'.

en: get to know, learn, find out
note: The perfect cognōvī 'I have found out' means 'I know'. Romance dropped the g (co(g)nōscere > conoscere, conocer, connaître); English know and Greek γιγνώσκω share the root.

ex.t: Fēlīx quī potuit rērum cognōscere causās.
ex.en: Happy the man who has been able to learn the causes of things. (Vergil, Georgics 2.490)

note: From co- + agō, 'drive together'. Cogent arguments 'compel' assent; coāgulum is what drives milk together into curds. Spanish coger is a different verb (colligere).

ex.en: The enemy were forced to surrender.

note: Its oldest sense was 'farmyard, enclosure'. Spoken cōrtem became the courtyard and then the royal court, so cohort and court are one word.
A rare Greek loan for a punch (used in the Gospels for the blows struck at Jesus) became the everyday Romance word for any 'blow' — and English coup d'état.
'One chosen together' (con + legō): every Roman magistracy was shared, each consul having a collēga who could veto him.
Spanish coger 'take, grab' and French cueillir 'pick (flowers)' are both colligere; to cull is the same word through French.
Italian colle is inherited; its diminutive collina was borrowed by French, Spanish and Portuguese. English hill is a Germanic cognate (Grimm's k > h).
Spoken *colcāre gave French coucher 'put to bed' (hence couch), Romanian culca and — with a different twist — Spanish colgar 'hang'; colocar is the learned doublet.
French cou is Old French col with the l vocalised (col survives in 'collar' words like collier 'necklace'); Portuguese colo slid down from 'neck' to 'lap'.
Three meanings from one idea, 'tend': agrī cultūra 'tending the fields', cultus deōrum 'worship of the gods', and colōnia 'a settlement of farmers'.
Portuguese regularly drops l between vowels: colōrem > coor > cor, just as dolōrem > dor.
Spanish paloma and Portuguese pomba come from palumba 'wood-pigeon'; Columbus's Italian surname Colombo means 'dove'.
A colonel led a colonnello, a 'little column' of soldiers; English spells the Italian-French form but pronounces the variant coronel.
A poetic word borrowed from Greek κόμη; a comet is a 'long-haired' star. Unrelated to Spanish coma 'comma' (Greek κόμμα).
Spanish and Portuguese comer continue this compound 'eat up' (com- + edō); elsewhere the jokey mandūcāre 'chomp' won. Like edō it has short forms: comēs, comēst.
Literally 'one who goes with' (com- + eō). The emperor's comitēs became titled officials, and the count's territory was his comitātus, the county.

ex.t: Comes fācundus in viā prō vehiculō est.
ex.en: A talkative companion on a journey is as good as a carriage. (Publilius Syrus)
The son accompanies his father on the journey.

note: A soldier's 'leave' became French congé (congés payés 'paid holidays') and Italian commiato 'farewell'; Caesar uses the word mostly for supply convoys.
Vulgar *commandāre turned 'entrust' into 'order': French commander, English command. Spanish encomendar still means 'entrust', and Portuguese encomenda is an order or a parcel.

en: come and go, travel back and forth
note: Caesar's Belgae are bravest because traders seldom 'come and go' among them (minimē ad eōs mercātōrēs saepe commeant).
Like English commit, the Romance verbs specialised in wrongdoing (commettere un errore); Caesar's use is proelium committere, 'to join battle'.

ex.en: to join battle, start the fight (Caesar)

note: The Church sense 'share (in the sacrament)' gave the popular Spanish comulgar and Portuguese comungar, beside learned comunicar.

ex.en: This matter is common to all.

note: Dante called his poem a Commedia because it ends happily, in Paradise; the epithet Divina was added by later editors.
From parō 'prepare'. 'Procure' narrowed to 'buy' in Italian comprare, Spanish and Portuguese comprar and Romanian cumpăra.
Spanish cumplir 'fulfil' gives cumpleaños 'birthday', the day one 'completes' another year; English comply and compliment came from the same family through Italian and Spanish.
French replaced -pondre with -poser (composer, proposer), crossing pōnō with pausāre 'rest, set down'.
'Seize' became 'understand' in French comprendre (compare 'grasp'), but 'contain, embrace' in Romanian cuprinde.
Counting and recounting are one word: contar means both 'count' and 'tell' in Spanish and Portuguese, while French split compter 'count' from conter 'tell a tale'.
Not to be confused with cōnsilium 'advice, plan': a concilium (con- + calō 'summon') is a meeting, a cōnsilium what it decides — English council and counsel keep the pair apart.
The crowd 'running together' became a contest in every Romance language: concorso, concurso, concours.
Classical spelling condiciō, from con- + dīcō, 'a speaking together, agreement'; medieval scribes wrote conditio, as if from condō.
Livy dated Roman history ab urbe conditā (AUC), 'from the founding of the City', reckoned as 753 BC.

ex.en: from the founding of the City (Livy)

note: In Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian 'to lead together' became the everyday verb for driving a car.
The abbreviation cf. is the imperative cōnfer 'compare!'; the supine collātum gives collate.
'Make up, prepare' led to sweets: Italian confetti were sugared almonds thrown at carnival, French confiture is jam. Caesar's sense is grimmer — cōnfectus vulneribus 'worn out by wounds'.

en: trust, rely on (+ dat. or abl.)

note: Romance built a new verb on the participle cōnfessus (*cōnfessāre). Cōnfiteor 'I confess' is also the name of the penitential prayer of the Mass.
A compound of iaciō: the first syllable is long by position (con-yi-ciō). To conjecture is to 'throw together' the evidence.
A band 'sworn together', like Catiline's in 63 BC; English conjure drifted from 'swear together' to 'summon spirits by oath'.

ex.en: In vain the enemy try to cross the river.

note: Literally 'knowing together (with oneself)'; French conscience still covers both 'conscience' and 'consciousness'.

ex.en: a mind conscious of its own integrity (Vergil, Aeneid 1.604)

note: The Senate was addressed as patrēs cōnscrīptī, 'enrolled fathers' — 'conscript fathers' in old translations.

ex.en: conscript fathers (formal address to the Senate)

note: The Romance verbs restored the a of sacer (consacrare, consagrar) where Latin had weakened it to e in the compound.
'Follow up and catch' became 'obtain': Spanish conseguir is the everyday 'to get, manage to'. A consequence is simply 'what follows'.
Probably from sīdus 'star', 'to study the stars closely' — and its partner dēsīderō 'miss, long for' perhaps 'to miss (a star)'.
-lium became a palatal l: consiglio, consejo, conseil, conselho — exactly as in fīlius > figlio, hijo, fils, filho.

ex.en: to form a plan, make a decision

en: take up position, make a stand

ex.en: The column halted at the bank of the river.

en: first cousin (child of a mother's sister)
note: From soror 'sister'. Cōnsōbrīnus prīmus 'first cousin' was cut down to primo in Spanish and Portuguese, cōnsōbrīnus vērus 'true cousin' to Romanian văr, while French kept the noun itself.

ex.en: The mother comforts her weeping daughter.
The sailors catch sight of land in the distance.

en: breathe together, agree, act in harmony
(impers. cōnstat) it is agreed, it is well known
note: The commercial sense 'stand at (a price)' became the Romance verb 'to cost' and English cost. Cōnstat with accusative and infinitive means 'it is agreed that…'.

ex.t: Cōnstat Rōmam in septem collibus sitam esse.
ex.en: It is agreed that Rome lies on seven hills.

note: A tight binding became compulsion: costringere, contraindre and English constrain all mean 'force'; constrict kept the literal squeeze.

en: (perf. cōnsuēvī) be accustomed, be used to

note: A spoken form *cōstūmen gave Italian costume, Spanish costumbre and French coutume; English has custom from French and costume, 'customary dress', from Italian.

en: consul (one of the two chief annual magistrates of Rome)
note: Romans named the year after its two consuls: M. Tulliō Cicerōne C. Antōniō cōnsulibus is 63 BC.

en: look after, take thought for (+ dat.)
note: The case decides the meaning: cōnsulere aliquem 'to consult someone', cōnsulere alicuī 'to look after someone's interests'.
French consommer fused this verb ('complete') with cōnsūmere ('use up'); a consommé is a 'completed', fully reduced broth.

ex.en: The fire consumed the whole city.

note: The compound replaced simple suō 'sew' everywhere. Spoken *cōsere lost its n before s; French coudre inserts a glide d, as moudre does from molere.
Originally a word of augury: to mark out a templum, the patch of sky in which the augur watched for omens.
Caesar uses it constantly for 'hurry' (in Galliam contendit 'he hastened to Gaul') — 'strain oneself towards'.

ex.en: All fell silent and held their faces intent upon him. (Vergil, Aeneid 2.1)

note: From continēns 'holding together, unbroken' — terra continēns is land without a break, a continent.

ex.en: The Helvetii are hemmed in on every side by the nature of the terrain. (Caesar, Gallic War 1.2)

note: The ablative continuō is an adverb, 'immediately, without a break'.

en: (adv.) on the other hand, in reply
note: Late Latin (terra) contrāta, 'the land lying opposite (one's view)', gave French contrée and English country.

ex.en: The Romans fought against the Carthaginians.

en: debate (rhetorical exercise on a legal case)

note: Catullus will 'muddle' the count of his kisses so that no one can put the evil eye on a known number.

en: agree; (impers. convenit) it is fitting, it is agreed
note: Convenit 'it suits, it is agreed' lives on in French il convient and Italian conviene 'it's worth it'.

ex.en: The soldiers assembled at the gate.

note: A 'gathering' of monks or nuns became the convent (French couvent, with the n lost); covenant is the Old French word for an 'agreement'.
Its first meaning is 'prove guilty': English convict keeps the legal sense, convince the persuasion.
'Living together' (con- + vīvō): Cicero praised the Roman name as better than the Greek words for 'drinking together', since a dinner party is about sharing life.

ex.en: The general calls the soldiers together to an assembly.

note: The compound displaced simple operiō 'cover' in every Romance language; English kerchief and curfew hide its French form couvre-.
The Gospel baskets of leftover bread are cophinī. Through French the word became coffer and coffin — and today it covers the car: Italian cofano 'bonnet', French coffre 'boot'.
Medieval scribes multiplied a text into an 'abundance' (cōpia) of exemplars — hence copy. In Caesar the plural cōpiae means 'troops'.
From co- + apiō 'fasten'. A 'link' became a pair in Italian coppia and French couple, and a pair of linked lines in Spanish copla.
A later by-form of classical culīna. English took it twice: early enough to become kitchen, and again from French as cuisine.
A biscuit is bis coctus, 'twice baked'; the apricot is praecoquum 'early-ripening', which travelled through Greek and Arabic before returning to Europe.
English heart, Greek καρδία and Latin cor share one root. Spanish corazón is an enlarged form, and Romanian chose anima 'soul' (inimă) for the organ.

en: (adv.) face to face, in person, openly

ex.en: He spoke in the presence of the people.

en: Corinth (city on the Isthmus of Greece)
note: Like most city names it is feminine. Currants are 'raisins of Corinth', exported from the Corinthian gulf.

en: Cornelia, Roman woman's name (feminine of the clan name Cornelius)
note: Roman women usually bore only the feminine of their father's clan name: every daughter of a Cornelius was a Cornelia.
In battle the cornū dextrum and sinistrum are the right and left wings. Grimm's law turned the same root into English horn.
Portuguese coroa drops n between vowels (as lūna > lua). Romanian has the inherited cunună 'wreath' and the later loan coroană 'crown'.
French corps still writes the p and s of corpus though it pronounces neither; English borrowed the word three times — corpse, corps, corpus.

ex.en: A healthy mind in a healthy body. (Juvenal)

rel.n: from ad + ferrum 'grab with a hook'

note: Portuguese cortiça is cork, the bark of the cork oak — Portugal produces about half the world's supply.
From 'rib, flank' came the flank of the land (coast) and of a hill (Spanish cuesta, French côte); a cutlet is a 'little rib'.
Also spelled quotīdiānus, cottīdiānus; from cotīdiē 'every day'.

ex.t: pānem nostrum cotīdiānum dā nōbīs hodiē
ex.en: give us this day our daily bread

ex.t: Pānem nostrum cotīdiānum dā nōbīs hodiē.
ex.en: Give us this day our daily bread. (the Lord's Prayer)

note: Classical femur 'thigh' gave way to coxa 'hip', which slid down the leg: coscia, cuisse, coxa, coapsă all mean 'thigh'.
Every Romance language dropped crās for a form of māne 'in the morning'. To procrastinate is to put things off 'till tomorrow' (crāstinus).

ex.en: Tomorrow let him love who has never loved. (Pervigilium Veneris)

note: Spoken Latin voiced the initial c, probably under the influence of grossus 'thick': grasso, gras. Mardi gras is 'fat Tuesday'.
From crās 'tomorrow', which no Romance language kept: they all say 'in the morning' (māne). To procrastinate is to put off till tomorrow.

ex.en: They batter the gate with blow after blow.
I believe in one God. (the Nicene Creed)

note: Spanish and Portuguese criar 'bring up, breed' is the popular form; Portuguese crioulo, 'raised (in the colony)', gave Creole. In politics cōnsulēs creāre is 'to elect consuls'.
From 'crack, burst' came Spanish and Portuguese quebrar 'break' (with the r moved) and French crever 'burst; drop dead'.
The crescent is the 'growing' moon; French croissant is the same participle, and musical crescendo is Italian 'growing'.

ex.t: Crēscit amor nummī quantum ipsa pecūnia crēvit.
ex.en: Love of money grows as much as the money itself has grown. (Juvenal)

note: Its first meaning is the 'accusation' or verdict (from cernō 'decide'), and only later the deed itself.

ex.en: From a single crime learn what they all are. (Vergil, Aeneid 2.65)

note: Romance narrowed it to horsehair; crinoline was originally a stiff fabric of crin (horsehair) and lin (flax).
French crête marks the lost s with a circumflex, as in tête < testa and fête < festa.
Herodotus says Greeks in Egypt named the beast after the κροκόδειλος, the lizard of their own dry-stone walls.
From crux: 'to put on the cross'. Excruciating pain is literally pain 'out of the torture'.
From crūdus 'raw, bloody'. Spanish, French and Portuguese cruel lost the d between vowels; Italian crudele keeps it.

ex.en: The cruel tyrant terrifies the citizens.

note: From the root of cruor 'gore': raw meat is still bloody. French cru 'raw' (and a wine's cru 'growth') lost the d entirely.
Sanguis is the blood in the body, cruor the blood spilt from a wound — the root also of crūdus and crūdēlis.
Custard was first a pie with a crust (crustade); Spanish costra shows the r shifted out of the first syllable.
English cross came by a roundabout route — from Irish missionaries' cros through Old Norse. Crucial first meant 'cross-shaped', like a signpost at a fork in the road.

ex.en: Hail, O Cross, our only hope! (hymn Vexilla Regis)

note: Greek κρύσταλλος was 'ice'; rock crystal was thought to be ice frozen too hard ever to melt.
Hens 'lie on' their eggs: Italian covare and French couver mean 'to brood'; incubate is the learned form of the same idea.
The classical word for kitchen; spoken Latin replaced it with coquīna (cucina, cocina, cuisine), leaving culīna only in learned culinary words — and in English kiln.
Culprit is thought to be a law-French abbreviation, cul. prit, 'guilty, ready (to prove it)'.
Romance continues the diminutive cultellus: coltello, cuchillo, couteau.
Cicero's cultūra animī, 'tilling of the mind', is the metaphor behind 'culture' in its modern sense.
It is tacked onto personal pronouns — mēcum, tēcum, nōbīscum — and Spanish still says conmigo, contigo, literally 'with with-me'.
With the indicative it simply marks time ('when'); with the subjunctive it is circumstantial, causal ('since') or concessive ('although'). The old spelling quom shows its kinship with quī.

ex.t: Cum Caesar in Galliam vēnisset, Helvētiī lēgātōs mīsērunt.
ex.en: When Caesar had come into Gaul, the Helvetii sent envoys.

note: Spanish ¡es el colmo! and French c'est le comble! 'that's the limit' both picture a measure heaped to overflowing.
Incūnābula 'swaddling clothes' is the name for books printed before 1501, in the cradle of printing.
Q. Fabius Maximus earned the name Cūnctātor, 'the Delayer', for wearing Hannibal down by refusing pitched battle.

ex.t: Ūnus homō nōbīs cūnctandō restituit rem.
ex.en: One man restored our state by delaying. (Ennius, on Fabius)

note: Probably from coniūnctus 'joined together': all of a group taken as one body, unlike omnis 'every'.

ex.en: All the citizens gathered in the forum.

note: The wedge-shaped die for striking money gave English coin; in French coin came to mean 'corner'. Cuneiform script is 'wedge-shaped'.
Probably an Iberian word; Roman sappers named their siege tunnels cunīculī after rabbit burrows.
The late by-form cuppa gave Italian coppa, French coupe and English cup; a cupola is an upturned 'little tub'.
A spoken *cupiditia gave Spanish codicia and Portuguese cobiça 'greed'; its verb, Old French coveitier, gave English covet.
As a common noun it is feminine; personified as Venus's son, the Latin counterpart of Greek Ἔρως, it is masculine.

rel.n: via French, from the same root

note: No Romance language kept it; 'want' is velle in Italian, French and Romanian, and quaerere 'seek' in Spanish and Portuguese.
Shortened from aes Cyprium 'Cyprian metal', after the island's copper mines; chemistry's symbol Cu still names it.
Probably from quā rē 'for what reason'. Romance replaced it everywhere with 'for what?' phrases.
A Spanish cura is the priest who has the 'cure' (care) of souls, like an English curate; sēcūrus 'free from care' gave secure and sure.

en: curia (ancient division of the Roman people)
note: The Cūria Iūlia, the senate house begun by Caesar, still stands in the Forum; the Pope's government is the Roman Curia.

ex.en: The senators gather in the senate house.

note: With a gerundive it means 'have something done': pontem faciendum cūrāvit 'he had a bridge built'.

ex.en: Take care to stay well. (a common letter ending in Cicero)
the course of one's life; CV
The boys run to the river.

note: Belongs with currō 'run'; the Romance and English car words come instead from Gaulish carrus.
The cursus honōrum was the ladder of Roman offices: quaestor, praetor, consul. An Italian corso is a town's main avenue, once its racecourse.
In Romance this 'cut-off' word became the ordinary adjective 'short', ousting brevis.

ex.en: Who will guard the guards themselves? (Juvenal)

note: Greek 'round-eye'. The huge-block walls of Mycenae were called Cyclopean, as though only giants could have built them.
Italian (clavi)cembalo, the harpsichord, borrowed the name of the clashing cymbal.

ex.t: factus sum velut aes sonāns aut cymbalum tinniēns
ex.en: I have become like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal (1 Corinthians 13:1, Vulgate)

note: Greek 'dog-like': Diogenes and his followers lived shamelessly in public, like dogs.

en: Quirinius (P. Sulpicius Quirinius), governor of Syria at the census of Luke 2
note: The Vulgate spells his name after the Greek of the Gospel, Κυρήνιος; Roman historians call him Quirinius.

en: Daedalus, legendary Athenian craftsman, builder of the Labyrinth
note: His Labyrinth made his name a common noun: French dédale and Italian dedalo mean 'a maze'.
Built on damnum 'loss': originally 'to make someone pay, to fine'. Christian Latin narrowed it to eternal condemnation, the sense English damn inherited.
Latin -mn- became -nn- in Italian (danno), -ñ- in Spanish (daño) and -un- in Romanian (daună), as in scamnum → scaun 'chair'.

ex.en: I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts (Vergil)

en: Davus, typical slave's name in Roman comedy
note: Originally 'the Dacian', a slave from beyond the Danube; Terence and Horace both have a Davus.
Spoken Latin used dē + noun instead of the genitive ('the house dē Marcus'), so every Romance language now says 'of' with a descendant of dē.

ex.en: there is no arguing about tastes
The goddess Diana hunts in the woods.

note: From dē + habeō 'have (something) from someone', hence 'owe'; the sense 'must' grew out of moral debt. English debt got its silent b from scribes who knew dēbitum.

ex.t: sīcut et nōs dīmittimus dēbitōribus nostrīs
ex.en: as we forgive our debtors (Lord's Prayer)

note: Spanish deuda and French dette continue the neuter plural dēbita, reinterpreted as a feminine singular.
Romanian zece shows d → z before e and i, as in zi 'day' < diēs and zice 'say' < dīcere.
The 'tenth' month: the oldest Roman year began in March, which is why September–December are two months out of step with their numbers.
From dē + cadō 'fall'. Do not confuse with dēcīdō (long ī, from caedō) 'cut off, settle', the source of decide.
Decimāre was to execute every tenth man of a mutinous unit. French dîme 'tithe' (decima pars) is the popular form, and gave the American dime.
A classic false friend: French décevoir and Spanish decepcionar mean 'disappoint', not 'deceive'.
Grammarians spoke of 'bending' a noun through its cases, copying Greek κλίσις — hence declension.

ex.t: dulce et decōrum est prō patriā morī
ex.en: sweet and fitting it is to die for one's country (Horace, Odes 3.2)

note: Perfect also dēcurrī.

ex.en: to found a colony (lit. 'to lead out a colony')

note: The basic sense is 'ward off' (dēfendere iniūriam). French défendre also means 'forbid' — défense de fumer 'no smoking'.

ex.en: The soldiers were worn out with toil.

note: Dēfūnctus (vītā) 'having discharged (life)' became the polite word for the dead: Spanish difunto, French défunt.
English delight comes from Old French delitier; its -gh- was added by analogy with light, to which it is unrelated. Italian dilettante is 'one who takes delight'.

ex.t: aut prōdesse volunt aut dēlectāre poētae
ex.en: poets wish either to be useful or to delight (Horace, Ars Poetica 333)
Carthage must be destroyed (Cato the Elder)

note: French délice is masculine in the singular but feminine in the plural (de grandes délices) — a trace of the Latin plural-only noun.
Literally 'to leave the furrow' (dē + līra 'furrow') — a ploughman's image for going off track.

rel.g: dolphin; heir to the French throne

note: French dauphin is the inherited form; through the counts of the Dauphiné it became the title of the French king's eldest son.
Classical 'entrust (a task to someone)' became 'ask for' in spoken Latin: French demander and Italian domandare are the everyday words for 'ask'.
Built on mōnstrum, a portent the gods 'show'. The simple mōnstrāre is the everyday 'show' in Romance: mostrare, mostrar, montrer.
Literally 'containing ten (asses)'. It became the word for money itself in Italian, Spanish and Portuguese; its d. abbreviated the British penny until 1971.
English tooth is the same Indo-European word: Germanic lost the n (*tanþ-), as in English other beside German ander. A dandelion is a dent de lion 'lion's tooth'.
Spoken Latin said deōsum; it survives as Italian giù and Romanian jos 'down'. Its opposite is sūrsum 'upward' (sūrsum corda 'lift up your hearts').
Italian dipingere, the everyday 'to paint', is this very verb; French peindre is the simple pingere.
From plōrō 'wail aloud' — the verb behind French pleurer and Portuguese chorar 'weep'.
Grammarians called verbs like hortor 'deponent' because they had 'laid aside' their active forms.
Not 'depopulate' in origin: populor meant 'ravage' (perhaps from populus in an old sense 'army'). Caesar uses it of laying waste fields.

ex.t: Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid dērelīquistī mē?
ex.en: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matthew 27:46)
