note: Built on scandō 'climb' (ascend, scan). Italian scendere has dropped the prefix; Portuguese descer has lost the -nd-.
The Vulgate's in dēsertō 'in the wilderness' made the neuter a noun. Romanian deșert kept the sense 'empty, vain': its Bible's deșertăciune is 'vanity'.
French désir is the popular heir (via désirer); Spanish deseo and Portuguese desejo look similar but are often traced instead to dēsidia 'idleness, lust'.
Italian disegno 'drawing' was the key term of Renaissance art theory; French dessin, Spanish diseño and English design all spread from it. Cōnsul dēsignātus is the consul-elect.
From saliō 'leap'. A dēsultor was a circus rider who leapt from horse to horse — hence desultory 'jumping from one thing to another'.
Romance grammar calls an inflectional ending a desinenza/desinencia — 'the place where the word stops'.
From sōlus 'alone'. French je suis désolé 'I am so sorry' is the everyday descendant of 'left desolate'.
The noun dēspectus 'looking down on, contempt' became the Romance words for 'spite' — and English despite and spite.
Frequentative of dēspondeō 'promise away'; the spōnsa 'promised woman' became Italian sposa, Spanish esposa, French épouse.

ex.en: I will not let you down.
I see the better course and approve it; I follow the worse (Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.20–21)

note: From dētestor 'curse, call the gods to witness against'.
Irregular plural: dī (or deī), dīs, deōrum. Romanian Dumnezeu fuses Domine Deus 'Lord God'. Despite appearances it is unrelated to Greek θεός; its cousins are diēs and Iuppiter.

ex.en: a god from the machine (a contrived solution)

note: In a dēvōtiō a Roman general vowed himself and the enemy army to the gods of the underworld and then charged to his death, as the Decii famously did.
Also dextera, dexterum. Its opposite, sinister 'left', was the unlucky side and gave English sinister.

ex.en: to give one's right hand (as a pledge)

note: Greek diábolos 'slanderer' translated Hebrew satan 'adversary'. Romanian calls the devil drac, from Latin dracō 'dragon'.
Greek diá 'through' + lógos 'speech' — not 'two-speech', so a dialogue may have many speakers. Cicero brought Plato's philosophical dialogue into Latin.

en: Diana (goddess of hunting and the moon)
note: Romanian zână 'fairy' is the goddess herself, with the same d → z as zi 'day' < diēs.

en: Diaulus, a doctor turned undertaker in Martial

note: Imperative dīc (like dūc, fac, fer). The root *deik- meant 'point out', as in Greek δείκνυμι 'show' and Latin index 'pointer'.

ex.en: Tell me, Damoetas, whose flock is this? (Vergil, Eclogues 3.1)

note: In the Republic a lawful office limited to six months in a crisis; Caesar's dictātor perpetuus 'dictator for life' created the modern sense.
Frequentative of dīcō: Romans 'dictated' their letters to slaves. Italian dettare is the inherited form (ct → tt); Spanish dictar is learned.
The participle of dīcō; Italian detto 'the aforesaid' gave English ditto.

Masculine, but feminine for a fixed date (diē dictā). It lives on in Spanish día and Romanian zi, and hides in lunedì, lundi 'Monday' and midi 'noon'; Italian giorno and French jour come from diurnum.

ex.en: it is hard not to write satire (Juvenal 1.30)

note: The ending -tās, -tātis gave Italian -tà, Spanish -dad, French -té, Portuguese -dade and Romanian -tate.
'Carry apart, sort out': Justinian's Digesta was an arranged collection of legal rulings, and the stomach 'distributes' food.
Counting on the fingers made digit a word for numeral, hence digital. The silent g of French doigt was put back by scribes who knew digitus.
A Roman aristocrat's dignitās was his public standing — Caesar crossed the Rubicon to defend his. English dainty is the same word worn down in Old French.
Takes the ablative: dignus laude 'worthy of praise'. Romanian demn shows the regular gn → mn, as in lignum → lemn and signum → semn.

ex.t: dignus enim est operārius mercēde suā
ex.en: for the labourer is worthy of his hire (Luke 10:7)

note: The 'diligence' stagecoaches of 18th-century France were named for their speed (carrosse de diligence).

ex.en: love, and do what you will (Augustine)

note: dis- + medius 'middle': 'cut through the middle'. French demi is its popular heir; the others say 'half' with medius.
Spanish dimitir 'resign' and Portuguese demitir 'fire' are the same verb seen from opposite sides of the desk.

ex.en: now, Lord, you let your servant depart (Luke 2:29)

note: Spoken Latin dīrēctum 'what is straight' became the word for 'law' everywhere (diritto, derecho, droit, direito, drept), ousting iūs; outside Italy it also ousted dexter as 'right (hand)'.

ex.t: quae lūcis miserīs tam dīra cupīdō?
ex.en: why do the poor souls feel such a dreadful longing for the light? (Vergil, Aeneid 6.721)

note: Its participle discrētus 'separated' gave both English discrete 'separate' and discreet 'judicious' — one word spelled two ways.
Reduplicated perfect didicī. Romance replaced it with apprehendere 'grasp' — the same image as English 'catch on'.

ex.en: people learn while they teach (Seneca, Letters 7.8)

note: Perfect also discucurrī. Running to and fro became running through a subject: Italian discorso, English discourse.

ex.t: disiectam Aenēae tōtō videt aequore classem
ex.en: he sees Aeneas' fleet scattered over the whole sea (Vergil, Aeneid 1.128)

note: From pēnsō 'weigh': paying out was once weighing out. French dépenser 'spend' is the popular heir.
The neuter diurnum 'daily portion' displaced diēs in Italian giorno and French jour; English journey was first 'a day's travel', journal 'a daily record'.
Classical spelling dēversōrium, from dēvertō 'turn aside (for the night)'. Luke 2:7: there was no room for them in the inn.
Also contracted dīs, dītis (comparative dītior). Romance replaced it with Germanic *rīki 'powerful', the word of the new Frankish and Gothic lords; Romanian took Slavic bogat.
An individual is 'what cannot be divided', translating Greek ἄτομος.

ex.t: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs
ex.en: Gaul as a whole is divided into three parts (Caesar, Gallic War 1.1)

note: A dīvīnus was also a soothsayer. The Romance verbs for 'guess' — indovinare, adivinar, deviner, adivinhar — mean 'to divine' like one.
Dead emperors were declared dīvī (dīvus Iūlius, dīvus Augustus). Italian diva 'goddess' became the prima donna of opera.
Unlike other first-conjugation verbs it has a short a (dăre, dămus, dătis). Letters were headed data Rōmae 'given at Rome', which gave English date.

ex.en: I give so that you may give

note: Takes two accusatives, of the person and of the thing taught. Romance 'teach' came from *insignāre 'point out by signs'.

ex.en: The teacher teaches the boys their letters.

note: Romanian durea shows intervocalic l → r (sōlem → soare); Portuguese doer simply lost the l. Indolent first meant 'feeling no pain'.
Portuguese dor 'pain' lost its l, as in cor 'colour'. Romanian dor, from a related Late Latin dolus, means 'longing' — a word Romanians call untranslatable.

ex.en: you bid me, queen, renew an unspeakable grief (Vergil, Aeneid 2.3)

ex.t: dolus an virtūs, quis in hoste requīrat?
ex.en: trickery or courage — who would ask which, against an enemy? (Vergil, Aeneid 2.390)

note: Contracted to domna in speech: Italian donna is now simply 'woman', and madonna is 'my lady'. The elegiac poets called their mistress domina, making the lover her slave.
Church Latin diēs dominica 'the Lord's day' replaced diēs Sōlis 'the Sun's day' (still English Sunday) in every Romance language.
The 'master of the house' (domus). Contracted domnus, it became a title — Spanish don, Romanian domn 'Mr' — and through *dominiō 'lord's tower' French donjon and English dungeon.
An irregular perfect (domuī) for a first-conjugation verb. English tame is a native cognate; the p of French dompter is a scribal insertion.

Mixes second and fourth declension; locative domī 'at home', domum 'homewards', domō 'from home', all without a preposition. Spoken Latin preferred casa 'hut', but domus survives in Italian duomo, the 'house' of God.

ex.t: dōnec eris sospes, multōs numerābis amīcōs
ex.en: as long as you are prosperous, you will count many friends (Ovid, Tristia 1.9.5)

note: French made dōnāre its everyday 'give' (donner), abandoning dare. Two constructions: alicui aliquid dōnāre or aliquem aliquā rē dōnāre.

ex.en: I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts (Vergil, Aeneid 2.49)
Marcus is sleeping in his bedroom.

note: Spoken Latin dossum (rs → ss) gave French dos and Italian dosso. To endorse a cheque is to sign it on the back.
In Romanian drac came to mean 'devil'. Vlad the Impaler's father belonged to the Order of the Dragon and was called Dracul; Dracula is 'son of Dracul'.
From duo 'two': to doubt is to waver between two choices. Romanian (se) îndoi 'doubt' was built the same way on doi 'two'. English doubt took a silent b from Latin.

ex.en: when in doubt, (decide) for the accused

note: Portuguese duzentos still continues ducentōs directly; Italian and Spanish remade the word on 'two'.
Imperative dūc. In mātrimōnium dūcere is to marry a wife ('lead her home'). Only Romanian kept the simple verb (duce); elsewhere it lives in compounds such as condūcere.

ex.en: the Fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling (Seneca, Letters 107.11)

en: (iam dūdum) for a long time now

note: Old Latin duellum became bellum (du- → b-, as duonus → bonus). Medieval scholars linked it with duo 'two' and revived it for single combat — the duel.
French doux and Portuguese doce lost the l (vocalized or dropped before a consonant), as in French cou 'neck' < collum.

ex.en: it is sweet to play the fool at the right moment (Horace, Odes 4.12)

note: Romanian counts 11–19 as 'X over ten' (doisprezece), a Slavic-type pattern; the others continue duodecim.
English during was the participle of dure 'last': 'during the war' = 'the war lasting'. Romanian dura moved on to 'build'.

ex.t: dūrāte, et vōsmet rēbus servāte secundīs
ex.en: hold on, and keep yourselves for better days (Vergil, Aeneid 1.207)

note: Romanian prefers tare, from tālis, which drifted from 'such, excellent' to 'strong, hard'.

ex.en: the law is harsh, but it is the law
a woman led the enterprise (Vergil, Aeneid 1.364)

note: French ivre is the direct heir; everyday Italian ubriaco comes from a derived ēbriācus.
Italian avorio and French ivoire come from eboreus 'made of ivory'; the Iberian languages took an Arabic word, Romanian a Turkish one.
Fused with pronouns it built many Romance demonstratives: Italian questo and quello, French ce and celui, Romanian acest and acel.
Greek ekklēsía was the citizens' assembly 'called out' to meet; Christians used it for their community. Romanian chose basilica instead.
From ēdīcō 'proclaim'. A praetor's ēdictum, posted at the start of his year, set out how he would administer the law.
Its short forms ēs, ēst 'you eat, he eats' clashed with es, est 'you are, he is', so speakers switched to comedere (Spanish comer) and the slangy mandūcāre 'chomp' (mangiare, manger, mânca).
ē + dō 'give out'. Not to be confused with edō 'eat' (short e). Romance éditer/editar mean 'publish'; English edit is a back-formation from editor.
ex + fēmina. Caesar's traders bring in luxuries 'that tend to soften minds' (quae ad effēminandōs animōs pertinent).
ex + ferō, with the suppletive tulī, lātum: ēlātus 'raised up' gave English elated.

ex.en: He brought it about that everyone fled.

note: ex + frēnum 'bridle': a horse that has thrown off the bit.
Used only for emphasis or contrast, since the verb ending already shows the person. All the Romance forms go back to a spoken eo.

ex.t: ego sum via et vēritās et vīta
ex.en: I am the way, the truth and the life (John 14:6)

note: Literally 'out of the herd' (ē + grex). English egregious slid from 'outstanding' to 'outrageous'; Italian Egregio Signore still opens a polite letter.

ex.t: ēheu fugācēs, Postume, Postume, lābuntur annī
ex.en: alas, Postumus, Postumus, the fleeting years slip by (Horace, Odes 2.14)

note: Its participle ēlāpsus gives elapse. Not to be confused with ēlabōrō 'work out', which gives elaborate.
Rubbed amber attracts straws; in 1600 William Gilbert coined Neo-Latin ēlectricus 'amber-like' for the force.
It rendered Greek στοιχεῖον, which meant both 'letter of the alphabet' and 'basic constituent' — so elementa are the ABC of any subject.
In Homer Greek eléphās means only 'ivory'; the animal became familiar later. Romans met war elephants in Pyrrhus' and Hannibal's armies.
From levis 'light'. French élever also means 'bring up (children)' — an élève is a pupil.
Romanian alege is the everyday 'choose'; French élire is reserved for elections, and its participle gave élite 'the chosen'.
ē + līmen 'threshold': literally 'put out over the doorstep'.
ē + lūdō: to 'play out' an opponent, like a gladiator dodging a blow.

ex.t: quam diū etiam furor iste tuus nōs ēlūdet?
ex.en: how long will that madness of yours still mock us? (Cicero)

note: From mancipium 'taking in hand' (manus + capiō): a son was formally released from his father's 'hand' by a mock sale.
ē + menda 'fault': take the faults out. English has it twice: learned emend and French-borrowed amend.
Its original meaning was 'take' (still in exemplum 'something taken out' and sūmō < *sub-emō). Romance 'buy' comes from comparāre 'get together'.
Literally 'remove the sinews' (nervus 'sinew'). French énerver and its kin flipped to 'get on someone's nerves'; English enervate kept 'sap the strength'.
ē + nōrma 'carpenter's square': 'out of square', then 'excessive', then 'huge'.
Perfect also īvī. Spanish and Portuguese kept ir; French kept only its future (irai), and Romanian merge comes from mergere 'dive'. Its compounds — exeō, redeō, pereō, trānseō — are everywhere.

ex.en: go, make for Italy with the winds (Vergil, Aeneid 4.381)

note: Greek epískopos 'overseer'. Each vernacular wore it down differently: vescovo, obispo, évêque, bispo — and English bishop, which lost the first syllable entirely.
The everyday Romance 'letter' comes from littera (lettera, letra, lettre); French épître is the worn-down heir of epistula, used for the New Testament epistles.

ex.en: Cicero writes a letter to Atticus.

note: Equus died out, but its feminine survived in Spanish yegua, Portuguese égua and Romanian iapă. Dative and ablative plural equābus.
The equitēs, originally citizens rich enough to serve on horseback, became Rome's moneyed business class, ranking just below the senators.
Everyday Latin preferred caballus 'nag', which displaced equus everywhere; only the feminine equa survives (Spanish yegua). Greek ἵππος is a cognate, its initial h- and pp irregular.

ex.en: do not trust the horse, Trojans (Vergil, Aeneid 2.48)

note: A rare classical word with heirs in every Romance language. English urchin meant 'hedgehog' before 'scamp' — a sea urchin is a 'sea hedgehog' — and Italian riccio also means 'curl'.

ex.en: rescue me from these troubles, unconquered one (Vergil, Aeneid 6.365)

note: 'Wander' and 'go wrong' are one idea: a knight-errant wanders, an error strays from the truth.

ex.t: perdiderint cum mē duo crīmina, carmen et error
ex.en: though two charges ruined me, a poem and a mistake (Ovid, Tristia 2.207)

note: From ērudiō, 'take the roughness out' (ē + rudis 'rough, untrained').
From edō 'eat'. Italian esca is still bait, but Spanish yesca and Romanian iască became 'tinder' — food for the fire.
Seneca credits Cicero with coining it from esse 'to be' to render Greek ousía. French essence is also 'petrol' — the refined 'essence' of oil.
Romanian și 'and' comes from sīc 'thus, so'. The ampersand & is a ligature of the letters e and t.
Greek 'good news' (eu + ángelos 'messenger'). English gospel is a native calque, Old English gōdspel 'good tidings'.
Church Latin, from Greek εὐ 'good' + ἄγγελος 'messenger': the angel in Luke 2 says ēvangelizō vōbīs gaudium magnum.
A false friend from the same root: Romance eventuale/eventual means 'possible', English eventual means 'final'.

ex.en: the outcome is the teacher of fools (Livy 22.39)

note: Rare in classical Latin (which preferred vītō), yet it became the standard 'avoid' in every Romance language; inēvītābilis gave inevitable.
Ancient books were scrolls, and to read one you 'rolled it out' (librum ēvolvere) — the image behind evolution, an 'unrolling'.
ē before consonants, ex before vowels (and often before consonants too). As a prefix it lives on in Italian s- (sfuggire 'escape') and French é- (étendre 'stretch out').
A Late Latin word from exigō 'weigh'. A weighing became a test or attempt, and Montaigne's Essais — 'attempts' — gave us the literary essay.

ex.t: dēposuit potentēs dē sēde et exaltāvit humilēs
ex.en: he has put down the mighty from their seat and raised up the lowly (Luke 1:52)

note: From ex + agō 'drive out': a swarm is driven out of the hive, and the needle of a balance 'comes out' when weighing. Popular speech kept the bees (sciame, enjambre, essaim, enxame); scholars kept the examination.
A rare late verb from calidus 'hot', yet it lives on everywhere: Italian scaldare 'warm up', Romanian scălda 'bathe', English scald.

ex.en: glory to God in the highest (the Gloria of the Mass)

en: slip out, escape (from memory or the lips)
note: ex + cadō 'fall'. Not to be confused with excīdō (long ī) 'cut out', from caedō, which gives excise.
ex + clāmō 'shout'. Spanish llamar 'call' and Portuguese chamar are the popular heirs of clāmāre.
ex + claudō 'shut'. Aqua exclūsa 'water shut out' gave French écluse 'lock' and English sluice.
ex + crux 'cross': to torment as on the cross.

ex.t: ōdī et amō … nesciō, sed fierī sentiō et excrucior
ex.en: I hate and I love … I do not know why, but I feel it happen and I am in torment (Catullus 85)

note: ex + causa 'case, charge': to get someone out of a charge. Italian scusa! is the everyday 'sorry'.
From eximō 'take out': a sample taken out of the whole. English sample is a clipped example; Spanish ejemplo shows the popular x → j.

ex.t: longum iter est per praecepta, breve et efficāx per exempla
ex.en: the road through rules is long, through examples short and effective (Seneca, Letters 6.5)

note: Italian uscire and Romanian ieși are its direct heirs; Spanish salir and Portuguese sair come from salīre 'leap'.
Literally 'the trained body', from exerceō. French armée and Romanian armată come instead from armāta 'armed'.

ex.en: Caesar led the army into winter quarters.

note: ex + agō: 'drive out' → 'weigh out' → 'demand'. Exāctus 'weighed precisely' gave exact.

ex.en: I have completed a monument more lasting than bronze (Horace, Odes 3.30)

note: A famous false friend: Spanish éxito and Portuguese êxito mean 'success' — the good outcome — not 'exit'.

ex.en: the outcome justifies the deed (Ovid, Heroides 2.85)

note: From ōrdior 'lay the warp, begin a web': the first threads set on the loom. In rhetoric, the opening section of a speech.
ex + pēs 'foot': to free the feet from a snare; impediō is to entangle them. Italian spedire 'send (by post)' is the everyday heir.
Money was originally weighed (pendō 'weigh'). Italian spendere and English spend both come from expendere.
Spanish and Portuguese despertar 'wake up' are usually traced to a spoken *expertāre built on this verb's participle; Italian and French use 'watch' words (vigilāre).
French expérience still means both 'experience' and 'experiment', close to the Latin 'trial'.
From plānus 'flat': to smooth out the difficulties. Italian spianare still means 'flatten'.
An expletive was first a 'filler' word, padding out a line; swear words became the filler par excellence.
Perfect also explicuī, supine explicitum. Literally 'unfold' (plicāre 'fold'); Italian spiegare still means both 'explain' and 'unfurl'.
ex + plaudō 'clap': the audience 'clapped out' a bad actor. The sense 'blow up' (a noisy bursting out) dates from the 17th century.
ex + premō 'press'. Italian caffè espresso is 'pressed-out' coffee.

ex.en: They took the town by storm.

note: Participle of exquīrō 'search out'. 'Sought out' went three ways: Italian squisito 'delicious', English exquisite, and Portuguese esquisito 'odd' — a notorious false friend.
Carrying out a sentence turned 'execute' into 'put to death'. Exsequiae 'following (the body)' are funeral rites.
Also spelled exilium. Ovid wrote his Tristia in exile at Tomis on the Black Sea — today's Constanța in Romania.
Also spelled expectō. Literally 'look out for'; Italian aspettare and Romanian aștepta use the sister verb aspectāre, while Spanish and Portuguese esperar fuse 'wait' and 'hope'.
French éteindre and Romanian stinge 'put out (a light)' are the popular heirs; the others use the learned form.
A rare late word (from sūcus 'juice'), yet it gave the everyday 'dry, wipe' verbs: asciugare, enjugar, essuyer, enxugar.

ex.t: et exsultāvit spīritus meus in Deō salūtārī meō
ex.en: and my spirit has rejoiced in God my saviour (Luke 1:47)

ex.t: extemplō Libyae magnās it Fāma per urbēs
ex.en: at once Rumour goes through the great cities of Libya (Vergil, Aeneid 4.173)

note: ex + terminus 'boundary': for Cicero it meant 'banish'; the sense 'destroy utterly' comes from the Latin Bible.
From extrā 'outside': the outsider became 'strange' in Italian, French and English, while Romanian străin still means 'foreigner'.
Spanish haba is a textbook case of Latin f- becoming h- (now silent) in Castilian.
The French surnames Lefèvre and Lefebvre mean 'the smith' and come from faber, just like English Smith.
French forge and Spanish fragua are the worn-down inherited forms; fabbrica, fábrica and fabrique were borrowed again from written Latin. English fabric first meant 'a building'.
Also deponent fabricor. Its worn-down heirs are blacksmiths' words (forger, fraguar, English forge); fabricate came back later as a learned word.

ex.t: Mūtātō nōmine dē tē fābula nārrātur.
ex.en: Change the name, and the story is about you. (Horace)

note: In Iberia this colloquial verb for 'chatting' became the normal word for 'speak' (hablar, falar); Italy and France chose parabolāre 'talk in parables' instead.
Everyday Spanish says cara, but the old word survives in set phrases such as la faz de la tierra 'the face of the earth'.

ex.en: The descent to the underworld is easy. (Vergil)

note: Neutral 'deed' in origin (from faciō), it came to mean mostly 'misdeed', a shift Latin speakers felt as euphemism.
Italian fare and French faire come from a shortened spoken *fare; Spanish hacer keeps the full stem, with f- > h-. The passive is supplied by fīō 'become'.

ex.t: Faciāmus hominem ad imāginem et similitūdinem nostram.
ex.en: Let us make man in our image and likeness. (Genesis 1:26)

note: A perfect showcase of Latin -ct-: fatto, hecho, fait, feito, fapt (tt, ch, it, it, pt).
Latin fāgus, English beech and Greek φηγός share a root; in Greece, with few beeches, the name went to an oak.

ex.t: Tītyre, tū patulae recubāns sub tegmine fāgī
ex.en: Tityrus, you who lie under the cover of a spreading beech (Vergil, Eclogues 1)

note: French il faut 'it is necessary' comes from fallere in the sense 'be lacking': what is missing is what is needed.

ex.t: Falsus in ūnō, falsus in omnibus.
ex.en: False in one thing, false in everything. (legal maxim)

note: French faux 'scythe' is identical in form to faux 'false' (< falsus): two Latin words collapsed into one sound.

ex.t: Fāma, malum quā nōn aliud vēlōcius ūllum
ex.en: Rumour, the evil swifter than any other (Vergil, Aeneid 4.174)

note: Spanish hambre goes back to a spoken *famine, with f- > h- and -mn- > -mbr-, exactly as in hombre < hominem. The ablative is famē, a fifth-declension form.
From famulus 'servant': a Roman familia was everyone under the authority of the head of the house, slaves included. The old genitive survives in pater familiās.
A fānāticus was someone possessed by a temple's god; profānus was what lay 'in front of the shrine', outside the sacred ground.
From far 'emmer wheat', the Romans' oldest grain; a word inherited in every Romance language.
Literally 'what has been spoken' (from fārī), i.e. the gods' decree. The plural fāta, reinterpreted as a feminine, gave French fée 'fairy'; Portuguese fado is the song of fate.

ex.en: The fates will find a way. (Vergil, Aeneid 3.395)

note: The 'throat' of a river or a valley: Italian foce and Portuguese foz mean an estuary, Spanish hoz a gorge.

en: Faustulus, the shepherd who found and raised Romulus and Remus

note: Takes the dative. At sacrifices the call favēte linguīs 'favour with your tongues' meant 'keep holy silence' — say nothing ill-omened.
Torches led Roman wedding processions, so fax is also a poetic word for marriage.
Latin fel, English gall and Greek χολή (behind cholera and melancholy) go back to one word for the yellow-green bile.
The classical word, used for any small mouse-hunting animal, lost out to late Latin cattus — the source of gatto, gato, chat and English cat.
The root sense is 'fruitful', then 'lucky'. Romanian ferice (and everyday fericit 'happy') shows -l- between vowels turning into r, as in soare < sōlem.

ex.t: Fēlīx quī potuit rērum cognōscere causās.
ex.en: Happy the one who could learn the causes of things. (Vergil, Georgics 2.490)

note: Only French femme and Romanian femeie kept this as the ordinary word for 'woman'; elsewhere it narrowed to 'female' and domina or mulier took over.

ex.en: A woman led the enterprise. (Vergil, Aeneid 1.364)

note: Spanish and Portuguese renamed the window — ventana 'wind-hole', janela 'little door' — while Romanian fereastră kept the Latin word, with its n turned to r. The circumflex in fenêtre marks a lost s.
Literally 'little hay' (from fēnum), for its fine feathery leaves. Spanish hinojo also survives in de hinojos 'kneeling', from a different word, genuculum 'knee'.
Short for fera bēstia, the feminine of ferus 'wild'. Italian fiera means both 'wild beast' and 'trade fair' (< fēria) — two Latin words that fell together.
Usually follows the word it qualifies: omnēs ferē 'almost all'. With a negative it means 'hardly': nēmō ferē 'hardly anyone'.
Markets were held on feast days, hence 'fair'. Portuguese names its weekdays after Church Latin fēria secunda etc.: segunda-feira 'Monday', terça-feira 'Tuesday'.
Has no perfect system of its own (Latin uses percussī, ictum). French férir survives only in the phrase sans coup férir 'without striking a blow'.
A by-form of ferē, favoured by Livy and later prose writers.
Three unrelated stems make up its principal parts: fer-, tul- (cf. tollō) and lāt- (from *tlātos). The simple verb died out in Romance, but compounds like sufferre and offerre live on.

ex.en: I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts. (Vergil, Aeneid 2.49)

note: French fier and Italian fiero moved from 'wild' to 'proud'; Spanish fiero kept 'fierce'. Greek θήρ 'beast' is a cognate.
Spanish hervir, Portuguese ferver and Romanian fierbe kept this verb for 'boil'; Italian and French chose bullīre 'bubble' instead.
The Romance nouns come from the neuter plural fēsta (diēs 'feast days') taken as a feminine singular. The circumflex of fête marks the lost s.
The e of fideī is short, unlike diēī, because a consonant precedes it. Romans prized fidēs as the bond of every contract and alliance; Greek πείθω 'persuade' is from the same root.
French fils, with its pronounced s, continues the nominative fīlius rather than the accusative fīlium — a rare survivor of the Latin subject case. Vocative: fīlī.

ex.t: Fīlius meus es tū; ego hodiē genuī tē.
ex.en: You are my son; today I have begotten you. (Psalm 2:7)

note: Spanish helecho and Portuguese feto both come from filictum 'a place full of ferns', with the Spanish showing the usual f- > h-.
Portuguese fio dropped the l between vowels (as in voar < volāre), Romanian fir turned it into r (as in soare < sōlem).
The participle fissus 'split' gives fissure and nuclear fission.
The root meant 'knead clay or dough': English dough is a cognate, and Spanish heñir still means 'knead'. From kneading to shaping to inventing and faking.
In the plural fīnēs means 'borders' and so 'territory': in fīnēs Helvētiōrum. French and Italian made 'end' feminine (la fin, la fine), Spanish and Portuguese kept it masculine (el fin, o fim).
Serves as the passive of faciō in the present system, with factus sum as its perfect. The ī is long except before -er: fīō, fīunt, but fierī, fierem.

en: (Vulgate) the firmament, the vault of heaven
note: Jerome's word for the solid vault of the sky in Genesis 1, translating Greek στερέωμα, itself from στερεός 'solid'.
A ferme in Old French was land held for a fixed rent — hence English farm. Italian fermo drifted to 'still, motionless'.
Latin fl- goes three ways: Italian fi- (fiamma), Spanish ll- (llama), Portuguese ch- (chama), while French keeps fl-. Compare clāmāre: chiamare, llamar, chamar.

ex.t: Flectere sī nequeō superōs, Acheronta movēbō.
ex.en: If I cannot bend the gods above, I shall stir up the underworld. (Vergil, Aeneid 7.312)

note: Romance replaced it with plōrāre 'wail' (llorar, pleurer, chorar) and plangere 'beat the breast' (piangere, plânge). English feeble is flēbilis 'lamentable'.
Its compound afflāre 'blow on, sniff at' became 'find' in Spanish hallar, Portuguese achar and Romanian afla — like a hound picking up a scent.
English flower and flour are one word: flour was the 'flower', i.e. the finest part, of ground grain. Romance made the word feminine — except Italian il fiore.

ex.en: She is tossed by the waves but does not sink. (motto of Paris)

note: Only Italian kept it (fiume, with fl- > fi-); elsewhere rīvus 'brook' grew into the general word for river.
An 'influence' was an ethereal fluid believed to flow from the stars into people — and influenza was blamed on it.
The household hearth replaced ignis as the everyday word for 'fire' in every Romance language. Kepler borrowed focus for the 'burning point' of a lens.
From the root of fidēs 'trust': a pact sworn before the gods. Rome's Italian allies were foederātī.
Spanish feo and Portuguese feio 'ugly' are this word: oe became e and the d between vowels dropped out.

ex.en: Back to the sources! (cry of Renaissance humanists)

note: Italian fuori and French hors continue forīs, Spanish fuera and Portuguese fora its twin forās. Related to forēs 'double door' and English door.
Italian formaggio and French fromage are cheese 'shaped in a mould' (formāticus). Spanish has learned forma beside inherited horma.
French formidable has slid from 'fearsome' to 'great, terrific' — the same path as English terrific.
Spanish hermoso, Portuguese formoso and Romanian frumos continue this word: the edges of the Latin world kept it, while Italy and Gaul preferred colloquial bellus (bello, beau).

ex.en: The shepherd Corydon burned for handsome Alexis. (Vergil, Eclogues 2.1)

note: Romanian foarte became the everyday word for 'very' (foarte bine 'very well'), a use French fort also has in fort bien.
Third-declension adjectives form adverbs in -iter. Romance dropped the suffix and used the noun mente 'with a … mind': fortemente, fuertemente, fortement.

ex.t: Ō fortūnātōs nimium, sua sī bona nōrint, agricolās!
ex.en: O farmers, too fortunate, if only they knew their blessings! (Vergil, Georgics 2.458)

note: Spanish fuero, a town's charter of privileges, is the inherited form. Forensic first meant 'of the forum', i.e. of the law courts held there.
A doublet: French frêle and English frail are the worn-down inherited forms, fragile the learned one. From the root of frangō 'break'.
The nasal n belongs to the present only: frēgī, frāctum. English break is a cognate (Latin f- = English b-, as in frāter ~ brother).

ex.en: I shall break, but not bend. (motto)

note: Iberia replaced it with (frāter) germānus 'full brother': hermano, irmão. The old word lives on there for monks: Spanish fraile, Portuguese frade 'friar'.

ex.t: Atque in perpetuum, frāter, avē atque valē.
ex.en: And for ever, brother, hail and farewell. (Catullus 101)

note: Kept in all five languages, a neat demonstration of Latin x: frassino, fresno, frêne, freixo, frasin.
The bit that checks a horse now names the brakes of a car in four languages. The plural is often frēnī (masculine).
The classical sense is 'crowded, in large numbers': senātus frequēns is a well-attended senate. 'Often' came later.
Spoken Latin shortened it to *frigdus, whence Italian freddo and French froid. Romanian rece comes from recēns 'fresh'.
An affront is a blow 'to the forehead', i.e. to one's face. Spanish la frente 'forehead' but el frente 'front line'.
Romanian frunză is the everyday word for 'leaf', where the West uses folium (foglia, hoja, feuille).

ex.en: The tree is known by its fruit. (Matthew 12:33)

note: Caesar's constant worry was the rēs frūmentāria 'grain supply'. Iberia renamed wheat after trīticum (trigo), Romania after grānum (grâu).
One of five deponents that take the ablative: ūtor, fruor, fungor, potior, vēscor.
Romanian fugi has become the ordinary verb 'to run'. Spanish huir lost both the f- and the g.

ex.en: Time flies, never to return. (Vergil, Georgics 3.284)

note: French fronde gained an r. The 17th-century revolt against Mazarin was called the Fronde after the slings of Parisian street boys.
From fundus 'bottom': to lay the bottom of something. Not to be confused with fundō, fundere 'pour'.
Romance narrowed 'pour' to pouring molten metal, hence 'melt, cast': French fondre, fondue, English foundry. In Caesar, hostēs fundere is 'to rout the enemy'.
Romanian kept the verb fūrārī as a fura 'to steal'. The ferret got its name as a 'little thief'.
Table forks came late: Italian forchetta and French fourchette are 'little pitchforks'.

ex.t: Nātūram expellās furcā, tamen usque recurret.
ex.en: Drive nature out with a pitchfork, she will still come running back. (Horace)

note: In the Aeneid furor is the destructive passion that opposes pietās. Italian far furore 'be all the rage' gave English furore.
Time zones are husos horarios in Spanish and fusos horários in Portuguese, after the spindle shape of the zones on a globe.
Surprisingly, French Gaule does not come from Gallia but from Frankish *Walha 'foreigners' — the same root as Wales and Wallachia.

ex.t: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs.
ex.en: Gaul as a whole is divided into three parts. (Caesar)

note: Romans enjoyed the pun gallus 'rooster' / Gallus 'Gaul' — one reason the cockerel became an emblem of France.

en: the Garonne, river of south-western Gaul
note: Like most Latin river names it is masculine despite the -a: flūmen Garumna.
Semi-deponent: active present, but perfect gāvīsus sum 'I rejoiced'. In Romance 'rejoice' shifted to 'enjoy'.

ex.en: So let us rejoice while we are young. (student song)

note: French joie, from the plural gaudia taken as a feminine, was itself borrowed into Italian (gioia) and English (joy).

ex.t: Annūntiō vōbīs gaudium magnum: habēmus Pāpam.
ex.en: I announce to you a great joy: we have a Pope.

note: The first meaning is 'bud'; jewels were named for their bud-like gleam. Spanish yema and Portuguese gema became the 'bud' of the egg, the yolk.
French gendre and Portuguese genro squeezed out the vowel between n and r, French adding a d as in tendre < tenerum; Spanish yerno shows ge- > ye-.
A Roman's family name marked his gēns: Gāius Iūlius Caesar belonged to the gēns Iūlia. In Romance it became collective 'people'; Portuguese a gente even means 'we'.
Romance continued the diminutive genuculum; Spanish renamed the knee rotella 'little wheel', i.e. the kneecap. English knee and Greek γόνυ are cognates.
The root of gignō 'beget', Greek γένος and English kin: 'kind' as in 'what one is born as'. English gender and genre are the same word reaching English at different times.

en: the Germans, the Germanic peoples beyond the Rhine
note: Probably a Celtic name the Gauls gave their neighbours. Only Romanian german and English German name today's Germans with it; compare tedesco, alemán, allemand.

en: the lands east of the Rhine
note: French, Spanish and Portuguese named the country after the Alamanni, the tribe they knew best; Italian and Romanian keep the Latin name used by Caesar and Tacitus.
From frāter germānus 'full brother', the adjective alone replaced frāter in Spanish hermano and Portuguese irmão. French cousin germain is a first cousin.
bellum gerere 'wage war', rēs gestae 'things done, achievements'. Old French chansons de geste sang of deeds, and a geste became an English jest.

ex.en: The Achievements of the Divine Augustus

note: A reduplicated present, gi-gn-ō, exactly like Greek γί-γν-ομαι; the plain root gen- shows in genuī, genitum and genus.

ex.en: Hail, Emperor, those who are about to die salute you. (Suetonius)

note: The short stabbing sword of the legions gave way to the long cavalry spatha (Greek σπάθη), which supplied every Romance word for 'sword'.

ex.t: Omnēs quī accēperint gladium, gladiō perībunt.
ex.en: All who take the sword will perish by the sword. (Matthew 26:52)
Thus passes the glory of the world.

note: Often in the bad sense: Plautus' Mīles Glōriōsus is the braggart soldier.

ex.en: Steps to Parnassus (title of verse and music textbooks)

note: The Greeks called their land Ἑλλάς; the Roman name comes from Graecī, probably a tribe the Italians met first, extended to the whole people.

ex.en: Captive Greece took her savage conqueror captive. (Horace)
It's Greek; it can't be read. (medieval scribes)

note: The second stage of Roman schooling: after the litterātor taught reading, the grammaticus, usually a Greek, taught boys to read and explain the poets.
Spanish and Portuguese call hail 'little grains' (granizo); Italian and Romanian keep the Latin word.
Romanian grâu became the word for wheat itself. English corn is a native cognate.
grātiās agere 'give thanks' lies behind Italian grazie and Spanish gracias. grātiā + genitive means 'for the sake of': exemplī grātiā (e.g.).
French gré, from the neuter grātum, lives on in bon gré mal gré 'willy-nilly' and savoir gré 'be grateful'.
Spoken *grevis (reshaped after levis 'light') gave Italian greve and Romanian greu, the everyday word for both 'heavy' and 'difficult'. Grief is heaviness of heart.
Latin ēgregius 'outstanding, out of the flock' was praise; English egregious has turned it into blame.
Borrowed from Greek κυβερνάω 'steer a ship': government as the ship of state. Cybernetics comes from the same Greek verb.
Spanish me gusta and Portuguese gosto de 'I like' grew out of 'it tastes good to me'. French goûter is also the afternoon snack.
Medieval doctors blamed gout on drops of bad humour settling in the joints.

ex.en: Dripping water hollows out the stone. (after Ovid)

note: Spoken Latin built new tenses with it: the perfect (habeō factum → ho fatto, he hecho, j'ai fait) and the future (amāre habeō → amerò, amaré, aimerai). Spanish and Portuguese now use tenēre for plain 'own'.

ex.en: I have in mind, I intend

note: A frequentative of habeō: 'keep having (a place)'. English habitat is Latin 'it dwells', from the wording of old natural-history descriptions.

en: be stuck, be at a loss

note: The amphitheatre floor was strewn with sand to soak up blood — hence arena. Spanish arena and Portuguese areia still mean plain 'sand'. Also spelled arēna.
A spear planted in the forum marked a public sale (sub hastā vendere), which is why Italian asta means 'auction'.
Mostly negates single adjectives and adverbs: haud procul 'not far', haud dubiē 'undoubtedly', haud sciō an 'I am inclined to think'.
French lierre swallowed its own article: l'ierre was reanalysed as le lierre. Ivy was sacred to Bacchus and crowned poets.
Switzerland's official Latin name, Confoederātiō Helvētica, gives the CH on its cars, coins and web addresses. Their migration in 58 BC opens Caesar's Gallic War.
A man's oath; women swore by Castor (ēcastor). Also mehercle, mehercule.
Portuguese ontem means 'last night' (ad noctem). English yester- and Greek χθές are cognates. Also spelled here.
Romance dropped hiems and named winter with this adjective, (tempus) hībernum: inverno, invierno, hiver, iarnă. In Caesar, hīberna are the legions' winter camps.
Every Romance 'here' is hīc propped up by a pointing word: Italian qui (eccum hīc), Spanish aquí, French ici (ecce hīc). Distinguish hīc 'here' from hic 'this'.
As a pronoun it vanished, but it hides inside many Romance words: per hoc → però, pero 'but'; hāc hōrā → ahora, agora 'now'; ecce hoc → ce.

ex.en: In this sign you will conquer.

note: Its own adjective hībernus replaced it everywhere. Greek χειμών and Sanskrit hima- 'snow' (as in Himālaya) share the root.
Part of the place series hīc 'here' – hinc 'from here' – hūc 'to here', answering ubi? unde? quō? Compare illīc, illinc, illūc.
Spoken Latin dropped the h and the unstressed i: *Spania. Western Romance then added a prop vowel before s + consonant (España, Espagne), as in schola → escuela, école.
Greek ἱστορία meant 'inquiry, research', the word Herodotus used for his work. English history and story are one word borrowed twice.

ex.en: History is the teacher of life. (Cicero, De Oratore 2.36)

note: Contracted from hōc diē 'on this day'. French hui survives only inside aujourd'hui, literally 'on the day of today' — a doubled 'today'.
From hodiē 'today' (hōc diē).
French on 'one, we' continues the nominative homō, homme the accusative hominem. Spanish hombre shows -m'n- > -mbr-, like hambre < *famine.

ex.t: Homō sum: hūmānī nihil ā mē aliēnum putō.
ex.en: I am human: I consider nothing human foreign to me. (Terence)

note: An early loan from Greek ὥρα 'season, hour'. Italian ora also means 'now' (from hāc hōrā), like Spanish ahora.

ex.en: You know neither the day nor the hour. (Matthew 25:13)

note: English yard is a native cognate, and garden (via French jardin from Frankish) is a Germanic cousin of the same root. Spanish huerta, from the plural horta, is an irrigated market-garden plain.
One word for both sides of the bond of guest-friendship, as Italian ospite and French hôte still are.
Medieval hospitāle, a guest-house for pilgrims and the sick, split in French into hôpital and hôtel — and English borrowed hospital, hostel and hotel.
Byzantine ὁσπίτιον 'lodging' became the ordinary Modern Greek word for 'house', σπίτι.
English has three hosts, all Latin: the Host (hostia), a host 'multitude' (hostis 'army') and a host who entertains (hospes).
Originally 'stranger', then a public enemy (a personal one is inimīcus). Medieval hostis 'army' gave Spanish hueste, Romanian oaste and English 'a host of'.

ex.en: enemy of mankind (legal term for pirates)

note: Cicero's hūmānitās joined kindness to liberal education — the ancestor of 'the humanities'.
Related to homō and probably to humus 'earth': humans as earth-dwellers, as opposed to the gods of the sky.
French gésir lives on in ci-gît 'here lies' on tombstones, Spanish yacer in aquí yace. Do not confuse iaceō 'lie' with iaciō 'throw'.
In compounds the stem weakens to -iciō: ēiciō, iniciō, obiciō, subiciō, source of eject, inject, object, subject.

ex.en: The die is cast. (Caesar at the Rubicon)

note: From iaciō 'throw': cargo jettisoned to save a ship in a storm. Italian iattura now means 'bad luck'.
Italian già, Spanish ya and Portuguese já kept it; French déjà packs dē ex iam 'from already'. nōn iam = 'no longer', nōndum = 'not yet'.

ex.en: Now spring brings back its mild warmth. (Catullus 46)

note: Linked with Iānus, god of doorways. It survives only in Portuguese janela 'window', literally a 'little door'.

en: Janus (two-faced god of doorways and beginnings)

note: French y in il y a 'there is' and Spanish hay (ha + y) both hide ibi: 'it has there'.

ex.en: Where one is well off, there is one's homeland.

en: Icaria, Aegean island named after Icarus
Icarus, son of Daedalus, who flew too close to the sun
note: He fell into the sea off Samos, which was then called the Icarian Sea (mare Īcarium).
is + -dem (īdem < *is-dem, eundem < eum-dem). Romance replaced it with *metipsimus 'the very self', whence medesimo, mismo, même.

ex.en: Always the same. (motto of Elizabeth I)

note: Often answered by quod or ut: ideō… quod 'for this reason… that'.

en: the Ides (15th of March, May, July, October; 13th of other months)

note: Roman gourmets fattened geese on figs: iecur fīcātum 'fig-fed liver' shrank to fīcātum, ancestor of every Romance word for 'liver' — foie gras included.
Spoken *disiēiūnāre 'un-fast' became French dîner and English dine — a perfect Latin twin of English breakfast.
Declined on a Greek pattern: nom. Iēsūs, acc. Iēsum, all other cases Iēsū. The monogram IHS abbreviates Greek ΙΗΣΟΥΣ.

ex.en: Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews (INRI, John 19:19)

note: Usually placed second in its clause, unlike ergō and itaque, which tend to come first.
in- + (g)nāvus 'busy, active'. For Romans sloth and cowardice were one and the same failing.
No Romance language kept it: the hearth (focus) took over as 'fire'. The Vedic fire-god Agni is a cognate.
In Latin and in Romance it means 'not to know'; English ignore has drifted to 'pay no attention to' — a classic false friend.
Paired with hāc 'this way'. Daedalus: ībimus illāc, 'we shall go that way' — through the sky.
The parent of nearly every Romance definite article and third-person pronoun; Romanian attaches it to the end of the noun (lupul 'the wolf'). After a name it means 'that famous': Mēdēa illa.
Italian lì and là, Spanish allí and allá, French là all descend from illīc and its twin illāc 'that way'.
hūc et illūc 'hither and thither'. The series illīc 'there' – illinc 'from there' – illūc 'to there' parallels hīc – hinc – hūc.
Noble families kept wax imāginēs of their ancestors in the atrium and paraded them at funerals; having them made one a nōbilis.
In Latin it describes weakness of body or will; the meaning 'stupid' is modern.
Literally 'not good': in- + old mānus 'good', seen in the Mānēs, the 'kindly' spirits of the dead. Hence monstrous, then simply enormous.
Corrects what was just said, either contradicting it or going one better: immō vērō 'nay rather'.

ex.t: Vīvit? Immō vērō etiam in senātum venit.
ex.en: He lives? Why, he even comes into the senate! (Cicero, Against Catiline 1.2)

note: Caesar's impedīmenta are the army's baggage — the things that 'hobble the feet' of a marching column.
Literally 'shackle the feet' (in + pēs); its opposite expediō 'free the feet' gave expedite. French empêcher, Romanian împiedica and English impeach come from late impedicāre.
Under the Republic a victorious general was hailed imperātor by his troops; Augustus turned it into the ruler's title. Romanian împărat is a fully worn-down inherited form.
First the legal power to command armies (and to execute) held by consuls and praetors; only later the territory ruled.

ex.en: I have given them rule without end. (Vergil, Aeneid 1.279)

note: The person ordered goes in the dative: mīlitibus imperat ut… 'he orders the soldiers to…'. Compare iubeō, which takes the accusative and infinitive.
Kept everywhere for 'fill', though Italian and French add re- (riempire, remplir). Spanish henchir 'swell' and Portuguese encher show im- turning into en-.
'Fold into' became 'involve' and then 'employ': to employ someone is to fold them into your business. English imply, implicate and employ are all this verb. Also perfect implicuī, supine implicitum.
in + plōrō 'wail' — the same plōrāre that gave Spanish llorar and French pleurer 'weep'.
In Romance 'bring in' also came to mean 'matter, be important': Italian importa, Spanish importa, French il importe.
'Not up to standard' (probus), hence wicked, but also 'excessive, unrelenting' — the sense Italian improbo 'gruelling' keeps.
With the ablative it marks place (in urbe 'in the city'), with the accusative motion (in urbem 'into the city'). Romance kept the word but lost the case contrast.
Used of stately walking, and of emotions that 'come over' people: timor incessit exercitum 'fear seized the army'.

ex.t: Ast ego, quae dīvum incēdō rēgīna…
ex.en: But I, who walk as queen of the gods… (Juno in Vergil, Aeneid 1.46)

note: Incense is what is 'set alight' (incēnsum), and to incense someone is to set them ablaze with anger.
in + cadō 'fall'. Distinguish incīdō, incīdere 'cut into' (from caedō), the source of incision.
Only Romanian kept it (a începe); the West coined *cominitiāre (cominciare, commencer, começar). For the perfect, Latin usually prefers coepī 'I began'.
It became the clitic pronoun Italian ne and French en: j'en ai deux 'I have two of them'.
The Church's indulgentia, a remission of punishment for sin, became a flashpoint of the Reformation.
Its opposite is exuō 'take off'. Romanian îmbrăca 'dress' is *imbrācāre 'put into trousers' (brācae, a Gaulish garment).

ex.t: Rīsū ineptō rēs ineptior nūlla est.
ex.en: Nothing is sillier than a silly laugh. (Catullus 39)

note: in- + ars 'skill': first 'unskilled', then 'idle'. Physics' inertia is the 'idleness' of matter.
Literally 'not (yet) speaking' (in- + fārī). French enfant is the everyday word for 'child'; Iberian infante became a royal prince, and Italian fante a foot-soldier — hence infantry.

en: offerings to the dead, funeral rites
note: From īnferī 'those below', the dead. Catullus brings his brother's ashes these 'sad gifts'.
Church Latin's word for Hell, simply 'the region below'. Dante's Inferno made the Italian form international.
Conjugated like ferō, with assimilation in the perfect and participle: intulī, illātum. bellum īnferre 'make war on', signa īnferre 'advance the standards'.
Irregular comparison: īnferior, īnfimus or īmus. Its opposite is superus (superior, suprēmus / summus).
The grammarians' modus īnfīnītīvus is our infinitive: the verb form 'not limited' by person or number.
'Not firm' became the everyday word for 'sick' in Spanish enfermo; French infirmière 'nurse' and English infirmary come from the same word.
Spanish hinchar, Portuguese inchar, French enfler and Romanian umfla all mean 'swell' — what happens when you blow into something.
Inborn talent became the clever device it produces: French engin, English engine and engineer. In Brazil an engenho is a sugar mill.
One of Vergil's favourite words, constantly used in the Aeneid, yet it left no descendant in any Romance language.
The freeborn were expected to be candid; candour slid into naivety, so ingenuo, ingénu now mean 'naive' — a false friend for 'ingenious'.
in- + amīcus: a personal enemy, as against hostis, the enemy in war. In every Romance language it displaced hostis.
in- + aequus 'level, fair', with ae weakened to ī. Uneven ground (inīquus locus) was a tactical handicap long before iniquity was a sin.
in- + iūs: 'what is not right', a legal wrong. Romance narrowed it to verbal wrong (insult), English to physical harm. The ablative iniūriā means 'unjustly'.
in- + ops 'means, resources'. Caesar's armies are forever suffering inopia frūmentī, a shortage of grain.
Defective: mostly inquam, inquis, inquit, inquiunt. It always stands inside a direct quotation, like English 'said he': 'Ego,' inquit, 'veniam.'

ex.t: Inquiētum est cor nostrum, dōnec requiēscat in tē.
ex.en: Our heart is restless until it rests in you. (Augustine, Confessions 1.1)

note: Italian inseguire 'chase' continues it, remodelled on seguire 'follow'.
From in + sedeō 'sit in': an ambush is men sitting in hiding. Plural in form, singular in meaning.
Originally 'unaccustomed' (in- + soleō); behaving out of the ordinary came to mean behaving arrogantly.
From īnstituō 'set up'. Caesar's Gallic peoples differ 'in language, customs and laws' (linguā, īnstitūtīs, lēgibus).
In Rome an īnsula was also a block of flats, an 'island' surrounded by streets. The circumflex of French île marks the s of Old French isle.
in- + the root of tangō: 'untouched'. Every Romance language kept it as the word for 'whole'.

ex.en: The man of upright life and free of crime… (Horace, Odes 1.22)

note: inter + legō 'choose between'. Only Romanian kept it as the everyday verb (a înțelege); the West turned to intendere, comprehendere and capere.

ex.en: I believe so that I may understand. (Anselm)

note: 'Stretching the mind towards' something became 'understand' in Spanish and Portuguese, 'hear' in French entendre, and 'intend' in Italian and English.
inter sē is Latin's way of saying 'each other': inter sē amant 'they love one another'. Romanian între adds in-.

ex.en: In time of war the laws fall silent. (Cicero)

note: A tribune's intercessiō was his veto: he 'stepped between' a magistrate and the act.
inter + claudō. Caesar's word for cutting an enemy off from supplies or retreat: commeātū interclūdere.
English interest is the Latin impersonal interest 'it makes a difference' — in banking, the sum that 'is between' a loan and its repayment.
Literally the space 'between the stakes' (vallī) of a palisade.
Italian tra 'between, among' continues intrā (its twin fra comes from īnfrā).
Literally 'come upon' (in + veniō); an inventor 'finds' new things. Romance replaced it with trovare / trouver and encontrar 'run into'.

ex.en: I shall either find a way or make one. (attributed to Hannibal)
the Unconquered Sun (a late Roman god)

note: Literally 'look askance at' (in + videō) — the evil eye. Takes the dative: tibi invideō 'I envy you'.
French envie has softened to 'desire': j'ai envie de… 'I feel like…'. In Latin politics invidia is the odium a man attracts.

ex.en: while we talk, envious time will have fled (Horace)

note: The participle of invideō: 'looked at with the evil eye', hence hated and hateful.
Spanish and Portuguese convidar is the popular form, its prefix remade as con-. Despite appearances it is not related to invītus 'unwilling'.

ex.en: against Minerva's will, i.e. without natural talent (Horace)
she wrapped him in swaddling clothes (Luke 2:7)

note: From Hebrew Yoḥanan through Greek Ἰωάννης. Europe's favourite Christian name wore down differently in every language: Giovanni, Juan, Jean, João, Romanian Ion.
Latin's word for 'joke' became the Romance word for 'game', displacing lūdus. The plural is often neuter: ioca.
Indeclinable in the Vulgate, like most Hebrew names: Ioseph serves for every case.
Emphatic, not reflexive. Spanish ese and Portuguese esse 'that' come from ipse; with met- it formed *metipsimus, ancestor of mismo and même 'same'.

ex.en: He himself said it. (appeal to authority)

note: Everyday Romance prefers rabiēs (rabbia, rabia, rage) or cholera (colère). Seneca wrote three books Dē Īrā.
in + rīdeō. Remus 'laughing at' his brother's low walls jumped over them, and died for it.
The plain pronoun that points back to someone already mentioned (eum vīdī 'I saw him'). It barely survived in Romance, where ille took over; English got 'the id' from translators of Freud.
In Cicero iste often sneers: iste Verrēs 'that fellow Verres'. In Romance it moved closer to the speaker: Spanish este, Italian questo 'this'.
Latin had no single word for 'yes': one answered ita, ita vērō, sīc (whence Italian sì, Spanish sí) or repeated the verb.
Usually first in its clause. Do not confuse with ita-que 'and so (in this way)', stressed differently.
Clerks wrote item 'likewise' before each entry of an inventory, and the adverb became the English noun item.
Takes the accusative and infinitive: Caesar mīlitēs pugnāre iussit 'Caesar ordered the soldiers to fight'. Compare imperō + dative + ut.
The Mona Lisa is La Gioconda in Italian, 'the cheerful lady' — a pun on her husband's surname, del Giocondo.

en: Judaea, the Roman province around Jerusalem

ex.en: The judge is condemned when the guilty man is acquitted. (Publilius Syrus)

note: Spanish juzgar and Portuguese julgar squeeze four syllables into two: the unstressed -di- vanished.
Defeated armies were sent sub iugum, under a 'yoke' of three spears. Married couples (coniugēs) share a yoke; English yoke and Greek ζυγόν are cognates.

ex.en: to send under the yoke (to humiliate a defeated army)

en: Julia, Roman woman's name (feminine of the clan name Julius)

note: The month Quīntīlis was renamed Iūlius in 44 BC in honour of Gaius Julius Caesar, who was born in it.
From the root of iungō 'yoke'. The same draught animal became a mare in French and a donkey in Spanish and Portuguese.
Gin is short for Dutch genever, from Old French for the juniper berries that flavour it.
Iu-piter is 'Father Sky' (*Dyēu-pater), the same god as Greek Ζεὺς πατήρ. The stem Iov- names Thursday: giovedì, jueves, jeudi, joi.

ex.t: Quod licet Iovī, nōn licet bovī.
ex.en: What is allowed to Jupiter is not allowed to an ox.

note: Probably from iūs + agō, 'go to law': a quarrel that might end in court.

ex.t: nūllīus addictus iūrāre in verba magistrī
ex.en: bound to swear by the words of no master (Horace, Epistles 1.1.14)

note: Spoken dīrēctum 'what is straight' replaced it in every Romance language: diritto, derecho, droit, direito, drept. iūs gentium 'the law of nations'.

ex.en: The extreme of law is the extreme of injustice. (Cicero)

note: French jus and English juice come from this Roman broth, not from iūs 'law' — a homonymy Cicero exploited in his joke about iūs Verrīnum, 'Verres' law' or 'boar gravy'.

en: order, command (in practice only abl. iussū)
note: Defective: only the ablative iussū (+ gen.) is common, 'by order of'; its opposite is iniussū 'without orders'.

ex.en: Let justice be done, though the heavens fall.

note: Not an i-stem despite -is: genitive plural iuvenum. A Roman iuvenis could be anyone of fighting age, up to about forty.
The frequentative of its compound adiuvāre, adiūtāre, supplied the verb 'help' to every Romance language: aiutare, ayudar, aider, ajudar, ajuta.

ex.t: Forsan et haec ōlim meminisse iuvābit.
ex.en: Perhaps one day it will be a joy to remember even this. (Vergil, Aeneid 1.203)

en: the Kalends, first day of the Roman month
note: From calāre 'call out': a priest proclaimed the new month. Debts fell due on the Kalends, so a moneylender's ledger was a calendārium. Usually abbreviated Kal.

ex.en: on the Greek Kalends, i.e. never (a saying of Augustus)

note: The everyday Romance 'work' is often another word: fr. travail, es. trabajo, pt. trabalho come from tripālium, an instrument of torture.
Not to be confused with labor 'work': the long ā and the deponent forms mark it. The participle lāpsus gives English lapse, elapse, collapse.
Only Italian kept the general sense 'work'; elsewhere it narrowed to working the land or stone (fr. labourer 'plough'), and 'to work' became trabajar, travailler, trabalhar.
French lèvre continues the neuter plural labra taken as a feminine singular; Italian keeps the old plural in le labbra.
A model of what happened to -ct-: it. tt, es. ch, fr. and pt. it, ro. pt — latte, leche, lait, leite, lapte. Spanish made it feminine: la leche.
English alligator is Spanish el lagarto 'the lizard' run together into one word.
The arm muscle and the lizard share a name, as mūsculus 'little mouse' became 'muscle': the Romans saw small animals rippling under the skin.
Old Latin dacruma shows the root of Greek δάκρυ and English tear; the d- turned into l-, as in lingua from older dingua.

ex.en: there are tears for things (Vergil, Aeneid 1.462)

note: French pleurer and Portuguese chorar are the same word, plōrāre; Portuguese turns initial pl- into ch-, as in plēnus → cheio.
Named from lac 'milk' for its milky sap, and it went through the same -ct- changes: lattuga, lechuga, laitue.
A doublet: the popular form laguna kept the watery sense (the Venetian lagoon), the learned lacuna the abstract 'gap'.

en: Laecania, a woman mocked by Martial

note: Compounds weaken ae to ī: collīdere 'strike together', ēlīdere 'strike out' — hence English collision and elision.
Italian kept it in everyday use (lieto fine 'happy ending'). Applied to fields it means 'thriving', the sense Vergil opens the Georgics with.

ex.en: What makes the crops rich… (Vergil, Georgics 1.1)

note: 'Left' was a taboo-prone word everywhere: Latin had laevus and sinister, and the Romance languages kept neither, except Italian sinistro.
English lambent 'flickering softly' comes from flames that lick.
Portuguese drops a single -n- between vowels and nasalises the vowel: lāna → lã, as manus → mão.
lāna 'wool' + gerō 'carry'. Phaedrus' lāniger is the lamb facing the wolf.

en: Laocoon, Trojan priest killed with his sons by two sea-serpents
note: The marble Laocoön group in the Vatican, found in Rome in 1506, shows his death as Vergil tells it.
Everyday 'stone' in all five languages is the Greek loan petra; lapis lives on only in learned words and in lapis lazuli.
A hunter's noose became a shoelace (fr. lacet, en. lace) and, via Mexican Spanish, the cowboy's lasso.
A notorious false friend: Spanish largo means 'long', Italian largo 'wide', and neither means 'large' — while the Latin meant 'generous'.
Linnaeus called the grub a larva because it 'masks' the form of the adult insect.
English alas is Old French a las '(I am) weary'; French hélas is the same cry with hé.
Same root as Greek λανθάνω 'escape notice' and λήθη 'forgetting'; ἀλήθεια 'truth' is literally 'un-hiddenness'.
The inherited form is ladino, with -t- voiced to -d-: in medieval Spain it meant 'speaking Romance', later 'Judaeo-Spanish' and 'crafty'; in the Dolomites it names Ladin.
Italian Lazio shows -ti- before a vowel becoming z, as palātium → palazzo, pretium → prezzo.
Contracted from lavātrīna, a place for washing (lavāre).
Originally a hired soldier, then a brigand. The -t- is voiced in ladro, ladrón, ladrão; the two thieves crucified with Christ are les deux larrons.
Spanish ladrar 'bark' and ladrón 'thief' look related but come from lātrāre and latrō, which differ in vowel length.
Romance replaced it with largus 'generous' or with amplus — Spanish ancho shows -mpl- → -nch-.
Short a, neuter, genitive lateris — unlike lātus 'wide'. French côté comes from costa 'rib', as does English coast.
French louer 'praise' (laudāre) and louer 'rent' (locāre) have fallen together into one form.
Feminine despite -us, like most tree names (pīnus, fāgus, ulmus).
Italian students graduate cum laude and their marks are 'trenta e lode', thirty with praise.

en: of Lavinium, Lavinian (Lavinium: the town Aeneas founded in Latium)
note: Legend says Aeneas named the town after his Latin wife Lavinia.
Also lavātum in the supine. Romanian spăla is lavāre with two prefixes stacked on; English lavatory was at first a washbasin.
The -ct- series again: letto, lecho, lit, leito. In Spanish lecho is literary — the everyday bed is cama.
A doublet in every western language: learned legal beside popular loyal — the loyal man keeps the law of his oath.
The participle of lēgāre 'send with a commission'; Caesar's lēgātī commanded legions in his name.
From legō 'choose' — a levy of picked men. The Spanish city of León grew out of the camp of Legiō VII Gemina.
The root sense is 'gather' (col-lect, se-lect); reading is gathering letters with the eye. The -g- vanished in es. leer, fr. lire, pt. ler.
Spanish legumbre shows the -m'n- → -mbr- of hombre (hominem) and nombre (nōmen).
Festīnā lentē was Augustus' motto; the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius took it up with his dolphin-and-anchor device.
Romanian leu is also the currency, named after the Dutch 'lion thaler' once common in the Balkans.
All the Romance forms come from the accusative leporem; Italian and Spanish made the hare feminine (la lepre, la liebre).

en: Lesbia, Catullus' name for the woman he loved
note: A pseudonym, 'woman of Lesbos', honouring Sappho; Apuleius says her real name was Clodia, which has the same metrical shape.

en: Leuconoe, the woman addressed in Horace's carpe diem ode

note: Short e; not to be confused with lēvis 'smooth'. French léger is built on a Late Latin extension *leviārius.
From 'lift' to 'carry' to 'take': Spanish llevar and Portuguese levar mean 'carry', Romanian lua simply 'take'.

ex.en: The law is harsh, but it is the law.

note: Diminutive of liber 'book'; a 'little book' of accusations became the legal libel.
From libet 'it pleases'; the root is the same as in English love and lief ('I'd as lief').

ex.t: Libenter hominēs id quod volunt crēdunt.
ex.en: People gladly believe what they want to. (Caesar, Gallic War 3.18)

note: Long ī, unlike liber 'book', and it keeps its -e- (lībera) where liber drops it (librī).
Originally the inner bark of a tree, an early writing material. French le livre 'book' is a different word from la livre 'pound' (lībra).
The artēs līberālēs were the studies fit for a free man — hence the 'liberal arts'.
Literally 'the free ones': the freeborn children of a household, as opposed to its slaves.
French livrer drifted from 'set free' to 'hand over, deliver goods'; English deliver comes from its compound délivrer 'set free'.
The suffix -tās, -tātis gives it. -tà, es. -dad, fr. -té, pt. -dade, ro. -tate, en. -ty: cīvitās → città, ciudad, cité, cidade, cetate, city.
Impersonal, with the dative: mihi libet 'I feel like it'. Also libitum est in the perfect.
From libet 'it pleases'; Freud's term was taken straight from Latin.
The £ sign and the abbreviation lb are both lībra; the Italian lira was the 'pound' too.

en: a Liburnian galley, light fast warship
note: Named after the Liburni of the Dalmatian coast, whose swift pirate ships the Roman navy copied (also called Liburna).
Impersonal, with the dative: mihi licet īre 'I may go'. Perfect also licitum est.

ex.t: Quod licet Iovī, nōn licet bovī.
ex.en: What is allowed to Jupiter is not allowed to an ox.

note: Romanian turns -gn- into -mn-: lignum → lemn, signum → semn, cognātus → cumnat.
Spanish has a doublet: popular liar 'tie' and learned ligar 'bind; flirt'. A league is literally a 'binding' together.
The French fleur-de-lis and the Florentine giglio are the same flower; Spanish and Portuguese dissimilated l–l to l–r.
To eliminate (ē + līmen) is literally to put someone out over the threshold; subliminal is 'below the threshold' of awareness.
The Roman līmes was the fortified frontier line along the Rhine and Danube.
An adjective of līnum 'flax' used as a noun: a line was first a linen thread.
Old Latin dingua is the cognate of English tongue. In Romanian the labiovelar gu became b, as qu became p: lingua → limbă, aqua → apă, equa → iapă.
A little linen cloth became the Italian and Portuguese bedsheet but the French shroud.
Romanian in has lost its initial l-; English lingerie is French for 'linen goods'.

en: Linus, man's name; a friend addressed by Martial

note: Romans strained wine through a cloth or colander to clear it; Horace's vīna liquēs means 'get the wine ready'.
Every modern language narrowed it to drink: sweet liqueur in Romance, strong liquor in English. Not to be confused with the deponent verb liquor 'melt, flow'.
Old Latin stlīs. Its verb lītigāre 'go to law' gives litigate and litigious.
Singular: one letter of the alphabet. Plural litterae: a letter you send, or 'letters', learning.
Venetian lido 'beach' (the Lido of Venice) is the popular descendant; the other languages use the learned adjective lītorālis.
Livid first meant 'the colour of a bruise'; the sense 'furious' is an English development.
The plural is usually neuter loca 'places' (masc. locī = passages in a book). Spanish luego 'then' is the ablative locō 'on the spot'.
One Latin word for two leggy, armoured creatures: Romanian kept the insect, Italian and French the crustacean, Spanish both.
Spanish replaced it with largo, which is why es. largo 'long' and it. largo 'wide' are false friends.

ex.en: Art is long, life is short.

note: Replaced everywhere: Iberian hablar/falar come from fābulārī 'chat', Italian and French from Church Latin parabolāre 'speak in parables'.

en: Lucilius, friend of Seneca and addressee of his Moral Letters

note: The Romans explained it from lūx: a boy born at first light. Abbreviated L.
Romanian lucru 'thing, work' is the popular descendant (and lucra 'to work'): what one earns became what one does.
A clean -ct- set: lottare, luchar, lutter, lutar, lupta (Romanian ct → pt). Reluctant is 'struggling against'.
All five languages replaced it with iocārī 'to joke'. An illusion is a 'mocking', an allusion 'playing at' something.
Lūdus was also the elementary school and the gladiator school — training as 'play'.
Romanian lume means 'world', a shift modelled on Slavic, where one word meant both 'light' and 'world'; in Spanish and Portuguese the light became 'fire'.
Monday is lūnae diēs 'the moon's day': lunedì, lunes, lundi, luni. Portuguese lua has lost its -n-, as usual between vowels.
The wolf that suckled Romulus and Remus; the slang sense gave lupānar 'brothel'.
The p where native Latin would have qu suggests a loan from a Sabine-type dialect; Greek λύκος and English wolf are its cousins.

ex.en: Man is a wolf to man. (Plautus, Asinaria 495)

note: Prīmā lūce 'at first light' = at dawn. Lūcifer 'light-bringer' was the morning star long before it named Satan.
A false friend: in Romance it became 'lust', one of the seven deadly sins, while English luxury kept the sense of extravagance.

en: Lydia, kingdom in western Asia Minor
note: The kingdom of Croesus, where the first coins were struck. As a woman's name it means 'the Lydian girl'.
Spelt with y and ph through association with Greek νύμφη 'nymph'.
Borrowed from Doric Greek μαχανά, hence the ā. Italian macchina and Romanian mașină both also mean 'car'.
From māchina 'device': to engineer something, usually something bad.
The 'spots' of a net were its meshes: French maille gave chain mail. Italian macchia also means Mediterranean scrub — Corsican maquis, which named the wartime Resistance.
Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian build comparatives with magis (más grande, mais grande, mai mare); Italian and French use plūs (più grande, plus grand). French mais 'but' grew out of 'rather'.
Built on magis 'more' — the 'greater' man — just as minister is built on minus. Master, mister, maestro and maître are all this word.

ex.en: master of the horse (the dictator's deputy)

note: Really two words, magnō opere 'with great effort' — the same opus as in magnum opus.
Spoken Latin preferred grandis, which won everywhere; magnus survives in names — Charlemagne (Carolus Magnus), Magna Carta, Magna Graecia.

ex.en: Great is truth, and it prevails.

note: Crīmen laesae māiestātis, 'the crime of injured majesty' of the Roman people, survives in French lèse-majesté.
Comparative of magnus. The mōs māiōrum, 'the custom of the ancestors', was the unwritten constitution of Rome.
Properly an adjective agreeing with mēnsis: mēnse Māiō 'in the month of May'.
Romanian blestema 'curse' is blasphēmāre, the same word as English blame and blaspheme.
French malin softened from 'wicked' to 'clever, sharp'; le Malin is still the Devil.
Contracted from magis volō 'I want more': mālō, māvīs, māvult, mālumus, māvultis, mālunt.

ex.en: I would rather die than be dishonoured.

note: Short a; mālum with long ā is 'apple' — a pun medieval writers loved when retelling Eden.
Spanish manzana and Portuguese maçã are the 'Matian apple', a variety named after one Matius; French pomme is simply pōmum 'fruit'.
Italian cattivo is captīvus, from Christian captīvus diabolī 'the devil's prisoner'; French mauvais still hides malus inside *malifātius.
French mauve, with l vocalised before a consonant, gave English its colour word.
A nursery word found all over Europe. Linnaeus named the mammals after the breast.
Maundy Thursday takes its name from the antiphon Mandātum novum dō vōbīs 'A new commandment I give you' (John 13:34).
From 'entrust' to 'send': it. mandare, es./pt. mandar. French demander weakened from 'entrust, require' to plain 'ask' — a false friend of English demand.
A comic 'chomp' word in early Latin that ousted classical edere in French and Romanian; Spanish and Portuguese chose comedere 'eat up' instead.
'In the morning' became 'tomorrow': it. domani, fr. demain, ro. mâine — and Spanish mañana means both.
The simple verb died; the compound remanēre lives on in it. rimanere and ro. rămâne, and the noun mānsiō became French maison.
From manus 'hand'. The French call the English Channel la Manche, 'the Sleeve'.
A night's halt on a Roman road became the French house, maison, and the Spanish inn, mesón.
Feminine despite -us, and it stayed feminine: la mano, la main, a mão, mâna.
The medieval mappa mundī 'cloth of the world' gave map; French turned m- into n- in nappe, whence English napkin.
Probably 'belonging to Mars'. Abbreviated M., as in M. Tullius Cicero.
A neuter i-stem: ablative marī, plural maria. Gender wavers in Romance: il mare, el mar (but la mar to sailors), la mer.
The daisy is the 'pearl' flower in Romance; margarine was named for the pearly sheen of the acid it was first made from.
From Hebrew Miryam through Greek. Church Latin stresses the ī (Ma-RĪ-a), and so do Spanish María and Italian Maria.
Spanish mármol and French marbre dissimilated the repeated r; poets call the calm, gleaming sea marmor.
Tuesday is Mārtis diēs 'Mars's day': martedì, martes, mardi, marți. Poets use Mārs for battle itself.
The old Roman year began in March, which is why September to December are the 'seventh' to 'tenth' months.
Greek μάρτυς meant simply 'witness'; Christians applied it to those who bore witness with their death.
The Romance words come from the diminutive masculus; Spanish macho went on into English with its swagger.
Portuguese mãe lost the -d- (mātrem → madre → mãe); Romanian replaced it with the nursery word mamma.
From māter: timber is the 'mother-stuff' of the tree. The popular forms mean 'wood' — Madeira is 'the wooded island'.
Literally the state of being a māter. Everyday words come from casa 'house' (setting up house) or from marītāre.

en: the Marne, river of northern Gaul
note: A Gaulish name, 'the Mother' (the river goddess), which happens to look like Latin mātrōna; French Marne is its worn-down descendant.
In Caesar it nearly always means 'hasten' — to act while the moment is ripe.
French mûr shows how far French could wear a word down: mātūrum → meür → mûr.
Named after Mātūta, goddess of dawn; it. mattino and fr. matin are 'the morning (hour)'.
In dialogue maximē is a strong 'yes, certainly'.
Superlative of magnus. A maxim is a maxima sententia, a 'principal saying'.

ex.en: chief priest (a title now held by the Pope)

note: Not originally a sneer: Horace's aurea mediocritās is the 'golden mean'.
Classical Latin used it for 'inland', the middle of the land; only in late antiquity did it name the sea 'amid the lands'.
Like summus it usually means 'the middle of': in mediā urbe 'in the middle of the city'. French midi is medius diēs.

ex.en: into the middle of things (Horace, Ars Poetica 148)

note: Spanish meollo and Portuguese miolo moved from bone marrow to 'the core' of a matter or of a loaf.
Romanian miere shows a single -l- between vowels turning into -r-, as sōlem → soare, gula → gură.
Comparative of bonus. The -li- became a palatal l, spelt differently in each language: it. gl, es. j (now [x]), fr. ill, pt. lh.
Perfect in form, present in meaning ('I have it in mind'); the imperative is mementō.
Gen. pl. memorum. Vergil's Juno nurses a memor īra, an anger that does not forget.

ex.en: Muse, tell me the reasons (Vergil, Aeneid 1.8)

note: Its ablative became the adverb suffix: clārā mente 'with a clear mind' → chiaramente, claramente, clairement.

ex.en: a healthy mind in a healthy body (Juvenal 10.356)

note: Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian kept it (the n dropped before s already in Latin speech); Italian and French chose tabula 'plank'.
Moon and month share one root in Latin, Greek and English alike; Romanian simply uses lună 'moon' for 'month'.
From mētior 'measure'. Spanish and Portuguese mesura narrowed to 'moderation, courtesy'; their 'measure' is medida.
Probably from mēns — lying as 'devising in the mind'. All five languages turned the deponent into an ordinary active verb.
Romanian negustor 'merchant' is negōtiātor, from negōtium 'business'.
French marché shows ca- → cha- (cf. cantāre → chanter). Romanian piață is the town square, like Italian piazza.
From mercēs 'pay'.
Pay became favour: French merci 'thanks', and Spanish vuestra merced 'your grace' was worn down to usted 'you'.
Wednesday is Mercuriī diēs: mercoledì, miércoles, mercredi, miercuri — Portuguese alone uses quarta-feira.
Also deponent mereor. Stipendia merēre 'to earn pay' means 'to serve in the army'.
From an older *medī diē 'at mid-day'. English a.m. and p.m. are ante and post merīdiem.
Portuguese melro has swapped l and r; Romanian keeps the feminine of the Latin.
Merum (neuter) was neat wine — Romans normally drank theirs mixed with water.
The conical post at each end of the chariot track; in Italian, Spanish and Portuguese meta is now any goal or finish.
Greek μέταλλον was first a 'mine'. A medal is a metal disc, through Italian medaglia.
Spanish miedo and Portuguese medo are its only survivors; Italian and French took pavor instead (paura, peur).
Masculine vocative mī: mī fīlī 'my son'. French mon and Spanish mi continue unstressed forms used before a noun.
'Not a crumb' became a negative: Italian non è mica vero 'it isn't at all true', like French ne … pas 'not a step'.
The Romance 'soldier' is the man paid in solidī, the gold coins of the late empire.

ex.en: The Braggart Soldier (a comedy by Plautus)

note: The locative mīlitiae 'on campaign' pairs with domī 'at home': domī mīlitiaeque 'in peace and war'.
When maize arrived from America, Portuguese gave it the old grain's name, milho.
Indeclinable in the singular, but the plural mīlia is a noun: tria mīlia mīlitum 'three thousand (of) soldiers'. The Roman mile was mīlle passūs, a thousand paces.
Late Latin mināre 'drive (cattle) with shouts' gave French mener 'lead' and Romanian mâna 'drive'.

en: Minerva, goddess of wisdom and crafts
note: Identified with Greek Athena; as a common noun her name stands for natural talent.

en: not at all, by no means
note: In dialogue minimē is a firm 'no', as maximē is a firm 'yes'.
Built on minus as magister is on magis: the 'lesser' man, a servant. Government ministers are, in theory, still servants.
The popular forms mean a trade (it. mestiere, fr. métier) or a need: Spanish es menester 'it is necessary'.
Comparative of parvus. French moindre continues the nominative minor itself, not minōrem — a rare surviving nominative.
After death he became a judge of the dead; Dante's Minosse sorts the damned at the entrance to Hell (Inferno 5). Greek acc. Mīnōa.
Also the neuter of minor. It still subtracts when telling the time: las tres menos cuarto, trois heures moins le quart.
Participle of minuō. A minute is a pars minūta prīma, the 'first small part' of an hour; a menu is a detailed list.
The neuter plural mīrābilia 'wonderful things' became a feminine noun: meraviglia, maravilla, merveille.
Spanish milagro and Portuguese milagre swapped the r and the l (*miraglo → milagro).
From gazing in wonder to plain looking: Spanish mirar is the everyday 'look at'. A mirror is what you gaze into.
The adjective itself left no popular descendants; its family lives on through mīrārī, mīrābilia and mīrāculum.
Wine was always mixed with water, so Italian mescere means 'pour'; Portuguese mexer went from 'stir' to 'move, touch' (não mexe! 'don't touch!').

en: Misenum, cape and naval base on the Bay of Naples
note: Named after Misenus, Aeneas' trumpeter, buried on the headland. The elder Pliny commanded the fleet stationed here in AD 79.
Italian and Spanish miseria also means 'a pittance', a miserable sum.

rel.g: ledge seat in a choir stall

note: Literally having a heart (cor) for the wretched (miser).
Named after the dismissal at the end of the service; Christmas is 'Christ's Mass'.
From 'let go' to 'put': it. mettere, fr. mettre. Romanian alone kept 'send', through the compound trānsmittere.
