Contracted from *movibilis. Furniture is literally 'movables', as opposed to land and buildings.
Late Latin modernus 'of the present day' was built on modo 'just now'.
Hoc modō 'in this way', quem ad modum 'how'. The original sense is 'measure', as in moderate and modest.

ex.en: There is a due measure in things. (Horace, Satires 1.1.106)

note: Related to mūnīre 'fortify' and to mūrus (Old Latin moerus); English munition and ammunition share the root.

ex.en: the walls of lofty Rome (Vergil, Aeneid 1.7)

note: A molar is a grinding tooth (Spanish muela). Sprinkling mola salsa on a victim was immolāre — hence immolate.

ex.t: Tantae mōlis erat Rōmānam condere gentem.
ex.en: So great a task it was to found the Roman race. (Vergil, Aeneid 1.33)

note: Built on mola 'millstone'; the Moulin Rouge is the 'red mill'.
French mou keeps an older form mol before a vowel (un mol oreiller); a mollusc is a 'soft' animal.

en: movement; weight that turns the scale
note: Contracted from *movimentum. The small weight that tips a balance gave both 'importance' (momentous) and a moment of time.
Greek μοναχός 'solitary'. Munich (München) is named after its monks.
Worn down early in popular use: Portuguese mosteiro, Romanian mănăstire, English minster (Westminster).
A monumentum is 'something that reminds'; Juno Monēta, 'the Warner', gave her name to the mint in her temple — and so to money.
Coins were struck at the temple of Juno Monēta on the Capitol; English has the word twice, as mint and money.
Spanish montaña and French montagne come from a derivative *montānea; Spanish monte often means wild scrubland.

ex.en: The mountains will labour, and a ridiculous mouse will be born. (Horace, Ars Poetica 139)

note: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese dropped the n, French the s. A French montre 'watch' is what shows the time.
From moneō: a portent 'warns' of the gods' will.
Late Latin montānea (terra) 'mountainous land' replaced mōns as the word for 'mountain' in the west: montagna, montaña, montagne, English mountain.

ex.en: I have raised a monument more lasting than bronze. (Horace, Odes 3.30)

note: To linger is to dwell: French demeurer 'live, remain' comes from dēmorārī 'delay', while Spanish demora is still 'a delay'.
Remorse is conscience 'biting back' (re-mordēre); a morsel is a 'little bite'.
Future participle moritūrus 'about to die'. Greek βροτός (from *mrotós) and English murder share the root.

ex.en: Hail, emperor, those about to die salute you. (Suetonius, Claudius 21)

note: Lingering became living: French demeurer 'dwell' and Italian dimora 'abode' both come from the compound dēmorārī.
Short o diphthongised under stress: Spanish muerte, Romanian moarte.

ex.en: Death is certain, its hour uncertain.

note: The perfect participle of morior, used as an adjective.

ex.en: Of the dead, say nothing but good.

note: The neuter plural mōra was taken as a feminine singular, as folia gave foglia and feuille.
French mœurs is the inherited plural mōrēs. The adjective mōrālis was coined by Cicero to translate Greek ἠθικός.

ex.en: Oh the times, oh the customs! (Cicero, Against Catiline 1.2)

note: An emotion is what 'moves you out' (ē-movēre); French émouvoir is still 'to move' someone's feelings.
Replaced everywhere, by words meaning 'at hand', 'ready', 'on the spot' or 'running'.
English milk and Greek ἀμέλγω share the root; an emulsion is literally a 'milking out'.
Italian moglie continues the nominative mulier — a rare surviving nominative — while Spanish mujer and Portuguese mulher continue mulierem.
Portuguese multidão 'crowd' is everyday speech, with -tūdinem → -dão as in solidão.
The neuter of multus. French alone replaced it (beaucoup); Old French moult lives on only as a jocular archaism.
cite: multum, plūs, plūrimum; abl. multō 'by much' (+ comparative)
forms: plūs, plūrimum; abl. multō 'by much' (+ comparative)

note: -lt- went the way of -ct-: Spanish ch (multum → mucho, cultellum → cuchillo), Portuguese it (muito).

ex.en: not many things, but much (after Pliny the Younger)

note: Modelled on Greek κόσμος, which meant both 'adornment, order' and 'world'; the adjective mundus means 'neat, clean'.

ex.en: Thus passes the glory of the world.

note: From mūnus + capere: a town whose people 'took on the duties' of Roman citizenship.
Viam mūnīre is 'to build a road' — Roman roads were engineered like fortifications.
Perfect participle of mūniō used as an adjective; Cicero's mūnītissimus locus is the heavily guarded temple where the Senate met.
Gladiatorial games were a mūnus — a duty owed to the dead and a gift to the people. Commūnis is 'sharing the duties'.
Italian keeps a collective plural le mura for city walls, beside i muri for the walls of a house.
A rippling muscle looked like a little mouse (mūsculus) under the skin; Greek μῦς also means both 'mouse' and 'muscle'.

ex.en: Muse, tell me the causes. (Vergil, Aeneid 1.8)

note: A mosquito is a Spanish 'little fly'; French mouche is also a beauty spot.
Diminutive of mūs. Romanian mușchi is the inherited form; the mussel got the name from its shape.
Superstitious fear of the weasel led each language to replace its name with a flattering nickname: 'little lady', 'little godmother', 'little beauty', 'little bride'.

rel.n: via French; once mixed with must

note: Changing your address became the main sense in Spanish mudarse and Romanian a se muta.

ex.t: Tempora mūtantur, nōs et mūtāmur in illīs.
ex.en: Times change, and we change with them.

note: From mūtāre 'exchange': mūtuum dare 'to lend', mūtuum sūmere 'to borrow'.
Stands first in its clause and introduces an explanation; namque is a slightly stronger form.

rel.n: second part from Old English nǣp

note: An early loan into Old English: the 'nip' of turnip (and Scots neep) is nāpus.

ex.t: Mūtātō nōmine dē tē fābula nārrātur.
ex.en: Change the name, and the story is about you. (Horace, Satires 1.1.69)

note: Old Latin gnāscor — the g survives in cognātus 'kinsman'. Romance turned the deponent into an ordinary active verb.

ex.en: A poet is born, not made.

note: Spanish and Portuguese nariz come from nāris 'nostril' rather than nāsus. Ovid's family name Nāsō means 'Big-nose'.
Diēs nātālis 'birthday' became the Birthday of Christ: it. Natale, fr. Noël, pt. Natal (hence the Brazilian city).
From nāscor: a nation is a people of common birth.
Spanish Navidad 'Christmas' is nātīvitātem worn down in popular speech; the other languages chose nātālis.
French lost its descendant of natāre and now 'swims' with nager, from nāvigāre 'sail'.
From nāscor: a thing's nature is what it is 'born' as.
Perfect participle of nāscor. Age is 'born so many years': the accusative of extent with nātus.
nāvis + frangere: the 'breaking of a ship'.
From Greek ναῦς 'ship': nausea is literally seasickness.
A masculine of the first declension, like agricola and poēta: nauta bonus 'a good sailor'.
Its popular French descendant is nager, which now means 'swim'.

ex.t: Nāvigāre necesse est, vīvere nōn est necesse.
ex.en: To sail is necessary; to live is not. (Pompey, as reported by Plutarch)

note: The nave of a church is its 'ship'. Nāvis longa 'long ship' is a warship, nāvis onerāria a merchantman.
Attached to the first, emphasised word of the question; it expects no particular answer (compare nōnne and num).

en: (adv.) not, in prohibitions; nē … quidem 'not even'
note: The negative of ut in purpose clauses. After verbs of fearing it means 'that': timeō nē veniat 'I am afraid he will come'.
Greek νεφέλη 'cloud' and German Nebel 'fog' are cousins.
The short form of neque. Nec … nec 'neither … nor' lives on as né … né, ni … ni, nem … nem, nici … nici.
Found only as a neuter, almost always with esse or habēre: necesse est 'it is necessary', with an infinitive or a subjunctive.

ex.t: Necesse est multōs timeat quem multī timent.
ex.en: He whom many fear must fear many. (Publilius Syrus)

note: Late Latin narrowed necāre to 'kill by drowning', so its Romance descendants mean 'drown': fr. noyer, ro. îneca, it. annegare.
The opposite of fās 'what divine law allows'; both are indeclinable. Diēs nefāstī were days on which no public business could be done.
nec + legō 'not pick up' — the opposite of dīligō 'pick out, value', whence diligent.
The normal way to report a negative statement: negat sē ventūrum esse 'he says he will not come'.
nec + ōtium 'not-leisure': business is the absence of leisure. Italian negozio has come down to 'shop'.
From *ne-hemō 'not a man' (homō); it borrows its genitive and ablative from nūllus.

ex.en: No one provokes me with impunity. (motto of Scotland)

cite: nēmō, gen. nūllīus, dat. nēminī, acc. nēminem, abl. nūllō
forms: gen. nūllīus, dat. nēminī, acc. nēminem, abl. nūllō

note: Classical 'grandson', later also 'nephew'. Nepotism is favouring one's 'nephews' — a polite word for popes' sons.
An Italic water god identified with Greek Poseidon.
Latin avoids et nōn: 'and not' is normally one word, neque — and 'and no one' is neque quisquam.
Also spelled nēquicquam; from nē + quīquam 'not anything'.
In Latin a sinew, not a nerve: a man's nervī are his muscle and vigour — the sense in English 'nerve' (courage).
English nice first meant 'foolish', from nescius 'ignorant', like Spanish necio. Nesciō quis 'I-know-not-who' simply means 'someone'.
ne + uter 'not either': the neuter gender is neither masculine nor feminine. Genitive neutrīus, dative neutrī.
Death by violence, as opposed to natural mors; hence necō 'kill'. A Roman father held vītae necisque potestās, 'power of life and death'.
Nīdus and nest both go back to *ni-sd-o-, 'where (the bird) sits down'.
Latin had 'glossy black' niger and 'dull black' āter; only niger survived. Italian nero has lost the g.
Short form nīl. Romance built its 'nothing' from positive words used with a negative: French rien is rem 'a thing'.

ex.en: Nothing in excess. (Terence, after Greek μηδὲν ἄγαν)
Unless the Lord (builds the house), it is in vain. (Psalm 127; motto of Edinburgh)

note: French net 'clean, clear' gave English twice: neat, and net as in net weight.
Perfect participle also nīxus. Not to be confused with nitor, nitōris (short i) 'brightness'.

ex.en: we strive for what is forbidden (Ovid)

note: Snow and nix are cousins: Latin lost an initial s-, and the old labiovelar shows up as the v of nivis.
Old Latin gnōbilis 'knowable', from (g)nōscō: the nobilēs were the 'well-known' families whose ancestors had held office.
Takes the dative: nēminī nocet 'he harms no one'. The innocent are those who 'do no harm' (in-nocēns).
Spanish nudo 'knot' (nōdus) and desnudo 'naked' (nūdus) look alike but come from different words.
Contracted from ne + volō. Nōlī / nōlīte with an infinitive is the usual negative command: nōlī timēre 'don't be afraid'.
Spanish nombre shows -m'n- → -mbr- (hominem → hombre, famine → hambre). In Gāius Iūlius Caesar, Iūlius is the nōmen, the clan name.

en: of Nomentum (a town north-east of Rome), Nomentan
note: The Via Nōmentāna that led there is still one of the main roads out of Rome.
From *ne oinom 'not one'. French split it into stressed non 'no' and unstressed ne, now usually propped up by pas.

ex.en: I shall not wholly die. (Horace, Odes 3.30)

note: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese remodelled it on novem 'nine'; the French of France counts in twenties instead.
nōn + -ne. Contrast num, which expects the answer 'no'.
Litotes in a single word: 'not none' = 'some'.
'Not never' = sometimes; compare numquam nōn 'never not' = always.
Noon was the nōna hōra, the ninth hour after sunrise (about 3 p.m.); when the church office said then moved earlier, the word moved to midday.
Normal first meant 'at right angles' — made with the set-square; geometry still calls a perpendicular a normal.
Spanish nosotros is 'we others', an emphatic form that became the normal one.
cite: nōs, gen. nostrum / nostrī, dat./abl. nōbīs

note: Old Latin gnōscō, cognate with Greek γιγνώσκω and English know. The perfect nōvī 'I have learned' means 'I know'.
A nostrum was a quack's 'our own' secret remedy.
From nota 'shorthand sign': the first notāriī were stenographers.
'Knowledge' became 'news' in Italian, Spanish and Portuguese — false friends of English notice.
The participle of nōscō; Romance uses the participle of the compound cognōscere instead.

rel.g: new, young; first of the season

note: French nouveau comes from this diminutive, not from novus; a novel was an Italian novella, a 'new story'.
French neuf is both 'nine' (novem) and 'new' (novum): sound change made them homophones.
A novus homō was the first of his family to reach the consulship — as Cicero was.

ex.en: A new order of the ages (on the Great Seal of the USA)

note: The -ct- series in full: notte, noche, nuit, noite, noapte. Nocte 'by night' is an ablative of time.

ex.en: One everlasting night must be slept. (Catullus 5.6)

note: French nuance, a shade of colour, comes from nue 'cloud' — the shifting tints of clouds.
Said of the bride, who 'veils herself' for the groom: nūbere alicui. The man dūcit uxōrem, 'leads home a wife'.
ne + ūllus 'not any'. Like ūnus, sōlus and tōtus it has genitive nūllīus, dative nūllī.

ex.en: No day without a line. (after Pliny the Elder on Apelles)

note: Opposite of nōnne, which expects 'yes'. In indirect questions it simply means 'whether'.

ex.en: You don't believe that, do you?

note: From nuere 'to nod': divine power is the 'nod' of a god, which sets things in motion.
French nombre 'number' is a false friend of Spanish nombre 'name' (nōmen).

en: Numitor, king of Alba Longa, grandfather of Romulus and Remus

note: Spanish and Portuguese nunca are inherited; Italian mai and French jamais are built on magis 'more'.
Replaced everywhere, mostly by phrases built on hōra 'hour'.

ex.en: Now is the time to drink. (Horace, Odes 1.37)

note: From nūbō. Plural only in Latin, and still plural in Italian le nozze and French les noces.
A fourth-declension feminine like manus; the Romance forms moved over to the -a class (nuora, nuera, noră).
English nurse is this word worn down through Old French nurice; the nurse was first the woman who fed the baby.
A god's nod was his command: from the same root comes nūmen 'divine will, godhead'.
A nucleus is a 'little nut', a kernel — hence nuclear.

ex.en: Oh the times, oh the customs! (Cicero, Against Catiline 1.2)

note: As a prefix ob- assimilates to the next consonant: occurrō, offerō, oppōnō, ostendō (obs-tendō).

ex.en: but endure with a stubborn mind, hold out (Catullus 8)

note: Mortem obīre 'to go to meet death' gave the noun obitus 'death', hence English obituary.
Participle of ob-edō 'eat away at': one who has 'eaten himself' fat.

en: throw in the way, put before
note: ob + iaciō 'throw': an object is literally 'something thrown in front of' the mind, an objection something thrown in the way.
Portuguese obrigado 'thank you' is literally '(I am) obliged', with the popular change of l to r after a consonant.
Grammarians call reported speech ōrātiō oblīqua and the cases other than the nominative cāsūs oblīquī.
Vulgar Latin rebuilt the deponent from its participle oblītus as *oblītāre, the source of Spanish olvidar, French oublier and Romanian uita.
ob + audiō: to obey is 'to listen towards'. Romanian makes the same leap with asculta, which means both 'listen' and 'obey'.
Spoken Latin dropped the b (oscuro), and Portuguese went further to escuro; French obscur is a learned respelling of Old French oscur.
ob + sedeō: a hostage is 'one who sits (stays) in front' as a pledge. Caesar demands obsidēs from almost every tribe he defeats.
ob + sedeō 'sit before': to obsess was originally to besiege — an obsession is an idea that has laid siege to the mind.
Each language remade the verb on its own word for 'hold': ottenere on tenere, obtener on tener, obter on ter.
Simply ob viam 'towards the road / in the way'.
Originally 'lying in your path' — what you bump into is obvious.
From occidō 'fall towards': an occasion is what 'falls' your way, just as English chance comes from cadentia 'falling'. French d'occasion means 'second-hand'.
Present participle of occidō 'fall': (sōl) occidēns is where the sun goes down, (sōl) oriēns where it rises.
ob + cadō 'fall', with short i. Do not confuse with occīdō (ob + caedō) 'kill', with long ī.
ob + caedō 'strike, cut down'. Italian uccidere and Romanian ucide continue it; Spanish and Portuguese matar and French tuer replaced it.
Participle of occulō 'cover over', related to cēlō 'hide' and, far back, to English hell and hall (places that cover).
ob + capiō 'lay hold of'. 'Busy' is a later sense: French s'occuper de, Spanish estar ocupado.
ob + currō 'run towards'. Italian occorre has drifted to 'it is necessary'.

en: the Ocean (the outer sea encircling the earth)
note: For Greeks and Romans Ōceanus was a river-like sea flowing round the disc of the earth, as opposed to the inner sea, the Mediterranean.
A textbook case of Latin -ct-: Italian tt, Spanish ch, French and Portuguese it, Romanian pt — just as in nocte → notte, noche, nuit, noite, noapte.
The 'eighth' month, because the oldest Roman year began in March; September to December kept their numbers after January and February were put first.
Standard French counts eighty in twenties (quatre-vingts), while Swiss French says huitante.
Spoken Latin said oclus; -cl- then became Italian cchi, Spanish j, French il, Portuguese lh, Romanian chi.
A defective verb with only perfect-system forms: ōdī 'I hate', ōderam 'I hated', ōderō 'I shall hate'.
Spanish olor got its l from the related verb olēre 'to smell' (Spanish oler).
ob + an old verb *fendō 'strike', also hidden in dēfendō 'strike away, ward off'.
Irregular like ferō (obtulī, oblātum); spoken Latin regularized it as *offerīre, the source of offrire and offrir.
From *opificīna, the workplace of an opifex 'craftsman'. French usine is the worn-down popular form; Spanish oficina moved upstairs to mean 'office'.
From *opi-ficium 'work-doing'. Cicero's De Officiis 'On Duties' was the most-read moral handbook of the Renaissance.
Borrowed early from Greek ἔλαιον. In Spain and Portugal the Arabic word won for cooking oil: aceite, azeite.
Built on ollus, the old form of ille: 'at that time' — either past or future.

ex.t: Forsan et haec ōlim meminisse iuvābit.
ex.en: Perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even this. (Vergil, Aeneid 1.203)

en: Mount Olympus, home of the gods
note: Not the same place as Olympia in the Peloponnese, where the Olympic games were held.

ex.en: I believe in God the Father almighty. (Apostles' Creed)

note: Only Italian kept it (ogni, ognuno); elsewhere tōtus 'whole' took over. English bus is the dative plural ending of omnibus 'for everyone'.
Operam dare 'to give effort, to attend to'. It merged in spoken Latin with opera, the plural of opus.
From opera 'work': it became the ordinary Romance word for 'worker' — operaio, obrero, ouvrier.
Romance continues the compound cooperīre; its opposite aperīre 'open' gave aprire, abrir, ouvrir — and English aperture.
Impersonal, used with an accusative and infinitive: mē īre oportet 'I ought to go'.

ex.t: Ēsse oportet ut vīvās, nōn vīvere ut edās.
ex.en: You should eat to live, not live to eat. (Rhetorica ad Herennium)

note: Caesar's word for the fortified hill-towns of Gaul, such as Alesia and Bibracte; archaeologists still call them oppida.

en: place against, set in the way

note: Traditionally ob portum 'towards the harbour', said of a wind that drives you home — opportunity as a fair wind.
ob + premō: in compounds the e of premō weakens to i (opprimō, comprimō, exprimō), but the perfect keeps press-.
ob + pugnō: Caesar's standard verb for storming a town, as opposed to obsidēre 'blockade it'.
The nominative singular is hardly used. Cōpia 'abundance' is co-op-ia and inops means 'without resources'.
Superlative of bonus (bonus, melior, optimus). Leibniz's 'best of all possible worlds' gave French optimisme, then English optimism.
The older sense 'choose' lives on in English opt and option.

en: opus est (+ abl.): there is need of
note: The neuter plural opera 'works' was reanalysed as a feminine singular — Spanish obra, French œuvre, and Italian opera, 'the work' par excellence: a sung drama.

ex.en: This is the task, this the toil. (Vergil, Aeneid 6.129)
who first from the shores of Troy (Vergil, Aeneid 1.1)

note: Christian Latin used it for 'prayer'; in Spanish and Portuguese grammar oración, oração is also 'sentence, clause'.
Orbis terrārum 'the circle of lands' was the Roman way to say 'the world'.

ex.en: to the City and to the world (the papal blessing)

note: Related to ōrdior 'lay the warp, begin a web': first a row, then a rank of soldiers, a social class (ōrdō equester) and finally order in general.

ex.en: A new order of the ages (on the Great Seal of the USA)

note: Present participle of orior 'rise'. To orient a map or a church was originally to turn it towards the east.
A mixed verb: the infinitive orīrī is 4th conjugation, but the present (oritur, orimur) and the imperfect subjunctive (orerētur) usually follow the 3rd.
The first meaning is practical — Caesar 'equips' fleets and armies (nāvēs ōrnāre) — and only later 'decorate'.
Related to ōs 'mouth': the old sense is 'speak solemnly', as in ōrātor and ōrātiō.
A short word that Romance replaced with bucca 'cheek' (bocca, boca, bouche) and Romanian with gula 'throat' (gură). Not to be confused with os, ossis 'bone'.
Spoken Latin regularized it to *ossum, hence osso and hueso; Greek ὀστέον gives English osteo-.
Diminutive of ōs, 'little mouth'. The Romance kiss comes from Catullus' favourite word bāsium; the Romanian one from 'greeting'.
obs + tendō 'stretch out towards'. A later supine ostēnsum also occurs, the source of English ostensible.
Spoken ustium gave Italian uscio, French huis (à huis clos 'behind closed doors', huissier 'usher') and Romanian ușă, the everyday word for 'door'. Ostia was Rome's port at the mouth of the Tiber.
The circumflex of French huître marks a lost s (Old French oistre), the same s still visible in English oyster.
Business was defined as its absence: neg-ōtium 'non-leisure', whence Italian negozio 'shop', Spanish negocio and English negotiate.

en: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso, 43 BC – AD 17), poet of the Metamorphoses
note: Augustus exiled him to Tomis on the Black Sea — today Constanța in Romania, where Ovidiu is still a popular first name.
A very old Indo-European word: Latin ovis, Greek ὄϊς and English ewe all go back to the same source.
Spanish huevo shows the diphthong ue from stressed short o — but the Latin o here is long; spoken Latin had shortened it.

ex.en: from the egg to the apples — from start to finish (Horace)

note: From pāscō 'feed'. The Germanic word that replaced it in Romance (fourrage, foraggio) is itself a distant cognate, like English food and fodder.
Same root as pāx: peace was originally a settlement, an agreement 'fastened' between two sides.
To 'pacify' a creditor was to pay him: pācāre became pagare, pagar, payer and English pay.

en: slave who took a boy to school and supervised him; tutor
note: Literally 'child-leader' (παῖς + ἄγω): a slave, usually Greek, who walked the boy to school, carried his things and watched his manners. Only later did it come to mean a teacher.
A peninsula is a paene īnsula 'almost an island'; the penultimate is the 'almost last'.

en: it causes regret; mē paenitet: I regret
note: Impersonal: the person regretting is accusative, the cause genitive — mē paenitet stultitiae meae 'I regret my folly'.
From pāgus 'country district': first a villager, then a civilian (not a 'soldier of Christ'), finally a non-Christian.
Late Latin pāgēnsis 'of the district' gave French pays and Italian paese 'country'; a paysan was a countryman, hence English peasant.
Augustus lived on the Palatine, and the emperors' residence there turned the hill's name into the word for 'palace' across Europe.
A model for Latin -li- before a vowel: Italian gli, Spanish j, French ill, Portuguese lh, Romanian i (paglia, paja, paille, palha, paie).

ex.t: Pallida Mors aequō pulsat pede pauperum tabernās rēgumque turrīs.
ex.en: Pale Death knocks with equal foot at the huts of the poor and the towers of kings. (Horace, Odes 1.4)

note: The tree seems to be named after the hand, its fronds spread like fingers; the palm branch was the victor's prize.
Spanish párpado, French paupière and Romanian pleoapă hardly look alike, yet all continue this one word.
The by-form palumba became the everyday word for 'dove, pigeon' in Spanish (paloma) and Portuguese (pomba); Romanian porumbel is a diminutive of the same word.
French paludisme and Spanish paludismo 'malaria' are literally 'marsh sickness' — the same idea as Italian mal'aria 'bad air'.
English borrowed it twice: pole early, pale 'stake, fence' later via French — hence 'beyond the pale'. Romanian par shows the change of l to r between vowels.
Its participle passum gave passus 'a pace' (the legs spread) and passim 'spread about, everywhere'.
Genitive plural pānum, not *pānium. A companion (com- + pānis) is someone you break bread with.
A 'piece of cloth' became, via French, an English window pane and a panel.
A Greek nursery word for 'father' that became the title of the bishop of Rome.
Soldiers nicknamed their tents 'butterflies' for their flapping canvas wings — hence pavilion. French has kept both papillon and pavillon.
As a neuter noun pār meant 'a pair' (whence French paire, English pair); a peer is an 'equal'.
The parables of Jesus were his characteristic 'sayings', and parabola displaced verbum as the everyday word for 'word' in Italian, Spanish, French and Portuguese.
From an Old Iranian word for a walled park; the Greek translators of Genesis used it for the Garden of Eden.
Takes the dative: parce mihi 'spare me'. Its noun parsimōnia 'thrift' gives English parsimony.

ex.en: to spare the conquered and subdue the proud (Vergil, Aeneid 6.853)

note: Present participle of pariō 'give birth'. In Italian, Spanish and Portuguese it now means 'relative' — a false friend; 'parents' there are genitori, padres, pais.
In Latin the main sense is 'obey', but Romance kept only the visual one: parere, parecer, paraître, părea all mean 'seem'.
Latin distinguished pariēs (wall of a building) from mūrus (free-standing or city wall); Spanish keeps both pared and muro.
Future participle paritūrus. Its present participle parēns gave 'parent'.
From 'prepare (a defence)' to 'ward off, stop': Spanish and Portuguese parar 'stop', French parer, and para- 'against' in parachute and parasol.

ex.en: If you want peace, prepare for war. (after Vegetius)

note: French partir 'leave' first meant 'divide' (from partīrī), as in à partir de 'starting from'.

ex.t: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs.
ex.en: Gaul as a whole is divided into three parts. (Caesar, Gallic War 1.1)

note: pars + capiō 'part-taker'. Grammarians named the participle (participium) because it 'shares' in both verb and adjective.
Used as the positive of minus, minimē.
One of the few basic adjectives that died everywhere: piccolo, pequeño, petit, pequeno and mic all come from expressive words of the street.
Hebrew pesaḥ 'Passover' reached Latin through Greek. In Church Latin it is also an indeclinable neuter; the Romance forms show the influence of pāscua 'pastures' (the end of the Lenten fast).
Same root as pānis 'bread', pābulum 'fodder' and pāstor 'shepherd' — and English food and fodder.
In Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian the sparrow became the generic word for 'bird'.
From passus, participle of pandō 'spread out': 'scattered about'.
A Christian coinage from patior 'suffer': the Passion is Christ's suffering. 'Strong feeling' came later — feelings were something one 'underwent'.
A Roman pace was a double step (about 1.48 m); a thousand of them made a mile. French ne … pas originally meant 'not (even) a step'.
French kept both case forms: pâtre from nominative pāstor, pasteur from accusative pāstōrem.
pateō + faciō 'make open'; passive patefīō.
Diminutive of patina 'pan'. Spanish paella is named after the pan it is cooked in, not the food.
Royal 'letters patent' were open letters granting a privilege — hence both patent 'obvious' and the inventor's patent.
Grimm's law in action: Latin p corresponds to English f (pater–father, piscis–fish, pēs–foot). The Senate was addressed as patrēs cōnscrīptī.

ex.t: Pater noster, quī es in caelīs
ex.en: Our Father, who art in heaven

note: Present participle of patior: a hospital patient is 'one who suffers'.

ex.t: Quō ūsque tandem abūtēre, Catilīna, patientiā nostrā?
ex.en: How long, Catiline, will you go on abusing our patience? (Cicero)

note: Passive in form, active in meaning. Its participle passus gave passion and passive.
Short for terra patria 'land of the fathers'. Romance relearned it from books; the everyday words are paese, país, pays, țară.

ex.t: Dulce et decōrum est prō patriā morī.
ex.en: It is sweet and fitting to die for one's country. (Horace, Odes 3.2)

en: patrician, member of the old Roman nobility
note: The patricians were the descendants of the patrēs; the first name Patrick is Patricius.
Romance 'World Heritage' is patrimonio mondiale, patrimonio mundial, patrimoine mondial.
Its feminine gives patria (terra), 'the fatherland'.
The Roman patron protected his clients; in Romance he became the boss. English pattern is the same word — the master's model to be copied.
Classical Latin used it mostly in the plural; Romance kept the singular paucus 'little': poco, peu, pouco.

en: (paulō + comparative or ante/post) by a little
note: The name Paulus means 'small'.
A consonant-stem adjective: ablative paupere, genitive plural pauperum. Poor meant 'having little', not destitute (that was egēns).
Late Latin pausāre 'rest, halt' became Italian posare and French poser 'put down', the source of English pose — and it blended with pōnō in compose, expose, suppose.

en: pavement, hard floor (of rammed stone or tiles)
note: From pavīre 'beat, ram down'. In Italian a pavimento is an indoor floor, in British English a pavement is the footpath.
Spanish pavo shifted to the American turkey, so the peacock had to become pavo real, the 'royal pavo'.
Ordinary Italian paura and French peur both come from this word; Spanish and Portuguese say miedo, medo (from metus).
Related to pactum: a pāx was first a settlement fixed between two sides — often imposed on the defeated, as in the Pāx Rōmāna.
Italian Che peccato! and Romanian Păcat! both mean 'What a pity!'
Impeccable is literally 'unable to sin'.
From pectō 'comb'. Each language treated the -ct- in its own way: pettine, peine, peigne, pente, pieptene.
The -ct- pattern again: petto, pecho, peito, piept. French built its word on the stem pector-.
From pecus 'livestock': wealth was once counted in cattle.
English fee (Old English feoh 'cattle, property') is a native cognate. A separate noun pecus, pecudis (f.) means 'a single animal'.
From pēs 'foot'. Late Latin pedō 'walker' gave the chess pawn — the foot soldier of the board.
Comparative of malus (malus, pēior, pessimus). French pire continues the nominative pēior, Italian peggiore the accusative pēiōrem; the adverb pēius gave peggio and pis.
A Greek neuter in -us. Archipelago, Italian arcipelago, was first the Aegean, 'chief sea', and then any sea full of islands.
The everyday word for skin in all five languages; Latin cutis survives only in learned words (cutaneous).
Reduplicated perfect pepulī. Its frequentative pulsāre gave French pousser and English push.

en: the Penates, gods of the household store
note: From penus 'food store, larder'. Aeneas carried the Penates of Troy to Italy.
Intransitive pendeō 'hang' (2nd conj.) beside transitive pendō 'weigh' (3rd): to weigh something, you hung it on a balance.
Before coinage, metal was weighed out: hence 'weigh' → 'pay' (poenās pendere 'pay the penalty'), and compensate, expense, pension.
From penitus 'deep within' — the root also of penātēs, the gods of the inner store-room.
A diminutive of pēnis 'tail' — a painter's 'little tail'. Penicillin was named for the brush-like Penicillium mould.
Related to penes, penus and penetrāre: the idea of the innermost part.
A pen was a quill feather; Italian penna still means both. Spanish and French chose plūma 'down' instead.
A classic doublet: the popular form lost its n (pesare, pesar, peser 'weigh'), while the learned pensare, pensar, penser 'think' kept the idea of weighing things up.
As a prefix it means 'through' or 'thoroughly' (perficiō 'finish', perterreō 'terrify utterly'), and sometimes 'to ruin' (pereō, perdō).
per + capiō 'take thoroughly'. The old sense 'gather in' survives in French percevoir des impôts 'collect taxes'; Portuguese perceber is everyday 'understand'.
per + quatiō 'shake': in compounds qua- weakens to cu- (concutiō, discutiō, percutiō).
per + dō 'give away (to ruin)'. 'Lose' was a secondary sense in Latin (beside āmittō) but became the only one in every Romance language.

ex.t: Quem deus vult perdere, prius dēmentat.
ex.en: Whom God wishes to destroy, he first drives mad. (later proverb)

note: Caesar uses it for carrying a wall or ditch through to the end: mūrum perdūcere.
From per agrum 'across the fields', i.e. from beyond Roman territory. Dissimilation of r…r to l…r produced pellegrino, pèlerin and English pilgrim.
per + annus 'through the year'.

ex.en: I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze. (Horace, Odes 3.30)

note: per + eō 'go through (to the end)'; it serves as a passive of perdō: perdō 'I destroy', pereō 'I am destroyed'.
Participle of perficiō 'carry through': perfect means 'thoroughly done', which is why the perfect tense is the 'completed' one.
Conjugated like ferō: perferō, perferre, pertulī, perlātum.
per + fidēs: going 'through' (i.e. beyond) one's word. Romans liked to accuse the Carthaginians of Pūnica fidēs.
From per + regō 'keep straight on' — hence the perfect perrēxī.
Originally 'a trial', from the root of experior 'try'. Spanish peligro swapped the l and r (metathesis).
Same root as perīculum and experior: the expert is one who has been 'through trials'.
Literally 'let go through'. Takes a dative of the person: mihi permittit 'he allows me'.
per + nex, necis 'violent death'.
Active in meaning, from perōdī 'hate thoroughly': Daedalus Crētēn perōsus, 'sick of Crete'.
Caesar had himself named dictātor perpetuus a few weeks before the Ides of March.

ex.en: We must sleep one never-ending night. (Catullus 5)

note: From sevērus 'strict, serious': to keep thoroughly in earnest.

ex.en: To err is human, to persist (in error) is diabolical. (medieval proverb)

note: The 'Persian apple' reached Rome from the East; Italian pesca, French pêche and English peach all go back to persica.
First an actor's mask (probably from Etruscan), then the part played, then the human being. Grammar's first, second and third 'persons' are the roles in a dialogue.
Takes the dative: mihi persuāsit 'he convinced me'. Related to suāvis 'sweet' — persuasion makes a thing thoroughly agreeable.
What 'reaches to' you belongs to you: Spanish pertenecer, Portuguese pertencer and French appartenir all mean 'belong'.
A French parvenu 'upstart' is 'one who has arrived'.
Latin pēs, Greek πούς and English foot are cognates (p → f by Grimm's law). Romanian picior comes from a diminutive *petiolus.
Superlative of malus (malus, pēior, pessimus).
Perfect also petiī. Spanish and Portuguese pedir 'ask for' continue it; Italian and Romanian ask with quaerere.

ex.en: Ask, and it will be given to you. (Matthew 7:7)

note: A Greek loan that pushed native lapis aside in every Romance language.

ex.t: Tū es Petrus, et super hanc petram aedificābō ecclēsiam meam.
ex.en: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church. (Matthew 16:18)

note: Greek 'Rock', translating Aramaic Kēphā. In French Pierre is both 'Peter' and 'stone', so the Gospel pun survives intact.
Latin wrote Greek φ as ph; Italian, Spanish and Portuguese now write f, French and English keep ph.

ex.en: If you had kept quiet, you would have remained a philosopher. (after Boethius)

note: French peintre continues the nominative pictor, like pâtre from pāstor; Spanish and Portuguese pintor were reshaped on VL *pinctāre.

ex.en: As is painting, so is poetry. (Horace, Ars Poetica 361)

note: The great Roman virtue of Aeneas: duty to gods, father and homeland. Christian Latin added 'compassion', and English took both: piety and pity.
Spanish prenda 'pledge' came to mean 'item of clothing' — clothes being what people most often pawned.
Its soft iron shank bent on impact, so the enemy could not throw it back and was left with a useless shield.
Romanian păr 'hair' shows l turning to r between vowels (compare cer < caelum 'sky').
The nasal of the present (pingō) is missing in the participle pictum; spoken Latin blended the two as *pinctāre, hence pintar.
Also declined in the 2nd declension (pīnī). Like most trees it is feminine despite the ending -us.
An Indian spice that came through Greek; Spanish and Portuguese use pigmenta 'spices' instead.
A masculine first-declension noun. Pompey swept the pirates from the Mediterranean in a lightning campaign in 67 BC.
As with many fruits, the neuter plural pira became a feminine singular (pera, poire, pară).
The Pope's seal is the 'Fisherman's Ring' (ānulus piscātōris), after St Peter. French pêcheur 'fisherman' and pécheur 'sinner' differ only by an accent.
A fishpond (piscis) first, then any pool: now the Romance word for 'swimming pool'.
Spanish distinguishes a fish in the water (pez) from fish on the plate (pescado, 'fished'). English fish is a native cognate.
Vergil's stock epithet for his hero: pius Aenēās.

en: (placet) it seems good, it is resolved
note: Italian mi piace and Romanian îmi place 'I like it' keep the Latin dative construction mihi placet 'it pleases me'.
Causative of placeō: 'make pleased'. Note the long ā, against short a in placeō.
A perfect showcase of initial pl-: piaga, llaga, plaie, chaga. A 'stroke' sent by God became the plague.
Beating the breast in mourning became the ordinary word for 'cry' in Italian (piangere) and Romanian (plânge).
First the sole of the foot — a cutting was pressed into the soil with it. Italian pianta del piede and French plante du pied still mean 'sole'.
Italian piano is 'flat', 'softly', a building's floor and the pianoforte; Portuguese chão has come down to earth as 'ground, floor'.
Greek πλατεῖα (ὁδός) 'broad (street)'. Every Romance town has one: piazza, plaza, place, praça, piață.
English Plato is the Latin nominative; French and Romanian Platon reflect the stem of the other cases (Platōnis, Platōnem).
To explode (ex-plaudere) was to drive an actor off the stage by clapping; plausible first meant 'deserving applause'.

ex.en: Applaud! (the last word of Roman comedies)

note: plēbis scītum 'decision of the plebs', from scīscō 'decree'.
Also plēbēs, plēbēī (5th declension). In the 'Conflict of the Orders' the plebs won its own tribunes and, in time, access to every office.
The model for initial pl-: Italian pi-, Spanish ll-, Portuguese ch-, French and Romanian pl-. Spanish and Portuguese also have the learned pleno.
Plural of the rare plērusque; plēraque (neuter) also 'most things'.
Sailors 'folded' the sails on reaching port: Spanish llegar and Portuguese chegar mean 'arrive' — but Romanian pleca, from the same verb, means 'leave'.
Western Romance weeps with plōrāre (llorar, pleurer, chorar); Italian and Romanian with plangere (piangere, plânge).
Spanish and French write with it: pluma and plume are also 'pen'.
Hence the chemical symbol Pb; a plumber was a worker in lead, the stuff of Roman water pipes.
Superlative of multus (multus, plūs, plūrimus). Plūrimum as adverb: 'very much, most'.
Romance comparatives split: Italian più and French plus (from plūs) against Spanish más, Portuguese mais and Romanian mai (from magis).

ex.en: Further beyond. (motto of Charles V, on the Spanish arms)

cite: plūs, gen. plūris; pl. plūrēs, plūra

note: From pluit 'it rains' (French il pleut, Italian piove). A complete set for initial pl-: pioggia, lluvia, pluie, chuva, ploaie.
From the root of pōtō 'drink'.
From Greek ποινή 'blood-money'. The penalty became the pain: Spanish ¡Qué pena! 'What a pity!', French ça vaut la peine 'it's worth the trouble'.
An early borrowing of Greek Φοῖνιξ 'Phoenician'; the adjective Pūnicus shows the later sound change oe → ū (compare poena → pūniō).
A masculine of the 1st declension, like agricola and nauta. In Greek the poet is a 'maker'.

ex.en: A poet is born, not made.

note: French pouce is also an inch — a thumb's breadth. The gladiatorial 'thumbs down' is a modern guess: Juvenal only says pollice versō 'with thumb turned'.
A favourite of Caesar and Cicero, but Romance kept only prōmittere.
French pompes funèbres 'funeral directors' keeps the old sense of a solemn procession.
Caesar's ally, son-in-law and finally rival, beaten at Pharsalus in 48 BC and murdered in Egypt. The town is a different word: Pompēiī.
Classical 'apple' was mālum; pōmum meant any orchard fruit. French narrowed it to the apple, and Italian pomodoro 'golden apple' is the tomato.
English pound comes from the adverb pondō 'by weight' (lībra pondō 'a pound by weight'); the d of French poids is a scholar's false link with pondus.
French pondre has shrunk to hens laying eggs; French 'put' is mettre (mittere). Perfect posuī, participle positum.
Caesar had a timber bridge built across the Rhine in ten days (Gallic War 4.17).
Literally 'bridge-maker' (pōns + faciō), perhaps from duties at Rome's sacred wooden bridge. Caesar was pontifex maximus; the Popes inherited the title.
The populārēs (the Gracchi, Caesar) worked through the people's assemblies, against the senatorial optimātēs.
Very frequent in Caesar and Livy (agrōs populārī). Its link with populus 'people' is uncertain.
Short o: populus 'people' differs from pōpulus 'poplar'. Spanish pueblo is both 'a people' and 'a village'.

ex.en: the Senate and People of Rome

note: Spoken Latin *ploppus explains the pl- of Romanian plop and Italian pioppo, and the ch- of Spanish chopo and Portuguese choupo.
After 1066 the English peasant kept the pig while his Norman lord ate the pork (French porc). Farrow 'litter of pigs' is a native cognate.
Pliny reports that Nero ate leeks to keep his singing voice clear. French poireau and Portuguese alho-porro look unlike Italian porro, but all continue porrum.
Latin porta was a city gate, while a house door was iānua or ostium; Romance made porta the ordinary door.
Italian, French and Romanian also 'wear' clothes with it (portare, porter, purta); Spanish and Portuguese carry with levāre 'lift'.
From a root meaning 'crossing', shared with porta and English ford. Portus Calē (today Porto) gave its name to Portugal.
Reduplicated perfect poposcī; related to precor 'pray' and postulō 'demand'.
A late philosophical coinage from posse, translating Greek δυνατός; classical Latin said quod fierī potest.
Probably pot- 'master' + sedeō 'sit': to sit on something as its master.
pot- 'able' + sum. Spoken Latin rebuilt the odd infinitive posse as *potēre, the source of potere, poder, pouvoir, putea.

ex.en: They can, because they think they can. (Vergil, Aeneid 5.231)

note: 'After' became 'then, so' in Romance: Italian poi, Spanish pues, French puis, Portuguese pois, Romanian apoi.
post + eā '(after) that'; compare anteā 'before'.
Latin uses the perfect where English has the pluperfect: postquam vēnit 'after he had come'.
Superlative of posterus. The ablative postrēmō is the adverb 'finally'.

en: (+ gen. or acc.) on the day after
note: A contraction of posterō diē.
French postuler means 'apply for a job'; English postulate is something 'demanded' as a starting point.
French puissant comes from a spoken participle *possentem, built on posse.
Romans distinguished potestās (the legal power of an office), imperium (military command) and auctōritās (personal prestige).
French poison is the inherited form of pōtiōnem — a 'drink' turned sinister. English borrowed both poison and potion.

en: get possession of, acquire (+ abl., sometimes gen.)
note: Takes the ablative: urbe potītus est 'he took control of the city'; rērum potīrī 'to seize supreme power'.
Usually potius quam 'rather than'. Comparative of the old adjective potis 'able'.
Participle pōtus 'having drunk, drunk'. Ordinary Latin 'drink' is bibō.
As a prefix prae- 'before, ahead' gives Romance and English pre-: praeficiō, praemittō, praeferō.
prae + habeō 'hold out in front'. Its gerundive praebenda 'things to be supplied' became a clergyman's prebend and English provender.
prae + caput 'head first'. Rain and snow are precipitation because they fall headlong.
prae + capiō: to 'take (the lead) in advance' — hence to teach or order.
From praecipuus 'taken first, special' (prae + capiō).
Not to be confused with praedīcō (3rd conj.) 'foretell', the source of predict. Portuguese pregar 'preach' has a homonym pregar 'nail', from plicāre.
Participle of praeficiō 'put in charge'. A French préfet runs a département; a Brazilian prefeito runs a city.
A prelate is literally 'one preferred', set over others (praelātus).

en: put in command of, put in charge (acc. + dat.)
note: Labiēnum castrīs praeficit 'he puts Labienus in charge of the camp'.
prae + the root of (g)nāscor 'be born': 'before birth'.
A judgement passed in advance. French préjudice, Portuguese prejuízo and Romanian prejudiciu kept the legal sense 'harm, loss' — false friends for English speakers.
Caesar constantly 'sends ahead' cavalry or scouts. In logic a premise is a proposition 'sent before' the conclusion.
Probably prae + emō 'take before (others)': the first pick of the booty.
Participle of praesum 'be at hand'. A present (gift) is something brought into someone's presence.

en: the present moment (in praesentiā: for now)

note: Also praesēpe. The manger of Luke 2 gave Italian presepio and Portuguese presépio, the nativity scene; Spanish pesebre is the inherited everyday word.
From praesideō 'sit in front, preside'. In Italy a school's head is still il preside.
From praesideō 'sit in front, guard' — like a president, who 'sits before' an assembly. A Spanish presidio, once a frontier fort, is now a prison.
Late Latin praestāre 'to provide' became the Romance verb 'to lend': prestare, prestar, prêter.
From the adverb Late Latin made an adjective praestus 'ready', whence Italian presto and French prêt.

en: be in charge of, command (+ dat.)
note: Conjugated like sum; its participle praesēns gave 'present'.
The preterite is the 'gone-by' tense (tempus praeteritum).
*prae-itor 'one who goes in front', once the title of the consuls. The Praetorian Guard began as the escort of the general's tent, the praetōrium.
Italians and Romanians still lunch on it: pranzo, prânz.
Madrid's Prado museum is named after the meadow on which it was built.
Precarious first meant 'held by favour, obtained by entreaty' — and so insecure. Italian prego 'please; you're welcome' is 'I pray'.
Contracted in speech to prēndō, it became the basic 'take' of Italian and French (prendere, prendre). A prison is a 'seizing'.
In compounds e becomes i: opprimō, comprimō, exprimō, imprimō — whence oppress, compress, express, impress, print.
Greek for 'elder'. Worn down in speech to Italian prete, French prêtre, Romanian preot and English priest.
Spanish precioso is everyday 'lovely, beautiful'.

en: (operae pretium est) it is worth while
note: English price, prize and praise are all this one word, borrowed through French in different senses.
The nominative singular is hardly found; the plural precēs is the usual form.

en: (+ acc. or gen.) on the day before …
note: Used in Roman dates: prīdiē Īdūs Mārtiās '14 March', the eve of the Ides.
prīmō 'at first' (as opposed to later) versus prīmum 'first, for the first time' (in a sequence).

ex.en: she gave birth to her first-born son (Luke 2:7)

en: the first part of (prīmā nocte 'at nightfall')
note: Spanish and Portuguese primo 'cousin' is short for prīmus cōnsōbrīnus 'first cousin'.
prīmus + capiō 'taking first place'. Augustus called himself prīnceps 'first citizen' to avoid the hated rēx — hence 'the Principate'.

ex.en: In the beginning was the Word. (John 1:1)

note: A comparative with no positive; the superlative is prīmus.
Catullus offers his brother gifts 'in the ancient way of our fathers' (prīscō mōre parentum).
In Caesar simply 'former' (prīstina virtūs 'their old courage'); English pristine 'unspoiled' is a modern shift.
The neuter of prior used as an adverb.
Often split: prius … quam. With the subjunctive when the action is expected or prevented: priusquam hostēs venīrent 'before the enemy could come'.
Participle of prīvō 'deprive': a prīvātus was a citizen 'deprived' of public office.
prīvus 'single' + lēx 'law': a law for (or against) one individual.
French pour comes from prō (Old French por); in Spanish and Portuguese por, prō and per fell together.
From probus 'good': to test whether something is good. Spanish probar and Portuguese provar also mean 'taste' and 'try on'.
A former consul governing a province 'in place of a consul' (prō cōnsule), as Caesar governed Gaul.

en: far, far off, at a distance

note: Tacitus calls Pontius Pilate procūrātor of Judaea; in modern Romance the word belongs to lawyers and prosecutors.
prō + cūrā 'take care for'. Portuguese procurar is the everyday 'look for'; Spanish procurar means 'try'.
Livy lists the year's prodigies — rains of stones, talking oxen — which the state had to expiate.
prō + dō 'give forth': handing over to the enemy is betrayal; handing down to posterity is tradition.
Romance battles all come from battuālia, soldiers' fencing exercises (battuere 'beat').
prō fānō 'in front of the shrine' — outside the sacred precinct.
From prō factō 'as a fact'.
Caesar's word for marching off: Caesar in Galliam proficīscitur.
prō + fateor 'confess': a professor publicly declares his expertise.

ex.t: Ītaliam fātō profugus Lāvīniaque vēnit lītora
ex.en: came, an exile by fate, to Italy and the Lavinian shores (Vergil, Aeneid 1.2–3)

note: prō + fundus 'bottom'. Spanish everyday 'deep' is hondo, inherited from fundus itself.

ex.t: Dē profundīs clāmāvī ad tē, Domine.
ex.en: Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord. (Psalm 130)

ex.t: Iam nova prōgeniēs caelō dēmittitur altō.
ex.en: Now a new generation is sent down from high heaven. (Vergil, Eclogues 4.7)

note: prō + gradior 'step forward' (gradus 'step').
prō + habeō 'hold in front, keep away': hostēs itinere prohibēre 'bar the enemy from the road'.
A project is something 'thrown forward' into the future.
Literally 'send forth'; it displaced the classical polliceor as the Romance word for 'promise'.
Italians answer the phone with Pronto! 'ready'; Spanish pronto means 'soon'.
Comparative propius, superlative proximē; the adjective is proximus 'nearest'.
Romance hurries with newer words: Italian affrettarsi, Spanish apresurarse, Portuguese apressar-se, French se dépêcher.
Greek 'one who speaks for (a god)', not primarily 'one who foretells'.
From prope 'near'. In Caesar propinquī are a chieftain's kinsmen.
French propre means both 'own' and 'clean'; Italian proprio is also 'really, exactly'. Spanish propio lost its second r.
From prope 'near': what stands next to a thing can be its cause.
The opposite end of the ship is the puppis 'stern'.
From prō-vorsus 'turned forwards'; its feminine prōsa gave the word prose.
Short for prōsa ōrātiō 'straightforward speech' (from prōrsus), as opposed to verse (versus), which 'turns back' at the end of each line.
Sulla, and later Antony and Octavian, posted lists of citizens whom anyone could kill for a reward; Cicero died in the proscriptions of 43 BC.
Also prosper, prospera, prosperum. Traditionally explained as prō spē 'in accordance with hope'.
prō(d) + sum: the old d reappears before vowels — prōdest 'it helps', prōderam.
prō + tegō 'cover' (tēctum 'roof').
English has it twice: provide (learned) and purvey (through French pourvoir). Prūdēns 'prudent' is a contraction of prōvidēns.
First a magistrate's assigned task, then the territory he governed. Southern Gaul was simply Prōvincia 'the Province' — today's Provence.
Superlative of prope 'near'. Spanish has the learned próximo 'next' beside the inherited prójimo 'one's neighbour'.

ex.t: Dīligēs proximum tuum sīcut tē ipsum.
ex.en: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. (Matthew 22:39)

note: Contracted from prōvidēns 'foreseeing'.

en: tax farmer, contractor for public revenue
note: The hated collectors of the Gospels' 'publicans and sinners'; in English a publican later became the keeper of a public house.

en: of the people, public, of the state
note: Related to populus. Rēs pūblica 'the public thing' meant the state — and gave English republic.

en: it shames; (mē pudet) I am ashamed (+ gen.)
note: Impersonal like paenitet: mē pudet tuī 'I am ashamed of you'.
A diminutive of puer. Every Romance language replaced it: ragazza, chica, fille, menina, fată.
Keeps its e in all forms (puerī, puerō), unlike ager, agrī. Like Greek παῖς it could also mean a slave of any age.
From pugnus 'fist': originally a fist-fight.
Repugnant is literally 'fighting back' (re-pugnāre).
Latin -gn- comes out as Italian gn, Spanish ñ, Portuguese nh and Romanian mn (compare lemn < lignum).
Romance replaced it with colloquial bellus 'pretty' (bello, beau) and fōrmōsus 'shapely' (hermoso, formoso, frumos).
The Paris marché aux puces is the 'flea market'; Romanian purice shows l becoming r between vowels.
Any young animal, especially a chick; English foal is a native cognate from the time when the word meant just 'young one'.
Romanian plămân swapped the order of the consonants (pulmōnem → plămân).
Frequentative of pellō. French pousser and English push come from it — while Portuguese puxar, from the very same verb, means 'pull'.

ex.en: We are dust and shadow. (Horace, Odes 4.7)

note: Romans smoothed book-rolls and skin with it. Horace's sea wears itself out 'on the pumice rocks' of the volcanic coast.
From pungō 'prick'. French point can also negate (ne … point), like pas.
Reduplicated perfect pupugī.
From Poenī. Rome fought three Punic Wars (264–146 BC); 'Punic faith' was the Roman sneer for broken promises.
From poena 'penalty', with the old diphthong oe turned to ū — as in Poenī / Pūnicus, moenia / mūniō.
A pure i-stem: accusative puppim, ablative puppī.
From pūrus + agō 'make clean'.
The dye came from the murex shellfish and was so costly that purple meant power: senators wore a purple stripe, emperors the whole robe.
All five languages kept it — the village well was too basic to rename. English pit was borrowed by the early Germanic peoples.
The first meaning was 'prune, trim' — kept in Italian potare and Spanish and Portuguese podar — then 'settle (accounts)', 'reckon', 'think'. Compute, count, dispute and amputate all share it.

en: Pyramus, the Babylonian lover of Thisbe
note: Ovid's tale of the lovers who talk through a crack in the wall is staged as farce in A Midsummer Night's Dream and retold in earnest as Romeo and Juliet.
Church Latin '(the) fortieth (day)'. French carême (Old French quaresme) shows how drastically French wore down a long word.
English quarantine goes back to the Venetian quaranta giorni, the forty days a ship from a plague port had to wait before landing.
Romanian pătrat shows Latin qu- before a turning into p- (as in patru 'four'), while French carré simply lost the w-glide.
The descendants split the meaning: 'ask' in Italian chiedere and Romanian cere, but 'want, love' in Spanish and Portuguese querer (te quiero 'I love you').

cite: quaesō, defective verb: only quaesō, quaesumus

note: The quaestor was the 'investigator' (from quaerō); in modern Italy the questore heads the provincial police headquarters, the Questura.

en: of what kind? what sort of?
note: Romanian care and French quel come straight from quālis; in Romanian it even became the ordinary relative pronoun 'who, which', ousting quī.

ex.en: What an artist dies with me! (Nero's last words, Suetonius)

note: Coined by Cicero to translate Greek ποιότης 'what-sort-ness', building it from quālis exactly as the Greek was built from ποῖος.
With a superlative it means 'as … as possible': quam celerrimē 'as fast as possible', quam plūrimī 'as many as possible'.

en: and yet (at the start of a sentence)

ex.t: Quamquam animus meminisse horret luctūque refūgit, incipiam.
ex.en: Although my mind shudders to remember and has shrunk back in grief, I will begin. (Vergil, Aeneid 2.12)
How changed from what he was! (Vergil, Aeneid 2.274, of Hector)

note: From quam sī 'as if'. In Italian, Spanish and Portuguese the hedge 'as it were' became the everyday word for 'almost'.

ex.en: Like newborn babes (Introit of Low Sunday, after 1 Peter 2:2; hence the name Quasimodo)

note: Romanian patru shows the regular Romanian change of qu- + a to p- (aqua → apă). Latin, Greek τέσσαρες and English four all continue Indo-European *kʷetwōr-.

ex.en: There are four seasons of the year.

note: Romanian builds its teens as 'four-over-ten' (patru spre zece → paisprezece), the same pattern as Slavic, instead of inheriting the Latin forms.
Enclitic: it attaches to the word it adds, binding two closely linked ideas. It is the same Indo-European particle as Greek τε and Sanskrit ca.

ex.en: the Senate and the People of Rome (SPQR)

note: Latin qu- here is an assimilated p- (*perkʷus); the Germanic cognate is English fir, the same old tree-name applied to a conifer.
French qui and Italian chi continue the nominative quī, Spanish quien and Portuguese quem the accusative quem, while Romanian replaced the pronoun with care < quālis.

ex.en: He who is silent is taken to consent. (legal maxim)

cite: quī, quae, quod; gen. cuius, dat. cui
forms: quae, quod; gen. cuius, dat. cui

note: In Late and Biblical Latin, dīcō quia/quod … 'I say that …' began to replace the accusative-and-infinitive, the model for Romance 'that'-clauses with che and que.

ex.en: I believe because it is absurd. (proverbial, after Tertullian)

note: Only the first half declines (cuiusdam, cuidam); before -dam the m of quem, quam turns into n: quendam, quandam.

ex.en: A certain man gave a great supper. (Luke 14:16)

cite: quīdam, quaedam, quoddam (pron. quiddam); gen. cuiusdam, acc. quendam
forms: quaedam, quoddam (pron. quiddam); gen. cuiusdam, acc. quendam

note: In nē … quidem 'not even' the emphasized word sits between the two: nē ūnus quidem 'not even one'.
One word, three English loans: quiet (learned), quit and coy (both via Old French quite, coi). Spanish quedar 'to stay' comes from the derived verb quiētāre.
Indo-European *penkʷe (Greek πέντε, English five) became *kʷīnkʷe in Latin by assimilation; spoken Latin then dissimilated it again to *cinque, the source of every Romance form.
Quintessence is the quīnta essentia, the 'fifth element' (ether) that medieval philosophy added to earth, water, air and fire.
After sī, nisi, nē and num it loses its question sense and means 'anyone': sī quis 'if anyone'. Neuter quid gave the Romance word for 'what' everywhere.

ex.en: Who will guard the guards themselves? (Juvenal)

cite: quis, quid; gen. cuius, dat. cui, acc. quem, quid
forms: quid; gen. cuius, dat. cui, acc. quem, quid

note: Idiomatic with superlatives and reflexives: optimus quisque 'all the best people', suum cuique 'to each his own'.
cite: quisque, quaeque, quidque (adj. quodque); gen. cuiusque, dat. cuique
forms: quaeque, quidque (adj. quodque); gen. cuiusque, dat. cuique

ex.t: Quidquid id est, timeō Danaōs et dōna ferentēs.
ex.en: Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts. (Vergil, Aeneid 2.49)

note: Latin kept 'where at' (ubi), 'where to' (quō) and 'where from' (unde) apart; Romance merged them, rebuilding the word from dē + ubi/unde (Italian dove, Spanish donde).

ex.en: I am glad that you are well.

note: Literally quō modō 'in what manner'. This phrase, not classical ut, became the Romance word for both 'how' and 'as'.

ex.t: Hic iacet Arthūrus, rēx quondam rēxque futūrus.
ex.en: Here lies Arthur, the once and future king. (Malory)

note: It always follows the word it emphasizes: tū quoque 'you too', never quoque tū.

ex.en: You too, my son? (Caesar's legendary last words)

note: Its derivative quotus 'which in number?' gave quota pars 'the how-manieth part', hence quota; medieval quotāre 'to number (chapters)' gave English quote.

ex.en: As many people, so many opinions. (Terence)

note: A quotient is the answer to quotiēns? 'how many times?', the question a division asks.
French racine and Romanian rădăcină both come from the same diminutive *rādīcīna; radical means 'going to the root'.
French grenouille is the diminutive *rānucula with an added g-; ranunculus, 'little frog', is the buttercup, which grows where frogs live.
French ravir 'snatch away' also means 'delight' (ravissant 'ravishing'): being carried away. The Sabine women of legend were raptae, 'carried off'.
From reor 'reckon': first a 'reckoning, account', then reason itself. One Latin noun gave English reason (via French), ration and ratio.
French radeau is its descendant, through Occitan radel 'little raft'. Not related to English raft.
Recipe is the imperative 'take!' that headed every doctor's prescription, which is why prescriptions are still marked ℞.

ex.en: she laid him in a manger (Luke 2:7)

note: Built on cor, cordis 'heart', once thought the seat of memory: to 'bring back to the heart'. English 'learn by heart' keeps the same idea.
Spoken Latin preferred the compound dīrēctus, the source of French droit, Romanian drept and Italian diritto; English right and German recht are native cognates.
Spoken Latin reshaped it as *rendere under the influence of prendere 'take'. French rendre then gave English render, rent ('what is paid back') and rendezvous ('present yourselves').

ex.t: Reddite ergō quae sunt Caesaris Caesarī, et quae sunt Deī Deō.
ex.en: Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. (Matthew 22:21)

note: Every Romance language replaced it with a verb of turning or coming: Italian tornare, Spanish volver, Romanian se întoarce, French revenir.

ex.en: I want to go back home.

note: Like ferō it takes its participle from another root (lātum, old *tlātum), so English got both refer and relate from the same Latin verb.
Spanish, Portuguese and Italian real(e) means both 'royal' (< rēgālis) and 'real' (< reālis), hence Real Madrid 'Royal Madrid'. English has royal via French and regal from Latin.

ex.en: Hail, Queen, mother of mercy (medieval antiphon)

note: French règne kept only 'reign'; for 'kingdom' it uses royaume, from regimen reshaped after royal.
The root means 'make or keep straight': rēx is the one who sets things right, and rēgula, rēctus, regiō and English right all belong to the same family.

ex.t: Tū regere imperiō populōs, Rōmāne, mementō.
ex.en: Remember, Roman, to rule the peoples with your power. (Vergil, Aeneid 6.851)

note: One wooden ruler gave English three words: rule and rail through Old French, regular straight from Latin. Monks living by a Rule were 'regular' clergy.
The Romans already argued over its origin: Cicero derived it from relegere 'go over again carefully', the Christian Lactantius from religāre 'bind back'.

ex.en: So many evils could religion prompt. (Lucretius 1.101)

note: All five languages replaced it with laxāre 'loosen'. The root linqu- (perfect līquī) is the same as Greek λείπω 'leave'.
Italian rimanere and Romanian rămâne kept it; the west chose other verbs: quiētāre (Spanish quedar), restāre (French rester) and *fīgicāre 'fix' (Portuguese ficar).
From rēmex 'rower' (rēmus 'oar' + agō). Vergil calls wings rēmigium ālārum, 'the oarage of wings'.
Short e, unlike rēmus 'oar'. Killed by Romulus for leaping over the new walls of Rome.
Latin rēmus (from *ret-smos), Greek ἐρετμός and English row and rudder all come from one Indo-European verb 'to row'.
Its participle ratus 'reckoned, fixed' survives in prō ratā (parte) and English rate; Romance 'think' is pēnsāre 'weigh (up)'.

Romance replaced it with two vivid metaphors: afflāre 'sniff out' (Spanish hallar, Portuguese achar, Romanian afla) and probably *tropāre 'invent a verse' (Italian trovare, French trouver, like the troubadours).

en: pay in cash, do at once

note: Literally 'grab back' (prehendere 'seize'): Italian riprendere still means both 'take back' and 'scold', while French reprendre kept only the physical sense.
Its accusative requiem opens the Mass for the dead, which is how it became an English word; R.I.P. is requiēscat in pāce 'may he rest in peace'.

ex.en: Grant them eternal rest, O Lord.

en: rest in death, lie at peace

ex.en: may he (or she) rest in peace (R.I.P.)

note: Romance chose causa 'case' for 'thing'; rēs survives only in French rien 'nothing', from rem 'a thing' in negative sentences, just like English 'not a thing'.
Literally 'the public thing'. Both halves decline (reī pūblicae, rem pūblicam), and it is often written as one word, rēspūblica.

ex.t: Videant cōnsulēs nē quid rēs pūblica dētrīmentī capiat.
ex.en: Let the consuls see to it that the state suffers no harm. (the senate's emergency decree)

note: Horace: spatiō brevī spem longam resecēs, 'since life is short, prune back long hope'.

ex.t: Respice post tē! Hominem tē mementō!
ex.en: Look behind you! Remember that you are a man. (Tertullian, on the Roman triumph)

en: (of a jurist) give a legal opinion
note: Built on spondeō 'pledge solemnly': an answer was first a pledge given in return. It survives in all five languages, Romanian răspunde included.
'Be left over' became the ordinary French verb 'stay' (rester). English the rest 'remainder' is a different word from rest 'repose'.
Italy's Risorgimento, the 19th-century unification, is literally 'the rising again'.
Its descendants all mean 'network' today: Italian rete, Spanish la red (also 'the Internet'), French réseau.
Spoken Latin dē retrō 'from behind' became Italian dietro and French derrière.
From rēs 'matter, lawsuit': the reus is the party 'in the case'. English law keeps the feminine in mēns rea, 'guilty mind'.
Deponent in the present, but classical authors mostly use active perfect forms: revertī, revertit 'he returned'.
The same Indo-European word as Sanskrit rāj- (rajah) and the Gaulish -rīx of Vercingetorix; English rich is an ancient Germanic borrowing of the Celtic form.

ex.en: The king can do no wrong. (legal maxim)

en: Rhea Silvia, Vestal Virgin, mother of Romulus and Remus by Mars
note: Livy calls her Rhea Silvia, Ennius and Vergil Ilia. She has nothing to do with the Greek Titaness Rhea.
Hannibal's army crossed it on rafts and floating platforms in 218 BC, elephants included.
Latin had no separate verb for 'smile': subrīdēre 'laugh a little' gave Italian sorridere and French sourire.

ex.en: What stops one from telling the truth with a laugh? (Horace)
The mountains will go into labour, and a ridiculous mouse will be born. (Horace)

note: French has both the inherited raide 'stiff, steep' and the learned rigide: a typical popular/learned doublet.
Unrelated to Italian and Spanish rima 'rhyme', which comes from rhythmus.
To arrive is *ad-rīpāre, 'reach the bank'; river is rīpāria 'bank-land' via French, so the word for the bank came to mean the water itself.

ex.en: The camp is pitched on the bank of the river.

en: custom, manner (rītū + gen. 'in the manner of')

note: In Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian the 'brook' grew into 'river' (río, rio, râu), replacing flūmen. Rīvālēs were neighbours drawing on the same stream: rivals.
In Spain this word for hard oak timber became the ordinary word for 'oak', replacing quercus; robust is 'strong as oak'.
Roman laws were 'asked' of the people, so a rogātiō was a bill; the praerogātīva was the voting unit 'asked first', hence a prerogative. Romanian a se ruga is 'to pray'.
Town names take bare cases with no preposition: Rōmam 'to Rome', Rōmae (locative) 'at Rome', Rōmā 'from Rome'.

ex.en: All roads lead to Rome. (medieval proverb)

note: Romanian român 'Romanian' is the inherited form of Rōmānus. Old French romanz 'in the vernacular' gave romance, first a tale told in a Romance language rather than Latin.

en: Romulus, legendary founder and first king of Rome

note: Rosemary has nothing to do with roses or Mary: it is rōs marīnus, 'dew of the sea', a shrub of the Mediterranean coast.
The model noun of the first declension in many grammars (rosa, rosae, rosae, rosam, rosā). Romanian's everyday trandafir comes from Greek τριαντάφυλλο, 'thirty-petalled'.

ex.t: Stat rosa prīstina nōmine, nōmina nūda tenēmus.
ex.en: The rose of old remains only in its name; we hold mere names. (Bernard of Cluny)

en: (Rōstra, pl.) the speakers' platform in the Forum
note: The Forum platform was called the Rōstra because it was decorated with the rams of warships captured at Antium in 338 BC. In Spanish and Portuguese the 'snout' became the human face.
A textbook case of stressed short o breaking into a diphthong: Italian ruota, Spanish rueda, Romanian roată, while Portuguese roda kept the plain vowel.
Romance took 'red' from other Latin words: russus, russeus, rubeus, and vermiculus, the insect 'worm' that yielded red dye. English red and Greek ἐρυθρός share ruber's Indo-European root.
In Italian rumore has become simply 'noise'; a rumour there is una voce, 'a voice'.
Bankrupt is Italian banca rotta, 'broken bench': the failed money-changer's table was said to be smashed.
Probably 'broken rock', from rumpō 'break'.

en: in turn, on the other hand

note: Like domus and town names it takes no preposition: rūs 'to the country', rūrī 'in the country', rūre 'from the country'.

ex.t: Ō rūs, quandō ego tē aspiciam?
ex.en: O countryside, when shall I see you again? (Horace)

note: Church Latin, from Greek σάββατον (Hebrew šabbāt). French samedi and Romanian sâmbătă reflect a nasalized *sambatum, while English Saturday kept the pagan 'Saturn's day'.

en: Sabidius, the man Martial cannot love
note: Martial 1.32 (nōn amō tē, Sabidī) became Tom Brown's 'I do not love thee, Doctor Fell'.
What was sacer belonged to the gods and was cut off from ordinary use, so the word could mean both 'holy' and 'accursed'.

ex.en: the accursed hunger for gold (Vergil, Aeneid 3.57)

note: French serment 'oath' is the inherited form, already spelled sagrament in the Strasbourg Oaths of 842, the oldest French text; sacrement is its learned twin.
Christian Latin used saeculum for 'this world' as opposed to the Church, hence secular clergy and secular society.

ex.en: for ever and ever (lit. 'into the ages of ages')

note: No Romance language kept it: Italian spesso is spissus 'thick, crowded' and French souvent is subinde 'immediately after, repeatedly'.

ex.t: Gutta cavat lapidem, nōn vī sed saepe cadendō.
ex.en: A drop hollows the stone not by force but by falling often. (proverb, after Ovid)

note: The word for a pig's 'bristle' became the western word for 'silk', first used of the fine thread itself.
It left no descendants, and despite appearances it is not the source of savage, which comes from silva 'forest'.
Romanian sare shows its typical l → r between vowels (salem → sare). English salt and Greek ἅλς are cognates; salad (and sauce) are 'salted' things.

ex.en: with a grain of salt (after Pliny)

note: Formed from sāl 'salt', but the popular claim that soldiers were paid in salt has no ancient evidence; the exact link is unknown.
One Latin leap went in every direction: Italian salire 'go up', Spanish salir and Portuguese sair 'go out', French saillir 'stick out'; only Romanian sări still means 'jump'.
Spanish sauce 'willow' is a false friend for English sauce. Willow bark gave salicylic acid, the ancestor of aspirin.
A salsa (rēs), 'salted thing', became Spanish salsa and French sauce; the derivative salsīcia gave sausage.
A different word from saltus 'leap'. Varus' legions were destroyed in AD 9 in the saltus Teutoburgiēnsis, the Teutoburg Forest.
Raising a glass, Italians say salute!, Spaniards ¡salud! and Portuguese saúde!, all 'health!'. Roman letters opened with salūtem dīcit 'sends greeting'.

ex.en: The welfare of the people shall be the supreme law. (Cicero)

en: pay one's respects to, call on

ex.en: Hail, Emperor, those who are about to die salute you. (Suetonius)

note: A Church Latin word for Greek σωτήρ; classical Latin said servātor. Spanish and Portuguese gave the name to El Salvador and to Salvador da Bahia.

cite: salvē, pl. salvēte; salvēre iubeō 'I bid you good day'
forms: pl. salvēte; salvēre iubeō 'I bid you good day'

note: English safe and save both came through French sauf, which also means 'except' (sauf erreur 'barring error'), as do Spanish salvo and English save.
A sanction is both an approval and a penalty because a law's sānctiō was the clause that fixed the punishment for breaking it.
Spanish sangre comes from sang(ui)nem → *sangne, with n → r as in hombre < hominem. Sanguine 'optimistic' recalls the medieval humour of blood.

ex.en: A sound mind in a sound body. (Juvenal)

note: The Romance 'wise' (sabio, sage) comes from a spoken *sapius, implied by Petronius' nesapius 'ignorant'. Homo sapiens is 'wise man'.

ex.en: A word to the wise is enough. (Plautus, Terence)
The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. (Psalm 111:10)

note: 'Have taste, have sense' became the Romance verb 'to know', replacing scīre everywhere except Romanian (ști). Spanish sabe a … still means 'it tastes of …'.

ex.en: Dare to be wise! (Horace; Kant's motto of the Enlightenment)

en: soap (originally a hair dye or pomade)
note: Pliny describes sāpō as a Gallic invention for reddening hair; the word is Germanic, the ancestor of English soap. Spanish jabón shows the Old Spanish shift of s- to x- (sh).
Kepler applied this word for a prince's bodyguard to the moons 'attending' Jupiter in 1611.
French assez is ad satis 'to sufficiency'. English sad first meant 'sated, weary' and comes from the same Indo-European root.
Italian kept sasso, but elsewhere the Greek loan petra won (piedra, pierre, piatră). Saxifrage is the 'stone-breaker' plant that grows in rock cracks.
Romanian scaun is the everyday 'chair'. English shambles were butchers' benches (Old English scamel < scamellum) long before they meant a mess.
To scan verse was to 'climb' it foot by foot, marking each step. Italian scendere 'go down' is the compound dēscendere.
Greek σχολή meant 'leisure', the free time spent in discussion. Note the Romance prothetic vowel: escuela, escola, école.

ex.en: We learn not for life but for school. (Seneca's complaint, usually quoted the other way round)

note: Contracted from scīre licet 'one may know', just as vidēlicet (viz.) is vidēre licet 'one may see'.
Spoken Latin swapped the sounds to *stincilla, whence French étincelle and, via Old French estenceler 'to sparkle, ornament', English stencil.
Only Romanian kept it (a ști); the others switched to sapere. English nice goes back to nescius 'not knowing', via Old French nice 'silly'.

ex.en: I know that I know nothing. (after Socrates)

note: Western Romance put a vowel before s + consonant (escribir, escrever, Old French escrire, now écrire); Italian and Romanian did not.
Coins stamped with a coat of arms were named after the shield: the Italian scudo, the French écu and the Portuguese escudo.
It always points back to the subject and so has no nominative; sibi and suī are its dative and genitive, suus its possessive. All five languages kept it as se.
cite: sē, gen. suī, dat. sibi, acc./abl. sē (sēsē); no nominative
forms: gen. suī, dat. sibi, acc./abl. sē (sēsē); no nominative

note: An insect is a creature 'cut into' segments, a calque of Greek ἔντομον; English saw and scythe go back to the same root.
From sequor: the 'following' one. A ventus secundus follows the ship, so rēs secundae means 'good fortune'. The second of time is the pars minūta secunda, the 'second small division' of an hour.
sē- 'without' + cūra 'care': first 'carefree', even 'careless', only later 'safe'. English sure (via French) and secure (learned) are a doublet.
No Romance language kept sed: Italian ma, French mais and Portuguese mas come from magis 'rather', Spanish pero from per hoc.

ex.en: The girl is not sleeping but reading.

note: French and Italian keep the Latin type up to 16 (seize, sedici), Spanish only to 15 (quince); after that they count 'ten and six' (dieciséis, dix-sept, diciassette).
Spanish and Portuguese ser 'to be' blends esse with sedēre (Old Spanish seer 'sit'); Romanian a ședea still means 'sit, stay'. English sit is a native cognate.

ex.en: The boy is sitting on a chair.

note: The Holy See is the papal 'seat'; a siege, via French, was an army 'sitting down' before a town.

en: (sella curūlis) official chair of a magistrate
note: From sedeō 'sit'. The 'seat' became the 'saddle' almost everywhere; only Spanish silla is still a chair (a saddle is silla de montar).
From Indo-European *sem- 'one, together', like simul, semper and simplex, Greek ἅμα and English same.

ex.en: Once a year one may go mad. (medieval proverb)

en: Semiramis, legendary queen of Assyria, said to have walled Babylon

ex.en: Always faithful. (motto of the US Marine Corps)

ex.t: Senātus haec intellegit, cōnsul videt; hic tamen vīvit.
ex.en: The senate knows this, the consul sees it; and yet this man lives. (Cicero, Against Catiline)

note: From senex 'old man'. Cicero's dialogue on old age is Cato Maior dē senectūte.
Irregular stem: gen. senis, pl. senēs, senum. Romance chose vetulus for 'old', but the comparative senior lived on as 'lord, sir'.

en: (as noun) an elder; (in the census) a man over 45
note: The comparative of senex became the polite word for 'lord, sir'. French even kept two case forms: sire from nominative senior, seigneur from accusative seniōrem.
From sentiō 'think': an opinion, a senator's vote, a judge's verdict, then a pithy saying and finally a grammatical sentence.
Italian sentire also means 'hear' and French sentir 'smell'. English scent is that French verb, spelled with a later, spurious c.
French sevrer 'to wean (a baby)' is the inherited form; through Anglo-French it gave English sever.
Greek ἑπτά shows Greek initial s- turning into h- (compare sex/ἕξ, sāl/ἅλς). September was the seventh month of the old Roman year, which began in March.
The 'seventh' month of the oldest Roman year, which began in March. Like all month names it is really an adjective (mēnsis September), hence Kalendae Septembrēs.

en: (pl. septentriōnēs) the seven stars of the Plough
note: septem triōnēs, 'the seven plough-oxen': the stars of the Great Bear wheeling around the northern sky.
Late Latin septimāna, '(a period) of seven (days)', became the word for 'week' in all five languages.
Standard French counts soixante-dix 'sixty-ten', but Belgians and the Swiss say septante. The Septuagint is the Greek Bible of the 'seventy' translators.
French Seine is the name worn down by regular sound change; the other languages took the French form.

en: the Sequani, Gallic people of the upper Saône (Franche-Comté)

note: Spoken Latin turned the deponent into an active *sequere, the source of seguire, seguir and suivre; English sue and suit came from it through French.
In classical Latin it is relaxed conversation; Horace called his satires sermōnēs, 'chats'. Church Latin turned it into the preacher's sermon.
English season, via French saison, is satiōnem, 'sowing (time)'; English sow and seed are native cognates.
The 'late (hour)' became the Romance evening: Italian sera, Romanian seară, French soir; Spanish and Portuguese say tarde, from tardē 'late'.

ex.en: No one can serve two masters. (Matthew 6:24)
