note: Italian serbare is the inherited form; elsewhere 'keep' is Germanic *wardōn (guardar, garder). Despite appearances, servō is probably unrelated to servus.
Medieval serfs were servī. Austrians and Bavarians still greet each other with Servus!, '(your) servant', and Italian ciao is the same courtesy, from Venetian s'ciavo '(your) slave'.

ex.en: Servant of the servants of God (title of the Pope)

en: sesterce, Roman coin worth a quarter of a denarius
note: From sēmis tertius 'the third (as) a half', i.e. 2½ asses; written HS, from IIS (two and a sēmis). Gen. pl. sēstertium in sums of money.
Romanian turns s before short e (which first became ie) into ș: sex → șase, septem → șapte, sedēre → ședea; compare long ē in sēra → seară.
Originally the ordinal sextus 'sixth', like Quīntus and Decimus. Abbreviated Sex.
The Roman day counted hours from sunrise, so the sixth hour was noon: Spanish siesta, the midday rest, is (hōra) sexta.
Romanian says dacă for 'if', but sī survives as să, the particle of the subjunctive: vreau să plec 'I want to leave'.

ex.en: If you want peace, prepare for war. (after Vegetius)

note: Latin answered yes with sīc 'thus (it is)', the source of Italian sì and Spanish sí. French oui instead comes from hoc ille, and the langue d'oc was named after its 'yes', oc < hoc.

ex.en: Thus passes the glory of the world.

ex.t: Sīcut erat in prīncipiō, et nunc et semper.
ex.en: As it was in the beginning, is now and ever shall be. (Gloria Patri)

note: Cōnsīderāre and dēsīderāre (English consider, desire) are probably built on sīdus, perhaps from augurs studying the stars, though the link is debated.
Romanian semn shows Latin -gn- turning into -mn- (lignum → lemn). The signa were the legion's standards: signa īnferre, 'carry the standards forward', meant 'attack'.

ex.en: In this sign you will conquer. (Constantine's vision)

note: Latin had two verbs: sileō for stillness and taceō for not speaking. Romance kept taceō (tacere, taire, tăcea), while Spanish and Portuguese chose callar, calar.

ex.en: For laws fall silent in the midst of arms. (Cicero)

note: Silvāticus 'of the woods' gave French sauvage and English savage. Romanian pădure 'forest' is palūs 'marsh'.

ex.en: The wolf lives in the forest.

note: From silva 'wood': the kings of Alba were the Silviī, descended from Aeneas' son Silvius, born in the forest.
Its verb similāre 'be like' became Italian sembrare and French sembler 'seem' (English resemble). The superlative simillimus doubles the l, like facillimus.

ex.en: Simplicity is the seal of truth.

note: Late Latin īnsimul became Italian insieme and French ensemble; Spanish and Portuguese say junto(s), from iūnctus 'joined'.
The popular story of sine cērā 'without wax' (sculptors hiding flaws) is a myth; the real origin is uncertain.
Italian senza comes from absentiā 'in the absence (of)', Romanian fără from forās 'outside'. A sinecure is an office sine cūrā, 'without care (of souls)'.

ex.en: a condition without which (it is) not: an essential condition

en: one each, one at a time
note: Spanish sendos still means 'one each'; Romanian singur means 'alone'; the French sanglier is the singulāris porcus, the boar that roams alone.
Roman augurs, facing south, held the left (the east) to be lucky; the Greek view that the left is ill-omened won out. Spanish izquierdo is Basque, French gauche Germanic.

ex.en: Let the little children come to me. (Mark 10:14)

en: fold of the toga; bosom, lap
note: The mathematical sine is a medieval mistranslation: an Arabic word for 'chord' was misread as jayb 'fold, pocket' and rendered sinus.
Kept in four languages (suocero, suegro, sogro, socru); French switched to the polite beau-père. Greek ἑκυρός is a cognate, with the usual Greek s- → h-.
French soleil is the diminutive *sōliculus; Romanian soare shows l → r between vowels. Greek ἥλιος and English sun share the Indo-European root.
From solum 'ground, sole of the foot'. The flatfish is named for its sandal shape.
Semi-deponent: active in the present (solet 'he usually …'), passive in form in the perfect (solitus est). Spanish uses it exactly the same way: suele llover 'it usually rains'.

en: (as noun) gold coin of the late Empire
note: Constantine's gold solidus became the word for pay (Italian soldo, Spanish sueldo); a soldier (Italian soldato) is literally a 'paid man'.

ex.en: Where they make a desert, they call it peace. (Tacitus, Agricola)

en: (nōn sōlum … sed etiam) not only … but also
note: The neuter of sōlus 'alone', with long ō; not to be confused with solum 'ground, soil'.
Short o, unlike sōlus 'alone' and sōl 'sun': that is why Italian suolo and Spanish suelo have a diphthong while solo and sol do not.
Like ūnus, tōtus and nūllus it has genitive -īus and dative -ī. Nōn sōlum … sed etiam: 'not only … but also'.
cite: sōlus, sōla, sōlum (gen. sōlīus, dat. sōlī)

note: Spanish sueño merges somnium 'dream' and somnus 'sleep'. Romanian vis 'dream' is vīsum, 'a thing seen'.
Greek ὕπνος (hypnosis) is a cognate: both come from *swepnos, with s- → h- in Greek and -pn- → -mn- in Latin.
From sordēs 'dirt'. Mourners and defendants wore dirty clothes (sordidātī) to show grief.
Spanish hermana and Portuguese irmã come from (soror) germāna 'full sister'. French sœur continues the nominative soror itself, a rare survival of a Latin nominative.
Romans drew lots (sortēs) to learn the gods' will; Spanish suerte became 'luck', French sort also 'spell', and a sorcerer was first a caster of lots.

ex.en: Fate, monstrous and empty (Carmina Burana, 'O Fortuna')

note: A Greek loan for the late Roman cavalry sword; it replaced gladius in the west (spada, espada, épée). The Italian card suit spade gave English spades.
Medieval merchants listed goods by 'kind' (speciēs), so the same word became French épice and English spice.
Romance 'look' came from a Germanic word for 'guard' (guardare, regarder) or from mīrārī 'marvel at' (Spanish mirar).
A neat set for Latin -cul-: Italian specchio, Spanish espejo, Portuguese espelho, exactly like oculus → occhio, ojo, olho.
Borrowed from Greek. Portuguese espelunca has sunk to 'a seedy dive', while American cavers go spelunking.
English spurn, originally 'kick away', is a native cognate. Romance rebuilt 'despise' from pretium 'price, value' (disprezzare, despreciar, mépriser).
The short noun died out and was replaced by derivatives of spērāre (speranza, esperanza, espoir). Spēs was also a goddess with temples in Rome.
From spīrō 'breathe'. Christian Latin used it for the Spīritus Sānctus, translating Greek πνεῦμα, which also means 'breath'.

ex.t: Spīritus quidem prōmptus est, carō autem īnfirma.
ex.en: The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. (Matthew 26:41)

note: Italian spesso is also the everyday adverb 'often', replacing saepe: things that come thick and fast.

ex.en: gloriously false (Horace, of a noble lie)

note: A Roman engagement was a formal pledge: the spōnsa is the 'promised' bride, hence Italian sposa, French épouse, English spouse. In Spanish esposas are also handcuffs.
Its diminutive sportula was the basket of food (later a cash handout) a patron gave his clients at the morning call.

en: thread of life (spun by the Fates)
note: English stamina is the Latin plural: the 'threads' of life spun by the Fates, hence staying power.
From stō 'stand': first 'without moving', then 'on the spot'. Hospital English still says stat! for 'at once'.

ex.en: the existing state of affairs (lit. 'the state in which')

note: Spanish estrella and Portuguese estrela picked up an r; Romanian stea lost the -ll-. Greek ἀστήρ and English star share the same root.

ex.en: Hail, star of the sea (medieval hymn to Mary)

note: A via strāta was a 'paved road'. The Germanic tribes borrowed it on the continent, so English street and Italian strada are the same Latin participle.
The point used on wax tablets came to mean 'manner of writing', then style in general. The y of style comes from a false link with Greek στῦλος 'pillar'.
Spanish and Portuguese estar became a second verb 'to be' (for states and locations); French été 'been' is its participle, grafted onto être.

ex.en: Each man's day stands fixed. (Vergil, Aeneid 10.467)

note: 'Tighten' went in surprising directions: French étreindre 'embrace', Spanish estreñir 'constipate'. The participle strictus gave the words for 'narrow' (stretto, estrecho, étroit, estreito) and English strait.

en: be eager for, be keen on (+ dat.)

note: Stupidus first meant 'stunned, struck dumb', not dull-witted; stupendous is the gerundive, 'to be marvelled at'.
The root is 'sweet' (suāvis, Greek ἡδύς, English sweet): to advise was to make something sweet to someone.
Romanian sub and Portuguese sob continue it directly; Italian sotto and French sous come from the adverb subtus. With motion it takes the accusative: sub montem 'up to the foot of the hill'.

en: draw up, haul up (ships onto land)

note: Spanish and Portuguese subir 'go up' come from 'come up from below'; Italian subire and French subir kept 'undergo'.
Italian subito now means 'right away'; English sudden came through French from subitāneus.
What 'comes next' simply happens: Italian succedere and Spanish suceder mean 'happen', a trap for English speakers.
sub + currere, 'run up (to help)': ¡Socorro! is still the Spanish and Portuguese cry for 'help!'.
Latin sūdor, Greek ἱδρώς and English sweat all come from Indo-European *sweid-. A sūdārium, 'sweat-cloth', became the Italian sudario, the holy shroud.
Its perfect sustulī and participle sublātum are borrowed from tollō. Spoken Latin remade it as a regular *sufferīre, the source of soffrire, sufrir, souffrir and Romanian suferi.

en: (+ dat.) belong to: mihi est 'I have'
note: Spoken Latin regularized esse to *essere (essere, être); Romanian a fi takes its infinitive from fierī 'become', though e and sunt still come from est and sunt. English is and Greek ἐστί share the root of est.

en: the top of (summus mōns 'the top of the mountain')
note: A superlative of superus. Like medius and extrēmus it often names a part: summus mōns is 'the top of the mountain', not 'the highest mountain'.
Every Romance language kept only the compound cōnsuere 'sew together'. English sew is a native cognate.

en: over, above, on top of (+ acc.)
note: Romanian spre 'towards' continues super; English over and Greek ὑπέρ are cognates. With the ablative it often means 'about': super hāc rē 'concerning this matter'.
From super: 'above (others)'. Rome's last king was Tarquinius Superbus, 'the Proud'; over time the word slid from 'arrogant' to 'magnificent'.

ex.en: To spare the conquered and wear down the proud in war. (Vergil, Aeneid 6.853)

en: (in law) a building standing on land
(m. pl. superī) the gods above; the living

ex.t: Flectere sī nequeō superōs, Acheronta movēbō.
ex.en: If I cannot bend the gods above, I will move the underworld. (Vergil, Aeneid 7.312)

note: First a kneeling in prayer or sacrifice; probably from the kneeling of the condemned it came to mean execution, and in Romance 'torture'.
Absurdus first meant 'out of tune, jarring'. The mathematical surd translates an Arabic term for a 'deaf' (irrational) root.

ex.en: We do not sing to the deaf. (Vergil, Eclogues 10.8)

note: sub + rapiō 'snatch from underneath'; also spelled subripiō. Its participle surreptus gives surreptitious.

ex.en: Lift up your hearts! (from the Mass)

note: English swine and sow and Greek ὗς are cognates; in Romance the word gave way to porcus.

en: acknowledge (a newborn child) as one's own
his own, her own, its own, their own (reflexive)
(m. pl. suī) one's own people: friends, family, troops
note: Reflexive: it points back to the subject (Caesar suōs mīlitēs laudat 'Caesar praises his own men'); for someone else's, Latin uses eius. Romance dropped the restriction and made it the ordinary 'his, her, their'.

en: Syria, Roman province in the Near East

note: Latin b went three ways here: Italian tafano has an unusual f, Portuguese tavão a v, and French taon dropped it altogether.
A diminutive of tabula. Under the lēgēs tabellāriae (from 139 BC) Romans voted by secret written ballot on tabellae.
Roman tabernae were the one-room shops lining every street; Tres Tabernae ('Three Shops') was a stop on St Paul's road to Rome.
A diminutive of taberna 'hut': first a soldier's tent, then in the Vulgate the portable sanctuary of the Israelites.
Boards laid on trestles became the 'table' in Italian and French; Spanish and Portuguese kept the sense 'plank' and use mesa (< mēnsa) for the furniture.

ex.en: a scraped-clean tablet, a blank slate

rel.g: to keep quiet about; se taire 'fall silent'

note: Spanish callar and Portuguese calar replaced it with *callāre, from Greek khaláō 'let down, lower' (the voice, like a sail).

ex.en: by their silence they shout (Cicero, against Catiline)

note: Originally the participle of taceō. The historian Tacitus bore it as a family name.
Torches led the bride to her new home, so taeda stands for marriage itself.
French replaced it with ennui, from (esse) in odiō 'to be hateful' — the same source as English annoy.

en: talent (a weight, or sum of money)
note: A talent was a huge weight of silver; the sense 'natural gift' comes from the Gospel parable of the servants who must put their talents to use (Matthew 25).
Still everywhere in the West: Italian tale e quale 'exactly alike', Spanish ¿qué tal? 'how's it going?', French tel quel 'as is'.
Spanish topo shows the same al → o as alter → otro; French taupe turned the l into a vowel (al → au).
Spoken Latin enlarged it to *tālō, -ōnis 'heel'. Sheep's knucklebones (tālī) served as dice. English talon meant 'heel' before it meant a bird's claw.

ex.t: Nātūram expellās furcā, tamen usque recurret.
ex.en: You may drive out nature with a pitchfork, yet she will keep coming back (Horace).

note: English tandem began as a university joke for a carriage with horses harnessed one behind the other — that is, 'at length'.

ex.t: Quō usque tandem abūtēre, Catilīna, patientiā nostrā?
ex.en: How long, pray, Catiline, will you abuse our patience? (Cicero)

note: The everyday 'touch' verbs of Italian and French come from an imitative *toccāre 'to knock' (English touch is borrowed from French); tangere survives in Iberian verbs for plucking strings and ringing bells.
Spanish tan 'so' is a clipped tanto; Romanian atât fused it with eccum 'behold'.
The adverb tardē 'late' became the Spanish and Portuguese word for 'afternoon' (la tarde, a tarde); Romanian târziu continues a derivative *tardīvus.
Latin au became o in Italian and Spanish and ou in Portuguese, but Romanian kept it (taur, like aur < aurum).
A textbook case of Latin -ct-: Italian tt, Spanish ch, French and Portuguese it/t. Originally the participle of tegō 'cover'.
Latin tegō, Greek stégō 'cover' and English thatch share one root; Romance replaced the verb with cooperīre 'cover completely'.
-gul- went the way of -cul-: Spanish teja and Portuguese telha match ojo and olho from oculus.
From *tex-la (texō 'weave'). French toilette, a little cloth on the dressing table, became the dressing itself and finally the room: English toilet.
The poets' word for 'earth'; prose used terra, and terra is what survived. The element tellurium was named after it in 1798.
One of the four cardinal virtues, beside prūdentia, iūstitia and fortitūdō. Spanish templanza has the same r → l as templar.

rel.g: to temper; to warm slightly; to tune

note: French tremper 'soak' (Old French temprer, with the r moved) keeps the smith's sense: steel is tempered by plunging it into water. Spanish templar swapped r for l.
First 'a stretch of time, weather' (from tempus); the bad-weather sense won. Romanian furtună 'storm' is Latin fortūna, come back via Greek sailors' speech.
Originally a patch of sky or ground marked out by an augur for taking omens — hence contemplārī 'to contemplate'.

ex.en: In the temple they pray to the goddess.

ex.t: et nē nōs indūcās in temptātiōnem
ex.en: and lead us not into temptation (the Lord's Prayer)

note: The basic meaning is 'feel, try out' — Portuguese tentar is still plain 'to try'. English tempt and attempt both came through French.
French temps carries a silent p restored from Latin spelling; English tense (of verbs) is the Old French tens 'time'.

ex.t: sed fugit intereā, fugit irreparābile tempus
ex.en: but meanwhile it flies, time flies beyond recall (Vergil)

note: A tent is something 'stretched' (Late Latin tenta); extend, attend, intend and pretend are all compounds.

ex.en: And they stretched out their hands in longing for the farther shore (Vergil).

note: Spanish tinieblas (with a diphthong and l for r) and Portuguese trevas (heavily worn down) are the popular descendants.

ex.en: The light shines in the darkness (John 1:5).

en: Tenedos, island off Troy where the Greek fleet hid
note: Greek second-declension islands are feminine. Today it is the Turkish island of Bozcaada.
In Spanish and Portuguese 'hold' became the ordinary verb 'to have' (tengo, tenho), leaving habēre as the auxiliary.

ex.en: Grasp the subject; the words will follow (Cato the Elder).

note: In Romanian 'tender' became the everyday word for 'young' (tânăr). French tendre grew a d, as gener → gendre.
English thin is a native cognate: both go back to the root 'stretch' seen in tendō.
A neat set of sound changes: Italian tiepido diphthongizes, Spanish tibio softens p to b, French tiède keeps little more than the stressed syllable.

ex.en: O three and four times blessed! (Vergil)

note: Every Romance language found a new word for 'back': Spanish espalda is the shoulder blade, Portuguese costas the ribs. ā tergō means 'from behind'.
Terminus was also the god of boundary stones. English term first meant a fixed limit of time — as in a school term.

ex.en: the limit before which (the latest possible date)

note: Romanian țară means 'country' (Țara Românească 'Wallachia'); for 'earth' it uses pământ, from pavīmentum 'pavement'.
The participle territus 'frightened, terrified' is often used as an adjective. To deter is literally 'to frighten off'.
French tiers survives only as 'a third' (le tiers état, the Third Estate); the ordinal troisième is a new formation from trois.

rel.n: via Old French: an assaying pot

note: Late Latin slang called the head a 'pot' (compare English 'nut'), and it stuck: French tête, Italian testa, Romanian țeastă 'skull'. English test was a pot for assaying gold.
The Old and New 'Testaments' translate Greek diathḗkē, which meant both 'covenant' and 'will'.
In Italian and French the word for the evidence came to mean the person giving it: testimone, témoin 'witness'.
Romanian martor 'witness' is Latin martyr — itself Greek for 'witness'. The diminutive testiculus 'little witness' gave English testicle.

ex.en: One witness is no witness (legal maxim).

note: From testa 'shell'. Roman soldiers locked their shields overhead into a testūdō to approach enemy walls.
A text is something 'woven' (textus) — the image of writing as weaving is Roman. Latin x came out as ss, j, s, c and s in the five languages.

en: Thais, woman's name (a famous courtesan's name)
note: The courtesan of Menander and Terence; Dante puts a Taide among the flatterers in Hell (Inferno 18).
Greek théatron is 'a place for watching' (theáomai 'watch'). Rome's first permanent stone theatre was Pompey's, built in 55 BC.
'Gift of god' (θεός + δῶρον): the same two elements, reversed, make Dorothea.
From Greek thermós 'hot' (thermometer, thermos). The thermae of Caracalla and Diocletian were among the largest buildings of Rome.
French trésor picked up an extra r. English has it twice: treasure via French and thesaurus, a 'storehouse' of words, straight from Latin.

ex.t: Ubi enim est thēsaurus tuus, ibi est et cor tuum.
ex.en: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also (Matthew 6:21).

en: Thisbe, the Babylonian girl loved by Pyramus

note: Accusative Tiberim, ablative Tiberī. Italian Tevere is the popular development, with b → v and i → e.
Also genitive tigridis. Probably an Iranian word for 'sharp, swift' — the same name as the river Tigris.
-li- before a vowel became palatal gl in Italian tiglio, and vanished in Romanian tei (as in filius → fiu).
Short i became e in all the popular forms (temere, temer, teme). French craindre is tremere 'tremble', reshaped under Gaulish influence.

ex.en: I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts (Vergil).

note: French teindre, peindre (pingere) and plaindre (plangere) share the same -ngere → -ndre change.
Cicero's freed secretary was called Tīrō; his 'Tironian notes' were the first Latin shorthand, and the Tironian sign for et (⁊) still appears on Irish road signs.
Spanish has a learned título and a popular tilde (the ~ over ñ) — both from titulus. English tittle, the dot on an i, is the same word again.
From tegō 'cover'. Vergil calls the Romans the gēns togāta, 'the toga-wearing people'.

ex.en: Let arms yield to the toga (Cicero).

note: Wildly irregular: perfect sustulī, participle sublātum (borrowed from sustollō and the old root of lātus). Italian togliere kept the sense 'take away'.

ex.t: Agnus Deī, quī tollis peccāta mundī
ex.en: Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world

note: French tondeuse (shears, lawnmower) and Romanian tunde 'cut hair' continue it; the tōnsūra was the monk's shaven crown.
English thunder is a native cognate; astonish and stun come from *extonāre 'to strike with thunder'.
From torqueō 'twist': an engine powered by twisted ropes, then torture. Spanish and Portuguese tormenta 'storm' come from the neuter plural tormenta.
Romanian toarce means 'spin wool' and also 'purr' — the cat 'spins'. English torch is probably *torca 'twisted (straw)'.
A torrent is a 'boiling', rushing stream (torrēns); toast and Spanish tostar come from the participle tostus.

ex.en: As many people, so many opinions (Terence).

note: Genitive tōtīus, dative tōtī. Spoken Latin doubled the t (*tottus), whence Italian tutto and French tout; in all five languages it became the word for 'all'.

ex.en: You are all beautiful, my love (Song of Songs).

note: The frequentative of trahō 'drag': 'handle' became 'treat, negotiate' — Italian trattato, French traité, English treaty.
To hand someone over is to betray them: Italian tradire, French trahir — hence the quip traduttore, traditore 'translator, traitor'. English tradition and treason are the same word.
The sense 'translate' — leading a text across into another language — was given to it by the humanist Leonardo Bruni around 1400.
Greek tragōidía means 'goat-song'; why goats is still debated.
In Spanish and Portuguese 'drag' became 'bring' (traer, trazer); in French it narrowed to 'milk (a cow)' — traire.

ex.en: Each is drawn by his own delight (Vergil).

note: Only the participle trāiectus 'a crossing' lives on, in words for a route or journey.
French très 'very' is trāns: 'across, beyond' → 'exceedingly'. In Spanish tras it means 'behind, after'.
trāns + scandō 'climb across'. Hannibal to his men: you are climbing over the walls of Rome itself.
Perfect also trānscucurrī.

ex.en: Thus passes the glory of the world.

note: Its participle trānslātus gave English translate — a text 'carried across'.
trāns + saliō 'jump'. Remus' jump over the new wall gives the verb its most famous moment.
Spoken *traversus lost the n, giving Spanish a través de, French à travers and Portuguese através de 'through, across'.
Italian il Trecento '(the) 300s' names the 1300s, the century of Dante and Giotto.
Romanian alone counts the teens as 'three over ten' (trei-spre-zece), following a Slavic pattern.
Spanish, French and Romanian prefer *tremulāre, 'to keep trembling'. Tremendous is 'that should make you tremble'.
The dais on which a tribune or other magistrate sat to give judgement — hence 'court of law'.
From tribus 'tribe'. The tribūnī plēbis could veto any magistrate's act; the Gracchi made the office famous.

ex.en: to give each his due (Roman law)

note: Dative and ablative plural tribubus. Traditionally linked with trēs — the three original tribes of Rome.
Greek 'three couches': diners reclined, three to a couch, on three sides of a low table.
Spoken Latin stressed *trigínta and dropped the g, hence trenta, treinta, trente.
The procession of a victorious general up to the Capitol. The trump of card games is a worn-down triumph.
Where three roads meet, everyone chats — hence trivial 'commonplace'. Medieval schools called grammar, rhetoric and logic the trivium.
Also called Īlium — hence the Iliad.

ex.t: Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs …
ex.en: I sing of arms and the man who first from the shores of Troy … (Vergil)

note: English thou is a native cognate. Brazilian Portuguese has largely replaced tu with você (< vossa mercê 'your grace').
The straight Roman signal trumpet; the modern brass tuba was named after it in the 19th century.
Guarding is 'watching over': a tutor was a guardian, tuition was guardianship, and intuition is 'looking into'.
In Roman law a tumultus was a sudden military emergency close to home — above all a Gallic invasion.
Ibero-Romance and Romanian built their 'then' on it: Spanish entonces, Portuguese então, Romanian atunci.
Italian has a popular tonaca 'friar's habit' beside the learned tunica.
A disorderly crowd; the verb turbō 'throw into confusion' comes from it, hence disturb and perturb.
French troubler and Romanian tulbura both come from a derivative *turbulāre; English trouble is the French word.
The turbine (named in French in the 1820s) and the turbo are 'spinning things'.
From turba 'commotion'. Phaedrus' wolf complains that the lamb has made his water muddy (turbulentam).
Spanish torpe softened from 'shameful' to 'clumsy'.
Accusative turrim (or turrem), ablative turrī (or turre).

ex.en: tower of ivory (title of the Virgin Mary)

note: Accusative tussim. Medical pertussis is 'severe cough'.
Originally the participle of tueor 'guard'. All of Romance says 'safe' with sēcūrus instead.
The hand-drum of Cybele's ecstatic cult; anatomy borrowed it for the eardrum.
Greek týrannos meant any ruler who seized sole power outside the constitution, not necessarily a cruel one.
The Greek name for the Etruscans (Τυρρηνοί); the sea west of Italy still bears it.
French où is ubi and Italian dove is dē ubi; Spanish donde and Portuguese onde come instead from unde 'whence'.

ex.en: Where I prosper, there is my homeland.

note: The Latin form comes from a Greek dialect variant with l (Olysseús), perhaps through Etruscan — hence English Ulysses.
Genitive ūllīus, dative ūllī. Its negative nūllus 'none' gave English null.
Feminine despite -us, like most Latin tree names. English elm is a native cognate.
Gallia Ulterior was 'Further Gaul', beyond the Alps; an ulterior motive lies beyond what is shown.
Superlative of the stem ulter- 'beyond' (comparative ulterior). In Italian and Spanish it is the everyday word for 'last'.

ex.en: farthest Thule, the end of the world (Vergil)

en: beyond, on the far side of
note: Italian oltre and French outre (outre-mer 'overseas') are the popular forms.

ex.en: nothing further beyond — the limit (said to be written on the Pillars of Hercules)

note: An imitative word every language reshaped its own way: urlare, aullar, hurler, uivar, urla.
English navel and Greek omphalós are cognates. French nombril grew out of l'ombril, with the article fused on and l turned into n.
Spanish and Portuguese sombra gained an s-, probably from sub umbrā 'in the shade'. An umbrella is Italian for a 'little shade'.
Spanish hombro shows the usual m'r → mbr (as hominem → hombre); French replaced it with épaule < spatula.
Also spelled hūmidus; the h, kept in English humid and French humide, comes from a mistaken link with humus 'earth'.
Mostly in questions and negative clauses; nec umquam 'and never'.
A twelfth of anything — of a pound (an ounce) or of a foot (an inch). English got the same word twice.
English water, Greek hýdōr and Latin unda share one root. Spanish onda is a physical or hair wave; a sea wave is ola.
'Whence' became plain 'where' in Spanish donde, Portuguese onde and Romanian unde.
Italian, French and Romanian continue the diminutive ungula; Greek ónyx and English nail are cognates.
Also spelled ungō. Greek Christós 'anointed' is rendered in Latin by ūnctus.
From ūnus: a 'single' perfect pearl, or an onion grown as a single bulb — whence French oignon and English onion. Christian writers used it (feminine) for 'unity', our union.
In Roman law any corporate body; the medieval ūniversitās magistrōrum et scholārium was a guild of teachers and students.
Literally 'turned into one' (ūnus + versus); the neuter ūniversum 'the whole' became our universe.
In all five languages it also became the indefinite article: un, una, um, un.
cite: ūnus, ūna, ūnum (gen. ūnīus, dat. ūnī)

note: City people were supposed to be polished: urbanity is the opposite of rusticity.
Every Romance language replaced it: cīvitās 'citizenship, community' gave città, ciudad, cidade, and French ville is a Roman vīlla.

ex.en: to the City and to the world (papal blessing)

note: Its compound combūrō gave combustion. Romance 'burn' verbs come from cremāre (quemar) or ardēre (arde).
Greek árktos is a cognate — the Arctic lies under the Great Bear. Germanic avoided the old name: bear means 'the brown one'.
A model set: c voiced to g in Spanish and Portuguese, vanished in French ortie, while Romanian urzică turned the t into z.

en: all the way, right up to
note: French jusque (jusqu'à 'until') is probably dē usque.
Interest is the price for the 'use' of money; only later did usury mean excessive interest. French usure means both 'usury' and, as a derivative of user 'wear out', 'wear and tear'.
ūsus est (+ abl.) 'there is need of'. Formed from the participle of ūtor.

en: (+ subj.) so that, in order that
note: With the indicative it means 'as' or 'when'; with the subjunctive it introduces purpose ('in order that') or result ('so that').

ex.en: As you sow, so shall you reap (Cicero).

note: neuter 'neither of the two' gave grammar its neuter gender — neither masculine nor feminine.

ex.en: doctor of both laws (civil and canon)

ex.t: Omne tulit pūnctum quī miscuit ūtile dulcī.
ex.en: He wins every vote who mixes the useful with the pleasant (Horace).

note: Cicero's De Officiis weighs the honestum 'the honourable' against ūtilitās 'expediency'.

en: if only, would that (introducing a wish)
note: With the present or perfect subjunctive for a possible wish, the imperfect or pluperfect for one that can no longer come true.
Takes the ablative: gladiō ūtī 'to use a sword'. The Romance verbs are built on the participle ūsus (*ūsāre).

ex.en: Use it and be happy (inscription on Roman gifts).

note: The neuter of uter 'which of two', used to open a double question: utrum … an …
French raisin 'grape' is racēmus 'cluster'; English raisin narrowed it to the dried fruit. The uvula is a 'little grape'.
It left no descendants: Romance used mulier (moglie), fēmina (femme), spōnsa 'betrothed' (esposa) and socius 'companion' (Romanian soție).
Jenner's smallpox vaccine came from cowpox (variolae vaccīnae), so every vaccine is, etymologically, 'cow stuff'.
A vacātiō was an exemption from duty — hence vacation.
The Romance words come from spoken variants of the same root: Italian vuoto and French vide from *vocitus, Spanish vacío and Portuguese vazio from *vacīvus.

The Romance verbs 'to go' are patchworks: Italian vado, Spanish voy, French vais and Portuguese vou are vādō, while other forms of the same verbs come from īre (Spanish ir, French irai) and from other roots.
Italian guado and French gué show the Germanic w- → gu-/g- (as in guerra, guerre), helped by the Frankish cognate *wad.

ex.en: Woe to the conquered! (the Gaul Brennus, in Livy)

note: Vanilla is Spanish vainilla, 'little sheath' — the seed pod. Italian guaina and French gaine again show a Germanic-style gu-/g-.
The vagus nerve 'wanders' from the brainstem down into the abdomen.
A contraction of validē 'strongly' (from validus).
valē 'be well!' was the Roman goodbye. Spanish vale 'OK' is the same form: 'it is worth it, it's fine'.

ex.t: Sī valēs, bene est; ego valeō.
ex.en: If you are well, that is good; I am well (standard letter opening).

note: Also spelled vallēs. French val survives in place names and in aval 'downstream' (à val); everyday French says vallée.
English wall is an early borrowing: the Germanic peoples met Roman ramparts all along the frontier.
From vānus 'empty'; more common in the compound ēvānēscō.

ex.en: Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity (Ecclesiastes).

note: Portuguese vão lost its n as in mão (manus); em vão, en vain, în van all copy Latin in vānum.
French vair, the mottled squirrel fur of heraldry, is the popular descendant — and perhaps the true material of Cinderella's slipper (pantoufle de vair).

ex.en: A woman is ever a fickle and changeable thing (Mercury in Vergil).

note: Singular 3rd declension (vās, vāsis), plural 2nd (vāsa, vāsōrum). Spanish vaso is the everyday 'drinking glass'; in Caesar vāsa colligere means 'to pack up the baggage'.
Blended with Germanic *wōst- 'waste', it gained a gu-/g-: Italian guastare and French gâter 'spoil', Spanish gastar 'spend' — spending as laying waste.
The first meaning is 'empty, desolate' — the link with English waste.
Augustan poets revived this old word for 'seer' to present themselves as inspired; possibly related to Irish fáith 'prophet'.
Attached to the second word, like -que: plūs minusve 'more or less'.
The verb itself left no Romance descendants (only learned vehiculum words), but English way, wagon and weigh (originally 'carry') are native cognates.
vel … vel 'either … or' (the choice is free, unlike aut … aut); the logician's 'or' sign ∨ is said to stand for vel.
French vélo 'bicycle' is short for vélocipède 'swift-foot'.
The plural vēla became a feminine 'sail' (vela, la voile) while the singular gave 'veil'; to reveal is to 'unveil'.
Portuguese veia lost the n between vowels, as in lua < lūna.
From vēnum dō 'give for sale'; its passive partner is vēneō 'be sold' (vēnum eō).
Italian veleno swapped one n for l (dissimilation); English venom came through French venin.
A venial sin is a 'pardonable' one, as opposed to a mortal sin.
Portuguese vir lost the n between vowels (compare ter < tenēre).

ex.en: I came, I saw, I conquered (Caesar).

note: Only Romanian kept it (vâna 'to hunt'); the West switched to *captiāre. Venison first meant any hunted game.
A ventriloquist 'speaks from the belly' (venter + loquor).
English wind is a native cognate (Germanic w = Latin v); Romanian vânt shows its typical â before n.
Her day, Veneris diēs, is still Friday in Italian venerdì, Spanish viernes, French vendredi and Romanian vineri (English Friday is Frigg's day, a Germanic translation).
Spoken Latin prīma vēra 'early spring' gave primavera and Romanian primăvară; French printemps is prīmum tempus 'first time (of year)'.
For everyday 'word' Romance chose parabola: parola, palabra, parole, palavra; Romanian cuvânt is conventus 'assembly'. English word is a native cognate.

ex.en: In the beginning was the Word (John 1:1).

note: Fear mixed with awe: the compound revereor gave revere and reverend.

en: Vergil (Publius Vergilius Maro), poet of the Aeneid
note: The later spelling Virgil arose from a fancied link with virgō 'maiden' or virga 'magic wand'.
Spanish verdad shows the regular -tātem → -dad (cīvitātem → ciudad).
Red dye was made from insects taken for 'little worms' — so Portuguese vermelho, the ordinary word for 'red', is literally 'wormy'.
English worm is a native cognate; Italian vermicelli are 'little worms'.
Spanish barrer and Portuguese varrer still mean 'sweep'; Spanish turned the v into b, as in many words.
Diminutive of versus. The numbered 'verses' of the Bible are versiculī in Spanish and Portuguese.
From vertō 'turn': the plough turns at the end of a furrow, and the poet at the end of a line.

en: towards, in the direction of (after the noun: Rōmam versus)
note: Italian verso 'towards' continues it; English versus 'against' comes from medieval legal Latin.
Spanish and Portuguese verter means 'to pour' (turning out a jug) and also 'to translate'. English -ward (toward, backward) is a native cognate.
English very first meant 'true' (Chaucer's 'verray parfit gentil knyght'), from Old French verai, now vrai.
Spoken Latin said *berbīx, whence French brebis 'ewe' and Romanian berbec 'ram'.
Each language did something different: Spanish vejiga, Portuguese bexiga (with b-), Romanian bășică (with b- and ș).
French guêpe got its gu- from Germanic *wapsa, a cognate of English wasp. The Vespa scooter was named for its buzz.
Also genitive vesperis. 'The evening before' a feast gave Spanish víspera 'eve' and the church office of vespers; Greek hésperos is a cognate.
Her eternal fire in the Forum was tended by the six Vestal Virgins; her Greek counterpart Hestía, 'hearth', bears a related name.

en: (as noun, f.) a Vestal Virgin, priestess of Vesta
note: Six Vestals kept Vesta's sacred fire burning for thirty years of service; a Vestal who broke her vow of chastity was buried alive.

en: your, yours (of more than one person)
note: Romance continues the older form voster (matching vōs): Italian vostro, Spanish vuestro, French votre.
To investigate is to follow the footprints (in + vestīgāre).

ex.en: The footprints frighten me — all lead into the lion's den (Horace).

note: French vêtir lost its s before t; the circumflex marks the gap (vêtement < vestīmentum).

en: Vesuvius, volcano above the Bay of Naples
note: Its eruption in AD 79, which buried Pompeii and Herculaneum, is described by the younger Pliny in two letters to Tacitus.
From vetus 'old': a soldier who had served his time, often settled on land in a veteran colony.
Veto is simply 'I forbid', the word with which a tribune blocked a measure. Italian vietato 'forbidden' is on every sign.
Spoken Latin preferred the diminutive vetulus > *veclus, source of vecchio, viejo, vieux, velho, vechi — a classic -cl- set.
French and English voyage come from viāticum 'provisions for the road' — still the name of the last communion given to the dying.

ex.t: Ego sum via, et vēritās, et vīta.
ex.en: I am the way, the truth and the life (John 14:6).

note: From vīcus 'village, street': your neighbour lives in the same quarter.
First the animal killed at a sacrifice; the sense 'person harmed' is modern.
Old English borrowed it as wīc — the -wick/-wich of Warwick, Norwich, Greenwich. Greek oîkos 'house' is a cognate.
From vidēre licet 'one may see'. English viz. abbreviates it; the z is a medieval sign for -et.
The passive videor means 'seem'. English wit and wise are native cognates, as is Greek eîdon 'I saw' (originally with w-).

ex.en: I see the better course and approve it; I follow the worse (Ovid).

note: English widow is a native cognate (Germanic w = Latin v); the root means 'separated, bereft'.

en: night watch (a quarter of the night)
note: The Roman night was divided into four vigiliae; Caesar's prīmā vigiliā means 'in the first watch'. French veille also means 'the day before'.

ex.en: in the first watch of the night (Caesar)

note: French veiller 'watch' gave surveillance — 'watching over'.
French vingt keeps a silent g put back from the Latin spelling.
The country estate became the settlement around it: French ville now means 'city'. A villain was first a farm labourer (villānus).
From vinciō 'bind'. In vinculīs 'in chains, in prison'.
From vīnum + dēmō 'take off'. English vintage is French vendange, reshaped after vintner.
In Western Romance it became the plain verb 'to avenge', and English borrowed avenge, revenge and vengeance from French.
-ne- before a vowel became a palatal n: vigna, viña, vigne, vinha. Caesar's vīneae were roofed sheds that protected sappers.
English wine was borrowed with the Roman wine trade, early enough to keep the w- sound that Latin v still had.
Traditionally explained as vīvipara 'bearing live young' — and vipers do.
No Romance language kept it — homō took over everywhere. Its cognate survives in English werewolf ('man-wolf') and world ('age of man').

ex.en: I sing of arms and the man (Vergil).

note: Italian vergine and French vierge show the popular change of short i to e; Spanish virgen keeps the church's Latin vowel.
Spoken Latin shortened it to *virdis, giving verde in four languages.
Literally 'manliness' (vir 'man'): Roman virtūs was above all courage. Italian virtuoso 'excellent, skilled' came into English through music.

ex.en: Virtue comes after cash (Horace, mocking the money-minded).

note: Irregular: acc. vim, abl. vī; plural vīrēs, vīrium 'strength'. English vim (as in 'vim and vigour') is the accusative.

en: undertaker (who carried out paupers' corpses at night)
note: Also vespillō; the Romans derived it from vesper 'evening', since the poor were buried after dark.
A person's 'look' became the face: Italian viso, French visage.
The classic lenition set: Italian keeps the t, Spanish and Portuguese soften it to d, French loses it entirely (vie).

ex.en: Art is long, life is short.

note: A centurion's badge of rank was a vine-staff. Romanian viță de vie 'grapevine' joins vītis and vīnea.

ex.en: I am the vine, you are the branches (John 15:5).

note: Italian has both a learned vizio 'vice' and a popular vezzo 'little habit, charm' (vezzoso 'charming').
Romance uses the compound ēvītāre; English inevitable is 'unavoidable'.
When Caesar says the Britons dye themselves with vitrum, he means woad, not glass.
The diminutive vitellus won out. English veal is Norman French veel: the meat got a French name, the living calf kept an English one.
Romanian alone replaced it, with Slavic trăi; viu 'alive' (< vīvus) survives.

ex.en: While we live, let us live.

rel.n: 'alive', as in 'the quick and the dead'

note: English quick originally meant 'alive' and is a native cognate (Germanic kw- = Latin v-), as is Greek bíos 'life'.
Romance switched to clāmāre 'shout', whose cl- turned into chi-, ll-, ch- and che-: chiamare, llamar, chamar, chema.

ex.t: Multī enim sunt vocātī, paucī vērō ēlēctī.
ex.en: For many are called, but few are chosen (Matthew 22:14).

note: Romanian builds its future on it — voi cânta 'I will sing' — exactly as English does with its cognate will. Spanish and Portuguese say querer (quaerere 'seek').

ex.t: Ferē libenter hominēs id quod volunt crēdunt.
ex.en: People generally believe what they want to believe (Caesar).

note: French voler also means 'to steal' — from falconry, where the hawk 'flies at' and seizes its prey. Portuguese voar lost the l between vowels.
From volvō 'roll'. Fortune's wheel turns (Fortūna volūbilis); English voluble kept only the rolling tongue.
A book was a roll (volvō 'roll'); 'volume' then came to mean a book's bulk, then any bulk — and finally loudness.
Portuguese vontade dropped the l between vowels, as in voar < volāre.
The Epicureans' highest good; in Romance and English it took on a sensual tinge (volupté, voluptuous).
Spanish volver 'to return' (volver a … 'to do again') is the everyday descendant; a revolution is a full 'rolling round'.
Spanish vos survives as a singular 'you' in much of Latin America; the plural vosotros is vōs + alterōs 'you others'.
From voveō 'promise to a god'. Spanish boda 'wedding' is the plural vōta, the marriage vows; English got the word twice, as vow and vote.
A vowel is a 'voiced' letter (vōcālis).

ex.en: The voice of the people is the voice of God.

en: Vulcan, god of fire and smiths
note: His forge was imagined under Etna and the island of Vulcano — hence every volcano.
Dante's De vulgārī ēloquentiā defended writing in the common tongue — Italian il volgare.
Neuter despite its -us. Jerome's Bible became the Vulgate, the 'popular' (vulgāta) edition.

ex.en: I hate the uninitiated crowd and keep it away (Horace).

note: Every Romance language replaced it; Italian ferita and Spanish herida are participles of ferīre 'strike'.
French renard is the fox's name in the medieval Roman de Renart; it drove out Old French goupil (< vulpēcula).
In Romanian vultur means 'eagle'; Spanish buitre and Portuguese abutre show v turning into b.
Only Italian kept it (volto); the others found new 'faces': Spanish cara (Greek 'head'), Portuguese rosto (rōstrum 'beak'), French visage, Romanian față.
A Greek loan; through *zēlōsus it also gave French jaloux and English jealous — zeal and jealousy are one word. Spanish celos means 'jealousy'.
The mild west wind that announces spring; the native Latin name is Favōnius.
Literally a belt; ancient geographers girded the globe with five 'belts' — the torrid, two temperate and two frigid zones.
Originally an adjective, ἀ- 'not' + βυσσός (= βυθός) 'bottom': 'bottomless'. Spanish abismo and French abîme go back to a Late Latin superlative *abyssimus.

ex.en: and darkness was upon the face of the deep (Genesis 1:2, Septuagint)
fine and good: the Athenian ideal of a gentleman

cmp: ἀμείνων / βελτίων / κρείττων, ἄριστος / βέλτιστος / κράτιστος

en: Agamemnon (king of Mycenae, leader of the Greeks at Troy)

note: In Classical Attic it often means 'be content with, put up with'; the Septuagint and NT made it the main verb for love, as in Modern Greek σ' αγαπώ 'I love you'.

ex.t: οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον
ex.en: for God so loved the world (John 3:16)

cite: ἀγαπάω, ἀγαπήσω, ἠγάπησα, ἠγάπηκα, ἠγάπημαι, ἠγαπήθην

ex.t: οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός

note: γγ was pronounced ng as in finger: ἄγγελος sounded angelos, which is why Latin wrote angelus and evangelium.
cite: ἀγγέλλω, ἀγγελῶ, ἤγγειλα, ἤγγελκα, ἤγγελμαι, ἠγγέλθην

note: Jewish Greek used it for God's messengers, translating Hebrew mal'akh 'messenger'; through Latin angelus this sense reached every Western language.

ex.t: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ὁ ἄγγελος· μὴ φοβεῖσθε
ex.en: and the angel said to them: do not be afraid (Luke 2:10)

note: From ἀγέλη 'herd'. Aristotle sets the merely gregarious animal (ἀγελαῖον ζῷον) beside the political one; Modern αγελαίος has sunk to 'vulgar'.

ex.t: Ἅγιος ὁ Θεός, ἅγιος ἰσχυρός, ἅγιος ἀθάνατος
ex.en: Holy God, holy and mighty, holy and immortal (the Trisagion hymn)

note: The Italian port of Ancona was founded by Greeks from Syracuse and named Ἀγκών after the elbow-shaped promontory sheltering its harbour.

cite: ἀγνοέω, ἀγνοήσω, ἠγνόησα, ἠγνόηκα, ἠγνόημαι, ἠγνοήθην

note: Prose prefers the compound κατάγνυμι 'smash'. Sappho's γλῶσσα ἔαγε 'my tongue is broken' uses the intransitive perfect.

ex.en: To an unknown god (an Athenian altar inscription, Acts 17:23)

note: First the gathering of the people (ἀγείρω 'gather'), then the place where they gathered, the civic and commercial heart of the city. Modern αγορά is the market and 'shopping'.
Classical Attic mostly said ὠνέομαι for 'buy'; the Koine sense 'buy' is the one that lives on in Modern Greek.
cite: ἀγοράζω, ἀγοράσω, ἠγόρασα, ἠγόρακα, ἠγόρασμαι, ἠγοράσθην

en: live in the fields, camp out in the open
note: ἀγρός 'field' + αὐλή 'courtyard': the shepherds of Luke 2:8 were ἀγραυλοῦντες, spending the night out in the fields.
Sappho: τρόμος δὲ παῖσαν ἄγρει 'trembling seizes me all over'. Related to ἄγρα 'hunting, catch'.
Greek ἀγρός, Latin ager and English acre are three descendants of one Indo-European word for 'field'.
Cognate with Latin agō; note the reduplicated aorist ἤγαγον. English -agogue 'leader' words: pedagogue (the slave who took a boy to school), demagogue, synagogue ('a bringing together').
cite: ἄγω, ἄξω, ἤγαγον, ἦχα, ἦγμαι, ἤχθην

note: Greek life was 'agonistic': athletics, drama and lawsuits were all ἀγῶνες. The πρωταγωνιστής was the actor who took the first part.
Romance agonia narrowed to the last struggle before death, English agony to extreme pain, while Modern Greek αγωνία is everyday 'anxiety, suspense'.
ἀ- + δαμάω 'tame': the 'unconquerable' substance. Late Latin diamas, reshaped under the influence of words in dia-, gave diamond, while the learned form survives as adamant.
ἀ- + δέος 'fear': in Athens an ἄδεια was a grant of immunity. Modern άδεια is a permit (άδεια οδήγησης 'driving licence') or time off work.
Literally 'from the same womb': copulative ἀ- 'same' + δελφύς 'womb'.

ex.en: doing wrong is worse than being wronged (Plato, Gorgias)

cite: ἀδικέω, ἀδικήσω, ἠδίκησα, ἠδίκηκα, ἠδίκημαι, ἠδικήθην

note: Personal 'unable' vs impersonal ἀδύνατόν ἐστι 'it is impossible'. Modern αδύνατος means 'weak' or 'thin', while αδύνατο is 'impossible'.
Attic contraction of Homeric ἀείδω (Μῆνιν ἄειδε, θεά). Its noun ᾠδή 'song' lives on in ode, melody, rhapsody, comedy, tragedy and parody.
Also αἰεί; same root as αἰών 'age' and Latin aevum. Between article and participle it means 'at the time': ὁ ἀεὶ βασιλεύων 'whoever is king at the time'.

ex.en: God is always doing geometry (a saying Plutarch attributes to Plato)

note: In Homer ἀήρ (then feminine) is the hazy lower air, as opposed to the bright αἰθήρ above. Latin borrowed āēr, whose descendants include Italian aria (also 'tune') and French air.
ἀ- + θάνατος 'death'. Herodotus calls the Persian king's 10,000 elite troops the Ἀθάνατοι 'Immortals', because every fallen man was at once replaced.

en: Athena (goddess of wisdom, crafts and war)

note: Plural like Θῆβαι and Μυκῆναι, but singular Αθήνα in Modern Greek. Note the old adverbs Ἀθήνησι 'at Athens', Ἀθήναζε 'to Athens', Ἀθήνηθεν 'from Athens'.

ex.en: men of Athens (the orators' standard address)

cite: ἀθροίζω, ἀθροίσω, ἤθροισα, ἤθροικα, ἤθροισμαι, ἠθροίσθην

en: Ajax (name of two Greek heroes at Troy)

note: English gypsy is a clipped 'Egyptian', from the mistaken belief that the Roma came from Egypt; Copt is the same Greek word, passed through Coptic and Arabic.
εἰς Ἅιδου (sc. δόμον) 'to the house of Hades' means 'to the underworld, to death'; NT ᾅδης. Ancient folk etymology made it ἀ-ϊδής 'the Unseen'.

ex.en: Shame, Argives! (Iliad 5.787; still a Modern Greek exclamation)

note: From αἴθω 'burn, shine': the shining upper air of the gods, above the misty ἀήρ. Aristotle's fifth element, and much later the name of an anaesthetic.
Poetic, Ionic and biblical; Attic prose says ἐπαινέω. Like ἐπαινέω it keeps a short ε in the σ-tenses (ᾔνεσα).

ex.t: αἰνούντων τὸν θεὸν καὶ λεγόντων· δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις θεῷ
ex.en: praising God and saying, Glory to God in the highest (Luke 2:13–14)

cite: αἰνέω, αἰνέσω, ᾔνεσα, ᾔνεκα, ᾔνημαι, ᾐνέθην

ex.t: βλέπομεν γὰρ ἄρτι δι’ ἐσόπτρου ἐν αἰνίγματι
ex.en: for now we see through a mirror, in a riddle (1 Corinthians 13:12)

ex.t: τί ποτε λέγει ὁ θεός, καὶ τί ποτε αἰνίττεται;
ex.en: what does the god mean, and what is his riddle? (Plato, Apology 21b)

note: Zeus' αἰγίς, a goatskin shield, gave English aegis. Modern γίδι is the diminutive αἰγίδιον with its first syllable worn away.
From αἱροῦμαι 'choose': a chosen course, then a philosophical school; the Church made it a wrongly 'chosen' belief.
The aorist εἷλον comes from another root, like English go/went. Its passive meaning 'be taken' is usually expressed by ἁλίσκομαι.
cite: αἱρέω, αἱρήσω, εἷλον, ᾕρηκα, ᾕρημαι, ᾑρέθην

en: set out, start (by land or sea)
note: Contracted from Homeric ἀείρω. Its compound ἐπαίρω, aorist ἐπῆρα, was reshaped into παίρνω, the everyday Modern Greek verb 'take'.
cite: αἴρω, ἀρῶ, ἦρα, ἦρκα, ἦρμαι, ἤρθην

note: With a participle: ashamed of doing what one does; with an infinitive: ashamed to do it (and so does not).

ex.en: ask, and it will be given to you (Matthew 7:7)

cite: αἰτέω, αἰτήσω, ᾔτησα, ᾔτηκα, ᾔτημαι, ᾐτήθην

ex.en: the blame is the chooser's; God is blameless (Plato, Republic 617e)

note: From αἰτία 'cause; blame'. It keeps ᾱ after ι in the σ-tenses (αἰτιάσομαι). Aesop's moral: people who fail through their own weakness τοὺς καιροὺς αἰτιῶνται, 'blame circumstances'.
Literally 'caught by the spear': αἰχμή 'spearpoint' + ἁλίσκομαι 'be taken'.

ex.en: for ever and ever (lit. to the ages of the ages)

en: the Academy (grove and gymnasium outside Athens)
note: Named after the hero Akademos, whose grove outside Athens held the gymnasium where Plato taught from about 387 BC.

ex.en: a man with an unclean spirit (Mark 1:23)

note: ἀ- + κάμνω 'grow weary'. Homer's fire is ἀκάματον πῦρ; Sophocles' Earth is ἄφθιτον, ἀκαμάταν 'imperishable, untiring'.
Epic; Sappho's ἄκαν is the Aeolic form. Homer's ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ, 'they all fell hushed in silence', follows many a startling speech.
ἀ- + κλέος 'fame'. Herodotus wrote so that great deeds might not become ἀκλεᾶ, 'unsung' (Ionic contraction of ἀκλεέα).

en: be in full bloom, be at one's peak
note: From ἀκμή 'point, prime'. Thucydides judged the war would be great because both sides entered it ἀκμάζοντες, 'at the peak of their power'.

ex.en: it stands on the razor's edge (Iliad 10.173)
he who has ears, let him hear (Matthew 11:15)

note: Later Greek moved from 'exact' to 'scarce, hard to get' to 'expensive'; Modern Greek has learned ακριβής 'exact' and popular ακριβός 'dear'.
In predicate position it means 'the top of': ἄκρον τὸ ὄρος 'the top of the mountain'. An acrobat (ἀκροβάτης) is one who walks on tiptoe.
Contracted from ἀέκων (ἀ- + ἑκών 'willing'). It agrees with the subject where English uses an adverb: ἄκων ἀπῆλθεν 'he left unwillingly'.
A stock figure of Greek comedy, set against the self-deprecating εἴρων, from whom English irony gets its name.
-algia 'pain' forms medical words; nostalgia (νόστος 'homecoming' + ἄλγος) was coined by a Swiss doctor in 1688 for soldiers' homesickness.

en: warmth, heat (of the sun or a fire)
note: Opposed to ψῦχος 'cold': in Aesop's fable the Sun's ἀλέα does what the North Wind could not.

ex.t: πρὶν ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι τρὶς ἀπαρνήσῃ με
ex.en: before the cock crows, you will deny me three times (Matthew 26:34)

note: Built on ἀ- + λήθω 'escape notice' (cf. λήθη 'forgetting'): truth as what is 'not hidden', an etymology Heidegger made much of.

ex.t: καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν, καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς
ex.en: and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free (John 8:32)

note: From ἀληθής 'true'. The moral of the boy who cried wolf: liars are not believed even ὅταν ἀληθεύωσι, 'when they tell the truth'.

ex.en: Christ is risen! — Truly he is risen! (Easter greeting, still in use)

note: From ἅλς 'sea'. The everyday Modern word ψαράς comes from ψάρι 'fish', itself from ὀψάριον 'relish (eaten with bread)'.

ex.en: I will make you fishers of men (Matthew 4:19)

en: man of Halicarnassus (Greek city in Caria, modern Bodrum)
note: Herodotus' Ionic form is Ἁλικαρνησσεύς, gen. Ἁλικαρνησσέος. The city's tomb of Mausolus, the Mausoleum, gave English mausoleum.
Serves as the passive of αἱρέω; its aorist ἑάλων (ἥλων) and perfect ἑάλωκα are active in form, passive in meaning. Modern Greeks call the fall of Constantinople in 1453 η Άλωση.
ἀλκυονίδες ἡμέραι, the 'halcyon days', were calm winter days when the bird was believed to nest on the sea; the English h- comes from a false link with ἅλς 'sea'.

cite: ἀλλάττω, ἀλλάξω, ἤλλαξα, ἤλλαχα, ἤλλαγμαι, ἠλλάχθην

rel.n: formal; usual ο ένας τον άλλον

note: Neuter ἄλλο has no -ν, like τοῦτο and αὐτό. Doubled it expresses variety: ἄλλος ἄλλα λέγει 'different people say different things'.
ἄλλως τε καί, literally 'both otherwise and', means 'especially'.
τὰ ἄλογα (ζῷα) were 'the dumb animals'; in medieval Greek τὸ ἄλογον narrowed to 'the horse', and άλογο replaced ἵππος as the everyday word.
Greek turned initial s- into h-: ἅλς = Latin sāl, as ἕξ = sex and ἑπτά = septem.

ex.t: ὑμεῖς ἐστε τὸ ἅλας τῆς γῆς
ex.en: you are the salt of the earth (Matthew 5:13, Koine ἅλας)

ex.t: Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ
ex.en: I am the Alpha and the Omega (Revelation 1:8)

ex.t: πόλλ’ οἶδ’ ἀλώπηξ, ἀλλ’ ἐχῖνος ἓν μέγα
ex.en: the fox knows many things, but the hedgehog one big thing (Archilochus)

en: (+ dat.) together with, at the same time as
note: ἅμα τῇ ἡμέρᾳ or ἅμα ἕῳ 'at daybreak'. In Modern Greek άμα is a colloquial conjunction 'when, if'.

en: Amazon (one of a mythical race of warrior women)

note: Wagon, then carriage, then car: Modern αμάξι is the everyday word for a car.

ex.t: πάτερ, ἥμαρτον εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ ἐνώπιόν σου
ex.en: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you (Luke 15:18)

cite: ἁμαρτάνω, ἁμαρτήσομαι, ἥμαρτον, ἡμάρτηκα, ἡμάρτημαι, ἡμαρτήθην

note: In Aristotle's Poetics the tragic hero falls through some ἁμαρτία, an error of judgement rather than wickedness.

ex.t: ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ
ex.en: God, be merciful to me, a sinner (Luke 18:13)

en: (adj.) not drunken; a remedy against drunkenness
note: ἀ- + μεθύω 'be drunk': the purple stone was believed to keep its wearer sober.
Homer's formula τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη 'and answering him he said' treats a reply as an exchange; Modern αμοιβή means 'payment, fee'.
One of three comparatives of ἀγαθός: ἀμείνων 'better (in ability or worth)', βελτίων 'better (morally)', κρείττων 'stronger, superior'.

cite: ἀμελέω, ἀμελήσω, ἠμέλησα, ἠμέληκα, ἠμέλημαι, ἠμελήθην

en: from some point or other, from anywhere (Homeric)
note: From an old word ἁμός 'some' (cf. οὐδαμός 'none'): τῶν ἁμόθεν γε, θεά … εἰπέ 'of these things, goddess, starting where you will, tell us too' (Odyssey 1.10).

ex.t: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος, ὑμεῖς τὰ κλήματα
ex.en: I am the vine, you are the branches (John 15:5)

note: Late Latin amandula, a reshaping of amygdala, is the source of Italian mandorla, French amande and English almond.

en: ward off, keep off (something from someone)

ex.t: εἷς οἰωνὸς ἄριστος, ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ πάτρης
ex.en: one omen is best: to fight for one's country (Hector, Iliad 12.243)

note: Originally 'on both sides'. οἱ ἀμφὶ Σωκράτη 'those around Socrates' means his circle, or sometimes Socrates himself.
Shortened from ἀμφιφορεύς 'carried on both sides' (ἀμφί + φέρω), from its two handles.

Not translatable alone: with the optative it makes a potential ('would'), with past indicatives an unreal condition, and with the subjunctive in relative clauses it adds '-ever': ὃς ἂν ἔλθῃ 'whoever comes'.
Xenophon's Anabasis is the 'march up' from the coast into Asia. Modern ανεβαίνω has taken its ε from the aorist ἀνέβην.

cite: ἀναβάλλω, ἀναβαλῶ, ἀνέβαλον, ἀναβέβληκα, ἀναβέβλημαι, ἀνεβλήθην

note: Literally 'know again, recognize' the letters; ancient reading was normally aloud. Koine spelled it ἀναγινώσκω; Modern Greek keeps ανάγνωση 'reading' and αναγνώστης 'reader'.
cite: ἀναγιγνώσκω, ἀναγνώσομαι, ἀνέγνων, ἀνέγνωκα, ἀνέγνωσμαι, ἀνεγνώσθην
ἀναγκάζω, ἀναγκάσω, ἠνάγκασα, ἠνάγκακα, ἠνάγκασμαι, ἠναγκάσθην

ex.en: not even the gods fight against necessity (Simonides, quoted by Plato)

en: vine trained up a tree, climbing vine
note: ἀνά 'up' + δένδρον 'tree'. Aesop's fox sees grapes hanging from one, just out of reach.
Two spellings of 'thing set up (for a god)' split apart: ἀνάθημα 'votive offering' and ἀνάθεμα 'thing accursed' (Galatians 1:8).
Used of the god 'taking up' a question and replying: ἀνεῖλεν οὖν ἡ Πυθία μηδένα σοφώτερον εἶναι, 'the Pythia answered that no one was wiser' (Apology 21a).
cite: ἀναιρέω, ἀναιρήσω, ἀνεῖλον, ἀνῄρηκα, ἀνῄρημαι, ἀνῃρέθην
ἀναλίσκω, ἀναλώσω, ἀνήλωσα, ἀνήλωκα, ἀνήλωμαι, ἀνηλώθην

en: (Plato) recollection of what the soul knew before birth

ex.t: τοῦτο ποιεῖτε εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν
ex.en: do this in remembrance of me (Luke 22:19)

note: Already in Mycenaean Linear B as wa-na-ka (ϝάναξ), the palace king. Homer's Agamemnon is ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν 'lord of men'.
Plato's cave has its entrance ἀναπεπταμένην πρὸς τὸ φῶς, 'open to the light' (perfect passive participle).
From ἀνατέλλω 'rise': the east is where the sun rises, exactly like Latin oriēns 'rising', whence Orient.

cite: ἀναφέρω, ἀνοίσω, ἀνήνεγκα, ἀνενήνοχα, ἀνενήνεγμαι, ἀνηνέχθην

note: Egyptian Christians who withdrew into the desert were ἀναχωρηταί, whence anchorite. Greek airports label departures ΑΝΑΧΩΡΗΣΕΙΣ.
Cognate with Latin anima 'breath, soul' and animus 'mind': the root means 'breathe'.
ἀ(ν)- + ἐξετάζω 'examine closely'.

ex.t: ὁ δὲ ἀνεξέταστος βίος οὐ βιωτὸς ἀνθρώπῳ
ex.en: the unexamined life is not worth living for a human being (Plato, Apology 38a)

note: Originally 'first cousin'; in Byzantine Greek it shifted to 'nephew', the meaning of its Latin cognate nepōs (whence nephew, neveu, nipote).

en: man (as opposed to woman or boy)
note: Irregular: ἀνήρ, ἀνδρός, ἀνδρί, ἄνδρα, voc. ἄνερ, dat. pl. ἀνδράσι. Modern άντρας grew out of the accusative ἄνδρα.

ex.en: Tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns (Odyssey 1.1)
man is the measure of all things (Protagoras)

en: make stand up, raise (also from the dead)
note: Like ἵστημι: transitive in the present, future and first aorist ἀνέστησα; intransitive in the second aorist ἀνέστην and the perfect. Χριστὸς ἀνέστη 'Christ is risen' uses the intransitive aorist.
Also ἀνοίγω, the form Koine and Modern Greek kept. The strange augment ἀνέῳξα goes back to an old initial digamma (ϝοίγνυμι).

ex.en: knock, and it will be opened to you (Matthew 7:7)

cite: ἀνοίγνυμι, ἀνοίξω, ἀνέῳξα, ἀνέῳχα, ἀνέῳγμαι, ἀνεῴχθην

en: hold out, withstand, endure (+ dat. or πρός + acc.)
(mid. + gen.) cling to, hold on to
note: Aesop's traveller, ἀντεχόμενος τῆς ἐσθῆτος 'clinging to his clothes', resists the wind but cannot ἀντέχειν 'hold out' against the sun's heat.
Originally 'facing, opposite'; Latin ante 'before' is cognate. ἀνθ’ ὧν 'in return for which, because'.

ex.t: ὀφθαλμὸν ἀντὶ ὀφθαλμοῦ καὶ ὀδόντα ἀντὶ ὀδόντος
ex.en: an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth (Matthew 5:38)

cite: ἀντιλέγω, ἀντερῶ, ἀντεῖπον, ἀντείρηκα, ἀντείρημαι, ἀντερρήθην

note: From ἀνύω 'accomplish'. The fable's moral: τὸ πείθειν τοῦ βιάζεσθαι ἀνυτικώτερον, 'persuasion is more effective than force'.

ex.t: ὁδὸς ἄνω κάτω μία καὶ ὡυτή
ex.en: the way up and the way down are one and the same (Heraclitus)

note: ἄνω 'up' + -θεν 'from'. In John 3:3 γεννηθῆναι ἄνωθεν is both 'born from above' and 'born again'.
ἄξιος 'worthy' + λόγος 'account'. Thucydides expected his war to be ἀξιολογώτατον, 'the most worth recording' of all before it.
Originally 'weighing as much as' (ἄγω in the sense 'weigh'). At an Orthodox ordination the people still cry Ἄξιος! 'He is worthy!'

ex.t: ἄξιος γὰρ ὁ ἐργάτης τοῦ μισθοῦ αὐτοῦ
ex.en: for the worker deserves his wages (Luke 10:7)

cite: ἀξιόω, ἀξιώσω, ἠξίωσα, ἠξίωκα, ἠξίωμαι, ἠξιώθην
ἀπαγγέλλω, ἀπαγγελῶ, ἀπήγγειλα, ἀπήγγελκα, ἀπήγγελμαι, ἀπηγγέλθην

note: Ionic ἀγινέω is a by-form of ἄγω 'lead, carry'; Herodotus' Phoenicians came ἀπαγινέοντας φορτία, 'carrying cargoes' of Egyptian and Assyrian goods.
Attic takes the future and aorist from ἐρῶ and εἶπον. Greek signs read Απαγορεύεται το κάπνισμα 'Smoking is forbidden'.
cite: ἀπαγορεύω, ἀπερῶ, ἀπεῖπον, ἀπείρηκα, ἀπείρημαι, ἀπερρήθην

note: The opposite of παιδεία. The Cave is an image of our nature παιδείας τε πέρι καὶ ἀπαιδευσίας, 'in respect of education and the lack of it' (Republic 514a).

en: demand back, ask for what is owed
cite: ἀπαιτέω, ἀπαιτήσω, ἀπῄτησα, ἀπῄτηκα, ἀπῄτημαι, ἀπῃτήθην
ἀπαλλάττω, ἀπαλλάξω, ἀπήλλαξα, ἀπήλλαχα, ἀπήλλαγμαι, ἀπηλλάγην

note: From meeting a person to meeting a question: Modern απαντώ and απάντηση mean 'answer'.

cite: ἀπατάω, ἀπατήσω, ἠπάτησα, ἠπάτηκα, ἠπάτημαι, ἠπατήθην

note: ἀ- + πείθομαι 'obey'. Socrates cannot keep quiet, he says, because that would be τῷ θεῷ ἀπειθεῖν, 'disobeying the god' (Apology 37e).
ἀπό + εἰκάζω 'liken'. The Cave begins with the imperative ἀπείκασον, 'compare…' (Republic 514a).
Compound of εἰμί 'be' (impf. ἀπῆν, inf. ἀπεῖναι); not to be confused with ἄπειμι 'go away', from εἶμι.
Compound of εἶμι 'go' (inf. ἀπιέναι, impf. ἀπῄειν). In Attic its present has future meaning; ἀπέρχομαι and ἀπῆλθον supply the other tenses.
ἀ- + πέρας 'limit'. For Anaximander the source of all things was τὸ ἄπειρον, 'the Boundless'.
ἀπέχω was the word written on receipts, 'I have received in full', which explains the Gospel phrase below.

ex.en: do not be unbelieving, but believing (John 20:27)

note: Cognate with Latin ab and English of/off. Modern από takes the accusative: από την Αθήνα 'from Athens'.

en: turn out, result, come to pass

cite: ἀποβάλλω, ἀποβαλῶ, ἀπέβαλον, ἀποβέβληκα, ἀποβέβλημαι, ἀπεβλήθην

ex.en: This is the display of the inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassus (Herodotus' opening, Ionic)

cite: ἀποδείκνυμι, ἀποδείξω, ἀπέδειξα, ἀποδέδειχα, ἀποδέδειγμαι, ἀπεδείχθην

note: From ἀποδείκνυμι 'show forth'. Herodotus' Ionic ἀπόδεξις is the 'setting-forth' of his research; for Aristotle and Euclid ἀπόδειξις is strict logical proof; a Modern Greek απόδειξη is also a till receipt.

ex.en: this is the setting-out of the inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassus (Histories, opening)

en: give back, return, pay (what is due)

ex.t: ἀπόδοτε οὖν τὰ Καίσαρος Καίσαρι καὶ τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τῷ θεῷ
ex.en: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's (Matthew 22:21)

cite: ἀποδίδωμι, ἀποδώσω, ἀπέδωκα, ἀποδέδωκα, ἀποδέδομαι, ἀπεδόθην

en: (mid. and aor. ἀπέδυν) strip oneself, undress
note: The North Wind and the Sun compete over which can strip a traveller; the undressing room of a gymnasium was the ἀποδυτήριον.
cite: ἀποδύω, ἀποδύσω, ἀπέδυσα / ἀπέδυν, ἀποδέδυκα, ἀποδέδυμαι, ἀπεδύθην

note: Latin apothēca, worn down in popular speech, became Italian bottega and Spanish bodega; French boutique came via Provençal. An apothecary was first a storekeeper.
Serves as the passive of ἀποκτείνω: ἀπέθανεν ὑπὸ τῶν πολεμίων 'he was killed by the enemy'. The perfect is the simple τέθνηκα 'I am dead'.
A 'home away' (ἀπό + οἶκος). Unlike a Roman colōnia, a Greek ἀποικία was an independent city, tied to its mother city (μητρόπολις) by religion and sentiment.

en: grow weary, give up from exhaustion
(+ inf. or ptcp.) tire of doing

note: Attic aorist ἀπεκρινάμην; the NT prefers ἀπεκρίθην, as in ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν 'he answered and said'.

cite: ἀποκρύπτω, ἀποκρύψω, ἀπέκρυψα, ἀποκέκρυφα, ἀποκέκρυμμαι, ἀπεκρύφθην

note: Attic has no passive: 'be killed' is ἀποθνῄσκω ὑπό + gen.
Sophocles' ode on man also calls the lawless man ἄπολις, 'cityless'.

ex.t: ὁ ἄπολις διὰ φύσιν καὶ οὐ διὰ τύχην ἤτοι φαῦλός ἐστιν, ἢ κρείττων ἢ ἄνθρωπος
ex.en: he who is without a city by nature and not by chance is either a poor sort of being or more than human (Aristotle, Politics 1253a)

en: (mid. ἀπόλλυμαι, aor. ἀπωλόμην, pf. ἀπόλωλα) perish, be lost

ex.en: he was lost and is found (Luke 15:24)

en: Apollo (god of prophecy, music, healing and archery)

note: Plato's Ἀπολογία Σωκράτους is Socrates' defence speech, and anything but an apology; the sense 'expression of regret' developed later in English.

ex.t: νῦν ἀπολύεις τὸν δοῦλόν σου, δέσποτα
ex.en: now, Lord, you let your servant depart (the Nunc dimittis, Luke 2:29)

cite: ἀπολύω, ἀπολύσω, ἀπέλυσα, ἀπολέλυκα, ἀπολέλυμαι, ἀπελύθην
ἀπονέμω, ἀπονεμῶ, ἀπένειμα, ἀπονενέμηκα, ἀπονενέμημαι, ἀπενεμήθην
ἀποπέμπω, ἀποπέμψω, ἀπέπεμψα, ἀποπέπομφα, ἀποπέπεμμαι, ἀπεπέμφθην

en: be at a loss, be in doubt
cite: ἀπορέω, ἀπορήσω, ἠπόρησα, ἠπόρηκα, ἠπόρημαι, ἠπορήθην

note: Plato's early dialogues end in ἀπορία, the productive bewilderment of discovering that one does not know.

cite: ἀποστέλλω, ἀποστελῶ, ἀπέστειλα, ἀπέσταλκα, ἀπέσταλμαι, ἀπεστάλην
ἀποστερέω, ἀποστερήσω, ἀπεστέρησα, ἀπεστέρηκα, ἀπεστέρημαι, ἀπεστερήθην

note: In Attic it could mean a naval expedition; Christian use made it 'one sent out', above all the Twelve.

en: (mid.) cut off for oneself, carve off a share
cite: ἀποτέμνω, ἀποτεμῶ, ἀπέτεμον, ἀποτέτμηκα, ἀποτέτμημαι, ἀπετμήθην

note: Its noun ἀποθήκη 'storehouse' became Latin apothēca, whence English apothecary, Spanish bodega and French boutique.
cite: ἀποτίθημι, ἀποθήσω, ἀπέθηκα, ἀποτέθηκα, ἀποτέθειμαι, ἀπετέθην

note: In the Antigone ode man wears away (ἀποτρύεται) Earth, highest of the gods, with his ploughs year after year.

cite: ἀποφέρω, ἀποίσω, ἀπήνεγκα, ἀπενήνοχα, ἀπενήνεγμαι, ἀπηνέχθην

ex.en: do not touch me (Noli me tangere, John 20:17)

en: after all, as it turns out
note: Postpositive; not to be confused with interrogative ἆρα. It often marks a realization: οὐκ ἄρα 'not after all'.
Leaves the question open, like Latin -ne; ἆρ’ οὐ expects 'yes' (Latin nōnne), ἆρα μή expects 'no' (Latin num).
Contracted from ἀ-εργός 'not working'. Argon, discovered in 1894, was named for being chemically 'lazy'. A different ἀργός means 'bright, swift'.
Neuter, like γένος: Ἄργος, Ἄργους — not ἀργός 'idle'. Its people, the Ἀργεῖοι, are one of Homer's names for all the Greeks.

ex.t: οἱ δὲ ἔστησαν αὐτῷ τριάκοντα ἀργύρια
ex.en: and they paid him thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15)

en: (ἀρέσκει μοι) I am content; I resolve
note: Modern Greek built a new present αρέσω on the aorist ἤρεσα. Μου αρέσει 'it pleases me' = 'I like it', just like Spanish me gusta.
Not only moral: a horse, a knife or a field has its ἀρετή, the excellence proper to it. In the Meno Socrates asks whether ἀρετή can be taught.
The Book of Numbers is Ἀριθμοί in the Septuagint. Logarithm was coined in 1614 by John Napier from λόγος 'ratio' + ἀριθμός.
Probably a euphemism, 'the better one', to avoid naming the unlucky side; εὐώνυμος 'of good name' is another word for 'left'.

ex.t: αἰὲν ἀριστεύειν καὶ ὑπείροχον ἔμμεναι ἄλλων
ex.en: always to be the best and to stand above the rest (Iliad 6.208)

note: The Arctic is the region under the Bear, the northern constellation; Antarctic is 'opposite the Bear'. Latin ursus is a cognate.

cite: ἁρμόζω, ἁρμόσω, ἥρμοσα, ἥρμοκα, ἥρμοσμαι, ἡρμόσθην

note: First a carpenter's joint (ἁρμόζω 'fit together'), then the fitting together of musical notes.

ex.en: but he denied it before them all (Matthew 26:70)

en: strive to win, try to save
note: Epic; future and aorist are shared with αἴρομαι. Odysseus was ἀρνύμενος ἥν τε ψυχὴν καὶ νόστον ἑταίρων, 'striving to win his own life and his comrades' return' (Odyssey 1.5).

cite: ἁρπάζω, ἁρπάσομαι, ἥρπασα, ἥρπακα, ἥρπασμαι, ἡρπάσθην

rel.n: a Persian word reshaped to look Greek

note: ἀ- + ῥώννυμι 'strengthen' (ἔρρωσο 'farewell!' is literally 'be strong'). In Modern Greek it is the everyday word for 'ill'.

en: Artaxerxes (name of Persian kings, esp. Artaxerxes II, 404–358 BC, brother of Cyrus the Younger)
Artemis (goddess of hunting, wild animals and childbirth)

ex.en: Great is Artemis of the Ephesians! (Acts 19:28)

note: Ancient anatomists found arteries empty in corpses and thought they carried air, hence the shared name with the windpipe, the τραχεῖα ἀρτηρία 'rough artery', whence trachea.
The humble ψωμίον, a morsel of bread, displaced ἄρτος in everyday speech; άρτος survives in church and in words like αρτοποιείο 'bakery'.

ex.t: τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον δὸς ἡμῖν σήμερον
ex.en: give us this day our daily bread (Matthew 6:11)
in the beginning was the Word (John 1:1)

note: Active ἄρχω 'be first, rule'; middle ἄρχομαι 'make a beginning (of one's own part)'. Both take the genitive.
cite: ἄρχω, ἄρξω, ἦρξα, ἦρχα, ἦργμαι, ἤρχθην

note: ἀ- + σβέννυμι 'quench'. Homer's gods laugh with ἄσβεστος γέλως, 'unquenchable laughter'; the same word gave asbestos and the lime used to whitewash island houses.

ex.t: ἡ γὰρ δύναμις ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται
ex.en: for power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9)

note: From ἀσθενής 'weak' (ἀ- + σθένος 'strength'); Modern ασθενής is a 'patient'.

ex.t: ἐπεὶ δὲ ἠσθένει Δαρεῖος καὶ ὑπώπτευε τελευτὴν τοῦ βίου
ex.en: when Darius fell ill and suspected the end of his life was near (Xenophon, Anabasis 1.1.1)

note: First used of crafting objects, then of athletic training; the ἀσκητής was an athlete before he was a hermit, whence ascetic.
cite: ἀσκέω, ἀσκήσω, ἤσκησα, ἤσκηκα, ἤσκημαι, ἠσκήθην

en: Asclepius (god of medicine, son of Apollo)
note: The Romans called him Aesculapius; his staff with a single serpent is still the emblem of medicine.

ex.t: ὦ Κρίτων, τῷ Ἀσκληπιῷ ὀφείλομεν ἀλεκτρυόνα
ex.en: Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius (Socrates' last words, Phaedo 118a)
either with it or on it (a Spartan mother handing her son his shield; Doric, quoted by Plutarch)

note: Herodotus says the Greeks call Σύριοι the people whom foreigners call Ἀσσύριοι; the name Syria is probably a clipped Assyria.
From ἄστυ 'town', as Latin urbānus comes from urbs: city manners became wit. Modern αστείο is 'a joke'.
One Indo-European word with three outcomes: ἀστήρ, Latin stēlla, English star. Asterisk is from the diminutive ἀστερίσκος. Dative plural ἀστράσι.

ex.t: ἐθεώρουν τὸν σατανᾶν ὡς ἀστραπὴν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ πεσόντα
ex.en: I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18)

en: town, city (esp. the town of Athens)
note: ἄστυ is the physical town, πόλις the city-state and its citizens; an Athenian going into town from Piraeus or the country went εἰς ἄστυ.
ἀ- + σφάλλω 'trip up': 'not liable to fall'. Modern ασφάλεια is 'safety', 'insurance' and an electrical 'fuse'.
ἀ- + σχολή 'leisure': business is the absence of leisure, exactly like Latin negōtium (nec + ōtium). σχολή itself became 'school'.

Usually plural in Homer. Odysseus' men perished σφετέρῃσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν, 'through their own recklessness' (Odyssey 1.7), and Zeus soon complains that mortals blame the gods for woes they bring on themselves.
ἅτε + participle gives a cause the speaker vouches for (ἅτε παῖς ὤν 'since he was a child'), while ὡς + participle gives an alleged one.
In Homer ἄτη is the god-sent blindness that drives a hero to ruin — Agamemnon blames Ἄτη, eldest daughter of Zeus (Iliad 19); in tragedy it is the ruin itself. Doric ἄτα.
ἀ- + τέμνω 'cut'. Democritus' indivisible particles; Latin rendered the same idea as indīviduum, and Modern άτομο means both 'atom' and 'individual'.
Socrates was famous for his ἀτοπία, his 'out-of-placeness'; in Plato ἄτοπον often means 'absurd'.

en: (du. and pl. Ἀτρεΐδαι) the two sons of Atreus
note: A Homeric patronymic in -ίδης 'son of'. In Iliad 1.7 Ἀτρεΐδης τε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν is Agamemnon, 'lord of men'.

rel.n: from the Attic order in architecture

note: Really an adjective, ἡ Ἀττικὴ (γῆ) 'the Attic land'. Attic is also the name of the Athenian dialect, the classical standard.

en: in turn, on the other hand
note: αὖθις is an extended form. In argument αὖ marks the next point: ἐάντε δ’ αὖ λέγω 'and if, on the other hand, I say…' (Apology 38a).
From 'doer of the deed', especially a murderer, to 'one with authority'. Byzantine αφέντης passed into Turkish as efendi.
Latin took it over as aula 'palace, hall'; in Italian and Spanish an aula is now a classroom.
A double-reed pipe rather than a flute; it accompanied the tragic chorus. Hydraulic comes from the water-organ, ὕδραυλις (ὕδωρ + αὐλός).

ex.t: ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι
ex.en: he must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30)

cite: αὐξάνω, αὐξήσω, ηὔξησα, ηὔξηκα, ηὔξημαι, ηὐξήθην

ex.t: φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνῄσκομεν
ex.en: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die (1 Corinthians 15:32)

note: Homer's word for 'but' (= ἀτάρ, δέ), often opening a new step in the story: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί 'but when…'.
αὐτός + ἀρκέω 'suffice'. For Aristotle the πόλις exists because no individual has αὐτάρκεια; whoever needs nothing is 'either a beast or a god'.
αὐτίκα μάλα 'this very instant'. In Attic argument αὐτίκα can also introduce an example, 'for instance'.

en: one's own master, with full powers
living by one's own laws, independent

note: Three uses by position: αὐτὸς ὁ βασιλεύς 'the king himself', ὁ αὐτὸς βασιλεύς 'the same king', αὐτόν 'him'. Modern αυτός is the demonstrative 'this' and the third-person pronoun.

ex.en: he himself said it, i.e. Pythagoras said so (ipse dixit; Doric)

note: The everyday Modern Greek word for 'neck' is λαιμός; αυχένας is formal and medical.

en: (mid.) take away for oneself, rob (someone of something)
cite: ἀφαιρέω, ἀφαιρήσω, ἀφεῖλον, ἀφῄρηκα, ἀφῄρημαι, ἀφῃρέθην
ἀφανίζω, ἀφανιῶ, ἠφάνισα, ἠφάνικα, ἠφάνισμαι, ἠφανίσθην

note: ἀ- + φθίνω 'waste away'. Achilles' κλέος ἄφθιτον 'undying fame' (Iliad 9.413) matches Vedic ákṣiti śravas, an inherited phrase of Indo-European poetry.
Modern αφήνω 'leave, let' grew out of the aorist ἀφῆκα; colloquial άσε 'let!' is its worn-down imperative.

ex.t: καὶ ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν

cite: ἀφίημι, ἀφήσω, ἀφῆκα, ἀφεῖκα, ἀφεῖμαι, ἀφείθην

note: Usually with εἰς or ἐπί + acc. Greek airports still label arrivals ΑΦΙΞΕΙΣ, from the noun ἄφιξις.

en: (intr., mid.) stand away from, revolt from (+ gen.)
note: Thucydides' word for allies who 'stood away from', i.e. revolted from, Athens. Transitive in the first aorist ἀπέστησα, intransitive in the second aorist ἀπέστην.
Hesiod derives her name from ἀφρός 'foam', since she rose from the sea-foam; the etymology is popular, not historical.

en: foam, froth (of the sea, of the mouth)

ex.t: ἄφρων, ταύτῃ τῇ νυκτὶ τὴν ψυχήν σου ἀπαιτοῦσιν ἀπὸ σοῦ
ex.en: fool! this very night your soul is demanded of you (Luke 12:20)

note: From ἄχθος 'burden': to feel weighed down. Takes a dative of the cause or a participle (ἄχθομαι ἀκούων 'I am annoyed to hear').

en: Achilles (the greatest Greek hero at Troy)
note: Homer spells it with one or two λ (gen. Ἀχιλῆος). The Achilles tendon recalls the post-Homeric story of the heel by which Thetis held him when dipping him in the Styx.

ex.en: Sing, goddess, the wrath of Achilles, son of Peleus (Iliad 1.1)

note: Also ἄχρις before vowels; a synonym of μέχρι, which Modern Greek kept.
English bathos comes from Pope's mock treatise Peri Bathous (1727) on the art of sinking from the sublime to the ridiculous.

ex.t: ὦ βάθος πλούτου καὶ σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως θεοῦ
ex.en: O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! (Romans 11:33)

note: The simple verb is mostly poetic; prose prefers compounds (ἀνα-, ἀπο-, ἐκ-, εἰσ-βαίνω). Modern μπαίνω 'go in' and βγαίνω 'go out' continue ἐμβαίνω and ἐκβαίνω.
The rod-shaped microbes seen under 19th-century microscopes were named after the diminutive βακτήριον, 'little stick'.
Latin balneum (older balineum) is a loan from βαλανεῖον. Its Italian descendant bagno came back into Greek as μπάνιο, the everyday word for a bath or a swim.
A whole English family: problem, emblem, symbol, parable (παραβολή), hyperbole and devil (διάβολος 'one who throws across, slanderer').
cite: βάλλω, βαλῶ, ἔβαλον, βέβληκα, βέβλημαι, ἐβλήθην

note: A derivative of βάπτω 'dip'. Modern βαφτίζω also means simply 'give a name'.

ex.t: ἐγὼ μὲν ὑμᾶς βαπτίζω ἐν ὕδατι

note: Imitative: foreign speech sounded like 'bar-bar'. Originally neutral (Herodotus uses it of the Persians without contempt); 'savage' came later.
Cognate with Latin gravis: Indo-European gʷ- became β in Greek, g in Latin. The grave accent is ἡ βαρεῖα, the 'heavy' accent.
From βάσανος 'touchstone', used to test gold. In Athenian courts a slave's evidence counted only if taken under torture (βάσανος).
cite: βασανίζω, βασανιῶ, ἐβασάνισα, βεβασάνικα, βεβασάνισμαι, ἐβασανίσθην

note: Accent decides: βασίλεια (short final -α) 'queen', βασιλεία 'kingdom', βασίλειον 'palace'. Koine preferred βασίλισσα.
βασιλεύς without the article meant the Great King of Persia. In democratic Athens the ἄρχων βασιλεύς kept the old kings' religious duties.
The ingressive aorist ἐβασίλευσε means 'he became king'. In Modern Greek ο ήλιος βασιλεύει means 'the sun is setting'.
The basilica, a Roman public hall named from the Greek 'royal (portico)', became the shape of early churches; Romanian biserică 'church' descends from it.

ex.en: brekekekex koax koax (the frogs' chorus, Aristophanes)

note: From βαίνω (perfect βέβηκα 'stand firm'). Modern βεβαίως 'certainly' is a common reply.

cite: βεβαιόω, βεβαιώσω, ἐβεβαίωσα, βεβεβαίωκα, βεβεβαίωμαι, ἐβεβαιώθην

note: The force has turned inward: Modern βιάζομαι is everyday 'I'm in a hurry'.
Diminutive of βίβλος 'papyrus', named after Byblos, the Phoenician port that exported it. τὰ βιβλία 'the books' became Latin biblia, misread as a feminine singular: the Bible.

ex.en: the book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ (Matthew 1:1)
