note: βίος is the life one leads, the stuff of a biography; ζωή is the fact of being alive. Cognate with Latin vīvus and old English quick 'living'.

ex.t: ὁ βίος βραχύς, ἡ δὲ τέχνη μακρή
ex.en: life is short, art is long (Hippocrates, Aphorisms 1.1; Latin ars longa, vita brevis)

note: The Attic aorist is athematic ἐβίων, like ἔγνων. Modern βιώνω means 'experience', βίωμα 'lived experience'.

ex.t: ὁ δὲ ἀνεξέταστος βίος οὐ βιωτὸς ἀνθρώπῳ
ex.en: the unexamined life is not worth living for a human being (Plato, Apology 38a)

note: Verbal adjective of βιόω 'live': οὐ βιωτόν 'not worth living'. Socrates: ὁ δὲ ἀνεξέταστος βίος οὐ βιωτὸς ἀνθρώπῳ (Apology 38a).
From βλάβη 'harm' (βλάπτω); the opposite of ὠφέλιμος 'useful'.

ex.t: ὁ δὲ λόγος ἐπὶ τῷ δηλοῦν ἐστι τὸ συμφέρον καὶ τὸ βλαβερόν
ex.en: speech exists to make clear what is beneficial and what is harmful (Aristotle, Politics 1253a)

note: Rare in classical prose (Plato, Xenophon), but now an everyday Modern Greek insult.

cite: βλάπτω, βλάψω, ἔβλαψα, βέβλαφα, βέβλαμμαι, ἐβλάβην

note: Late Latin blasphēmāre, worn down in Old French to blasmer, gave English blame; the learned twin blaspheme was borrowed later.
cite: βλασφημέω, βλασφημήσω, ἐβλασφήμησα, βεβλασφήμηκα, βεβλασφήμημαι, ἐβλασφημήθην

note: In Attic ὁράω is the usual 'see' and βλέπω 'look, have sight'; Koine and Modern Greek made βλέπω the normal verb for seeing.

ex.en: though I was blind, now I see (John 9:25)
the voice of one crying in the wilderness (Matthew 3:3)

note: βοή 'shout' + θέω 'run': to run at the cry for help. Takes the dative.
cite: βοηθέω, βοηθήσω, ἐβοήθησα, βεβοήθηκα, βεβοήθημαι, ἐβοηθήθην

rel.g: shaped like a bunch of grapes

en: be a member of the council (βουλή)
note: Active: deliberate for others, or sit on the council; middle: deliberate with oneself, make up one's mind.
cite: βουλεύω, βουλεύσω, ἐβούλευσα, βεβούλευκα, βεβούλευμαι, ἐβουλεύθην

en: council (esp. the Council of 500 at Athens)

ex.en: and the will of Zeus was being fulfilled (Iliad 1.5)

note: The augment is ἐ- or ἠ- (ἐβουλόμην / ἠβουλόμην). In Koine θέλω gradually took over, and the Modern future particle θα comes from θέλω ἵνα.
Herodotus uses it of the hills of Cyrene as a local word; it spread in Koine, and Modern βουνό has replaced ὄρος as the everyday word for 'mountain'.
Cognate with Latin bōs and English cow. The Bosporus is the 'Ox-ford', where Io, turned into a cow, crossed into Asia.
Literally 'cow-cheese' (βοῦς + τυρός), perhaps a reshaped Scythian word: Greeks and Romans cooked with olive oil and knew butter as a northern food and an ointment.

ex.t: πάντες μὲν τρέχουσιν, εἷς δὲ λαμβάνει τὸ βραβεῖον
ex.en: all the runners run, but only one receives the prize (1 Corinthians 9:24)

note: Adverb of βραδύς 'slow' (as in bradycardia).

ex.en: make haste slowly (Augustus' motto, Latin festīnā lentē)

note: Modern βράδυ 'evening' is the neuter used as a noun: 'the late (part of the day)'. The everyday Modern word for 'slow' is αργός.
Probably the comparative of βραχύς, 'the shorter (part of the arm)'. Borrowed early by Latin as bracchium, it became the everyday word for 'arm' in every Romance language.

ex.en: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths (Luke 2:12)

note: Attic says ὕει 'it rains' (Zeus understood); Koine and Modern Greek say βρέχει.

ex.en: he sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45)

note: From *mrotós 'dead, mortal': Greek grew a β between μ and ρ and then dropped the μ, while ἄμβροτος kept both. Cognate with Latin mors, mortālis.

en: depth of the sea, the deep

note: Medieval Latin bursa 'leather purse' gave English purse and bursar and the Romance words for 'bag'; the stock exchange sense is traced to a merchants' meeting place in Bruges.
The galaxy is the γαλαξίας κύκλος, the 'milky circle', i.e. the Milky Way.
Any man related by marriage; Modern γαμπρός keeps the 'bridegroom' and 'son-in-law' senses, with the usual Modern Greek spelling μπ for the sound mb.
Active for the man, middle for the woman: γαμεῖ γυναῖκα 'he takes a wife', γαμεῖται ἀνδρί 'she marries a man'. In Modern Greek γαμώ has become vulgar, and 'to marry' is παντρεύομαι.

ex.t: γάμος ἐγένετο ἐν Κανὰ τῆς Γαλιλαίας
ex.en: there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee (John 2:1)

note: Postpositive: it never stands first in its clause (ὁ γὰρ ἄνθρωπος…). καὶ γάρ = 'and indeed, for in fact'.
Declined like πατήρ (γαστρός, γαστρί, dat. pl. γαστράσι).
Enclitic that stresses the word before it; it fuses with ἐγώ into ἔγωγε 'I for my part'.
An irregular contract verb: the σ-forms keep a short α (γελάσομαι, ἐγέλασα).
The Homeric gods' ἄσβεστος γέλως, 'unquenchable laughter' (Iliad 1.599), is the source of the phrase 'Homeric laughter'.

ex.t: οἵη περ φύλλων γενεή, τοίη δὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν
ex.en: as is the generation of leaves, so is that of men (Iliad 6.146)

note: Γένεσις is the Septuagint's title for the first book of the Bible, the book 'of the origin' (of the world).

cite: γεννάω, γεννήσω, ἐγέννησα, γεγέννηκα, γεγέννημαι, ἐγεννήθην

note: γένος and Latin genus are exact cognates (both from *ǵénh₁os 'birth, kind'), and English kin comes from the same root.
The geranium is the 'crane's bill', named after its long beak-shaped fruit; English crane is a native cognate.
Sparta's council of elders was the γερουσία; Modern Greek uses γερουσία for 'senate'.
Same root (*ǵews-) as Latin gustus 'taste' and English choose: to 'taste' and then pick.
γῆ 'earth' + γράφω 'describe'; the term is usually credited to Eratosthenes (3rd c. BC), who also measured the earth's circumference.
Literally 'land-measurement': Herodotus (2.109) says it began in Egypt, where fields had to be re-measured after the Nile floods.
γῆ + ἔργον, an 'earth-worker'. The name George (Γεώργιος) means 'farmer'; Vergil's Georgics are poems on farming.
A contracted noun (γῆ, γῆς, γῇ, γῆν), so the accent is a circumflex throughout. As the goddess it is Γαῖα or Γῆ.

ex.t: ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
ex.en: in the beginning God made the heaven and the earth (Genesis 1:1, Septuagint)

note: Geriatric is a modern coinage from γῆρας and ἰατρός 'doctor'.
The Giants were sons of Gaia who fought the Olympians. The word reached English through Latin gigās, gigantis and Old French geant.
Koine already wrote γίνομαι, the form Modern Greek keeps. The perfect γέγονα means simply 'I am' (I have come into being).
γνω-, Latin (g)nō- (Old Latin gnōscō) and English know all continue one Indo-European root *ǵneh₃-. The aorist ἔγνων is athematic (ἔγνως, ἔγνω…).
cite: γιγνώσκω, γνώσομαι, ἔγνων, ἔγνωκα, ἔγνωσμαι, ἐγνώσθην

note: Athena is γλαυκῶπις, 'bright-eyed' or 'grey-eyed'; glaucoma is named for the greyish sheen of the affected eye.
The owl stamped on Athenian silver coins made 'owls' slang for money.

ex.en: an owl to Athens (proverb: coals to Newcastle)

note: Latin dulcis is generally explained as the same old word with the first consonant changed (*dlukus → dulcis vs. *glukus → γλυκύς).
Hieroglyph comes from ἱερογλυφικὰ (γράμματα), 'sacred carved (letters)'.
Attic γλῶττα vs. Ionic and Koine γλῶσσα (like θάλαττα/θάλασσα); Modern Greek continues the Koine form. A γλῶσσα was also a rare word needing a 'gloss'.

ex.en: they began to speak in other tongues (Acts 2:4)

note: κατὰ γνώμην 'according to one's wish'; in the sense 'maxim' it gave English gnomic ('expressed in maxims').

rel.g: know (a person); get to know, meet

note: In Modern Greek γνωρίζω means knowing people (γνωρίζω τη Μαρία), while ξέρω means knowing facts — like French connaître vs. savoir.
cite: γνωρίζω, γνωριῶ, ἐγνώρισα, ἐγνώρικα, ἐγνώρισμαι, ἐγνωρίσθην

note: Its negative ἄγνωστος appears in Paul's 'altar to an unknown god' (Acts 17:23); agnostic was coined from it by T. H. Huxley in 1869.
Latin genū and English knee are cognates. Modern γόνατο was rebuilt from the oblique stem γονατ-.
Grammar is the γραμματικὴ τέχνη, the 'art of letters'; glamour is a Scots alteration of grammar, once meaning occult learning.

ex.en: woe to you, scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 23:13)

note: Irregular: γραῦς, γραός, γραΐ, γραῦν, voc. γραῦ.
In Athenian law a γραφή was a public prosecution that any citizen could bring, as opposed to a δίκη, a private suit.
The original meaning was 'scratch', as in English carve, a native cognate. Graft comes from Greek γραφεῖον 'stylus', through Latin and Old French, because the shoot looks like a pencil.

ex.en: what I have written, I have written (John 19:22)

cite: γράφω, γράψω, ἔγραψα, γέγραφα, γέγραμμαι, ἐγράφην

note: A Koine verb made from ἐγρήγορα, the perfect of ἐγείρω ('I am awake'). From it came the name Γρηγόριος 'watchful', and Modern γρήγορος 'quick', first meaning 'wide awake'.

cite: γυμνάζω, γυμνάσω, ἐγύμνασα, γεγύμνακα, γεγύμνασμαι, ἐγυμνάσθην

note: Greek athletes trained γυμνοί, naked. Because philosophers taught in the gymnasia (the Academy, the Lyceum), the word came to mean a school, as in Modern Greek and German.
The nominative γυνή stands apart from the stem γυναικ- (acc. γυναῖκα, voc. γύναι). English queen goes back to the same Indo-European word for 'woman'; Modern γυναίκα is made from the accusative.
Related to γόνυ 'knee', the body's angle.
Socrates spoke of a δαιμόνιον, an inner divine sign that warned him off certain actions; the charge of 'new divinities' (καινὰ δαιμόνια) helped condemn him.
Originally a neutral divine power allotting one's lot — hence εὐδαίμων 'happy', 'with a good δαίμων'. Christian usage turned it into the demon.

ex.en: a man's character is his fate (Heraclitus)

cite: δάκνω, δήξομαι, ἔδακον, δέδηχα, δέδηγμαι, ἐδήχθην

note: Latin lacrima (Old Latin dacruma) and English tear are cognates; the change d → l is a Latin peculiarity.
The dactyl (– ⏑ ⏑) is a long joint followed by two short ones, like a finger. The date fruit got its name from the finger-like shape.
Mostly poetic; Homer's Hector is ἱππόδαμος, 'horse-taming'. Latin domō and English tame share the root.
One of Homer's three names for the Greeks, beside Ἀχαιοί and Ἀργεῖοι. Vergil's Laocoön says timeo Danaos et dona ferentes, 'I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts'.

en: Darius (king of Persia: Darius I, 522–486 BC; Darius II, 423–404 BC)
note: From Old Persian Dārayavauš, 'holding firm the good'. Darius I sent the expedition defeated at Marathon; Darius II was the father of Artaxerxes II and Cyrus the Younger.
Hebrew names are left undeclined in the Greek Bible: ἐν πόλει Δαυίδ 'in the city of David' (Luke 2:11). Editions also spell it Δαβίδ or Δαυείδ.
The nymph Daphne became a laurel to escape Apollo, and the laurel became his tree; victors at the Pythian Games were crowned with it.
Postpositive (δ’ before a vowel). μέν… δέ… sets two things side by side ('on the one hand… on the other'), and ὁ δέ means 'and he' at the start of a new clause.

en: it is necessary, one must (+ acc. + inf.)
note: An impersonal form of δέω 'lack': literally 'it is lacking', hence 'it is needed'. τὰ δέοντα = 'what is needed, one's duty'.

ex.t: δεῖ δὲ χρημάτων, καὶ ἄνευ τούτων οὐδέν ἐστι γενέσθαι τῶν δεόντων
ex.en: money is needed, and without it nothing that is needed can be done (Demosthenes, Olynthiac 1.20)

note: Same root (*deyḱ- 'point out') as Latin dīcō (first 'show', then 'say') and English teach and token. A παράδειγμα is a 'model shown alongside'.
cite: δείκνυμι, δείξω, ἔδειξα, δέδειχα, δέδειγμαι, ἐδείχθην

note: The dinosaur is a δεινὸς σαῦρος, a 'terrible lizard'. Sophocles plays on the double sense 'terrible/wondrous' in his famous ode on man.

ex.t: πολλὰ τὰ δεινὰ κοὐδὲν ἀνθρώπου δεινότερον πέλει
ex.en: many things are wondrous, but none more wondrous than man (Sophocles, Antigone 332)

note: In the New Testament the κυριακὸν δεῖπνον is 'the Lord's supper' (1 Corinthians 11:20).
δέκα, Latin decem and English ten are one Indo-European numeral (*déḱm̥); Greek δ and Latin d correspond to Germanic t.
ἡ δεκάτη (μοῖρα) was 'the tenth', a tithe or a 10% tax.

rel.g: dolphin; heir to the French throne

note: Plural in form, like Ἀθῆναι: the place is simply 'the Delphians'. The Greeks believed it was the ὀμφαλός, the navel of the earth.
Rhododendron = 'rose tree'. Modern δέντρο shows the usual shift νδ → ντ.
ἡ δεξιά (χείρ) is 'the right hand', also a pledge given with it. As in Latin dexter, the right hand is the skilful, lucky one.
A passive deponent (aorist ἐδεήθην). Modern Greek has narrowed it to 'pray', and δέηση means 'prayer'.
From δέρω 'flay': a δέρμα is what is stripped off.
Plato's Phaedo is set in the δεσμωτήριον where Socrates drank the hemlock.
From δεσμός 'bond, chain'. Aeschylus' Προμηθεὺς Δεσμώτης is 'Prometheus Bound'; Plato's cave-dwellers are δεσμῶται.
Vocative δέσποτα, with recessive accent. In Modern Greek ο Δεσπότης is the everyday word for a bishop.
Deuteronomy is the 'second law'. In Modern Greek Monday is Δευτέρα, the 'second' day of the week.
A διάδημα was a band 'tied round' the head. Like other two-syllable -έω verbs, δέω contracts only ε + ε/ει (δεῖς, δεῖ, but δέομεν, δέουσι).
cite: δέω, δήσω, ἔδησα, δέδεκα, δέδεμαι, ἐδέθην

en: lack, be in want of (+ gen.)
note: The active is mostly idiomatic; its everyday forms are impersonal δεῖ 'it is necessary' and middle δέομαι 'need, ask'.
cite: δέω, δεήσω, ἐδέησα, δεδέηκα, δεδέημαι, ἐδεήθην

note: Postpositive; it highlights the word before it (πολλοὶ δή 'very many', νῦν δή 'just now') and is often ironic: ὁ σοφὸς δή 'the wise man, if you please'.
From δηλέομαι 'hurt, damage'; Ionic and poetic. The Oath promises to keep patients ἐπὶ δηλήσει καὶ ἀδικίῃ, 'from harm and injustice'.
Often personal where English is impersonal: δῆλός ἐστιν ἀδικῶν 'he is clearly doing wrong' (lit. 'he is clear doing wrong').

cite: δηλόω, δηλώσω, ἐδήλωσα, δεδήλωκα, δεδήλωμαι, ἐδηλώθην

note: δῆμος + ἄγω, 'leader of the people': neutral at first, it soon became a term of abuse for Cleon and other populists.
Literally 'one who works for the people' (δήμιος + ἔργον). In Plato's Timaeus the δημιουργός is the divine craftsman who shapes the world.
δῆμος + κράτος 'power'. Modern Greece is officially the Ελληνική Δημοκρατία, 'Hellenic Republic'.
Attica was divided into about 140 demes, and every citizen was registered in one. Modern δήμος means a municipality and δήμαρχος a mayor.
δημοσίᾳ 'publicly, at public expense'; τὸ δημόσιον 'the state treasury'. Modern δημόσιος υπάλληλος is a civil servant.
δή + enclitic πού 'perhaps': a confident 'surely' that assumes the hearer agrees, as in οὐ γὰρ δήπου ψεύδεταί γε 'for surely he is not lying' (Apology 21b).
A stronger δή, frequent in dialogue: τί δῆτα; 'what then?', οὐ δῆτα 'certainly not'.

en: (+ acc.) because of, on account of
note: Modern Greek για 'for' is διά worn down in everyday speech, while the learned prefix δια- survives intact (διάβαση, διάλογος).
Diabetes comes from διαβήτης, 'one that passes through', a siphon — the disease was named for the large amounts of urine.
From διαβάλλω 'throw across, slander'. Socrates' defence begins by tracing the old διαβολή against him; the διάβολος 'slanderer' became the Devil.
From διαβάλλω 'slander': the devil is literally 'the Slanderer', the Septuagint's rendering of Hebrew satan 'accuser'. English devil came through Latin diabolus.
From διαδέχομαι 'take over in turn'. The Διάδοχοι were Alexander's generals who carved up his empire; in Modern Greek ο διάδοχος is the heir to the throne.
Η Καινή Διαθήκη is the 'New Testament' (Covenant). Latin rendered the legal sense 'will' with testāmentum, whence English testament.
The diaeresis (¨) marks a 'division' of two vowels that would otherwise form a diphthong, as in Greek ϊ. Modern διαίρεση also means arithmetical division.
cite: διαιρέω, διαιρήσω, διεῖλον, διῄρηκα, διῄρημαι, διῃρέθην

note: Greek doctors prescribed a whole δίαιτα — food, exercise, sleep — which narrowed to 'diet'. An Athenian διαιτητής was an arbitrator.
In Greek medicine δίαιτα and διαιτήματα cover a patient's whole regimen — food, exercise, bathing, sleep — not only what he eats.
Diacritics are marks that 'distinguish' letters — like the accents and breathings of Greek.
cite: διακρίνω, διακρινῶ, διέκρινα, διακέκρικα, διακέκριμαι, διεκρίθην

note: A passive deponent. Dialectic, ἡ διαλεκτικὴ τέχνη, is the Socratic art of reaching truth through question and answer.

en: leave an interval, leave a gap
stop for a while, pause (+ participle)
note: Aesop's tortoise οὐ διέλιπε τρέχουσα, 'never stopped running'.
cite: διαλείπω, διαλείψω, διέλιπον, διαλέλοιπα, διαλέλειμμαι, διελείφθην

note: The prefix is δια- 'through', not δι- 'two': a dialogue can have any number of speakers.

cite: διαλύω, διαλύσω, διέλυσα, διαλέλυκα, διαλέλυμαι, διελύθην

note: A passive deponent (aor. διενοήθην). Its present participle lives on as Modern Greek ο διανοούμενος 'the intellectual'.
From διασπείρω 'scatter (seed)'. Modern Greek η διασπορά refers above all to Greeks living abroad.

ex.en: he continues to be well-disposed to the people

note: The noun διατριβή meant 'pastime', then 'study, discourse'; English made it a bitter tirade, Modern Greek a doctoral thesis.
cite: διατρίβω, διατρίψω, διέτριψα, διατέτριφα, διατέτριμμαι, διετρίβην

note: Latin differō is built exactly like διαφέρω (dis- + ferō, cognate with φέρω), so English differ mirrors the Greek word part for part without being borrowed from it.
cite: διαφέρω, διοίσω, διήνεγκα / διήνεγκον, διενήνοχα, διενήνεγμαι, διηνέχθην

ex.t: ἀδικεῖ δὲ καὶ τοὺς νέους διαφθείρων
ex.en: and he does wrong by corrupting the young (charge against Socrates, Xenophon, Memorabilia 1.1.1)

cite: διαφθείρω, διαφθερῶ, διέφθειρα, διέφθαρκα, διέφθαρμαι, διεφθάρην

note: Playwrights 'taught' (ἐδίδασκον) their plays to the chorus, so the poet was the διδάσκαλος. In everyday Modern Greek the word has lost its first syllable: δάσκαλος.

en: teach (+ acc. of person and thing)

ex.t: ἐγὼ τοῦτον οὐδὲν διδάσκω, ἀλλ’ ἐρωτῶ πάντα
ex.en: I am teaching him nothing, only asking him everything (Plato, Meno 82e)

cite: διδάσκω, διδάξω, ἐδίδαξα, δεδίδαχα, δεδίδαγμαι, ἐδιδάχθην

note: The root δω/δο is the same as Latin dō, dōnum. A δόσις is 'a giving' (a dose), and an ἀντίδοτον something 'given against' poison.

ex.t: δός μοι πᾶ στῶ καὶ τὰν γᾶν κινάσω
ex.en: give me a place to stand and I will move the earth (Archimedes, in Doric)

cite: δίδωμι, δώσω, ἔδωκα, δέδωκα, δέδομαι, ἐδόθην

en: (intr.: aor. διέστην, perf. διέστηκα) stand apart; quarrel, be at odds
note: ἐξ οὗ δὴ τὰ πρῶτα διαστήτην ἐρίσαντε 'from the time when those two first parted in strife' (Iliad 1.6): διαστήτην is a dual.
cite: διίστημι, διαστήσω, διέστησα / διέστην, διέστηκα, —, διεστάθην
δικάζω, δικάσω, ἐδίκασα, δεδίκακα, δεδίκασμαι, ἐδικάσθην

en: Dikaiopolis ('Just-City'), the farmer hero of Aristophanes' Acharnians
note: A speaking name: δίκαιος 'just' + πόλις 'city'. In Aristophanes (425 BC) he makes a private peace with Sparta so that he can go back to his farm.

en: (+ inf.) bound, having the right to
note: τὸ δίκαιον 'justice, one's right'; in Modern Greek το δίκαιο also means 'law' as a discipline (αστικό δίκαιο 'civil law').

ex.t: ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται
ex.en: the righteous shall live by faith (Romans 1:17)

note: The central question of Plato's Republic is τί ἐστι δικαιοσύνη; 'what is justice?'
Athenian popular courts had hundreds of citizen jurors chosen by lot; the jury that tried Socrates numbered about 500.
In Athens the δικασταί were ordinary citizens, and speakers addressed them as ὦ ἄνδρες δικασταί.

en: (acc. δίκην + gen.) in the manner of
note: Idioms: δίκην δίδωμι 'pay the penalty', δίκην λαμβάνω 'punish'; δίκην κυνός 'like a dog'. Δίκη personified is the daughter of Zeus.
The Internet is το Διαδίκτυο in Modern Greek, a learned coinage from δια- + δίκτυον.
διοίκησις 'administration' became a Roman administrative district under Diocletian, and the Church took the word over for a bishop's diocese.
cite: διοικέω, διοικήσω, διῴκησα, διῴκηκα, διῴκημαι, διῳκήθην

en: Dionysus (god of wine, ecstasy and theatre)
note: Athenian tragedy and comedy were performed at his festival, the Great Dionysia. The Romans usually called him by his other Greek name, Bacchus (Βάκχος).
From *diwyos 'of the sky', the root of Ζεύς, Διός and Latin deus, dīvus: δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς 'godlike Achilles' (Iliad 1.7).

en: that (after verbs of knowing, later Greek)

note: A contracted adjective (διπλόος → διπλοῦς). A δίπλωμα was a document folded double, the source of diploma and diplomacy.
From *dwis, like Latin bis (old duis) and English twice.

ex.t: δὶς ἐξαμαρτεῖν ταὐτὸν οὐκ ἀνδρὸς σοφοῦ
ex.en: to make the same mistake twice is not the mark of a wise man (Menander)

note: Through Latin discus one Greek word gave English disc, dish and desk.
A dichotomy is a 'cutting in two'. Modern δίχως 'without' grew out of δίχα.
Like ζάω it contracts to η, not α: διψῶ, διψῇς, διψῇ, inf. διψῆν.

ex.t: μακάριοι οἱ πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τὴν δικαιοσύνην
ex.en: blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matthew 5:6)

note: In court ὁ διώκων is the prosecutor ('the pursuer') and ὁ φεύγων the defendant ('the one fleeing').
From δοκέω: 'what seems right', hence a resolution or a philosophical tenet.

en: (δοκεῖ μοι) it seems good to me, I decide
note: Future and aorist are built on δοκ-σ- (δόξω, ἔδοξα). τὸ δοκοῦν 'opinion' and δόξα come from the same verb.

ex.t: ἔδοξε τῇ βουλῇ καὶ τῷ δήμῳ
ex.en: resolved by the Council and the People (opening of Athenian decrees)

note: The δοκιμασία was the scrutiny every Athenian official had to pass before taking office.
cite: δοκιμάζω, δοκιμάσω, ἐδοκίμασα, δεδοκίμακα, δεδοκίμασμαι, ἐδοκιμάσθην

note: Odysseus is πολύτροπος and the master of δόλος; the Trojan Horse was his δόλος. Roman law took it over as dolus (malus), 'fraud'.
Plato sets δόξα 'opinion' against ἐπιστήμη 'knowledge'. In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew 'glory', the sense that dominates in Christian and Modern Greek.

ex.en: glory to God in the highest (Luke 2:14)

note: Originally 'wood', related to English tree and to δρῦς 'oak'. A δορυφόρος was a bodyguard; Modern Greek uses it for 'satellite', just as Latin satelles meant 'bodyguard'.
A telling shift: Modern δουλειά simply means 'work, job'.

ex.t: οὐ δύνασθε θεῷ δουλεύειν καὶ μαμωνᾷ
ex.en: you cannot serve God and mammon (Matthew 6:24)
behold the handmaid of the Lord (Luke 1:38)

note: Also an adjective, 'slavish, servile'. Paul calls himself δοῦλος Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ, 'slave of Christ Jesus' (Romans 1:1).

cite: δουλόω, δουλώσω, ἐδούλωσα, δεδούλωκα, δεδούλωμαι, ἐδουλώθην

note: Probably 'the sharp-sighted one', from δέρκομαι 'see'. The Athenian lawgiver Δράκων gave English draconian.
Originally 'a handful' (of iron spits, ὀβελοί, used as money), from δράττομαι 'grasp'. It was the Modern Greek currency until the euro (2002).
Mainly poetic and Attic, a weightier synonym of ποιέω and πράττω; δραστικός 'active, effective' gave English drastic.

ex.en: the doer must suffer (Aeschylus, Libation Bearers 313)

cite: δράω, δράσω, ἔδρασα, δέδρακα, δέδραμαι, ἐδράσθην

note: A palindrome 'runs back again'; the dromedary is the 'running' camel. In Modern Greek δρόμος is the ordinary word for road or street.
Feminine despite -ος. Drosophila, the fruit fly, is the 'dew-lover'.
Dryads are tree-nymphs. δρῦς, δόρυ 'spear-shaft' and English tree share one Indo-European root for 'wood, tree'.
Inflected like a middle μι-verb (δύνασαι, δύναται); imperfect ἐδυνάμην or ἠδυνάμην. τί δύναται τοῦτο; 'what does this mean?'
Aristotle's δύναμις 'potentiality' is the opposite of ἐνέργεια 'actuality'. Alfred Nobel named dynamite after it in 1867.

ex.t: τὰ ἀδύνατα παρὰ ἀνθρώποις δυνατὰ παρὰ τῷ θεῷ ἐστιν
ex.en: what is impossible with men is possible with God (Luke 18:27)

note: Often indeclinable; gen. and dat. δυοῖν, an old dual form. Latin duo and English two are cognates.
Menander's comedy Δύσκολος is 'The Grouch'. Modern Greek keeps only the sense 'difficult' (εύκολος 'easy' is its opposite).
δυσ- 'ill' + τύχη 'fortune', the opposite of εὐτυχής. The prefix δυσ- lives on in English dys- (dyslexia).
The root aorist ἔδυν is intransitive ('I sank, set'). The sun's setting, δύσις/δυσμαί, gave the Modern Greek word for 'the West', η Δύση.
cite: δύω, δύσω, ἔδυσα / ἔδυν, δέδυκα, δέδυμαι, ἐδύθην

note: δύο + δέκα, like Latin duodecim. The Dodecanese are the 'twelve islands'.
Same root as δόμος and Latin domus. Modern Greek signs reading ΔΩΜΑΤΙΑ offer 'rooms' to let.

en: (acc. δωρεάν as adv.) freely, for nothing
note: Modern δωρεάν 'free (of charge)' is the frozen ancient accusative.

ex.en: freely you have received, freely give (Matthew 10:8)

note: From the root of δίδωμι. Theodore and Dorothy are 'gift of God'; Pandora is 'all-gifted'.

ex.en: gifts persuade even the gods, as the saying goes (Euripides, Medea 964)

note: From εἰ + ἄν, also contracted to ἤν or ἄν; Modern Greek αν 'if' continues the shortened form.
Attic contracts to ἦρ, ἦρος. ἔαρ and Latin vēr come from one Indo-European word for spring; Modern Greek calls it the 'opening', άνοιξη.
No nominative, since a reflexive refers back to the subject. Modern Greek expresses 'myself' with ο εαυτός μου, 'my self'.
cite: ἑαυτοῦ, ἑαυτῆς, ἑαυτοῦ; contracted αὑτοῦ, αὑτῆς

note: Augments to ει- (imperfect εἴων, aorist εἴασα); οὐκ ἐάω often means 'forbid'.
cite: ἐάω, ἐάσω, εἴασα, εἴακα, εἴαμαι, εἰάθην

note: The Greek Old Testament is called the Septuagint, Latin for 'the Seventy', after the legend of its seventy(-two) translators — hence the abbreviation LXX.
ἐγγύα, πάρα δ’ ἄτα 'give a pledge, and ruin is near' was one of the sayings of the Seven Sages displayed at Delphi.
Comparative ἐγγυτέρω, superlative ἐγγύτατα. Also used as an improper preposition with the genitive: ἐγγὺς τῆς πόλεως.
The perfect ἐγρήγορα 'I am awake' gave the Koine verb γρηγορέω and the name Gregory.

ex.en: he has risen, he is not here (Mark 16:6)

cite: ἐγείρω, ἐγερῶ, ἤγειρα, ἐγρήγορα, ἐγήγερμαι, ἠγέρθην

ex.t: θεέ μου θεέ μου, ἱνατί με ἐγκατέλιπες;
ex.en: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matthew 27:46)

cite: ἐγκαταλείπω, ἐγκαταλείψω, ἐγκατέλιπον, ἐγκαταλέλοιπα, ἐγκαταλέλειμμαι, ἐγκατελείφθην

note: ἐγκύκλιος παιδεία was the 'all-round' general education; a misreading of the phrase as one word gave Renaissance Latin encyclopaedia.
Originally a song sung in the κῶμος, the festive procession honouring a victor.
Literally 'a thing in the hand' (ἐν + χείρ): first a hand-dagger, then a handbook, like Epictetus' Enchiridion.
The nominative is used only for emphasis; μου, μοι, με are unemphatic enclitics, and Modern Greek keeps εγώ, μου, με. Latin ego and English I (Old English ic) are cognates.

ex.t: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωή
ex.en: I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6)

cite: ἐγώ, ἐμοῦ/μου, ἐμοί/μοι, ἐμέ/με; pl. ἡμεῖς

note: A καθέδρα was a chair; Latin cathedra became the bishop's throne, and the church that houses it is the cathedral.
Attic prose prefers ἐθέλω, poetry and Koine θέλω. Modern θέλω also supplied the future particle θα (θέλω ἵνα → θε να → θα), much as Romance built its future on habēre.
In the New Testament τὰ ἔθνη and οἱ ἐθνικοί are 'the nations', i.e. non-Jews; English ethnic long meant 'heathen' before its modern sense.
Aristotle links ἦθος 'character' to ἔθος 'habit' (Nicomachean Ethics 2.1): virtue of character is formed by habituation.
With the indicative for simple and contrary-to-fact conditions, with the optative for remote ones; with a subjunctive it becomes ἐάν.
From the root of εἶδον 'I saw' (originally ϝιδ-), the same as Latin videō. A kaleidoscope shows 'beautiful forms' (καλὰ εἴδη).
In Homer the εἴδωλον is the insubstantial image of a dead person; biblical Greek used it for the images of pagan gods.
The neuter participle of ἔοικα, mostly in εἰκός ἐστι 'it is likely/reasonable'. Argument from τὸ εἰκός, probability, was a staple of Greek rhetoric.
Doric ϝίκατι keeps the lost digamma (w-) that also shows in Latin vīgintī. Before a vowel often εἴκοσιν.
Mainly poetic; the compound ὑπείκω is commoner in prose. Its sense in Sappho 31 (οὐδ’ ἒν ἔτ’ εἴκει) is disputed.
An iconoclast is an 'image-breaker', from the Byzantine controversy of the 8th–9th centuries over religious images.
ἐστί, Latin est and English is all go back to *h₁ésti. The present is enclitic except accented ἔστι 'there is, it is possible'; Modern είμαι has taken middle endings.

ex.t: ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ ἄλφα καὶ τὸ ὦ
ex.en: I am the Alpha and the Omega (Revelation 1:8)

note: In Attic prose εἶμι supplies the future of ἔρχομαι; infinitive ἰέναι, participle ἰών. Latin eō, īre is a cognate.

en: shut out, keep away, prevent (+ gen. or inf.)
note: Some editors write εἵργω (rough breathing) for 'shut in' and εἴργω for 'shut out'.
Personified Εἰρήνη was one of the Horai, daughters of Zeus; the name Irene means 'peace'.
The common noun εἰρήνη 'peace' used as a name; Aristophanes wrote a comedy called Εἰρήνη (Peace, 421 BC).
εἰρήνη 'peace' + ποιέω 'make'.

ex.t: μακάριοι οἱ εἰρηνοποιοί, ὅτι αὐτοὶ υἱοὶ θεοῦ κληθήσονται
ex.en: blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God (Matthew 5:9)

note: The εἴρων 'dissembler' pretends to know less than he does; Socratic εἰρωνεία is the classic example.

en: speak ironically, not mean what one says
note: The εἴρων pretends to know less than he does. Socrates expects the jury to hear even his sincerity ὡς εἰρωνευομένῳ, 'as if he were being ironic' (Apology 38a).
Older Attic and Ionic ἐς. Modern Greek σε (στο = εἰς τό) is εἰς worn down, and now covers both 'in' and 'into'.
From *sems 'one', like Latin semel 'once' and English same. A hyphen joins two words ὑφ’ ἕν, 'into one'.
cite: εἷς, μία, ἕν (gen. ἑνός, μιᾶς, ἑνός)

en: arrive at, come into, reach (a place)
note: Herodotus' ἐσαπικνέεσθαι shows three Ionic habits: ἐς for εἰς, no aspiration (ἀπ- for ἀφ-), and uncontracted -έε-.
ἡ εἰσβολή is both 'invasion' and 'mouth of a river'; Modern εισβολή keeps the first sense.
cite: εἰσβάλλω, εἰσβαλῶ, εἰσέβαλον, εἰσβέβληκα, εἰσβέβλημαι, εἰσεβλήθην

note: Feminine, like ὁδός 'road', of which it is a compound. Greek doors still read ΕΙΣΟΔΟΣ and ΕΞΟΔΟΣ.

en: carry in, bring in, lead into

ex.t: καὶ μὴ εἰσενέγκῃς ἡμᾶς εἰς πειρασμόν
ex.en: and lead us not into temptation (Matthew 6:13)

cite: εἰσφέρω, εἰσοίσω, εἰσήνεγκα / εἰσήνεγκον, εἰσενήνοχα, εἰσενήνεγμαι, εἰσηνέχθην

note: Often in indignant questions: εἶτα οὐκ αἰσχύνῃ; 'and then you are not ashamed?'
A perfect with present meaning; pluperfect εἰώθειν 'I used to'. τὸ εἰωθός is 'custom, habit'.
ἐξ before vowels; Latin ex is cognate. In Modern Greek the prefix survives as ξε- (ξεφεύγω 'escape', ξεκινώ 'set out').

ex.en: (you can tell) the lion from its claw (proverb)

note: With the article it stands in predicate position: ὁ ἀνὴρ ἕκαστος or ἕκαστος ὁ ἀνήρ. καθ’ ἑκάστην (ἡμέραν) 'every day'.
Literally a sacrifice of a hundred oxen (ἑκατόν + βοῦς), though in Homer any great offering.
ἑκατόν, Latin centum and English hundred all go back to *ḱm̥tóm; the ἑ- is probably from ἕν 'one'.
Modern βγαίνω 'go out' is ἐκβαίνω with the κβ simplified to βγ. τὸ ἐκβάν 'the outcome'.

ex.t: ἐξέβαλεν πάντας τοὺς πωλοῦντας καὶ ἀγοράζοντας ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ
ex.en: he drove out all who were selling and buying in the temple (Matthew 21:12)

cite: ἐκβάλλω, ἐκβαλῶ, ἐξέβαλον, ἐκβέβληκα, ἐκβέβλημαι, ἐξεβλήθην

note: ἔκδοσις 'a giving out' became Modern έκδοση 'edition', and ἐκδότης 'publisher'.
cite: ἐκδίδωμι, ἐκδώσω, ἐξέδωκα, ἐκδέδωκα, ἐκδέδομαι, ἐξεδόθην

note: Neuter ἐκεῖνο without -ν (like ἄλλο, αὐτό). With a noun in predicate position: ἐκεῖνος ὁ ἀνήρ 'that man'. Modern Greek keeps it unchanged.
From ἔχω + χείρ, 'holding one's hands'. The sacred truce around the Olympic Games was the Ὀλυμπιακὴ ἐκεχειρία.
From ἐκκαλέω 'call out': the Athenian assembly of citizens summoned by herald. Christians took the word for their congregation, and through Latin ecclesia it became the Romance word for 'church'.

ex.t: ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ οἰκοδομήσω μου τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
ex.en: on this rock I will build my church (Matthew 16:18)

note: An eclipse, ἔκλειψις, is literally a 'failing' of the sun's or moon's light.
cite: ἐκλείπω, ἐκλείψω, ἐξέλιπον, ἐκλέλοιπα, ἐκλέλειμμαι, ἐξελείφθην

note: Vergil's Eclogues (Latin ecloga) are 'selected pieces'. Modern Greek εκλογές are 'elections'.
Aristotle's distinction of τὰ ἑκούσια and τὰ ἀκούσια, voluntary and involuntary acts, underlies later ideas of legal responsibility.
Attic -ττ-, Koine -σσ-; Modern Greek follows Koine: εκπλήσσω, έκπληξη 'surprise'.
cite: ἐκπλήττω, ἐκπλήξω, ἐξέπληξα, ἐκπέπληγα, ἐκπέπληγμαι, ἐξεπλάγην

note: From ἐξίστημι 'put out of place': ecstasy is 'standing outside oneself'.
Probably 'holder, stay' (from ἔχω), the defender of Troy. English to hector, 'bully', comes from the name used for swaggering bullies in the 17th century.

en: willing, of one's own free will
note: Used predicatively where English uses an adverb: ἑκὼν ἀπῆλθεν 'he left willingly'. Its opposite is ἄκων.
Latin olīva is an early loan from the older Greek form ἐλαίϝα. The olive tree was Athena's gift to Athens.
Latin oleum, an early borrowing from ἔλαιον, gave Italian olio, French huile and English oil. Modern λάδι comes from a diminutive.
The future ἐλῶ, ἐλᾷς, ἐλᾷ is inflected like a contract verb in -άω. Xenophon's Anabasis repeats ἐντεῦθεν ἐξελαύνει 'from there he marches on'.
cite: ἐλαύνω, ἐλῶ, ἤλασα, ἐλήλακα, ἐλήλαμαι, ἠλάθην

note: Masculine or feminine (ὁ/ἡ ἔλαφος).
The Socratic ἔλεγχος tests a claim by questioning until it collapses. In Modern Greek έλεγχος is any check: έλεγχος εισιτηρίων 'ticket inspection'.
The Greek prayer Κύριε ἐλέησον was kept untranslated in the Latin Mass as Kyrie eleison.
cite: ἐλεέω, ἐλεήσω, ἠλέησα, ἠλέηκα, ἠλέημαι, ἠλεήθην

note: Church Latin eleēmosyna was worn down in popular speech into French aumône, Spanish limosna, Portuguese esmola and Old English ælmesse, English alms.

ex.t: μακάριοι οἱ ἐλεήμονες, ὅτι αὐτοὶ ἐλεηθήσονται
ex.en: blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy (Matthew 5:7)

ex.t: οὐ νέμεσις… τοιῇδ’ ἀμφὶ γυναικὶ πολὺν χρόνον ἄλγεα πάσχειν
ex.en: no blame… to suffer woes so long for such a woman (the Trojan elders on Helen, Iliad 3.156–157)

note: Attic ὁ ἔλεος; Koine also τὸ ἔλεος, -ους. Aristotle says tragedy works through ἔλεος and φόβος, pity and fear.

ex.en: freedom or death (motto of the Greek War of Independence, 1821)

note: Latin līber 'free' is a cognate: both derive from a root meaning 'people', the free being full members of the community.

ex.en: and the truth will set you free (John 8:32)

cite: ἐλευθερόω, ἐλευθερώσω, ἠλευθέρωσα, ἠλευθέρωκα, ἠλευθέρωμαι, ἠλευθερώθην

note: In Homer ἐλέφας means only 'ivory'; the animal itself appears in Greek from Herodotus on.
Augment εἱ- (imperfect εἷλκον). Modern ελκυστικός 'attractive' comes from the by-form ἑλκύω.
cite: ἕλκω, ἕλξω, εἵλκυσα, εἵλκυκα, εἵλκυσμαι, εἱλκύσθην

note: Greeks still call their country Ελλάδα (formal Ελλάς). 'Greece' comes from Latin Graecia, from Graecī, the Romans' name for the Greeks (Greek Γραικοί).
In Christian usage Ἕλλην came to mean 'pagan', so the Byzantines called themselves Ῥωμαῖοι; the old name returned with the modern national revival.
Xenophon's Ἑλληνικά is his 'Greek History'; Modern τα ελληνικά is 'Greek (language)'.
In Hesiod's tale only Ἐλπίς stayed inside Pandora's jar when the evils flew out.

ex.t: νυνὶ δὲ μένει πίστις, ἐλπίς, ἀγάπη, τὰ τρία ταῦτα
ex.en: and now faith, hope and love abide, these three (1 Corinthians 13:13)

note: From ἕλωρ 'booty', related to ἑλεῖν 'take'. The wrath made heroes ἑλώρια … κύνεσσιν, 'prey for dogs' (Iliad 1.4).
A trireme's ἔμβολον was the bronze ram on its prow; ramming (ἐμβάλλειν) was the main tactic of Greek naval warfare.
cite: ἐμβάλλω, ἐμβαλῶ, ἐνέβαλον, ἐμβέβληκα, ἐμβέβλημαι, ἐνεβλήθην

note: ἐν + βρύω 'swell, teem': 'that which grows within'.
Possessive adjective of ἐγώ, with the article: ὁ ἐμὸς πατήρ 'my father'. Modern Greek uses enclitic μου instead (ο πατέρας μου).
From πεῖρα 'trial', which shares its root with Latin experior, perītus and English experience.
An ἐμπόριον was a trading-station or port market; it reached English via Latin emporium. Modern εμπόριο means 'commerce'.
ἐν, Latin in and English in are one word. Modern Greek replaced it with σε (from εἰς), but it survives in set phrases such as εν τάξει 'OK' and εν τω μεταξύ 'meanwhile'.

ex.en: in the beginning was the Word (John 1:1)

note: τοὐναντίον (= τὸ ἐναντίον) 'on the contrary'. Modern εναντίον and ενάντια both mean 'against'.
ἕν + δέκα. In Athens οἱ Ἕνδεκα, 'the Eleven', were the officials in charge of prisons and executions.
Modern ντύνω 'dress' is ἐνδύνω after the loss of its unstressed first vowel.

ex.en: put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13:14)

cite: ἐνδύω, ἐνδύσω, ἐνέδυσα, ἐνδέδυκα, ἐνδέδυμαι, ἐνεδύθην

note: Usually placed after its noun: τοῦ κέρδους ἕνεκα 'for the sake of profit'. Also ἕνεκεν, and in Koine εἵνεκεν.
Aristotle's term (ἐν + ἔργον, 'being at work'), the actuality that realizes a δύναμις 'potential'. Physics borrowed it much later.
ἐν + θυμός 'spirit': 'to have in mind'. Modern θυμάμαι 'I remember' is ἐνθυμοῦμαι without its first syllable; ενθύμιο is a souvenir.
Contracted from ἔνι οἵ 'there are (those) who'.
Greek added a vowel in front of the old numeral seen in Latin novem and English nine. Plotinus' Enneads are 'groups of nine' treatises.
From *en-sekʷ-. Livius Andronicus' Latin Odyssey renders it with the cognate insece: virum mihi, Camēna, insece versūtum.

ex.en: tell me, Muse, of the man (Odyssey 1.1)

note: Very common in narrative to open a new scene: ἐνταῦθα δή 'just then, at this point'.
Dysentery, δυσεντερία, is a 'bad (state of the) bowels'.
Xenophon's Anabasis advances stage by stage with the formula ἐντεῦθεν ἐξελαύνει 'from there he marches on'.

ex.t: ἐντολὴν καινὴν δίδωμι ὑμῖν, ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους
ex.en: a new commandment I give you, that you love one another (John 13:34)

en: meet with, fall in with (+ dat.)

note: A Koine preposition (ἐν + ὤψ 'face'), very frequent in the Septuagint and New Testament.

ex.t: ἥμαρτον εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ ἐνώπιόν σου
ex.en: I have sinned against heaven and before you (Luke 15:18)

note: Greek turned initial s- into h- (the rough breathing): ἕξ ~ sex, ἑπτά ~ septem, ἅλς ~ sāl.
Modern εξαίρεση 'exception' and εξαιρετικός 'excellent' (originally 'exceptional') come from it.
cite: ἐξαιρέω, ἐξαιρήσω, ἐξεῖλον, ἐξῄρηκα, ἐξῄρημαι, ἐξῃρέθην
ἐξαπατάω, ἐξαπατήσω, ἐξηπάτησα, ἐξηπάτηκα, ἐξηπάτημαι, ἐξηπατήθην

ex.t: ἐντεῦθεν ἐξελαύνει σταθμοὺς τρεῖς παρασάγγας εἴκοσιν
ex.en: from there he marches three stages, twenty parasangs (the recurring formula of Xenophon's Anabasis)

cite: ἐξελαύνω, ἐξελῶ, ἐξήλασα, ἐξελήλακα, ἐξελήλαμαι, ἐξηλάθην

en: it is allowed, permitted (+ dat. + inf.)
note: Imperfect ἐξῆν; the participle ἐξόν 'it being allowed' is used as an accusative absolute. ἐξουσία 'authority' comes from it.

ex.t: ὁ δὲ ἀνεξέταστος βίος οὐ βιωτὸς ἀνθρώπῳ
ex.en: the unexamined life is not worth living for a human being (Plato, Apology 38a)

cite: ἐξετάζω, ἐξετάσω, ἐξήτασα, ἐξήτακα, ἐξήτασμαι, ἐξητάσθην

note: In Athens the ἐξηγηταί were official interpreters of sacred law.
From ἔξειμι 'go out': of colours that run and of memories that fade. Herodotus writes so that men's deeds may not become ἐξίτηλα with time.
Feminine like ὁδός. Modern Greek also uses the plural τα έξοδα for 'expenses' (money going out).
From ὅρκος 'oath': the exorcist binds the demon by solemn oath to leave.

ex.t: ἐδόθη μοι πᾶσα ἐξουσία ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς
ex.en: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (Matthew 28:18)

note: ἐξωτικός 'from outside' gave exotic. ἔξω τῆς πόλεως 'outside the city'.
ἔξω 'outside' + -θεν 'from'.

en: (ἔοικε) it is fitting, it is likely
note: A perfect with present meaning. ὡς ἔοικε 'as it seems' is a favourite phrase of Plato's speakers; the participle εἰκώς gives εἰκός 'likely'.
Modern γιορτή is ἑορτή with the ε- turned into a γι- sound; it also means a person's name day.

en: his own, her own, its own (Homeric possessive)
note: Also ὅς, ἥ, ὅν, easily mistaken for the relative: ὃν κατὰ θυμόν 'in his own heart', ἥν τε ψυχήν 'his own life' (Odyssey 1.4–5). From *sewos, cognate with Latin suus.
The sophists 'professed' (ἐπηγγέλλοντο) to teach virtue for a fee; from the same idea Modern Greek has επάγγελμα 'profession'.
The σ-tenses keep a short ε (ἐπῄνεσα), and the future is middle in form.
cite: ἐπαινέω, ἐπαινέσομαι, ἐπῄνεσα, ἐπῄνεκα, ἐπῄνημαι, ἐπῃνέθην

en: (+ gen.) above, over; (of numbers) more than
note: ἐπί + ἄνω 'up'. Modern πάνω 'up, on' is the same word without its first syllable.
ἐπεὶ τάχιστα 'as soon as'. With ἄν + subjunctive it becomes ἐπήν/ἐπάν 'whenever'.

en: episode (in tragedy, the scene between two choral odes)
note: ἐπί + εἴσοδος, an 'additional entrance' of actors; the term comes from Aristotle's Poetics. Modern επεισόδιο also means a scuffle or incident.

en: (+ gen.) on, upon; in the time of
(+ dat.) on, at, by; for, on condition of
note: With all three cases: ἐπὶ Κύρου 'in the time of Cyrus', ἐφ’ ᾧ 'on condition that', ἐπὶ τοὺς πολεμίους 'against the enemy'. Modern Greek says δύο επί τρία for 'two times three'.

ex.t: τῶν ὄντων τὰ μέν ἐστιν ἐφ’ ἡμῖν, τὰ δὲ οὐκ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν
ex.en: of the things that exist, some are up to us and some are not (Epictetus, Enchiridion 1)

en: (mid.) call on for help, call in
note: The shepherd boy amused himself ἐπιβοώμενος τοὺς κωμήτας, 'calling on the villagers for help'.

cite: ἐπιβουλεύω, ἐπιβουλεύσω, ἐπεβούλευσα, ἐπιβεβούλευκα, ἐπιβεβούλευμαι, ἐπεβουλεύθην

note: First a verse inscription on a tomb or dedication, later any short witty poem.

ex.t: ὦ ξεῖν’, ἀγγέλλειν Λακεδαιμονίοις ὅτι τῇδε κείμεθα, τοῖς κείνων ῥήμασι πειθόμενοι
ex.en: stranger, tell the Spartans that here we lie, obedient to their words (epitaph for Thermopylae, Herodotus 7.228)

note: Sappho's ’πιδεύης is the Aeolic/epic form ἐπιδευής: τεθνάκην δ’ ὀλίγω ’πιδεύης 'little short of dying' (fr. 31).
An ἐπίδειξις was a sophist's showpiece lecture; epideictic oratory is the rhetoric of praise and blame.
cite: ἐπιδείκνυμι, ἐπιδείξω, ἐπέδειξα, ἐπιδέδειχα, ἐπιδέδειγμαι, ἐπεδείχθην

note: Aristotle's ἐπιείκεια 'equity' corrects the law where its general wording fails a particular case.
In Plato's divided soul τὸ ἐπιθυμητικόν is the appetitive part, ruled by reason with the help of spirit.

en: (mid.) call to one's aid, invoke; appeal to
cite: ἐπικαλέω, ἐπικαλῶ, ἐπεκάλεσα, ἐπικέκληκα, ἐπικέκλημαι, ἐπεκλήθην

en: press upon, attack, press hard (+ dat.)

note: In the Iliad the ἐπίκουροι are Troy's allies. The philosopher Epicurus bore the name, which means 'helper'.
Same root as λανθάνω 'escape notice' and λήθη 'forgetfulness': to forget is to let something slip by unnoticed.
From ἐπιλαμβάνω 'seize upon'. It was called 'the sacred disease', a name the Hippocratic treatise On the Sacred Disease rejects.

en: take care of, see to (+ gen.)
note: From μέλει 'it is a concern'. Socrates urged the Athenians ἐπιμελεῖσθαι τῆς ψυχῆς, 'to care for the soul'.

en: (of bread) daily; for the coming day; needful (meaning disputed)
note: Found almost nowhere outside the Lord's Prayer; Origen already thought the evangelists coined it. 'Daily' follows the Old Latin cottīdiānus, while Jerome wrote supersubstantiālis in Matthew.

ex.t: τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον δὸς ἡμῖν σήμερον
ex.en: give us this day our daily bread (Matthew 6:11)

note: Known from Sappho 31: ἐπιρρόμβεισι δ’ ἄκουαι 'my ears hum'. From ῥόμβος, the whirring bull-roarer.
Attic prose prefers ἐπισκοπέω in the present. Modern επισκέπτομαι 'visit', επισκέπτης 'visitor'.
The 'overseer' of a Christian community. Through Latin episcopus came Old English biscop, English bishop, and the Romance words, all worn down from the same Greek.
Inflected like ἵσταμαι (ἐπίστασαι, ἐπίσταται; imperfect ἠπιστάμην). Its noun is ἐπιστήμη.
For Plato ἐπιστήμη is secure knowledge, as opposed to δόξα 'opinion'. Modern Greek uses it for 'science'.

cite: ἐπιστρέφω, ἐπιστρέψω, ἐπέστρεψα, ἐπέστροφα, ἐπέστραμμαι, ἐπεστράφην

rel.g: funeral oration; the Good Friday bier

note: Pericles' Funeral Oration in Thucydides (2.35–46) is the most famous ἐπιτάφιος. In the Orthodox Church the Επιτάφιος is the flower-decked bier of Christ carried in procession on Good Friday.

cite: ἐπιτείνω, ἐπιτενῶ, ἐπέτεινα, ἐπιτέτακα, ἐπιτέταμαι, ἐπετάθην

note: ἐπιτελέα ποιεῖν = ἐπιτελεῖν 'fulfil': the physician swears to make the Oath ἐπιτελέα, 'fulfilled'.
τὰ ἐπιτήδεια, the army's supplies, are a constant concern in Xenophon's Anabasis.
An ἐπίθετον is something 'put on' — an added word, an epithet; ἐπίθεσις is an 'attack'.
cite: ἐπιτίθημι, ἐπιθήσω, ἐπέθηκα, ἐπιτέθηκα, ἐπιτέθειμαι, ἐπετέθην

note: Greek signs read δεν επιτρέπεται 'not allowed'; επιτροπή 'committee' is a body 'entrusted' with a task.
cite: ἐπιτρέπω, ἐπιτρέψω, ἐπέτρεψα, ἐπιτέτροφα, ἐπιτέτραμμαι, ἐπετράπην

note: The Christian feast celebrates the 'manifestation' of Christ; Modern Greek calls it Θεοφάνεια or Φώτα and uses επιφάνεια for 'surface'.

en: put one's hand to, attempt (+ inf.)
note: ἐπί + χείρ 'lay a hand on'. Modern επιχείρηση is an 'enterprise', both a business and a military operation.
cite: ἐπιχειρέω, ἐπιχειρήσω, ἐπεχείρησα, ἐπικεχείρηκα, ἐπικεχείρημαι, ἐπεχειρήθην

note: Imperfect εἱπόμην, aorist ἑσπόμην. Latin sequor is a cognate, with the s- that Greek turned into the rough breathing.
Originally ϝέπος, from the same root as Latin vōx 'voice'.
Athens' ten tribes were named after the ten Eponymous Heroes. Modern το επώνυμο is a surname.
In Athenian courtship the older ἐραστής pursued the younger ἐρώμενος; the pair is central to Plato's Symposium and Phaedrus.

en: love, be in love with (+ gen.)
note: The object is in the genitive. The aorist is passive in form: ἠράσθην 'I fell in love'.
The augment is εἰ- (εἰργαζόμην) because the stem once began with ϝ (ϝεργ-).
Originally ϝέργον, a cognate of English work. Greek writers love the contrast λόγῳ μέν… ἔργῳ δέ 'in word…, but in fact…'.

ex.en: in word…, but in deed… (a favourite antithesis of Thucydides)

note: The ἐρημίτης was a 'desert-dweller', the early Christian ascetic: hence hermit.

ex.en: the voice of one crying in the wilderness (Mark 1:3)

en: vie with, compete (+ dat.; περί + gen. 'about')
note: From ἔρις 'strife'. The Iliad's quarrel begins when Agamemnon and Achilles διαστήτην ἐρίσαντε, 'parted in strife' (1.6).
Accusative ἔριν. Eris threw the golden apple that led to the judgment of Paris; Hesiod distinguishes a good Strife (competition) from a bad one (war).

ex.t: ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων;
ex.en: what word has escaped the fence of your teeth? (Homeric formula)

note: An ἑρμηνεύς was an interpreter or translator. Plato's Cratylus connects the word with Hermes, messenger of the gods — a popular etymology.
cite: ἑρμηνεύω, ἑρμηνεύσω, ἡρμήνευσα, ἡρμήνευκα, ἡρμήνευμαι, ἡρμηνεύθην

en: herm (pillar with a head of Hermes)
note: The Romans identified him with Mercury. 'Hermetically sealed' refers to Hermes Trismegistus, legendary founder of alchemy. The mutilation of the Herms in 415 BC shook Athens before the Sicilian expedition.
In Attic the present is usually supplied by ἐρωτάω, while ἠρόμην serves as the aorist.
From ἕρπω 'creep', a cognate of Latin serpō, whence serpent.
ἐρυθρός, Latin ruber and English red share one root. Herodotus' Ἐρυθρὰ θάλασσα includes the Arabian Sea and Persian Gulf, not just today's Red Sea.
In Attic only the present indicative is common; the other present forms and the future come from εἶμι. Modern Greek keeps έρχομαι with aorist ήρθα, from ἦλθα.

ex.en: I came, I saw, I conquered (Caesar's veni, vidi, vici in Plutarch's Greek)

note: Passionate desire, as opposed to φιλία 'friendship' and Christian ἀγάπη. Modern Greek still says έρωτας for being in love.
Modern ρωτάω/ρωτώ has dropped the unstressed initial vowel; ερώτηση 'question' keeps it.
cite: ἐρωτάω, ἐρωτήσω, ἠρώτησα, ἠρώτηκα, ἠρώτημαι, ἠρωτήθην

note: From ϝεσ- 'clothe', the root of Latin vestis and English wear.
Suppletive: ἐσθ-/ἐδ- (like Latin edō, English eat) and aorist ἔφαγον, which gives -phagus: a sarcophagus is a 'flesh-eater'.

ex.t: φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνῄσκομεν
ex.en: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die (1 Corinthians 15:32)

note: A poetic synonym of ἀγαθός, frequent in Homer and in Theognis, where οἱ ἐσθλοί are the aristocrats.
ἑσπέρα and Latin vesper are cognates. The Hesperides guarded golden apples at the western edge of the world.

ex.t: ἔσονται οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι καὶ οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι
ex.en: the last will be first, and the first last (Matthew 20:16)

note: Attic also εἴσω. ἐσωτερικός 'inner' gave esoteric, 'for the inner circle'; exoteric and exotic come from ἔξω.
Athenian ἑταιρεῖαι were political clubs, which helped organize the oligarchic coup of 411 BC. Modern εταιρεία is a company or firm.
Homer's word for the companions of Achilles and Odysseus. The feminine ἑταίρα came to mean a courtesan.
Attic crasis gives ἅτερος and θάτερον (= τὸ ἕτερον). ὁ μὲν… ὁ δὲ ἕτερος 'the one… the other'.
οὐκέτι/μηκέτι 'no longer'; ἔτι καὶ νῦν 'even now'. Modern Greek still uses έτι in έτι περισσότερο 'even more'.

ex.en: prepare the way of the Lord (Mark 1:3)

cite: ἑτοιμάζω, ἑτοιμάσω, ἡτοίμασα, ἡτοίμακα, ἡτοίμασμαι, ἡτοιμάσθην

note: Originally ϝέτος; Latin vetus 'old', literally 'of many years', comes from the same root.
εὖ πράττω 'fare well', εὖ ποιέω 'treat well'. As the prefix εὐ- 'good, well' it lives on in countless English words.

ex.en: fare well (Plato's greeting at the head of his letters)

note: The Annunciation, Ευαγγελισμός (25 March), is also Greece's national day, the traditional start of the 1821 revolution.
εὐ + ἄγγελος 'messenger'. English gospel is a translation of it: Old English gōd spel, 'good news'.
For Aristotle εὐδαιμονία, a whole life of activity in accordance with virtue, is the highest human good.
εὐ + δαίμων: one who has a good divine power watching over his lot. Comparative εὐδαιμονέστερος.

A biblical word. In Luke 2:14 the reading εὐδοκίας (gen.) gives 'among men of (God's) good pleasure', the Vulgate's hominibus bonae voluntātis 'men of good will'; the Byzantine text has εὐδοκία, 'goodwill among men'.

cite: εὐεργετέω, εὐεργετήσω, εὐηργέτησα, εὐηργέτηκα, εὐηργέτημαι, εὐηργετήθην

note: An honorary title for public benefactors and kings, such as Ptolemy III Euergetes; Jesus mocks it in Luke 22:25.
Every Athenian official faced εὔθυναι, an audit of his accounts and conduct, at the end of his term — hence Modern ευθύνη 'responsibility'.
Mark's Gospel uses εὐθύς 'immediately' about forty times, often as καὶ εὐθύς 'and at once'.
Originally of people (easy to satisfy), the opposite of δύσκολος 'grumpy'; in Modern Greek it simply means 'easy'.

ex.t: εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου
ex.en: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord (Matthew 21:9)

cite: εὐλογέω, εὐλογήσω, εὐλόγησα, εὐλόγηκα, εὐλόγημαι, εὐλογήθην

note: The Furies were euphemistically called Εὐμενίδες, 'the Kindly Ones' — the title of Aeschylus' play.
Contracted from εὔνοος (εὐ + νοῦς), declined like νοῦς: εὔνους, εὔνου, εὔνῳ.
Traditionally explained as εὐνή 'bed' + ἔχω: 'keeper of the bedchamber' at Eastern courts.

en: have plenty of, find means (+ gen.)
note: The ordinary Modern Greek verb for 'can', μπορώ, comes from εὐπορῶ 'I have the means'.
cite: εὐπορέω, εὐπορήσω, ηὐπόρησα, ηὐπόρηκα, ηὐπόρημαι, ηὐπορήθην

note: Attic augments to ηὑ- or leaves εὑ-. Modern βρίσκω has dropped the first vowel.

ex.en: I have found it! (Archimedes in the bath)

cite: εὑρίσκω, εὑρήσω, ηὗρον / εὗρον, ηὕρηκα / εὕρηκα, ηὕρημαι / εὕρημαι, ηὑρέθην / εὑρέθην

en: piety, reverence (towards gods, parents, the dead)
note: Its opposite ἀσέβεια 'impiety' was the formal charge against Socrates (γραφὴ ἀσεβείας).
εὐ + τύχη. In Modern Greek good luck has become happiness: ευτυχία, ευτυχισμένος 'happy'.

en: use of words of good omen
note: At a sacrifice the call εὐφημεῖτε meant 'speak only words of good omen', i.e. keep holy silence. A euphemism likewise avoids an ill-omened word.
A Hellenistic word (εὐ + χάρις). The Eucharist is 'the thanksgiving'; Modern ευχαριστώ is the everyday 'thank you'.

ex.en: and he took bread, gave thanks and broke it (Luke 22:19)

note: Homer's heroes say εὔχομαι εἶναι 'I proudly claim to be'. Latin voveō 'vow' is a cognate; Modern εύχομαι means 'wish'.
ἐπί + ἥβη 'youth'. Athenian ephebes did two years of military training; Modern έφηβος is any teenager.
ἐπί + ἡμέρα. Mortals are ἐφήμεροι, 'creatures of a day', in Greek poetry; a Modern Greek newspaper is an εφημερίδα, a 'daily'.

ex.t: ἐπάμεροι· τί δέ τις; τί δ’ οὔ τις; σκιᾶς ὄναρ ἄνθρωπος
ex.en: creatures of a day! What is anyone? What is no one? Man is a dream of a shadow (Pindar, Pythian 8)

en: set over, set upon; put in charge
(intr.: aor. ἐπέστην, perf. ἐφέστηκα) stand over, stand by; come upon suddenly; be in charge

ex.en: and an angel of the Lord stood before them (Luke 2:9)

cite: ἐφίστημι, ἐπιστήσω, ἐπέστησα / ἐπέστην, ἐφέστηκα, ἐφέσταμαι, ἐπεστάθην

note: Sparta's five ephors were elected yearly and could check even the kings. Modern Greece has an έφορος αρχαιοτήτων, 'superintendent of antiquities'.
ὁ ἐχθρός is a personal enemy, ὁ πολέμιος an enemy in war. Comparison ἐχθίων, ἔχθιστος.
Echidna, half woman and half snake, is the mother of monsters in Hesiod; zoologists gave her name to the spiny anteater.

en: (+ adv.) be in a state: καλῶς ἔχει 'it is well'
note: From *seǵʰ-: the lost s- explains imperfect εἶχον (from ἔσεχον) and the rough breathing of the future ἕξω. Like Romance habēre, Modern έχω forms the perfect: έχω γράψει 'I have written'.

ex.en: I have in mind, I intend

note: With the indicative of past events, with ἄν + subjunctive of the future: ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ 'until he comes'. Also an improper preposition in Koine: ἕως τῆς σήμερον 'until today'.
Attic declension: ἕως, ἕω, ἕῳ, acc. ἕω. Homeric Ἠώς, the rosy-fingered goddess of dawn, shares her name's root with Latin aurōra and English east and Easter.

ex.t: ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς
ex.en: when early-born, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared (Homeric formula)

rel.g: alive (orig. sense, cf. 'the quick and the dead')

note: Contracts to η, not α: ζῶ, ζῇς, ζῇ, inf. ζῆν; classical Attic prefers the aorist ἐβίων (from βιόω). Modern Greek ζω is the same verb, still with the same contraction.

ex.t: ζῶ δὲ οὐκέτι ἐγώ, ζῇ δὲ ἐν ἐμοὶ Χριστός
ex.en: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20)

note: A rare word in antiquity that became the ordinary Modern Greek for 'hot': ζεστό νερό, κάνει ζέστη.

ex.en: you are neither cold nor hot (Revelation 3:15)

note: Same root as Latin iungō and iugum and English yoke: Greek ζ- here reflects an original y-. Herodotus uses it of Xerxes 'yoking' the Hellespont with a bridge of boats.

rel.n: day of Tiw, the Germanic sky-god

note: Ζεύς, Διός, Διί, Δία continue Indo-European *dyēus 'bright sky'; Ζεῦ πάτερ is the exact counterpart of Latin Iuppiter, originally a vocative 'father Sky'.
Like πλέω, a disyllabic -έω verb that contracts only ε + ε/ει: ζεῖ but ζέουσι.

rel.n: via Late Latin zēlōsus, Old French gelos

note: English zeal and jealous are the same Greek word, one learned and one through popular French: Late Latin zēlōsus gave French jaloux and Italian geloso.
In Attic law ζημία is the standard word for a penalty; in Modern Greek ζημιά is any damage, and ζημία a business loss.

cite: ζημιόω, ζημιώσω, ἐζημίωσα, ἐζημίωκα, ἐζημίωμαι, ἐζημιώθην
ζητέω, ζητήσω, ἐζήτησα, ἐζήτηκα, ἐζήτημαι, ἐζητήθην

note: From the parable of the wheat and the tares (Matthew 13), in which an enemy sows weeds among the wheat: hence Italian seminare zizzania and French semer la zizanie 'to sow discord'.
Also masculine ὁ ζυγός. Greek, Latin iugum, Sanskrit yugám and English yoke are one of the textbook Indo-European cognate sets.

ex.t: μικρὰ ζύμη ὅλον τὸ φύραμα ζυμοῖ
ex.en: a little leaven leavens the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5:6)

note: Literally 'one who draws living things'; Modern Greek still says ζωγράφος and ζωγραφική for painting.
ζωή is life as a living state, shared with animals; βίος is a life as lived, a career. Ironically English biology takes βίος for the natural-science sense.

ex.t: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωή
ex.en: I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6)

note: Greek geographers divided the earth into five 'belts' (torrid, temperate, frigid), which is how a word for a girdle became English zone.

ex.en: man is by nature a political animal (Aristotle, Politics)

note: Not to be confused with ἦ 'truly' or ἦ 'I was', which differ only in breathing and accent.

ex.en: either with it or on it (a Spartan mother handing her son his shield)

note: 'Lead' and 'consider' in one verb, exactly as in Latin dūcō, which also means both: to lead a thought to its conclusion.

en: enjoy oneself, take pleasure in (+ dat.)

note: The key term of Epicurean ethics: ἡδονή as the absence of pain in the body and of disturbance in the soul, a far cry from modern 'hedonism'.
Greek ἡδύς, Latin suāvis and English sweet share one root *swād-; initial s- became the rough breathing in Greek, as in ἕξ ~ sex, ἑπτά ~ septem.
Aristotle derives ἠθική ('ethics') from ἔθος 'habit': character is formed by what we repeatedly do.
A present with perfect meaning: ἥκω 'I have come, I am here'; the imperfect ἧκον means 'I had come'.

ex.t: ἥκω νεκρῶν κευθμῶνα καὶ σκότου πύλας λιπών
ex.en: I have come, leaving the hiding-place of the dead and the gates of darkness (Euripides, Hecuba 1)

note: Amber rubbed with cloth attracts light objects; in 1600 William Gilbert called this force ēlectricus 'amber-like', the source of electricity and Modern Greek ηλεκτρισμός.
Greek ἥλιος (earlier ἠέλιος, Doric ἅλιος), Latin sōl and English sun go back to one Indo-European word; helium was first detected in the spectrum of the sun.

ex.en: the sun is new each day (Heraclitus)

note: Modern εμείς replaced the initial η- with ε- by analogy with εγώ; the clitic μας 'us, our' comes from the accusative ἡμᾶς.
Everyday Modern Greek drops the unstressed initial vowel, μέρα, but keeps it in καλημέρα 'good morning'.

ex.t: μία χελιδὼν ἔαρ οὐ ποιεῖ, οὐδὲ μία ἡμέρα
ex.en: one swallow does not make a spring, nor does one day (Aristotle)

rel.g: (pl. οι ημέτεροι) our own people, cronies (formal, ironic)

note: Literally 'half-donkey' (ἡμι- + ὄνος); also feminine ἡ ἡμίονος.
Prefix ἡμι- and Latin sēmi- are cognates (Greek h- < s-). Modern μισός, μισό 'half' is the same word with its unstressed first syllable worn away.
'Rein-holder' (ἡνία + ἔχω): the famous bronze Charioteer of Delphi is ὁ Ηνίοχος in Modern Greek.
Greek and Latin cooks both called goose liver 'fig-fattened' (συκωτόν, iecur ficātum): hence Modern Greek συκώτι and Italian fegato, Spanish hígado, French foie.
The name means 'glory of Hera', the goddess who persecuted him; Ἡράκλεις! and Latin mehercule are everyday oaths.

en: Herodotus (c. 484–425 BC), historian of the Persian Wars
note: Cicero called him pater historiae, 'the father of history'. He wrote in Ionic.
ἤ 'or' + the particle τοι; it gives the first of two alternatives extra weight.

en: be weaker than, give way to (+ gen.)

note: Attic -ττ- corresponds to Ionic and Koine -σσ- (ἥσσων, θάλασσα); Modern Greek inherited the Koine form, as in ήσσονος σημασίας 'of lesser importance'.
The Homeric form; Attic says ἕως, ἕω (Attic 2nd declension). Dawn, the east and the spring goddess behind English Easter share one Indo-European root.

ex.t: ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς

note: Attic θάλαττα, Ionic and Koine θάλασσα; Modern Greek continues the Koine form. The word has no Indo-European etymology and was probably taken from a pre-Greek language of the Aegean.

ex.en: the sea! the sea! (the cry of Xenophon's Ten Thousand)

note: Personified as Θάνατος, twin brother of Ὕπνος 'Sleep' in Hesiod and Homer.
The stem is ταφ- (τάφος 'tomb', ἐτάφην): Greek avoids two aspirates in successive syllables, so *θαφ- appears as θαπ-/ταφ- (Grassmann's law).

en: be of good courage, take heart
be confident about, not fear (+ acc.)
note: Ionic and Koine θαρσέω; the imperative θάρσει 'take heart!' is common in the Gospels. Modern θαρρώ has drifted to 'I reckon, I think'.

ex.en: take heart, it is I; do not be afraid (Matthew 14:27)

ex.t: μάλα γὰρ φιλοσόφου τοῦτο τὸ πάθος, τὸ θαυμάζειν
ex.en: this feeling, wonder, is very much the mark of a philosopher (Plato, Theaetetus)

cite: θαυμάζω, θαυμάσομαι, ἐθαύμασα, τεθαύμακα, τεθαύμασμαι, ἐθαυμάσθην

note: θαῦμα 'wonder' + ποιέω 'make'. Plato compares the low wall in the Cave to the screen above which puppeteers show their puppets.
Not θέα 'sight' — only the accent differs. θεά is mainly poetic; Attic prose says ἡ θεός, especially of Athena.
Literally 'place for watching' (θεάομαι + -τρον, the suffix of instruments and places).

A Greek family word that conquered the western Mediterranean: Late Latin thīus gave Italian zio, Spanish and Portuguese tío/tio, ousting Latin avunculus (which survives in French oncle, English uncle).
Poetic and Koine form of Attic ἐθέλω, hence the augment ἠ-. Medieval θέλει ἵνα 'wants that' wore down to θα, the Modern Greek future marker: θα γράψω.

ex.en: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice (Matthew 9:13)

note: 'What is laid down' (root of τίθημι); οὐ θέμις ἐστί 'it is not right, not allowed by divine law'.
'Gift of god' (θεός + δῶρον); Dorothea is the same two words in reverse order.
Used for both genders (ἡ θεός 'the goddess', beside θεά). Despite the look-alike, θεός is not related to Latin deus, which belongs with Ζεύς, Διός.

ex.en: a god from the machine (deus ex machina)

en: serve, attend to, take care of
cite: θεραπεύω, θεραπεύσω, ἐθεράπευσα, τεθεράπευκα, τεθεράπευμαι, ἐθεραπεύθην

note: In the Iliad Patroclus is Achilles' θεράπων: not a slave but a noble companion who serves him.
Θερμοπύλαι 'Hot Gates' is named after its hot springs.
An action noun from τίθημι 'put': a thesis is what one 'lays down' for discussion, as synthesis is 'putting together'.

en: be a spectator at a festival
cite: θεωρέω, θεωρήσω, ἐθεώρησα, τεθεώρηκα, τεθεώρημαι, ἐθεωρήθην

note: A θεωρός was a 'spectator' sent by a city to watch the games or consult an oracle; philosophers turned the watching inward, and θεωρία became contemplation, then theory.
Plural in form, like Ἀθῆναι; the city of Cadmus, Oedipus and Antigone.
From τίθημι 'put': a place to put things. Its compound ἀποθήκη 'storehouse' became Latin apothēca, whence Italian bottega 'shop', Spanish bodega 'cellar' and French boutique.
From a root meaning 'suckle', also in θηλή 'nipple' and Latin fēmina ('one who gives suck') and fīlius.
Cognate with Latin ferus, fera 'wild (beast)', the source of English feral and fierce.

cite: θηρεύω, θηρεύσω, ἐθήρευσα, τεθήρευκα, τεθήρευμαι, ἐθηρεύθην

rel.n: via Latin thēriaca, Old French triacle

note: A diminutive of θήρ that lost its diminutive force. English treacle began as θηριακή, an antidote against the bites of wild beasts, sweetened with syrup.
The 'treasuries' at Delphi and Olympia were small temple-like buildings in which cities stored their offerings.

ex.t: ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρός σου, ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου
ex.en: for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:21)

note: In Attic prose the present and aorist are normally the compound ἀποθνῄσκω, ἀπέθανον, while the perfect is simple τέθνηκα 'I am dead'. Modern πεθαίνω was rebuilt from ἀπέθανα.

ex.t: ὃν οἱ θεοὶ φιλοῦσιν ἀποθνῄσκει νέος
ex.en: whom the gods love dies young (Menander)

en: make a noise, raise an uproar
note: Athenian juries and assemblies were noisy: Socrates repeatedly begs μὴ θορυβεῖτε, 'don't shout me down'.
cite: θορυβέω, θορυβήσω, ἐθορύβησα, τεθορύβηκα, τεθορύβημαι, ἐθορυβήθην

ex.en: do not make an uproar, men of Athens (Socrates in Plato's Apology)

en: Thucydides (c. 460–400 BC), Athenian historian of the Peloponnesian War
note: An Athenian general exiled after failing to save Amphipolis (424 BC), he wrote his history to be 'a possession for all time' (κτῆμα ἐς αἰεί).
In Herodotus a word for cult practice; in the New Testament and later, 'religion' in general, which is its only sense in Modern Greek.

en: hair (single hair; pl. hair of the head)
note: The stem is *θριχ-, but two aspirates cannot stand in successive syllables, so it shows τριχ- (τριχός, θριξί): a classic case of Grassmann's law.
Declined like πατήρ and μήτηρ (θυγατρός, θυγατρί, θυγατέρα). English daughter and German Tochter are exact cognates; Latin replaced the word with fīlia.

ex.t: θάρσει, θύγατερ· ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε
ex.en: take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well (Matthew 9:22)

note: Originally the 'breath' or 'smoke' of life (cognate with Latin fūmus); in Homer the seat of emotion and will, in Plato the spirited part of the soul. Modern θυμός and θυμώνω mean only 'anger, get angry'.
Greek θ-, Latin f- and English d- regularly correspond, from Indo-European dh-: θύρα ~ forēs ~ door, θυμός ~ fūmus.

cite: θύω, θύσω, ἔθυσα, τέθυκα, τέθυμαι, ἐτύθην

note: Modern γιατρός shows a regular change: an initial ι before a vowel hardened to γι- (ἰατρός → γιατρός, Ἰωάννης → Γιάννης).
From the root of ἰδεῖν 'to see' (Latin videō, English wit): an idea is first of all a 'look'. Plato's Ideas are the true 'looks' of things, visible only to the mind.
Opposed to κοινός 'common' and δημόσιος 'public'. In Modern Greek ο ίδιος mostly means 'the same' (το ίδιο 'the same thing').

ex.t: εἰς τὰ ἴδια ἦλθεν, καὶ οἱ ἴδιοι αὐτὸν οὐ παρέλαβον
ex.en: he came to his own, and his own did not receive him (John 1:11)

note: In democratic Athens the ἰδιώτης was the citizen without public role, then the layman as opposed to the expert; Latin idiōta 'uneducated person' took the last step towards English idiot.
Originally the aorist middle imperative of ὁράω (ἰδοῦ 'see!'), accented differently as a fixed exclamation; very frequent in the Septuagint and New Testament.

ex.t: ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν
ex.en: behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son (Matthew 1:23)

note: Greek rough breathing for s- again: ἱδρώς ~ Latin sūdor ~ English sweat.

rel.g: sanctuary; altar area of a church

note: A poetic by-form of ἵζω (< *si-sd-ō, like Latin sīdō). Sappho's ἰσδάνει shows Aeolic σδ for ζ and no rough breathing.
Mostly met in compounds: ἀφίημι 'let go, forgive', συνίημι 'understand' (lit. 'send together'), μεθίημι 'release'. Modern αφήνω 'leave, let' continues ἀφίημι.
cite: ἵημι, ἥσω, ἧκα, εἷκα, εἷμαι, εἵθην

note: Greek rendering of Hebrew Yēšūaʿ; declined Ἰησοῦς, Ἰησοῦ, Ἰησοῦ, Ἰησοῦν, voc. Ἰησοῦ. The Septuagint uses the same form for Joshua.
Odysseus' island home, and in Cavafy's poem the destination that matters less than the journey.
A suppliant clasping an altar or a person's knees was under the protection of Zeus Ἱκέσιος; violating him was sacrilege, the theme of Aeschylus' Suppliants.

ex.t: ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός
ex.en: for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7)

note: A by-form of εἴλλω / εἱλέω 'roll'. In the Antigone ode the ploughs go ἰλλομένων ἀρότρων ἔτος εἰς ἔτος, 'turning to and fro year after year'.
From ἵμερος 'longing'. Sappho's γελαίσας ἰμέροεν 'your lovely laughter' shows the Aeolic loss of the rough breathing.

en: in order that, so that (+ subj./opt.)
note: Koine used ἵνα-clauses ever more widely instead of the infinitive; reduced to να, it is the Modern Greek subjunctive particle: θέλω να γράψω 'I want to write'.

ex.en: I eat in order to live (saying attributed to Socrates)

note: Cognate with Latin vīrus 'poison, slime'; Modern Greek gave the old word the new meaning of the Latin one, so ιός is 'virus'.

rel.n: via Latin and Old French giu

en: of a horse or horses, equine
note: From ἵππος. Sophocles' ἱππείῳ γένει 'with the offspring of horses' probably means mules drawing the plough.

en: (pl., at Athens) the Knights, the second property class

note: Ἵππος, Latin equus and Sanskrit áśva- are cognates. The everyday Modern word άλογο comes from ἄλογον 'irrational (animal)', much as Latin caballus 'nag' replaced equus in Romance (cavallo, caballo).
In Herodotus' constitutional debate (3.80) Otanes says rule by the many has 'the fairest name of all, ἰσονομία'.

rel.n: from the perfect ἕστηκα via Koine στήκω

note: The reduplicated present *σί-στη-μι (cf. Latin sistō) lost its σ- to the rough breathing. The aorist ἔστησα is transitive 'I set up', ἔστην intransitive 'I stood'.

ex.t: δός μοι πᾶ στῶ καὶ τὰν γᾶν κινάσω
ex.en: give me a place to stand and I will move the earth (Archimedes, Doric)

cite: ἵστημι, στήσω, ἔστησα / ἔστην, ἕστηκα, ἕσταμαι, ἐστάθην

note: An ἵστωρ is 'one who knows' (root of οἶδα, Latin videō): Herodotus calls his work an 'inquiry', and the word came to mean the account that results.

ex.en: this is the presentation of the inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassus (Herodotus 1.0, Ionic)

note: Literally 'that which stands' (ἵστημι). Penelope's ruse was weaving and unweaving a web on her ἱστός; Modern Greek ιστοσελίδα 'web page' reuses the word for the Internet.
From the root of οἶδα 'know' (*wid-): the one who knows. Its derivative ἱστορία 'inquiry' gave history and story. The Oath calls on all the gods ἵστορας ποιεύμενος, 'making them my witnesses'.
Also two-termination: πολλὰς δ’ ἰφθίμους ψυχάς 'many mighty souls' (Iliad 1.3). Probably related to ἶφι 'by might'.
The early Christian symbol ΙΧΘΥΣ is an acrostic: Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Θεοῦ Υἱὸς Σωτήρ, 'Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour'. Everyday Modern Greek says ψάρι.

cite: καθαίρω, καθαρῶ, ἐκάθηρα, κεκάθαρκα, κεκάθαρμαι, ἐκαθάρθην

note: Aristotle's Poetics says tragedy achieves, through pity and fear, the κάθαρσις of such emotions; whether this is purgation or purification is still debated.
A cathedral is the church that houses the bishop's cathedra; through popular Latin the same word became English chair, French chaise and Portuguese cadeira.

en: (impers. καθήκει) it is fitting, it is one's duty
note: The Stoic τὸ καθῆκον 'what is appropriate' was rendered by Cicero as officium, the title of his De Officiis; Modern Greek καθήκον is simply 'duty'.
κατά + poetic ἧμαι 'sit'; it has only present-system forms (imperfect ἐκαθήμην, 3 sg. ἐκάθητο or καθῆστο). Modern κάθομαι continues it with a regular -ομαι ending.

en: (intr.: aor. κατέστην, perf. καθέστηκα) be established, become
cite: καθίστημι, καταστήσω, κατέστησα / κατέστην, καθέστηκα, καθέσταμαι, κατεστάθην

note: From καθ’ ὅλου 'on the whole'; the 'catholic' Church is the 'universal' one.
Classical writers often print it as two words, καθ’ ὅλου. In Modern Greek it means 'at all': δεν ξέρω καθόλου 'I don't know at all'.
Pronounced [ke] in Modern Greek; the abbreviation κ.λπ. (καὶ τὰ λοιπά) is the Greek 'etc.'

ex.en: you too, my son? (Caesar's last words, in Suetonius)

note: καινός is new in kind, novel; νέος is new in time, young. ἡ Καινὴ Διαθήκη is the New Testament, and English -cene (Eocene, Pliocene) is καινός.
χρόνος is time as duration, καιρός the critical moment. Modern καιρός means 'weather' as well as 'time', exactly like Italian tempo, Spanish tiempo and French temps.
A Latin loanword: the Greek spelling with κ shows that Latin c was pronounced [k] before ae in Caesar's day.

ex.t: ἀπόδοτε οὖν τὰ Καίσαρος Καίσαρι καὶ τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τῷ θεῷ
ex.en: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's (Matthew 22:21)

note: Attic also κάω. The stem καυ- appears in καῦμα 'heat' and καύσιμα 'fuel', still Modern Greek words.
cite: καίω, καύσω, ἔκαυσα, κέκαυκα, κέκαυμαι, ἐκαύθην

note: κακός has several comparisons: κακίων, κάκιστος 'more base, basest'; χείρων, χείριστος 'worse, worst' in quality; ἥττων 'weaker'.

ex.en: no one is bad willingly (Socratic maxim)

en: (κακῶς ἔχειν) be in a bad way

note: Latin calamārium was the case for reed pens and ink; the squid, with its ink sac, was named after it, hence Italian calamari.

The future καλῶ looks like the contracted present, and the perfect stem κλη- (κέκληκα, ἐκλήθην) is the one in ἐκκλησία, the 'called-out' assembly that became Latin ecclēsia, Italian chiesa and French église.

ex.t: πολλοὶ γάρ εἰσιν κλητοί, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοί
ex.en: for many are called, but few are chosen (Matthew 22:14)

cite: καλέω, καλῶ, ἐκάλεσα, κέκληκα, κέκλημαι, ἐκλήθην

note: Superlative of καλός (comparative καλλίων).

ex.en: for the fairest (inscribed on the golden apple of Eris)

note: The classical ideal of the gentleman was καλὸς κἀγαθός, 'fine and good'. In Modern Greek καλός means 'good', while 'beautiful' is ωραίος.

ex.en: a fine and good man, a gentleman

note: The nymph Καλυψώ, who kept Odysseus hidden for seven years, is 'she who conceals'.
A vaulted room became Latin camara/camera 'room' (Italian camera, French chambre); the photographic camera is short for camera obscura, a 'dark chamber'.
A Semitic word (Hebrew gāmāl) that reached Europe through Greek; also feminine ἡ κάμηλος.

ex.t: εὐκοπώτερόν ἐστιν κάμηλον διὰ τρυπήματος ῥαφίδος διελθεῖν
ex.en: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle (Matthew 19:24)

note: Greek κάμινος passed through Latin camīnus to Italian camino and French cheminée, and on to English chimney.
Modern Greek's commonest verb, κάνω 'do, make', is this verb: 'toil at' weakened in Byzantine Greek to 'make, do', replacing ποιέω and πράττω.
A measuring rod; the sculptor Polyclitus wrote a treatise called Κανών on ideal proportions, and the Church used the word for the list of authoritative books.
Homeric κραδίη; καρδία, Latin cor, cordis and English heart all continue Indo-European *ḱerd-.

ex.en: blessed are the pure in heart (Matthew 5:8)

note: Hippocratic doctors compared a tumour with its swollen veins to a crab; Latin cancer, a cognate, carried the same metaphor.
The fruit is 'what is plucked': same root as Latin carpō (carpe diem, 'pluck the day') and English harvest.
Pilgrims purified themselves in its water before consulting the oracle; later poets made it a spring of poetic inspiration.
Καστωλοῦ πεδίον, the plain of Castolus, was the mustering-ground of the Persian forces in the west, which Darius put under Cyrus' command (Anabasis 1.1.2).
Merchants' Greek κατὰ μῆνα 'per month' entered Vulgar Latin as cata 'each', whence Spanish and Portuguese cada.

en: go down to the sea (from inland)

ex.en: I went down yesterday to the Piraeus (first words of Plato's Republic)

note: κατά 'down' + γῆ 'earth'; Plato's prisoners live ἐν καταγείῳ οἰκήσει σπηλαιώδει, 'in an underground, cave-like dwelling'.

en: condemn, give judgment against (+ gen. of person)
cite: καταγιγνώσκω, καταγνώσομαι, κατέγνων, καταγέγνωκα, καταγέγνωσμαι, κατεγνώσθην

note: The Septuagint's word for Noah's Flood; Greek myth had its own in the flood of Deucalion.
Modern καταλαβαίνω 'understand' is to 'grasp' with the mind, the same metaphor as Latin comprehendere and English get it.
cite: καταλαμβάνω, καταλήψομαι, κατέλαβον, κατείληφα, κατείλημμαι, κατελήφθην
καταλείπω, καταλείψω, κατέλιπον, καταλέλοιπα, καταλέλειμμαι, κατελείφθην

note: Travellers 'unloosed' their animals for the night, hence 'lodge': κατάλυμα is the inn with no room in Luke 2:7.
cite: καταλύω, καταλύσω, κατέλυσα, καταλέλυκα, καταλέλυμαι, κατελύθην
καταπονέω, καταπονήσω, κατεπόνησα, καταπεπόνηκα, καταπεπόνημαι, κατεπονήθην

en: end, conclusion (of a play or life)
note: In drama the καταστροφή is the final 'down-turn' of the plot, which is how the word came to mean disaster.

cite: καταφρονέω, καταφρονήσω, κατεφρόνησα, καταπεφρόνηκα, καταπεφρόνημαι, κατεφρονήθην

note: In Sappho 31.13 the Aeolic form κακχέεται (κακ- for κατα- before χ) is the usual restoration of a corrupt line: 'sweat pours down me'.
cite: καταχέω, καταχέω, κατέχεα, κατακέχυκα, κατακέχυμαι, κατεχύθην

note: As with ἔρχομαι, Attic uses κάτειμι for the future. κατέρχομαι is the technical word for an exile 'coming back down' to his city.

cite: κατέχω, καθέξω, κατέσχον, κατέσχηκα, κατέσχημαι, κατεσχέθην

note: Formed from κατήγορος 'accuser', so the augment is inside: κατηγόρησα. Literally 'speak against (someone) in the ἀγορά'.
cite: κατηγορέω, κατηγορήσω, κατηγόρησα, κατηγόρηκα, κατηγόρημαι, κατηγορήθην

note: Aristotle's ten 'categories' are the kinds of thing that can be 'said against', i.e. predicated of, a subject.

ex.en: upside down, topsy-turvy (lit. up and down)

note: From καίω 'burn'. Late Latin cauma, the heat of midday when everything rests, is the probable source of Italian calma, French calme and English calm.

en: (as perf. pass. of τίθημι) be placed, be established

ex.t: ὦ ξεῖν’, ἀγγέλλειν Λακεδαιμονίοις ὅτι τῇδε κείμεθα, τοῖς κείνων ῥήμασι πειθόμενοι
ex.en: stranger, tell the Spartans that here we lie, obeying their words (Simonides, on the dead of Thermopylae)

ex.t: ὁ στρατηγὸς κελεύει τοὺς στρατιώτας μένειν
ex.en: the general orders the soldiers to stay

cite: κελεύω, κελεύσω, ἐκέλευσα, κεκέλευκα, κεκέλευσμαι, ἐκελεύσθην

note: For the atomists Leucippus and Democritus, reality consisted of atoms and τὸ κενόν, the void.
From κεντέω 'prick': the centre is where the fixed point of the compass pricks the surface.

ex.en: it is hard for you to kick against the goads (Acts 26:14)

note: The Κεραμεικός, the potters' quarter of Athens, was also its main cemetery.
Gen. also κέρως. Greek κ ~ English h by Grimm's law: κέρας ~ horn, καρδία ~ heart, κύων ~ hound.
Its derivative κεφάλαιον 'main point, sum' gives Modern κεφάλαιο 'capital; chapter', a perfect parallel to Latin caput → capitulum, capitale (but κεφαλή and caput are not related).

ex.en: I have a headache (lit. I hurt in the head)

note: Epicurus taught in a garden in Athens, so his school was called simply ὁ Κῆπος, 'the Garden'.
Heralds were sacred and inviolable even in war; their staff, the κηρύκειον (Doric καρύκειον), became Latin cādūceus, the snake-entwined wand of Hermes.
Attic -ττ-, Koine κηρύσσω; Modern Greek keeps the Koine form: κηρύσσω πόλεμο 'declare war'.
cite: κηρύττω, κηρύξω, ἐκήρυξα, κεκήρυχα, κεκήρυγμαι, ἐκηρύχθην

note: The 'great fish' that swallowed Jonah is a κῆτος in the Septuagint and Matthew 12:40.
The professional singer's lyre travelled via Arabic qītāra to Spain and became the guitarra; Modern Greek has taken the word back as κιθάρα 'guitar'.

en: run a risk, be in danger
(+ inf.) be likely to, it seems that
note: Plato's Socrates uses κινδυνεύω + infinitive as a modest 'I dare say': κινδυνεύεις ἀληθῆ λέγειν 'you are probably right'.
cite: κινδυνεύω, κινδυνεύσω, ἐκινδύνευσα, κεκινδύνευκα, κεκινδύνευμαι, ἐκινδυνεύθην

note: The cinema is short for cinématographe, 'motion-writer'; Modern Greek calls it κινηματογράφος.

ex.en: that which moves without being moved (Aristotle, Metaphysics)

cite: κινέω, κινήσω, ἐκίνησα, κεκίνηκα, κεκίνημαι, ἐκινήθην

note: In Aristotle κίνησις covers all change, not just locomotion; his God is the 'unmoved mover', τὸ κινοῦν ἀκίνητον.
Attic also spells it κλάω (κλα(ί)ω in school lists).

ex.en: to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15)

note: Cognate with Latin clāvis 'key' and claudō 'shut'; Latin clāvicula 'little key' gave the anatomists' clavicle, the bone Greek doctors also called κλείς.
Older Attic κλῄω. Modern κλείνω, κλειστός 'closed' and κλειδαριά 'lock' all belong here.
cite: κλείω, κλείσω, ἔκλεισα, κέκλεικα, κέκλεισμαι, ἐκλείσθην

note: Achilles chooses a short life with κλέος ἄφθιτον, 'imperishable fame', a phrase matched word for word in Vedic Sanskrit. The same word ends many names: Περικλῆς, Σοφοκλῆς, Ἡρακλῆς.
Modern κλέφτης shows the regular change πτ → φτ; under Ottoman rule the κλέφτες were outlaw guerrillas celebrated in folk song.

cite: κλέπτω, κλέψω, ἔκλεψα, κέκλοφα, κέκλεμμαι, ἐκλάπην

en: inherit, be heir to (+ gen.; NT + acc.)
note: κλῆρος 'lot, allotted land' + νέμω 'distribute': the heir receives his share of the family land.

ex.t: μακάριοι οἱ πραεῖς, ὅτι αὐτοὶ κληρονομήσουσι τὴν γῆν
ex.en: blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5)
