cite: κληρονομέω, κληρονομήσω, ἐκληρονόμησα, κεκληρονόμηκα, κεκληρονόμημαι, ἐκληρονομήθην

note: 'One who receives (νέμομαι) the allotment (κλῆρος)'.
Athens filled most offices by lot (κλῆρος). The clergy are those whose 'lot' is the Lord; a clerk was originally a cleric, the man who could write.
Greek geographers divided the world into κλίματα by the 'slope' of the sun's rays at each latitude, so a climate was first a band of the globe.
Greeks dined reclining on κλῖναι; κλινική (τέχνη) was medicine practised at the bedside.
Greek grammarians thought of inflected forms as 'leanings' away from the upright nominative: κλίσις, Latin dēclīnātiō, and casus, πτῶσις 'fall'.
cite: κλίνω, κλινῶ, ἔκλινα, κέκλικα, κέκλιμαι, ἐκλίθην

note: Early Christians called the dead 'those who have fallen asleep' (οἱ κεκοιμημένοι), and their burial place a κοιμητήριον 'dormitory': the source of cemetery in every western language.
ἡ κοινὴ διάλεκτος 'the common dialect' was the Greek of Alexander's empire and of the New Testament, the ancestor of Modern Greek.

en: share, have a share in (+ gen.)

note: Aristotle's ἡ πολιτικὴ κοινωνία, the political community, is what Modern Greek simply calls κοινωνία 'society'; the Eucharist is η Θεία Κοινωνία.
From the 'eternal punishment' (κόλασις αἰώνιος) of Matthew 25:46, Modern Greek κόλαση simply means 'hell', its opposite being παράδεισος.
A humble Koine word (the soldiers 'buffeted' Jesus, ἐκολάφισαν) that became Latin colaphus, popular *colpus: hence Italian colpo, Spanish golpe and French coup, as in coup d'état.
A comet is a 'long-haired star', named for its streaming tail.

cite: κομίζω, κομιῶ, ἐκόμισα, κεκόμικα, κεκόμισμαι, ἐκομίσθην

note: A κόμμα was a short clause 'cut off' from a sentence; the name passed to the punctuation mark that sets it off.
cite: κόπτω, κόψω, ἔκοψα, κέκοφα, κέκομμαι, ἐκόπην

ex.en: go to the crows! (= go to hell; common in Aristophanes)

note: The pupil is called κόρη 'little girl' because you see a tiny figure of yourself in another's eye; Latin pūpilla 'little doll', whence English pupil, is the same image.

cite: κοσμέω, κοσμήσω, ἐκόσμησα, κεκόσμηκα, κεκόσμημαι, ἐκοσμήθην

note: The Pythagoreans first called the universe κόσμος, 'the beautiful order'; Latin mundus imitates both meanings. Modern κόσμος also means 'people': είχε πολύ κόσμο 'it was crowded'.

ex.t: οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον
ex.en: for God so loved the world (John 3:16)

ex.t: κοῦφον γὰρ χρῆμα ποιητής ἐστιν καὶ πτηνὸν καὶ ἱερόν
ex.en: for a poet is a light and winged and holy thing (Plato, Ion)

note: The twelve baskets of leftovers at the feeding of the five thousand were κόφινοι; through Latin cophinus the word became French coffre 'chest' and English coffin.
An imitative word for the raven's cry; the perfect κέκραγα has present meaning 'I am shouting'. Very common in the Gospels for the cries of the possessed.

cite: κρατέω, κρατήσω, ἐκράτησα, κεκράτηκα, κεκράτημαι, ἐκρατήθην

note: Superlative of κρατύς 'strong', used as a superlative of ἀγαθός beside ἄριστος and βέλτιστος; comparative κρείττων.
The -κρατία of δημοκρατία and ἀριστοκρατία. Modern Greek κράτος means 'the state'.

ex.en: by force, with all one's might

note: Gen. κρέως, pl. κρέα (contracted from *κρέασ-ος, *κρέασ-α); English creosote is 'flesh-preserver' (κρέας + σῴζω).
Comparative of ἀγαθός in the sense 'stronger, superior'; Ionic and Koine κρείσσων. κρείττων λόγου 'beyond words'.
The root meant 'sift, separate': Latin cernō (discern, crīmen, discrīmen) is its cognate. Judging is separating the guilty from the innocent.

ex.en: judge not, that you be not judged (Matthew 7:1)

cite: κρίνω, κρινῶ, ἔκρινα, κέκρικα, κέκριμαι, ἐκρίθην

note: Hippocratic doctors used κρίσις for the decisive day when a fever turns towards recovery or death, the origin of the modern 'crisis'.

en: (theatre) one of the judges of the contest

note: Latin crypta 'vault' became popular *crupta and then Italian grotta, so a crypt and a grotto are the same Greek word.
cite: κρύπτω, κρύψω, ἔκρυψα, κέκρυφα, κέκρυμμαι, ἐκρύφθην

note: From κρύος 'frost': ancient writers thought rock crystal was ice frozen so hard it could never melt.
The perfect κέκτημαι 'I have acquired' means 'I own', just as οἶδα 'I have seen' means 'I know'.
Prose uses the compound ἀποκτείνω, whose passive is supplied by ἀποθνῄσκω: ἀπέθανεν ὑπὸ τῶν πολεμίων 'he was killed by the enemy'. Modern σκοτώνω 'kill' is 'to darken (someone's eyes)'.

ex.en: a possession for all time (Thucydides on his History, 1.22)

note: Popular Modern Greek turns κτ into χτ: κτίζω → χτίζω, ὀκτώ → οχτώ, νύκτα → νύχτα.
An early nautical loan into Latin (gubernāre); the 'ship of state' metaphor turned steering into governing. Cybernetics, 'the art of steering', was coined from the same verb in 1948.
cite: κυβερνάω, κυβερνήσω, ἐκυβέρνησα, κεκυβέρνηκα, κεκυβέρνημαι, ἐκυβερνήθην

rel.g: captain (of a ship or aircraft); governor

note: κύκλος and English wheel both come from Indo-European *kʷékʷlos, a reduplicated word for the newly invented wheel.
In Plato's Phaedo Socrates says swans sing most beautifully just before death, out of joy at going to Apollo: the origin of the 'swan song'.

ex.t: γέγονα χαλκὸς ἠχῶν ἢ κύμβαλον ἀλαλάζον
ex.en: I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal (1 Corinthians 13:1)

note: A Homeric drinking cup; in Modern Greek it is the sports trophy, as in Κύπελλο Ελλάδος 'the Greek Cup'.
Greek-speaking Christians called a church κυριακόν (δῶμα) 'the Lord's house'; the word was borrowed into early Germanic and became English church, Scots kirk and German Kirche.
Originally an adjective 'having authority'. The Septuagint used Κύριος for the divine name; in Modern Greek κύριος and κυρία are simply 'Mr' and 'Mrs'.

en: Cyrus the Great (d. 530 BC), founder of the Persian empire
Cyrus the Younger (d. 401 BC), son of Darius II
note: Xenophon wrote about both: the Cyropaedia idealizes the elder Cyrus, and the Anabasis follows the younger one's march against his brother Artaxerxes II, which ended with his death at Cunaxa.
Also feminine ἡ κύων 'bitch'. Diogenes, who lived shamelessly in public, was nicknamed ὁ κύων, and his followers were the Cynics, 'the doggish ones'.

ex.en: what prevents me from being baptised? (Acts 8:36)

cite: κωλύω, κωλύσω, ἐκώλυσα, κεκώλυκα, κεκώλυμαι, ἐκωλύθην

note: From κώμη 'village'. Do not confuse with κομήτης 'long-haired', the source of comet.
Most likely 'the song (ᾠδή) of the κῶμος', the drunken revel; Aristotle reports a rival Dorian claim that it came from κώμη 'village', because comic players toured the villages.
A κωνωπεῖον was a bed with a mosquito net; via Latin it became English canopy and French canapé, a sofa (and the open sandwich that 'sits' on its bread).
In drama a κωφὸν πρόσωπον is a 'mute character' who appears on stage without speaking.
A pre-Greek word, like Κόρινθος with its -νθ- suffix; the Labyrinth of Minos at Knossos housed the Minotaur.

en: obtain by lot, get as one's share (+ gen. or acc.)

rel.g: win (in a lottery), happen to get

cite: λαγχάνω, λήξομαι, ἔλαχον, εἴληχα, εἴληγμαι, ἐλήχθην

note: A model 'Attic second declension' noun: λαγώς, λαγώ, λαγῷ, λαγών (Ionic and Homeric λαγωός).
From the root of λανθάνω 'escape notice'; Modern λαθρεπιβάτης is a 'stowaway', λαθρεμπόριο 'smuggling'.
The official name of the Spartan state was Λακεδαίμων. Spartans (Λάκωνες) were famous for terse replies, hence English laconic.
In Attic it is mere 'prattle'; in the New Testament it is the neutral verb 'speak', alongside λέγω.
cite: λαλέω, λαλήσω, ἐλάλησα, λελάληκα, λελάλημαι, ἐλαλήθην

note: The root is λαβ-/ληβ-: the present adds a nasal (λα-μ-β-άν-ω), the aorist ἔλαβον shows the bare root, the future λήψομαι the long grade.

ex.en: come and take them (Leonidas' reply when Xerxes demanded the Spartans' arms)

cite: λαμβάνω, λήψομαι, ἔλαβον, εἴληφα, εἴλημμαι, ἐλήφθην

note: Athenian festivals included a torch relay, the λαμπαδηδρομία, the model for the modern Olympic flame relay.
Modern Greeks call Easter Λαμπρή, 'the Bright (day)', from the candles lit at the midnight service.

ex.t: οὕτως λαμψάτω τὸ φῶς ὑμῶν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων
ex.en: let your light so shine before men (Matthew 5:16)

note: Greek puts the main idea in the participle: ἔλαθεν εἰσελθών 'he came in unnoticed'. ἀλήθεια 'truth' is literally 'un-concealment'.
The Attic form is λεώς (Attic declension), surviving in λεωφόρος 'highway'. Via Church Latin lāicus, 'one of the people', it gave English lay and laity.
From λάτρις 'hired servant'; in the Septuagint and New Testament it is service to God, and in Modern Greek σε λατρεύω means 'I adore you'.
A suppletive verb: the future ἐρῶ and aorist εἶπον come from other roots. τί λέγεις; can mean 'what do you mean?'.

ex.t: λέγει που Ἡράκλειτος ὅτι πάντα χωρεῖ καὶ οὐδὲν μένει
ex.en: Heraclitus says somewhere that everything moves on and nothing stays (Plato, Cratylus)

cite: λέγω, ἐρῶ / λέξω, εἶπον / ἔλεξα, εἴρηκα, εἴρημαι / λέλεγμαι, ἐλέχθην / ἐρρήθην

note: The original meaning of the root: 'gather' → 'count' → 'recount, tell'. Latin legō went the same way, 'gather' → 'read', which is why λόγος 'account, reckoning' and Latin lēctiō are so close.
The textbook example of Greek vowel gradation: λειπ- (present), λοιπ- (perfect λέλοιπα, λοιπός 'remaining'), λιπ- (aorist ἔλιπον).
cite: λείπω, λείψω, ἔλιπον, λέλοιπα, λέλειμμαι, ἐλείφθην

note: 'Work for the people' (λήϊτος 'public' + ἔργον): in Athens rich citizens paid for a chorus or a warship as a λειτουργία. Modern Greek uses it of any machine 'working' and of the Divine Liturgy.
Aristotle's Rhetoric treats λέξις as 'style'; in Modern Greek λέξη is the everyday word for 'word', and λεξικό for 'dictionary'.
From λεπρός 'scaly', from λέπω 'peel': the disease that makes the skin flake.
The widow's mite in Mark 12:42 is two λεπτά. Modern λεπτό 'minute' copies Latin pars minūta 'small part', the source of English minute.

rel.n: from Latin asper 'rough' (of new silver coins)

note: The root *leuk- 'shine' gives λευκός, Latin lūx and lūna, and English light. Everyday Modern άσπρος comes from Latin asper, used of freshly minted, rough and shining silver coins.
Latin leō, leōnis is an early loan from Greek, so every European word for the lion goes back to λέων; the Lion Gate of Mycenae shows how familiar the animal was to Bronze Age Greeks.

ex.en: (you know) the lion by its claw (proverb: the whole from a part)

note: 'Carrying the people' (Attic λεώς 'people' + φέρω): an ancient highway, then a modern avenue, and with -εῖον the Modern Greek word for a bus.

en: (Λήθη) Lethe, river of forgetfulness in the underworld
note: From the root of λανθάνω; its negation ἀλήθεια 'not-forgetting, un-concealment' is the Greek word for truth.
From λεία 'booty'. In John 18:40 Barabbas is a λῃστής; Modern ληστεία is 'robbery'.
A Semitic loan (Hebrew lĕbōnāh, 'the white (resin)'), like the name of Mount Lebanon, Λίβανος.

ex.t: ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτος ἐπ’ αὐτὴν βαλέτω λίθον
ex.en: let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her (John 8:7)

note: Thucydides reports that during the Athenian plague people argued whether an old oracle had foretold a λοιμός 'plague' or a λιμός 'famine', and remembered it to fit what happened, the two words being pronounced almost alike.
From λιμός 'hunger'; Attic ττ, elsewhere λιμώσσω.
Pindar's praise of λιπαραὶ Ἀθᾶναι, 'gleaming Athens', became the city's proud epithet.

rel.n: both from the same Italic word
via Medieval Latin litra, French litre

note: Sicilian Greeks borrowed the word from their Italic neighbours, whose form appears in Latin lībra 'pound' (lira, livre). Through Medieval Latin litra it ended up as the metric litre.
Herodotus calls the chroniclers of Persia and Egypt λόγιοι, 'men versed in tales'.
From λέγω in its old sense 'gather, count': first an 'account' or 'reckoning', then a statement and the reason behind it. Latin needed two words to translate it, ratiō and ōrātiō (or verbum).

ex.en: in the beginning was the Word (John 1:1)

cite: λοιδορέω, λοιδορήσω, ἐλοιδόρησα, λελοιδόρηκα, λελοιδόρημαι, ἐλοιδορήθην

note: The Iliad opens with Apollo's λοιμός on the Greek camp, Thucydides' Book 2 with the plague of Athens.
The λοιπ- grade of λείπω, 'left over'. καὶ τὰ λοιπά 'and the rest' is the Greek 'et cetera', abbreviated κ.λπ.; Modern λοιπόν is the everyday 'so, well'.
Apollo was called Λοξίας, 'the oblique one', because his oracles were notoriously ambiguous.
λούω is for washing the body, νίζω for hands and feet, πλύνω for clothes; Attic often contracts it (λοῦμαι, ἐλοῦτο).
A military term with Doric -ᾱγός even in Attic (cf. ξεναγός); frequent in Xenophon's Anabasis, and still the Greek army rank.
Thebes' elite ἱερὸς λόχος, the Sacred Band, gave its name to Ypsilantis' Sacred Band of 1821 in the Greek War of Independence.
Aristotle taught in the Λύκειον, a gymnasium sacred to Apollo Λύκειος; hence French lycée and Modern Greek λύκειο 'upper secondary school'.

cite: λυπέω, λυπήσω, ἐλύπησα, λελύπηκα, λελύπημαι, ἐλυπήθην

note: From λύπη 'pain, grief'. For Aristotle animal voice signals only τὸ λυπηρὸν καὶ ἡδύ, the painful and the pleasant; human speech can express the just and the unjust.
Lyric poetry was poetry sung to the lyre; the Modern Greek λύρα of Crete is, oddly, played with a bow.

ex.t: δοῦναι τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν
ex.en: to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45)
lighting a lamp in broad daylight, he said: 'I am looking for a human being' (Diogenes the Cynic)

en: ransom (mid.: get released for a price)
note: The model verb of Greek grammars, chosen because all its forms are regular. Modern λύνω 'untie, solve' adds a present -ν-.

ex.t: λυσόμενός τε θύγατρα φέρων τ’ ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα
ex.en: to ransom his daughter, bringing a boundless ransom (Iliad 1.13)

cite: λύω, λύσω, ἔλυσα, λέλυκα, λέλυμαι, ἐλύθην

note: Odysseus' men who ate the honey-sweet fruit of the Lotus-eaters (Λωτοφάγοι) forgot their homecoming.

en: by … (in oaths, + acc.; mostly negative: 'no, by …')
note: Usually negative (οὐ μὰ Δία 'no, by Zeus'), while νή swears 'yes, by …'. Modern Greek still swears μα τον Θεό 'by God!'.

en: magus, member of the Persian priestly caste
note: A Persian word for the priestly caste. The 'wise men' who follow the star in Matthew 2 are μάγοι ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν, 'magi from the East'.
Literally 'a thing learnt' (from μανθάνω). For the Pythagoreans the learnable sciences par excellence were arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and music, so τὰ μαθήματα narrowed to 'mathematics'.
Already in Aristophanes ὁ μακαρίτης is 'the late, the dear departed' — the dead are 'the blessed' — and Modern Greek uses it the same way.

ex.en: blessed are the poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3)

note: The long-vowel mark (ā) is called a macron, Greek μακρόν 'long (one)'.
The present adds a nasal infix and -αν- to the root μαθ-, which appears bare in the aorist ἔμαθον.
From μάντις 'seer'. The English suffix -mancy (necromancy, chiromancy) comes from μαντεία 'divination'.
The praying mantis was named for its prophet-like pose; μαντεῖον is an oracle, μαντεία the art of divination.
Named after μάραθον 'fennel'. The modern 42 km race (1896) recalls the runner said to have carried news of the victory of 490 BC to Athens.

ex.t: μηδὲ βάλητε τοὺς μαργαρίτας ὑμῶν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν χοίρων
ex.en: do not throw your pearls before swine (Matthew 7:6)

cite: μαρτυρέω, μαρτυρήσω, ἐμαρτύρησα, μεμαρτύρηκα, μεμαρτύρημαι, ἐμαρτυρήθην

note: A martyr is literally a 'witness': early Christians bore witness to their faith with their death, and the word narrowed to that sense.

ex.en: vanity of vanities, all is vanity (Ecclesiastes 1:2, Septuagint)

note: Originally the accusative of μάτη 'folly'; μάταιος 'vain' is its adjective.

ex.t: οὐθὲν γάρ, ὡς φαμέν, μάτην ἡ φύσις ποιεῖ
ex.en: for nature, as we say, does nothing in vain (Aristotle, Politics 1253a)

note: Modern μαχαίρι continues the diminutive μαχαίριον — Modern Greek is full of such neuter diminutives (παιδί, ψάρι, μάτι).

ex.t: πάντες γὰρ οἱ λαβόντες μάχαιραν ἐν μαχαίρῃ ἀπολοῦνται
ex.en: for all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52)

en: neut. as adv. μέγα: greatly, loudly
note: Only μέγας, μέγαν, μέγα are short; every other form uses the stem μεγαλ-, which Modern Greek generalised (μεγάλος).

ex.en: a big book is a big evil (Callimachus)

note: From μέθυ 'wine', cognate with English mead. The amethyst (ἀμέθυστος 'not drunk') was believed to ward off intoxication.

en: (pass.) mix with, have intercourse with (+ dat.)
note: Older editions spell it μίγνυμι; Attic inscriptions show μειγ-. The second aorist passive ἐμίγην is common.
cite: μείγνυμι, μείξω, ἔμειξα, μέμειχα, μέμειγμαι, ἐμείχθην

note: Comparative of μέγας. Modern Greek normally says μεγαλύτερος but keeps μείζων in formal phrases (μείζον θέμα 'a major issue').
μελαγχολία 'black bile' was the humour blamed for gloom → melancholy. Modern Greek μελάνι 'ink' is 'the black stuff'.

en: it is a care to, it concerns (+ dat. of person, gen. of thing)

rel.n: colloquial δε με μέλει 'I don't care'

note: Impersonal: the person who cares is dative, the thing cared about genitive. Compounds: ἐπιμελέομαι 'take care of', ἀμελέω 'neglect'.

cite: μελετάω, μελετήσω, ἐμελέτησα, μεμελέτηκα, μεμελέτημαι, ἐμελετήθην

ex.en: practice is everything (Periander, one of the Seven Sages)

note: Greek μέλι and Latin mel are cognate. μέλισσα (Attic μέλιττα) 'bee' is the honey-maker — hence the name Melissa; it is still the Modern Greek word for bee.
'The honey one', from μέλι. Attic has ττ where Ionic, Koine and Modern Greek have σσ (μέλισσα).

en: be likely to, be destined to
note: Usually with a future infinitive. Greek grammar calls the future tense ὁ μέλλων (χρόνος) 'the impending time', and Modern το μέλλον is 'the future'.

en: blame, find fault with (+ dat. or acc.)
on the one hand (answered by δέ)

rel.g: on the one hand (formal μεν … δε)

note: Usually left untranslated: it signals that a contrasting δέ is coming. Formal Modern Greek still uses μεν … δε.

ex.t: οἱ μὲν ἔφευγον, οἱ δὲ ἐμάχοντο
ex.en: some were fleeing, others were fighting

note: Homer's word for surging energy, from the root *men- 'have in mind', like Latin mēns and Sanskrit manas.
Modern Greek πού μένεις; means 'where do you live?'.
μέσος + ἡμέρα 'mid-day', with a glide β between μ and ρ. Like Latin merīdiēs, it also means 'south', where the sun stands at noon.
In Modern Greek μετά means only 'after'; 'with' is με, a worn-down μετά.

cite: μεταβάλλω, μεταβαλῶ, μετέβαλον, μεταβέβληκα, μεταβέβλημαι, μετεβλήθην

note: In Herodotus a μέταλλον is a mine; the sense 'metal' came from what was dug out of it.
Literally 'think afterwards' (μετά + νοῦς), i.e. change one's mind; the New Testament made it 'repent'.

ex.t: μετανοεῖτε· ἤγγικεν γὰρ ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν
ex.en: repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near (Matthew 3:2)

note: ἐν τῷ μεταξύ 'in the meantime' lives on as Modern στο μεταξύ.
The middle means 'send for (to oneself)': Κῦρον δὲ μεταπέμπεται 'but Cyrus he summons' (Anabasis 1.1.2).

en: share in, take part in (+ gen.)
raised off the ground, lofty, in mid-air
note: τὰ μετέωρα 'things aloft' were the subject of Aristotle's Meteorologica; the cliff-top monasteries of Thessaly are the Μετέωρα.
Adverb of μέτριος. μετρίως ἔχειν means 'to be fairly well, in a middling state'.
μέτρον ἄριστον 'moderation is best' was a saying of the Seven Sages; the metre (1795) took its name from μέτρον.

ex.en: man is the measure of all things (Protagoras)

en: not (in commands, wishes, conditions, purpose clauses)
note: οὐ denies facts; μή is used for what is willed, wished, feared or supposed. Modern Greek keeps exactly this split: δεν (from οὐδέν) vs μη(ν).

en: no longer, no more (μή-form of οὐκέτι)

note: Latin mālum 'apple' was borrowed from Doric μᾶλον. A homonym μῆλον means 'sheep, flock' in Homer.

en: (καὶ μήν) and moreover; (ἀλλὰ μήν) but surely

note: Months were counted by the moon: Greek μήνη 'moon' and μήν 'month', like English moon and month, share one root.

en: wrath (lasting, esp. of gods or heroes)
note: The first word of the Iliad — European literature begins with 'wrath'.

ex.en: Sing, goddess, the wrath of Achilles son of Peleus (Iliad 1.1)

note: A μητρόπολις was the mother-city of a colony; the Church reused it for a chief see, so a Greek bishop's cathedral is still the Μητρόπολη.
In tragedy a crane (μηχανή) swung gods onto the stage to resolve the plot.

ex.en: a god from the machine (Latin deus ex machina)

note: The perfect μέμνημαι 'I have been reminded' means 'I remember' — just like Latin meminī. In prose it is common as ἀναμιμνῄσκω.
Common in Homer and Herodotus where Attic would use αὐτόν, αὐτήν, αὐτό.
cite: μιν, enclitic, acc. sg. of all genders
forms: enclitic, acc. sg. of all genders

cite: μισέω, μισήσω, ἐμίσησα, μεμίσηκα, μεμίσημαι, ἐμισήθην

en: mina (weight and sum of money = 100 drachmas)
note: A Semitic loanword (Akkadian manû); sixty minas make a talent.
From μείρομαι 'receive a share': fate is one's allotted portion. Modern μοίρα is also a degree of angle or temperature.

ex.en: you shall not commit adultery (Exodus 20:14; Matthew 5:27)

note: Modern Greek μόλις also means 'just, as soon as': μόλις έφτασα 'I've just arrived'.
μοναχός 'solitary' became Latin monachus → English monk, Italian monaco, French moine; μοναστήριον → monastery (and Old English minster).
Ovid's dream-god Morpheus, who 'shapes' dreams, gave morphine its name.
In the parable of the prodigal son the father kills 'the fatted calf' (τὸν μόσχον τὸν σιτευτόν). A different μόσχος, from Persian, is musk.

ex.en: Tell me, Muse, of the man of many ways (Odyssey 1.1)

en: the arts of the Muses, literary and musical education

note: In Homer μῦθος is simply 'speech'; philosophers came to set μῦθος 'story' against λόγος 'reasoned account'.

ex.en: the fable shows that … (formula introducing the moral in Aesop)

note: The accent tells them apart: μυρίοι 'countless', μύριοι 'ten thousand' — the largest Greek number word.
Modern μυρίζω 'smell' and μυρωδιά 'scent' come from this word for perfume.
Greeks and Romans alike saw a 'mouse' running under the skin: μῦς and Latin mūsculus both mean 'muscle'.
From μύω 'close (lips, eyes)': initiates (μύσται) kept silent about the rites. The Orthodox Church calls the sacraments μυστήρια.
Modern Greek το μωρό 'the baby' is literally 'the silly one'. Attic accents the word μῶρος.
A trap for English speakers: ναί means 'yes'. Modern Greek 'no' is όχι, from emphatic οὐχί.
In Plato's Meno Socrates is likened to the νάρκη, the fish that numbs whoever touches it. Modern νάρκη is also a land- or sea-mine.
Irregular: ναῦς, νεώς, νηΐ, ναῦν; pl. νῆες, νεῶν, ναυσί, ναῦς. Cognate with Latin nāvis (→ navy, nave).

ex.t: αἱ νῆες εἰς τὸν λιμένα ἔπλεον
ex.en: the ships were sailing into the harbour

en: nectar, the drink of the gods

note: From νέμω 'deal out': the anger that gives each person his due.
Root of νόμος 'what is allotted → custom, law', νομός 'pasture, district' and νομάς 'nomad'.
cite: νέμω, νεμῶ, ἔνειμα, νενέμηκα, νενέμημαι, ἐνεμήθην

note: Originally νέϝος, matching Latin novus and English new. Neon (1898) is 'the new (gas)'; Naples is Νεάπολις 'New City'.
Greek and Latin both first meant 'sinew'; nerves proper were identified by Hellenistic anatomists. Modern τα νεύρα 'nerves' also means 'bad temper'.
A nod (νεῦμα) of Zeus' head decides the course of the Iliad; Latin nūmen 'divine power' is literally 'a nod'.
Aristophanes' Clouds (Νεφέλαι) mocks Socrates. Its sister word νέφος in Modern Greek mostly means Athens' smog cloud.
Attic 'second declension' (νεώς, νεώ, νεῴ, νεών). Homer and the NT have ναός, Herodotus νηός; Modern Greek ναός is a church.
Homer often exclaims νήπιος! 'the fool!' over a hero who cannot see his doom coming.
Feminine though 2nd declension (like ὁδός). The -nesia/-nese of place names is νῆσος.

ex.en: by this, conquer (Constantine's vision; Latin in hoc signo vinces)

cite: νικάω, νικήσω, ἐνίκησα, νενίκηκα, νενίκημαι, ἐνικήθην

note: Koine form (Jesus washing the disciples' feet, John 13); Attic prose says νίζω.

ex.en: wash your sins, not only your face (a palindrome inscribed on Byzantine fonts)

cite: νοέω, νοήσω, ἐνόησα, νενόηκα, νενόημαι, ἐνοήθην

note: From νόμος: first 'hold as customary', then 'believe, think'.

ex.t: θεοὺς οὓς ἡ πόλις νομίζει οὐ νομίζοντα
ex.en: not acknowledging the gods the city acknowledges (charge against Socrates, Plato, Apology 24b)

cite: νομίζω, νομιῶ, ἐνόμισα, νενόμικα, νενόμισμαι, ἐνομίσθην

note: Money is 'what custom sanctions': Aristotle notes it exists not by nature but by νόμος.
The great 5th-century debate set νόμος 'convention' against φύσις 'nature'.

ex.en: custom is king of all (Pindar, quoted by Herodotus 3.38)

note: Not νόμος 'law' — the accent differs. Herodotus uses it for the provinces of Egypt; Greece's modern prefectures are νομοί.

en: of the return home (νόστιμον ἦμαρ 'the day of homecoming')
note: From νόστος 'homecoming'. In later Greek it came to mean 'productive', then 'pleasant, tasty' — the only sense of Modern νόστιμος.
The Νόστοι were epics of the Greeks' homecomings from Troy. νόστιμος 'of the return, welcome' became Modern νόστιμος 'tasty'.
Contracted from νόος. For Anaxagoras Νοῦς is the cosmic Mind that set the world in order.

ex.en: I have in mind, I intend

note: Unaccented and enclitic, unlike temporal νῦν 'now'. Herodotus' μέν νυν 'well then' corresponds to Attic μὲν οὖν.

en: (νῦν δέ) but as it is, but in fact
note: Cognate with Latin nunc and English now. Modern Greek keeps νυν only in set phrases like νυν και αεί 'now and forever'.
The genitive νυκτός means 'by night'. Modern νύχτα comes from the accusative νύκτα, with κτ → χτ as in ὀκτώ → οχτώ.
Homer's Menelaus is ξανθός; Socrates' wife was Ξανθίππη 'Yellow Horse'.

en: the bond between host and guest
note: Ξενία, protected by Ζεὺς Ξένιος, bound host and guest and their descendants — Glaucus and Diomedes stop fighting because of it (Iliad 6).

en: Xenias (Arcadian commander of Cyrus' Greek mercenaries)
note: Xenophon introduces him as Ξενίας ὁ Παρράσιος, 'Xenias of Parrhasia' (Anabasis 1.1.2).
One word for both guest and host, bound by ξενία; Homer's form is ξεῖνος. Xenon (1898) is 'the stranger' gas.

ex.t: ὦ ξεῖν’, ἀγγέλλειν Λακεδαιμονίοις ὅτι τῇδε κείμεθα
ex.en: Stranger, tell the Spartans that here we lie (Simonides, on Thermopylae)

en: Xenophon (c. 430–354 BC), Athenian soldier and writer
note: His Anabasis, with the soldiers' cry θάλαττα, θάλαττα 'the sea, the sea!', is the classic first reading of Attic prose.
ξήριον, a drying powder for wounds, became Arabic al-iksīr → elixir. Xerography (Xerox) is 'dry writing'.
Modern Greek τρώω ξύλο 'eat wood' means 'get a beating'.
Thucydides and the tragedians write ξύν and ξυν- compounds (ξυμμαχία 'alliance') where later Attic has σύν.

en: (Homer; with μέν/δέ) he, she, it; this, that
note: In Homer ὁ, ἡ, τό is still mostly a demonstrative 'he, she, that'; Attic made it the article but kept ὁ μέν … ὁ δέ 'the one … the other'. Modern ο, η, το continues it.

en: obol (coin worth one sixth of a drachma)
note: Originally an iron 'spit' (ὀβελός): six spits made a handful, a δραχμή. The dead were buried with an obol for Charon's fare.
Points to what is present or about to be said (τάδε λέγει 'he speaks as follows'), whereas οὗτος points back to what has been mentioned.

ex.en: This is the presentation of the inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassus (opening of the Histories)

note: ὁδός 'road' + πόρος 'passage'.
A feminine of the 2nd declension. Its compounds gave English method ('way after'), exodus ('way out') and period ('way round').

ex.t: ὁδὸς ἄνω κάτω μία καὶ ὡυτή
ex.en: the road up and the road down are one and the same (Heraclitus)

note: Latin Ulixes comes from a variant such as Ὀλυσσεύς; his epic, the Ὀδύσσεια, gave English 'odyssey'.
A perfect with present meaning: 'I have seen' → 'I know' (root ϝιδ-, as in εἶδον 'I saw' and Latin videō). Pluperfect ᾔδη = 'I knew'.

ex.en: I know one thing: that I know nothing (later summary of Socrates' words)

note: From οἰδέω 'swell'; poetic.
-δε marks motion towards: οἴκαδε 'homewards', beside οἴκοι 'at home' and οἴκοθεν 'from home'.

cite: οἰκέω, οἰκήσω, ᾤκησα, ᾤκηκα, ᾤκημαι, ᾠκήθην

note: From οἰκέω 'dwell'.
Modern Greek's everyday 'house', σπίτι, came from Latin hospitium via Byzantine ὁσπίτιον.

ex.t: ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ τοῦ πατρός μου μοναὶ πολλαί εἰσιν
ex.en: in my Father's house are many rooms (John 14:2)

cite: οἰκοδομέω, οἰκοδομήσω, ᾠκοδόμησα, ᾠκοδόμηκα, ᾠκοδόμημαι, ᾠκοδομήθην

note: Originally ϝοῖκος with a digamma — hence the cognate Latin vīcus 'village', which reached English place names in -wich.
A participle: ἡ οἰκουμένη (γῆ) 'the land being inhabited'. The Ecumenical Patriarch is patriarch of 'the whole world'.

ex.t: ἐξῆλθεν δόγμα παρὰ Καίσαρος Αὐγούστου ἀπογράφεσθαι πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην
ex.en: a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered (Luke 2:1)

note: Originally ϝοῖνος, related to Latin vīnum. Greeks drank wine mixed with water (κρᾶσις 'mixing'), whence Modern κρασί.

ex.en: wine and truth (proverb; cf. Latin in vino veritas)

note: Attic often contracts it to οἶμαι (impf. ᾤμην); Plato's Socrates uses it constantly in polite understatement.

en: such as, of the kind that
(οἷός τέ εἰμι + inf.) I am able to

note: Hera sent a gadfly to drive Io across the world; the 'sting' became any frenzy, and in Modern Greek poetic inspiration.
A present with perfect meaning: οἴχεται 'he is gone'; with a participle, οἴχεται φεύγων 'he is off and away'.
Birds of prey feast on the dead in Iliad 1.5; because their flight was watched for signs, the word came to mean 'omen'.

ex.t: εἷς οἰωνὸς ἄριστος, ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ πάτρης
ex.en: one omen is best: to fight for one's country (Hector, Iliad 12.243)

note: Modern λίγο 'a little' has shed the initial ὀ-, as ὀδόντιον became δόντι.

ex.en: all but, almost (lit. 'to lack a little')

en: (mid. ὄλλυμαι, aor. ὠλόμην, pf. ὄλωλα) perish, be ruined
note: In prose usually compounded as ἀπόλλυμι. The perfect ὄλωλα 'I am undone' is a tragic cry.
From *solwos, cognate with Latin salvus. καθ’ ὅλου 'on the whole' gave catholic 'universal'.

en: Mount Olympus, home of the gods

note: As a common noun ὅμηρος means 'hostage' — and Modern Greek όμηρος still does.

en: be in company with, associate with (+ dat.)
note: From ὅμιλος 'throng'. Modern Greek's everyday 'speak', μιλάω/μιλώ, is ὁμιλῶ without its first vowel.
Modern Greek μάτι 'eye' descends from the diminutive ὀμμάτιον, not from the prose word ὀφθαλμός.

ex.en: I swear by Apollo the healer (Hippocratic Oath)

cite: ὄμνυμι, ὀμοῦμαι, ὤμοσα, ὀμώμοκα, ὀμώμομαι, ὠμόθην
ὁμολογέω, ὁμολογήσω, ὡμολόγησα, ὡμολόγηκα, ὡμολόγημαι, ὡμολογήθην

note: Athens' central square, Πλατεία Ομονοίας, is 'Concord Square'.

en: centre, hub (Delphi as the navel of the earth)
note: Zeus released two eagles from the ends of the earth; they met at Delphi, where a carved stone ὀμφαλός marked the centre of the world.
Aesop's fox, unable to reach the grapes, says ὄμφακές εἰσιν, 'they're unripe' — the origin of 'sour grapes'.
Distinguish ὅμως 'nevertheless' from ὁμῶς 'equally'. Modern όμως is the everyday 'however'.
Also the grammatical term 'noun' — Latin nōmen is both its cognate and its translation.

ex.en: what is your name? (lit. what name is to you?)

cite: ὀνομάζω, ὀνομάσω, ὠνόμασα, ὠνόμακα, ὠνόμασμαι, ὠνομάσθην

ex.en: a donkey at the lyre (proverb for someone with no ear for culture)

en: nail (of finger or toe); claw, hoof

note: ὀξύμωρον 'sharp-dull' is itself an oxymoron. The related ὄξος 'vinegar' gave Modern ξίδι.
From ὀξύς 'sharp, quick'.

ex.en: come and take them (Leonidas, when ordered to give up his arms)

note: Modern Greek ο οποίος 'who, which' is this indirect interrogative turned relative pronoun.
Modern που, the all-purpose relative 'who, which, that', is ὅπου worn down.
Three roots: ὁρα- (present), ὀπ- (ὄψομαι, ὤφθην) and ἰδ- (εἶδον, cf. Latin videō). The imperfect ἑώρων has a double augment.
cite: ὁράω, ὄψομαι, εἶδον, ἑώρακα, ἑώραμαι, ὤφθην

note: From the root of ἔργον 'work': a thing to work with. Aristotle's logical treatises are collectively the Organon, the 'tool' of thought.

en: reach for, stretch out to (+ gen.)

ex.t: πάντες ἄνθρωποι τοῦ εἰδέναι ὀρέγονται φύσει
ex.en: all men by nature desire to know (Aristotle, Metaphysics 980a)

note: Modern Greek ορίστε! 'here you are; yes?' is its imperative: '(please) command'.
cite: ὁρίζω, ὁριῶ, ὥρισα, ὥρικα, ὥρισμαι, ὡρίσθην

en: (intr. and mid.) start, rush, set out
cite: ὁρμάω, ὁρμήσω, ὥρμησα, ὥρμηκα, ὥρμημαι, ὡρμήθην

note: Because birds gave omens, ὄρνις also means 'omen'. Aristophanes' Birds is the Ὄρνιθες.
Not ὅρος 'boundary'. Mount Athos is Το Άγιον Όρος 'the Holy Mountain'.
Rough breathing and masculine — not ὄρος 'mountain'. Modern όροι are the terms of a contract.
The ὀρχήστρα was the round floor where the chorus danced; the word moved from the place to the musicians.
Its forms look like the article with accents (ὅς, ἥ, ὅ; οὗ, ἧς; ᾧ, ᾗ). Modern Greek replaced it with που and ο οποίος.

ex.t: ὃν οἱ θεοὶ φιλοῦσιν ἀποθνῄσκει νέος
ex.en: whom the gods love dies young (Menander)

en: sanctioned by divine law, pious, holy
note: ὅσιος is what divine law allows, often paired with δίκαιος (what human law allows). Orthodox monastic saints are styled Όσιος.

en: as great as, as much as
the very one who, the very thing which
note: The relative ὅς + intensive -περ. ὅπερ λέγω 'as I say' (Apology 21a); Euclid's ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι 'which was to be proved' is Latin quod erat dēmōnstrandum, Q.E.D.
Both halves decline (οὗτινος, ᾧτινι). The neuter is written ὅ τι to distinguish it from ὅτι 'that'.
Each year Athenians could scratch a name on potsherds; the 'winner' was exiled for ten years — ostracism (ὀστρακισμός).
Not to be confused with ὅ τι 'whatever'. Modern Greek keeps both: ότι 'that' and ό,τι 'whatever'.

ex.en: he says that his father is here

note: οὐ before consonants, οὐκ before a smooth vowel, οὐχ before a rough breathing (οὐχ ὁρῶ). It denies statements of fact; μή does the rest.
οὐδέ + εἷς 'not even one'. Modern Greek δεν 'not' is οὐδέν 'nothing' worn down.

ex.en: no one is bad willingly (Socratic maxim)

note: Accent matters: οὐκοῦν 'so then', οὔκουν 'not then, certainly not'.
An old aorist participle of ὄλλυμι, 'ruined, accursed', used as an adjective: μῆνιν … οὐλομένην 'the accursed wrath' (Iliad 1.1–2).
Postpositive: never first in its clause. μὲν οὖν 'well then; no, rather' is very common in Plato.
Modern Greek κάνω ουρά means 'stand in a queue'.
Often two-termination in the New Testament: πλῆθος στρατιᾶς οὐρανίου 'a multitude of the heavenly host' (Luke 2:13).

ex.t: Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς
ex.en: Our Father, who art in heaven (Matthew 6:9)

note: From οὖσα, the participle of εἰμί 'be'; Latin translated it essentia and substantia.
Modern Greek's demonstrative 'this', αυτός, comes from αὐτός, not from οὗτος. Forms in τ- (τοῦτο, ταῦτα) follow the pattern of the article.

ex.en: that's it! that's just what I meant (Aristophanes)

note: Matthew's 'debts' (Luke has ἁμαρτίας 'sins') probably reflects Aramaic, where one word means both debt and sin.

ex.t: καὶ ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν

note: The second aorist ὤφελον with an infinitive expresses an unattainable wish: ὤφελον θανεῖν 'would that I had died!'.

ex.t: ὀφθαλμὸν ἀντὶ ὀφθαλμοῦ καὶ ὀδόντα ἀντὶ ὀδόντος
ex.en: an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth (Matthew 5:38)

note: From the sense 'trouble' comes ἐνοχλέω 'annoy', Modern ενοχλώ 'bother'.
Diminutive of ὄψον, anything eaten with bread — above all fish. The boy at the feeding of the five thousand has δύο ὀψάρια (John 6:9); the word ousted ἰχθύς and became Modern ψάρι.
From the root of πάσχω (aor. ἔπαθον). The Stoic ideal was ἀπάθεια, freedom from passions → apathy.

en: paean: hymn of thanksgiving or battle-song
slave who escorted boys to school
note: Literally 'boy-leader': a household slave who walked the boy to his teachers and watched over him — not a teacher himself.
The model regular verb of many grammars. Modern παιδεύω has drifted to 'torment', while 'educate' is εκπαιδεύω.
cite: παιδεύω, παιδεύσω, ἐπαίδευσα, πεπαίδευκα, πεπαίδευμαι, ἐπαιδεύθην

note: Mind the accents: παιδιά 'play', παιδία 'little children' (pl. of παιδίον), παιδεία 'education'. Plato liked to play on them.
Like Latin puer, παῖ! was also how one called a slave. Vocative παῖ, dat. pl. παισί(ν).

ex.en: my son, may you be luckier than your father (Sophocles, Ajax 550)

en: long ago, in the old days
for a long time (up to now)

rel.g: formerly (in πάλαι ποτέ 'once upon a time')

note: With a present tense it means 'for a long time now': πάλαι θαυμάζω 'I have long been wondering'.

en: Pan, the goat-footed god of shepherds and wild places
note: Sudden groundless terror in lonely places or in armies was blamed on Pan — hence πανικὸν δεῖμα, panic.
From πᾶν 'all' + ἄκος 'cure'. The Hippocratic Oath swears by Apollo the healer, Asclepius, Hygieia and Panacea.

en: festival assembly, national festival (e.g. at Olympia)
note: πᾶν + ἄγυρις 'gathering' (= ἀγορά). Isocrates wrote his Panegyricus for such a festival; a Greek village πανηγύρι still celebrates its saint's day.

en: (πάνυ γε, πάνυ μὲν οὖν) certainly, quite so

ex.en: certainly, by all means (a standard reply in Plato)

en: (+ dat.) beside, at the house of; in the eyes of
(+ acc.) to, alongside; contrary to, beyond
note: Modern Greek says δέκα παρά πέντε 'five to ten' and παρά τον καιρό 'despite the weather'.
Christian Latin parabola 'parable' — Jesus' way of speaking — became the everyday Romance word for 'word', replacing verbum.

cite: παραγγέλλω, παραγγελῶ, παρήγγειλα, παρήγγελκα, παρήγγελμαι, παρηγγέλθην

note: From an Iranian word for a 'walled enclosure'; Xenophon describes the Persian kings' hunting parks.

ex.t: σήμερον μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ
ex.en: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43)

note: Its noun παράδοσις means both 'surrender, betrayal' and 'tradition' — exactly like Latin trādere, trāditiō.
cite: παραδίδωμι, παραδώσω, παρέδωκα, παραδέδωκα, παραδέδομαι, παρεδόθην
παραινέω, παραινέσω, παρῄνεσα, παρῄνεκα, παρῄνημαι, παρῃνέθην

note: Modern παρακαλώ is simply 'please' — and 'you're welcome'. The Holy Spirit as comforter is ὁ Παράκλητος.
cite: παρακαλέω, παρακαλῶ, παρεκάλεσα, παρακέκληκα, παρακέκλημαι, παρεκλήθην
παραλαμβάνω, παραλήψομαι, παρέλαβον, παρείληφα, παρείλημμαι, παρελήφθην

note: At Athens the γραφὴ παρανόμων was a prosecution of anyone who proposed an unconstitutional decree.

en: slip away, escape (one's notice or memory)

cite: παρασκευάζω, παρασκευάσω, παρεσκεύασα, παρεσκεύακα, παρεσκεύασμαι, παρεσκευάσθην

note: The Jewish 'Preparation' day before the Sabbath became the Greek name for Friday.
Suppletive like τρέχω: aorist παρέδραμον, participle παραδραμών.
From παραφράσσω 'fence alongside'.
Compound of εἰμί 'be'; impf. παρῆν. τὰ παρόντα = 'the present circumstances'.
Compound of εἶμι 'go' (impf. παρῄειν); its present has future meaning and serves as the future of παρέρχομαι.

en: (mid.) display, offer from one's own resources
cite: παρέχω, παρέξω, παρέσχον, παρέσχηκα, παρέσχημαι, παρεσχέθην

en: the Parthenon (temple of Athena Parthenos on the Acropolis)
note: 'The maiden's place', from παρθένος 'maiden': Athena Parthenos was the virgin goddess. Built under Pericles from 447 BC.

en: (intr.: aor. παρέστην, pf. παρέστηκα) stand by, be at hand, help
cite: παρίστημι, παραστήσω, παρέστησα / παρέστην, παρέστηκα, παρέσταμαι, παρεστάθην

note: In the theatre the πάροδοι were the side passages through which the chorus entered, singing its πάροδος.
παρά + οἰκοδομέω 'build'; augment and reduplication turn οἰ- into ῳ-: παρῳκοδομημένον 'built alongside' (Republic 514b).
Also the name of a famous painter, Parrhasius of Ephesus, rival of Zeuxis.
πᾶν + ῥῆσις 'saying everything': the Athenian citizen's right to speak his mind.

en: Parysatis, wife of Darius II, mother of Artaxerxes II and Cyrus the Younger
note: Xenophon says she loved Cyrus more than his elder brother and saved him when he was accused of plotting against the king (Anabasis 1.1.3–4).
πᾶσα πόλις 'every city', πᾶσα ἡ πόλις 'the whole city', ἡ πᾶσα πόλις 'the city as a whole'. Modern Greek keeps it in formal phrases (πάση θυσία 'at all costs').

ex.t: πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει
ex.en: all things are lawful for me, but not all things are helpful (1 Corinthians 6:12)

note: Indeclinable. From Aramaic pasḥā (Hebrew pesaḥ); early Christians linked it by wordplay with πάσχω 'suffer'.
Serves as the passive of ποιέω: εὖ πάσχειν 'be well treated' answers εὖ ποιεῖν 'treat well'. Its future πείσομαι looks just like that of πείθομαι.

ex.en: what will become of me? (lit. what am I to suffer?)

note: Greek π = Latin p = English f (Grimm's law): πατήρ, pater, father; πούς, pēs, foot.

ex.en: father of men and gods (Homer's title for Zeus)

note: Active 'stop someone', middle 'stop oneself'. Latin pausa (from παῦσις) gave English pause and, via pausāre, French poser and Italian posare.
cite: παύω, παύσω, ἔπαυσα, πέπαυκα, πέπαυμαι, ἐπαύθην

note: πεζὸς λόγος 'language on foot' (not riding on metre) is prose; Modern πεζογραφία = 'prose writing'.
The middle πείθομαι 'let oneself be persuaded' means 'obey'. The same root gives πίστις 'trust', cognate with Latin fidēs.
cite: πείθω, πείσω, ἔπεισα, πέπεικα, πέπεισμαι, ἐπείσθην

note: A πειρατής was one who 'makes attempts' on ships — Latin pīrāta, English pirate.
Modern δεν πειράζει means 'it doesn't matter, never mind'.
cite: πειράζω, πειράσω, ἐπείρασα, πεπείρακα, πεπείρασμαι, ἐπειράσθην

ex.t: καὶ μὴ εἰσενέγκῃς ἡμᾶς εἰς πειρασμόν
ex.en: and lead us not into temptation (Matthew 6:13)

note: Italian arcipelago 'chief sea' first meant the Aegean, then any sea dotted with islands.

en: (οἱ Πελοποννήσιοι) the Peloponnesians, Sparta and her allies
note: Thucydides calls his subject 'the war of the Peloponnesians and the Athenians'; the modern name 'Peloponnesian War' looks at it from the Athenian side.

en: peltast, light-armed soldier with a small shield (πέλτη)
(mid. πέλομαι) come to be, turn out
note: A poetic synonym of εἰμί; originally 'move, turn', the root of πόλος 'pivot' and κύκλος 'wheel'.

ex.t: πολλὰ τὰ δεινὰ κοὐδὲν ἀνθρώπου δεινότερον πέλει
ex.en: many things are wondrous, but nothing is more wondrous than man (Sophocles, Antigone)

note: Modern Πέμπτη 'Thursday' is the fifth day, counting from Sunday.

cite: πέμπω, πέμψω, ἔπεμψα, πέπομφα, πέπεμμαι, ἐπέμφθην

en: poor man (who works for his living)
note: Aristophanes distinguishes the πένης, who works and has nothing to spare, from the πτωχός, who has nothing at all (Wealth 552–4).

ex.t: μακάριοι οἱ πενθοῦντες, ὅτι αὐτοὶ παρακληθήσονται
ex.en: blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matthew 5:4)

note: One numeral, three faces: Greek π, Latin qu and English f all continue the same Indo-European *penkʷe.

en: Pentecost (the fiftieth day after Passover or Easter)

note: Enclitic; it is the -περ of ὥσπερ, ὅσπερ, καίπερ and ἐπείπερ. With a participle in Homer it is concessive — ἱέμενός περ 'eager though he was' (Odyssey 1.6) — a job Attic gives to καίπερ.
From πέρα 'beyond'. It keeps ᾱ after ρ in all tenses (περάσω).
Epic and tragic. Odysseus is the man who Τροίης ἱερὸν πτολίεθρον ἔπερσε, 'sacked the holy citadel of Troy' (Odyssey 1.2), hence his epithet πτολίπορθος 'sacker of cities'.

ex.en: On Nature (title of many early philosophical books)

note: The chained prisoners cannot περιάγειν τὰς κεφαλάς, 'turn their heads around'; later Plato calls education a περιαγωγή, a turning-around of the whole soul (Republic 518d).
cite: περιάγω, περιάξω, περιήγαγον, περιῆχα, περιῆγμαι, περιήχθην

note: In the Antigone ode man crosses the grey sea περιβρυχίοισιν περῶν ὑπ’ οἴδμασιν, 'passing under swells that roar about him'.

en: be superior to, get the better of, overcome (+ gen.)

ex.t: φιλοκαλοῦμέν τε γὰρ μετ’ εὐτελείας καὶ φιλοσοφοῦμεν ἄνευ μαλακίας
ex.en: we love beauty without extravagance and wisdom without softness (Funeral Oration, Thucydides 2.40)
and the glory of the Lord shone around them (Luke 2:9)

note: Aristotle's school, the Περίπατος, was named after its covered walk. Modern περπατάω/περπατώ is the everyday 'walk'.

ex.en: the Spirit descending like a dove (Mark 1:10)

ex.t: σὺ εἶ Πέτρος, καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ οἰκοδομήσω μου τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
ex.en: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church (Matthew 16:18)

en: son of Peleus, i.e. Achilles (Homeric patronymic)
note: Homeric patronymics in -ίδης / -ιάδης mean 'son of'. Πηληϊάδεω in Iliad 1.1 is the Ionic genitive (Attic -ου), its last two vowels pronounced as one syllable.

cite: πίμπλημι, πλήσω, ἔπλησα, πέπληκα, πέπλησμαι, ἐπλήσθην

en: painting on a panel; map; list

note: The future πίομαι has no σ. A συμπόσιον was a 'drinking-together' after dinner — hence Plato's Symposium.

ex.t: φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνῄσκομεν
ex.en: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die (Isaiah 22:13; 1 Corinthians 15:32)

cite: πίνω, πίομαι, ἔπιον, πέπωκα, πέπομαι, ἐπόθην

note: Stems πεσ- (future, aorist) and πτω- (perfect πέπτωκα, noun πτῶσις). Modern πέφτω shows the change πτ → φτ.

ex.en: I believe in one God (Nicene Creed)

cite: πιστεύω, πιστεύσω, ἐπίστευσα, πεπίστευκα, πεπίστευμαι, ἐπιστεύθην

note: Modern πίστη is also financial 'credit' (πιστωτική κάρτα 'credit card'), just as Latin crēditum comes from crēdō 'believe'.

ex.en: your faith has made you well (Mark 5:34)

note: Epic: Odysseus ὃς μάλα πολλὰ πλάγχθη, 'who was driven far off course' (Odyssey 1.1–2). The aorist passive drops the augment, as often in Homer.

cite: πλανάω, πλανήσω, ἐπλάνησα, πεπλάνηκα, πεπλάνημαι, ἐπλανήθην
πλάττω, πλάσω, ἔπλασα, πέπλακα, πέπλασμαι, ἐπλάσθην

note: πλατεῖα (ὁδός) 'broad street' became Latin platea and then Italian piazza, Spanish plaza, French and English place.
Diogenes Laertius says Πλάτων ('broad') was a nickname and his real name was Aristocles.
Comparative of πολύς (also spelt πλέων). The neuter πλέον, used as an adverb, survives in Modern πλέον 'more, any more'.

en: greed, wanting more than one's share
side (of a body, ship or figure)

ex.en: to sail is necessary, to live is not (Pompey, in Plutarch)

en: the people, the majority (in a democracy)

note: In Modern Greek πέντε πλην δύο is 'five minus two'.
Modern πληρώνω means 'pay' — filling up what is owed. πλήρωμα, a ship's full complement, is still a crew.
cite: πληρόω, πληρώσω, ἐπλήρωσα, πεπλήρωκα, πεπλήρωμαι, ἐπληρώθην

ex.t: ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν
ex.en: you shall love your neighbour as yourself (Matthew 22:39)

note: Compounds take aor. pass. -επλάγην (ἐξεπλάγην 'was astounded'). Modern πλήττω means 'be bored' — 'stricken' with tedium (πλήξη 'boredom').
cite: πλήττω, πλήξω, ἔπληξα, πέπληγα, πέπληγμαι, ἐπλήγην

note: From πλέω 'sail'. It ousted ναῦς and is Modern Greek's ordinary word for 'ship'.

ex.t: τὸ πλοῖον πρὸς τὴν νῆσον πλεῖ
ex.en: the boat is sailing to the island

note: Contracted from πλόος. When the wind fails, sailors take to the oars — the 'second voyage'.

ex.en: the second sailing, i.e. the next best way (Plato, Phaedo 99d)

note: Πλοῦτος, the blind god of wealth, gives Aristophanes' last play its title; Πλούτων 'the Rich One' is a name of Hades, lord of the riches underground.

ex.en: the wind (spirit) blows where it wishes (John 3:8)

note: Ionic and Aeolic ποία: Sappho feels herself χλωροτέρα δὲ ποίας, 'greener than grass' (fr. 31).
Modern Greek το πόθεν έσχες 'whence did you get it?' is the asset declaration required of politicians.
The poet is a ποιητής, a 'maker'. εὖ ποιεῖν 'treat well', κακῶς ποιεῖν 'harm'.

ex.t: ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
ex.en: in the beginning God made the heaven and the earth (Genesis 1:1, Septuagint)

cite: ποιέω, ποιήσω, ἐποίησα, πεποίηκα, πεποίημαι, ἐποιήθην

note: Latin borrowed poēta; its native word for an inspired poet was vātēs.
The Στοὰ Ποικίλη 'Painted Porch' in Athens, where Zeno taught, gave the Stoics their name.

ex.t: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός

note: Same root as ποιμήν 'shepherd': μία ποίμνη, εἷς ποιμήν 'one flock, one shepherd' (John 10:16).

en: of what kind? what sort of?
note: Modern ποιος has become simply 'who?', replacing ancient τίς.

ex.en: the Athenians were at war with the Spartans

cite: πολεμέω, πολεμήσω, ἐπολέμησα, πεπολέμηκα, πεπολέμημαι, ἐπολεμήθην

ex.t: πόλεμος πάντων μὲν πατήρ ἐστι, πάντων δὲ βασιλεύς
ex.en: war is father of all and king of all (Heraclitus)

note: A rare poetic verb related to πόλος 'turning-point; ploughed land'. Sophocles' man wears out the Earth ἱππείῳ γένει πολεύων, 'turning her up with the breed of horses'.
πόλις + ἕρκος 'fence': to fence a city in.
cite: πολιορκέω, πολιορκήσω, ἐπολιόρκησα, πεπολιόρκηκα, πεπολιόρκημαι, ἐπολιορκήθην

note: Used of grey hair and old age, and of the sea: πολιοῦ πέραν πόντου 'across the grey sea' (Sophocles, Antigone).
In place names: Νεάπολις → Naples, Κωνσταντινούπολις → Constantinople, which Greeks still call simply η Πόλη 'the City'.

ex.t: ἄνδρες γὰρ πόλις, καὶ οὐ τείχη οὐδὲ νῆες ἀνδρῶν κεναί
ex.en: for men are the city, not walls or ships empty of men (Thucydides 7.77)

note: Cicero rendered it rēs pūblica — hence 'Republic' as the English title of Plato's Πολιτεία.
Asked where he came from, Diogenes the Cynic replied κοσμοπολίτης 'a citizen of the world'.

ex.en: man is by nature a political animal (Aristotle, Politics 1253a)

rel.g: pole (of the earth, of a magnet)

note: Like μέγας, it has short forms only in πολύς, πολύν, πολύ; the rest use πολλ-. English 'hoi polloi' is οἱ πολλοί 'the many'.

ex.t: πολλὰ τὰ δεινὰ κοὐδὲν ἀνθρώπου δεινότερον πέλει
ex.en: many things are wondrous, and none more wondrous than man (Sophocles, Antigone 332)

note: The first epithet of Odysseus (Odyssey 1.1). Ancient critics already debated whether it meant 'much-wandering' or 'of many wiles'.

ex.en: tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns (Odyssey 1.1)

note: From the ribald abuse hurled from carts in Dionysiac processions, πομπεύω came to mean 'revile' — hence Modern πομπή 'disgrace'.

cite: πονέω, πονήσω, ἐπόνησα, πεπόνηκα, πεπόνημαι, ἐπονήθην

note: From πόνος 'toil' ('toil-ridden, wretched') to 'bad, wicked'; Modern πονηρός has softened to 'cunning'.

ex.t: ἀλλὰ ῥῦσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ

note: The Πόντος Εὔξεινος 'Hospitable Sea' is the Black Sea. The root first meant a path — over the sea in Greek, over a river in Latin pōns.
The aorist is passive in form (ἐπορεύθην). Modern τα πορεύομαι means 'I get by'.
The Βόσπορος is the 'cow-ford' where Io crossed; ἀπορία 'no way through' is perplexity.
Attic for πρόσω 'forwards'. Comparative πορρωτέρω 'further', superlative πορρωτάτω.
πόρρω 'far' + -θεν 'from'.
Byzantine emperors' children were πορφυρογέννητοι, 'born in the purple' chamber.

en: Poseidon, god of the sea, earthquakes and horses

ex.t: δὶς ἐς τὸν αὐτὸν ποταμὸν οὐκ ἂν ἐμβαίης
ex.en: you could not step twice into the same river (Heraclitus, in Plato's Cratylus)

note: Enclitic. In Modern Greek ποτέ normally means 'never' (δεν … ποτέ), while πότε asks 'when?'.

ex.t: πότερον ἐπιστήμη ἐστὶν ἡ ἀρετὴ ἢ οὔ;

note: Enclitic, so usually printed without an accent (που); distinct from interrogative ποῦ 'where?'. Χαιρεφῶντα γὰρ ἴστε που 'you know Chaerephon, I suppose' (Apology 20e).
Modern πού 'where?' keeps the accent; unaccented που means 'that, who' (from ὅπου).

ex.t: δός μοι ποῦ στῶ καὶ κινῶ τὴν γῆν
ex.en: give me a place to stand and I will move the earth (Archimedes)

ex.t: μακάριοι οἱ πραεῖς, ὅτι αὐτοὶ κληρονομήσουσιν τὴν γῆν
ex.en: blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5)

en: (intr. with adv.) fare: εὖ πράττειν 'fare well'
note: Ionic and Koine πράσσω. Perfect πέπραγα = 'have fared'. Plato signed his letters εὖ πράττειν 'fare well'.
cite: πράττω, πράξω, ἔπραξα, πέπραχα, πέπραγμαι, ἐπράχθην

en: it is fitting, it suits (+ dat. & inf.)
note: Modern Greek πρέπει has hardened into 'must': πρέπει να φύγω 'I must go'.
In prose a single ambassador is a πρεσβευτής, the plural πρέσβεις — envoys were chosen from the older men.

en: (NT, as noun) elder of a community
note: Comparative of πρέσβυς. The church 'elder' became Latin presbyter, worn down to English priest, French prêtre and Italian prete.

en: until (+ ἄν & subj., after a negative)

ex.t: πρὶν ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι τρὶς ἀπαρνήσῃ με
ex.en: before the cock crows, you will deny me three times (Matthew 26:34)

note: Unlike other prepositions πρό is not elided (προελθεῖν). Modern dates use π.Χ. = προ Χριστού 'before Christ'.
From προβαίνω 'walk forward': any beast that moves on in a herd; later narrowed to sheep.

en: come before, happen before, be born before
(οἱ προγεγενημένοι) predecessors, men of earlier times

note: πρό + δίδωμι 'give forward (into enemy hands)'; a traitor is a προδότης. Aorist προὔδωκα is a crasis of προ- + ἔδωκα.
cite: προδίδωμι, προδώσω, προὔδωκα, προδέδωκα, προδέδομαι, προὐδόθην

note: A preposition is 'put before' its noun — Latin praepositiō is a translation.
πρό + θεσμός 'what is laid down': a time set in advance. In Modern Greek it is the everyday word for 'deadline'.

en: send forth, hurl forth (esp. to Hades)
note: Epic: the wrath of Achilles πολλὰς δ’ ἰφθίμους ψυχὰς Ἄϊδι προΐαψεν, 'hurled many mighty souls to Hades' (Iliad 1.3).

en: lie before, be set in front
be set before one, be proposed (as a task, prize or subject)

rel.g: (impers.) it is a question of; (+ να) be going to

note: Serves as passive of προτίθημι. Modern Greek πρόκειται να means 'is going to', and περί τίνος πρόκειται; 'what is it about?'.

en: Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire for mankind
note: His name means 'Forethinker'; his foolish brother is Ἐπιμηθεύς 'Afterthinker'.
ἐκ προνοίας 'with forethought' was the Athenian legal term for premeditated homicide.

en: proxenos: citizen who looked after a foreign state's people in his own city
note: Modern Greek uses it for a consul, and προξενείο for a consulate.

en: (+ gen.) from; in the name of, by (in oaths)
(+ dat.) near, at; in addition to
(+ acc.) to, towards; against; with regard to

note: προσέχειν τὸν νοῦν is 'to turn the mind towards'; Modern πρόσεχε! means 'watch out!'.

en: it is fitting, it belongs to (+ dat. & inf.)

note: Greeks despised the Persian court prostration (προσκύνησις); Alexander's attempt to impose it caused a scandal. Orthodox believers still προσκυνούν icons.

en: take in addition, add, put on besides
(mid.) take to oneself; take on, enlist; take hold of
cite: προσλαμβάνω, προσλήψομαι, προσέλαβον, προσείληφα, προσείλημμαι, προσελήφθην

note: ὁ προστάτης τοῦ δήμου was the leading popular politician in Athens. Later anatomists named the gland 'standing before' the bladder.

cite: προστάττω, προστάξω, προσέταξα, προστέταχα, προστέταγμαι, προσετάχθην
προσφέρω, προσοίσω, προσήνεγκα / προσήνεγκον, προσενήνοχα, προσενήνεγμαι, προσηνέχθην

note: Like Latin persōna, the word went from 'mask' to 'dramatic role' to 'person' — including grammar's first, second and third person.
Thucydides separates the stated grievances from the ἀληθεστάτη πρόφασις, the 'truest cause' of the war: Sparta's fear of Athens' growth (1.23).
πρό + φημί: one who speaks for (or before) the god; at Delphi the προφῆται interpreted the Pythia.

en: early in the day, at dawn

ex.t: ἔσονται οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι καὶ οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι
ex.en: the last will be first, and the first last (Matthew 20:16)

note: Modern Greek turned initial πτ- into φτ-: πτερόν → φτερό, πτωχός → φτωχός, πτύω → φτύνω.

en: (pass.) be scared; flutter, be excited (with passion)

rel.g: be daunted (δεν πτοούμαι 'I am not deterred')

note: Sappho's καρδίαν ἐν στήθεσιν ἐπτόαισεν, 'set my heart fluttering in my breast', uses the Aeolic aorist ἐπτόαισεν (= ἐπτόησεν).
An epic enlargement of πόλις, built on its older by-form πτόλις.
Grammarians pictured the oblique cases as 'falling' away from the nominative; Latin cāsus (from cadō 'fall') is a translation of πτῶσις.
From πτώσσω 'cower': the beggar who cringes. Attic distinguishes him from the working poor man, the πένης.

en: the Pythia, Apollo's priestess and prophetess at Delphi
note: Named from Πυθώ, the old name of Delphi, where Apollo killed the serpent Python. She gave her answers seated on a tripod.

en: gate (usually pl. αἱ πύλαι, of a city)

note: Root πυθ-/πευθ-, the same as Sanskrit budh- 'awaken, perceive' — whence Buddha, 'the awakened one'.
From πύξος 'box-tree'. Modern πυξίδα is a magnetic compass, kept in a little box.
Attic prose usually takes the future and aorist from another verb (ἀποδώσομαι, ἀπεδόμην). Modern πουλάω/πουλώ shows ω → ου.
cite: πωλέω, πωλήσω, ἐπώλησα, πεπώληκα, πεπώλημαι, ἐπωλήθην

note: The enclitic πως means 'somehow'; Modern Greek likewise distinguishes πώς 'how?' from πως 'that'.
Comparison is irregular: ῥᾴων 'easier', ῥᾷστος 'easiest'. Its derivative ῥᾳδιουργία 'easy-going villainy' survives in Modern Greek ραδιουργία 'intrigue'.

ex.en: It is not easy to do this.

note: Literally a 'song-stitcher', from ῥάπτω 'stitch' + ᾠδή 'song': the rhapsode strung together the episodes of Homer in performance.
Greek medicine blamed many pains on 'flows' of humour through the body, hence rheumatism. Modern Greek ρεύμα is the everyday word for electricity: κόπηκε το ρεύμα 'the power went off'.

cite: ῥέω, ῥυήσομαι / ῥεύσομαι, ἔρρευσα, ἐρρύηκα, —, ἐρρύην

note: Plato split a sentence into ὄνομα (what you talk about) and ῥῆμα (what you say about it); the grammarians turned these into 'noun' and 'verb', and Modern Greek ρήμα means only 'verb'.
In democratic Athens οἱ ῥήτορες were in effect the politicians: the citizens who regularly spoke in the Assembly.
Greek ῥίζα, Latin rādīx (→ radical, radish) and English wort all go back to one Indo-European word for 'root'.

ex.en: Let the die be cast. (Caesar at the Rubicon, quoting Menander, as Plutarch reports)

cite: ῥίπτω, ῥίψω, ἔρριψα, ἔρριφα, ἔρριμμαι, ἐρρίφθην / ἐρρίφην

note: Homer's dawn is ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς, 'rosy-fingered Dawn'. The island of Rhodes (Ῥόδος) was popularly linked with the rose, which appears on its coins.
Probably from ῥέω 'flow': a ῥυθμός is a flow given regular shape. English rhythm keeps both the Greek rh and y.

ex.t: ἀλλὰ ῥῦσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ.
ex.en: But deliver us from evil. (Lord's Prayer, Matthew 6:13)

note: The Byzantines called themselves Ῥωμαῖοι 'Romans', so for centuries ρωμιός meant 'Greek', and ρωμιοσύνη still names the Greek Orthodox world.
Greeks could not miss that Ῥώμη 'Rome' sounded exactly like their word for 'strength', and poets played on it.
From Hebrew shabbat, passed through Greek and Christian Latin into the Romance names for Saturday. In the New Testament μία τῶν σαββάτων is 'the first day of the week'.
Sarcasm comes from σαρκάζω 'tear flesh like a dog', then 'bite one's lip, sneer'.
A Greek rendering of Old Persian xšaçapāvan 'protector of the realm'; a frequent figure in Herodotus and Xenophon.

en: (intr. in perf., 2 aor. ἔσβην) go out
note: Asbestos is ἄσβεστος 'inextinguishable'; in ancient Greek the word was also used of quicklime.
cite: σβέννυμι, σβέσω, ἔσβεσα, ἔσβηκα, ἔσβεσμαι, ἐσβέσθην
σεαυτοῦ, σεαυτῷ, σεαυτόν; f. σεαυτῆς, σεαυτῇ, σεαυτήν; contracted σαυτοῦ
forms: σεαυτῷ, σεαυτόν; f. σεαυτῆς, σεαυτῇ, σεαυτήν; contracted σαυτοῦ

note: From the same root comes σεβαστός 'revered', the Greek translation of the title Augustus; the name Sebastian comes from it.
Related to σέλας 'brightness'. Selenium was named for the moon because it was found alongside tellurium, named for the earth (Latin tellūs).
Related to σέβομαι. αἱ Σεμναί 'the Revered Ones' was the Athenian euphemism for the Furies.

en: show by a sign, indicate, signify
cite: σημαίνω, σημανῶ, ἐσήμηνα, σεσήμαγκα, σεσήμασμαι, ἐσημάνθην

note: From σιγή 'silence'. Socrates imagines being asked whether he could not live σιγῶν καὶ ἡσυχίαν ἄγων, 'keeping silent and quiet' (Apology 37e).
cite: σιγάω, σιγήσομαι, ἐσίγησα, σεσίγηκα, σεσίγημαι, ἐσιγήθην

note: The dative σιγῇ 'in silence' became Modern Greek σιγά 'slowly, softly', as in σιγά σιγά 'little by little'.

ex.en: Silence is an ornament to women. (Sophocles, Ajax 293; a proverbial line)

en: anything made of iron: sword, knife
note: Modern Greek's word for 'railway' is σιδηρόδρομος 'iron road', and the adjective σιδηροῦς 'of iron' gives Hesiod's iron age.
A παράσιτος was 'one who eats beside' another, at his table: a sponger, the stock flatterer of comedy, and later the biologist's parasite. The plural is neuter: τὰ σῖτα.

cite: σιωπάω, σιωπήσομαι, ἐσιώπησα, σεσιώπηκα, σεσιώπημαι, ἐσιωπήθην
σκάπτω, σκάψω, ἔσκαψα, ἔσκαφα, ἔσκαμμαι, ἐσκάφην

note: Attic prose uses σκοπέω for the present and σκέψομαι, ἐσκεψάμην, ἔσκεμμαι for the other tenses. The σκεπτικοί were philosophers who kept 'examining' and suspended judgement.
The σκηνή began as the hut behind the dancing floor where actors changed masks; its painted front became the 'scenery'.
The squirrel is σκίουρος 'shadow-tail', the animal that shades itself with its tail.

ex.en: Man is the dream of a shadow. (Pindar, Pythian 8)

note: Only the present system is used in Attic; the other tenses come from σκέπτομαι. The ἐπίσκοπος 'overseer' became Latin episcopus, English bishop, French évêque.
A Hellenistic word; classical prose says σκότος.

ex.t: καὶ τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει, καὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν
ex.en: and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:5)

note: Also neuter τὸ σκότος, -ους. Modern σκοτώνω 'kill' is literally 'to darken', since death brings darkness to the eyes.
In Homer σοφία is the skill of a carpenter; only later did it mean wisdom in general. Hagia Sophia in Constantinople is 'Holy Wisdom', not a saint.

ex.en: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. (Psalm 111:10, Septuagint)

note: Originally a neutral 'expert'; Plato's attacks on the fee-charging teachers gave the word its sneer.
Modern Greek από τα σπάργανα 'from the cradle' keeps the noun.

ex.t: εὑρήσετε βρέφος ἐσπαργανωμένον καὶ κείμενον ἐν φάτνῃ
ex.en: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger (Luke 2:12)

note: The state was officially Λακεδαίμων and its citizens Λακεδαιμόνιοι; their clipped speech gave English 'laconic' from Λακωνική.
διασπορά 'a scattering' named the Jewish communities abroad; σποράδην 'scattered' gives sporadic.
cite: σπείρω, σπερῶ, ἔσπειρα, ἔσπαρκα, ἔσπαρμαι, ἐσπάρην

note: Augustus' favourite motto, according to Suetonius, was Greek; the Latin version is festīnā lentē.
σπήλαιον 'cave' + -ώδης 'like'.
A treaty was sealed by pouring wine to the gods, so σπονδαὶ γίγνονται means 'a truce is made'. The slow spondee (– –) was the metre of libation hymns.

en: be serious about, devote oneself to
cite: σπουδάζω, σπουδάσομαι, ἐσπούδασα, ἐσπούδακα, ἐσπούδασμαι, ἐσπουδάσθην

note: A distance of 600 feet, the length of the original footrace at Olympia; the track was then named after the race. Plural also masculine: οἱ στάδιοι.
From ἵστημι. Thucydides' account of the στάσις at Corcyra is the classic analysis of civil war.
Greek στέγω 'cover', Latin tegō (→ toga, tēctum) and English thatch descend from one root meaning 'to cover'.
An ἀπόστολος is 'one sent out', an ἐπιστολή 'something sent', i.e. a letter. Modern Greek στέλνω is still the everyday 'send'.
cite: στέλλω, στελῶ, ἔστειλα, ἔσταλκα, ἔσταλμαι, ἐστάλην

en: deprive, rob (someone acc. of something gen.)
cite: στερέω, στερήσω, ἐστέρησα, ἐστέρηκα, ἐστέρημαι, ἐστερήθην

note: Victors at Olympia won only an olive στέφανος; Demosthenes' greatest speech is 'On the Crown'. In an Orthodox wedding the couple are still 'crowned' with στέφανα.

en: mark made by a pointed instrument

note: Zeno of Citium taught in the Painted Stoa (Στοὰ Ποικίλη) in the Athenian Agora, so his followers were 'the people of the porch', οἱ Στωικοί.

en: front, edge (of an army, a weapon)
note: στόμαχος first meant the throat or gullet, a 'mouth' leading inwards. John Chrysostom (Χρυσόστομος) was 'golden-mouthed' for his preaching.

en: natural affection (esp. of parents and children)
(mid.) serve as a soldier, take the field

rel.g: be called up, do military service

en: (at Athens) one of the ten elected generals
note: στρατός 'army' + ἄγω 'lead'. Athens elected ten στρατηγοί every year, and re-election made Pericles the leading man of the city.

ex.t: ἡ στρατιὰ πρὸς τὴν θάλατταν πορεύεται.
ex.en: The army is marching towards the sea.

note: A καταστροφή is an 'overturning', originally the final turn of a tragedy; the στροφή was the chorus's turn as it danced.
The ostrich was 'the big sparrow' or 'sparrow-camel'; Latin avis strūthiō became Old French ostrusce and English ostrich.
Doric τύ shows the original t- of Latin tū and English thou. Modern εσύ took its ε- by analogy with εγώ.

ex.en: You too, child? (Caesar's dying words to Brutus, according to Suetonius)

cite: σύ, σοῦ / σου, σοί / σοι, σέ / σε; pl. ὑμεῖς
forms: σοῦ / σου, σοί / σοι, σέ / σε; pl. ὑμεῖς

note: Literally 'judging with' someone, seeing things from their side. In Modern Greek it is the everyday 'sorry!'.

ex.t: Θουκυδίδης Ἀθηναῖος ξυνέγραψε τὸν πόλεμον τῶν Πελοποννησίων καὶ Ἀθηναίων.
ex.en: Thucydides, an Athenian, wrote the history of the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians. (Thucydides 1.1)

note: The Hippocratic Oath binds the physician by ὅρκον τόνδε καὶ συγγραφὴν τήνδε, 'this oath and this written covenant'.
Thucydides' first sentence: Θουκυδίδης Ἀθηναῖος ξυνέγραψε τὸν πόλεμον… — old Attic ξυν- for συν-.
cite: συγγράφω, συγγράψω, συνέγραψα, συγγέγραφα, συγγέγραμμαι, συνεγράφην

note: A συκοφάντης was literally a 'fig-revealer', but in Athens a malicious informer who blackmailed citizens with lawsuits; why figs, nobody knows for sure.
Athens had no public prosecutor, so any citizen could bring a charge; συκοφάνται made a living from threatening lawsuits. English shifted the word to 'toady'.
A συλλαβή is what is 'taken together', several letters pronounced as one: a syllable.
cite: συλλαμβάνω, συλλήψομαι, συνέλαβον, συνείληφα, συνείλημμαι, συνελήφθην
συλλέγω, συλλέξω, συνέλεξα, συνείλοχα, συνείλεγμαι, συνελέγην

note: τὸ συμβεβηκός 'what happens to belong' is Aristotle's term for an accidental property, translated into Latin as accidēns.

ex.en: What happened? (the same in Modern Greek: τι συνέβη;)

note: From συμβάλλω 'throw together': each party kept half of a broken knucklebone or coin, and matching the halves proved identity. The Christian creed was also called σύμβολον.

cite: συμβουλεύω, συμβουλεύσω, συνεβούλευσα, συμβεβούλευκα, συμβεβούλευμαι, συνεβουλεύθην

note: From συμπίνω 'drink together'. Plato's Symposium is the after-dinner party at which the guests take turns praising Eros.

cite: συμφέρω, συνοίσω, συνήνεγκα / συνήνεγκον, συνενήνοχα, συνενήνεγμαι, συνηνέχθην

note: Chaerephon συνέφυγε τὴν φυγὴν ταύτην: he went into exile with the democrats under the Thirty (404 BC) and came back with them (Apology 21a).

ex.en: A great disaster befell the city.

note: Older Attic spelling ξύν. Attic prose usually says μετά + gen. instead; σύν is poetic and Xenophontic, but as a prefix (συν-, συμ-, συλ-) it is everywhere.
A συναγωγή is a 'gathering': the Septuagint used it for the congregation of Israel, then for the building.
cite: συνάγω, συνάξω, συνήγαγον, συνῆχα, συνῆγμαι, συνήχθην

note: 'A sitting together' (ἕδρα 'seat'). The Jewish high council took the Greek word into Hebrew as Sanhedrin.
From σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ 'I share knowledge with myself'; Latin con-scientia is an exact calque, and English conscience comes from it.

en: be with, be together with (+ dat.)
associate with, be a disciple of
note: From εἰμί 'be'; a homonym σύνειμι from εἶμι means 'come together'. Plato's word for time spent with Socrates is συνουσία 'being together', which Modern Greek uses only of sex.

cite: συνίημι, συνήσω, συνῆκα, συνεῖκα, συνεῖμαι, συνείθην

en: (intr.: aor. συνέστην, perf. συνέστηκα) stand together, unite; be formed; meet in battle
cite: συνίστημι, συστήσω, συνέστησα / συνέστην, συνέστηκα, συνέσταμαι, συνεστάθην

en: share knowledge with, be privy to (+ dat.)
(σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ) be conscious, be aware (of oneself)
note: Perfect in form, present in meaning, like οἶδα. Its noun συνείδησις, like Latin cōnscientia, came to mean 'conscience'.

ex.t: οὔτε μέγα οὔτε σμικρὸν σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ σοφὸς ὤν
ex.en: I am not aware of being wise in anything, great or small (Plato, Apology 21b)

en: whole made of parts, organised body

note: From σφάλλω 'trip up, make fall'.

ex.t: ὁ βίος βραχύς, ἡ δὲ τέχνη μακρή, ὁ δὲ καιρὸς ὀξύς, ἡ δὲ πεῖρα σφαλερή
ex.en: life is short, the art long, opportunity fleeting, experiment treacherous (Hippocrates, Aphorisms 1.1)

cite: σφάλλω, σφαλῶ, ἔσφηλα, ἔσφαλκα, ἔσφαλμαι, ἐσφάλην

note: Reflexive possessive of the 3rd person plural. Odysseus' comrades perished σφετέρῃσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν, 'through their own recklessness' (Odyssey 1.7).
Its adverb σφόδρα 'very, exceedingly' is far commoner; the comparative adverb is σφοδρότερον 'more violently'.
Polycrates of Samos threw his precious signet ring into the sea to avert divine envy, only to find it in a fish served to him (Herodotus 3.41–42).
Leisure was what free men spent on talk and learning, so 'leisure' became 'lecture' and then 'school'. Its opposite ἀσχολία 'lack of leisure' meant business.

ex.en: I have leisure, I am at leisure.

note: Attic writes the iota subscript (σῴζω), Koine and Modern Greek drop it (σώζω). The same root gives σωτήρ 'saviour' and σωτηρία 'safety'.
cite: σῴζω, σώσω, ἔσωσα, σέσωκα, σέσωσμαι / σέσωμαι, ἐσώθην

ex.t: ἀδικεῖ Σωκράτης οὓς μὲν ἡ πόλις νομίζει θεοὺς οὐ νομίζων.
ex.en: Socrates is guilty of not acknowledging the gods the city acknowledges. (the indictment, in Xenophon, Memorabilia 1.1)

note: Ancient scholars observed that Homer uses σῶμα only of a corpse; the living body is δέμας or the limbs, γυῖα.

ex.en: The body is a tomb. (Orphic saying quoted by Plato)

note: A title of gods (Ζεὺς Σωτήρ) and Hellenistic kings (Ptolemy I Soter) before it became Christ's. The fish symbol ΙΧΘΥΣ spells Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Θεοῦ Υἱὸς Σωτήρ.

ex.en: They are deliberating about their safety.

note: Literally 'having a sound (σῶς) mind (φρήν)'. With wisdom, courage and justice it is one of the four cardinal virtues of Plato's Republic.

en: talent (weight of about 26 kg; sum of 6,000 drachmas)
note: The sense 'natural gift' comes from the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25), where servants are judged by how they use the money entrusted to them.
For classical writers it was a reproach; Christianity turned ταπεινοφροσύνη 'lowliness of mind' into the virtue of humility.

ex.t: ταράσσει τοὺς ἀνθρώπους οὐ τὰ πράγματα, ἀλλὰ τὰ περὶ τῶν πραγμάτων δόγματα.
ex.en: What upsets people is not things, but their opinions about things. (Epictetus, Handbook 5)

cite: τάττω, τάξω, ἔταξα, τέταχα, τέταγμαι, ἐτάχθην

ex.t: ἀνδρῶν γὰρ ἐπιφανῶν πᾶσα γῆ τάφος.
ex.en: For famous men the whole earth is their tomb. (Pericles' Funeral Oration, Thucydides 2.43)

note: From ταχύς. 'Quickly' slid into 'perhaps', and Modern Greek τάχα (μου) means 'supposedly, pretending'.
Enclitic and placed after the word it attaches, exactly like its Latin cognate -que.
Diminutive of τεῖχος 'wall'.
From τέκμαρ 'sign, goal'. Thucydides' method in a word: he infers (τεκμαιρόμενος) from evidence (τεκμήρια) where direct knowledge is impossible.

ex.t: τὰ τέκνα ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ μένει.
ex.en: The children stay in the house. (a neuter plural subject takes a singular verb)

note: The ἀρχιτέκτων is the 'chief builder'. In Mark 6:3 Jesus is called ὁ τέκτων.

en: (τὸ τελευταῖον, as adv.) at last, finally
note: From τελευτή 'end'.

cite: τελευτάω, τελευτήσω, ἐτελεύτησα, τετελεύτηκα, τετελεύτημαι, ἐτελευτήθην

ex.t: σκοπέειν δὲ χρὴ παντὸς χρήματος τὴν τελευτήν.
ex.en: One must look to the end of every matter. (Solon to Croesus, Herodotus 1.32)

cite: τελέω, τελῶ, ἐτέλεσα, τετέλεκα, τετέλεσμαι, ἐτελέσθην

note: The accusative τέλος is used as an adverb, 'finally'. It is the word that ends Greek films: ΤΕΛΟΣ.
The ablaut grades τεμ-, τομ-, τμ- run through its family: τόμος 'a cut piece' (of a papyrus roll), ἄτομος 'uncut', τμῆμα 'section'.
cite: τέμνω, τεμῶ, ἔτεμον, τέτμηκα, τέτμημαι, ἐτμήθην

note: Attic ττ against Ionic and Koine σσ (τέσσαρες), as in θάλαττα / θάλασσα; Modern Greek follows Koine. In compounds it is τετρα-: τετράγωνον 'square'.
cite: τέτταρες, τέτταρα; gen. τεττάρων, dat. τέτταρσι(ν)

note: Achilles' wrath made the heroes ἑλώρια … κύνεσσιν, 'prey for dogs' (Iliad 1.4): τεῦχε there is an unaugmented imperfect.
cite: τεύχω, τεύξω, ἔτευξα, τέτευχα, τέτυγμαι, ἐτύχθην

note: One word covered both art and technique; Latin ars translated it, so 'art' and 'technique' are twins in disguise.

ex.t: ὁ βίος βραχύς, ἡ δὲ τέχνη μακρή.
ex.en: Life is short, the art is long. (Hippocrates, Aphorisms 1.1; Latin ars longa, vita brevis)

note: A Homeric adverb revived as the international prefix tele-; Modern Greek reimported it in τηλέφωνο and calqued 'television' as τηλεόραση 'far-seeing'.

cite: τηρέω, τηρήσω, ἐτήρησα, τετήρηκα, τετήρημαι, ἐτηρήθην

note: One Indo-European root *dʰeh₁- 'put' gives τίθημι (reduplicated, with θ > τ), Latin faciō and English do. θέσις 'placing' yields thesis, hypothesis, synthesis.
cite: τίθημι, θήσω, ἔθηκα, τέθηκα, τέθειμαι, ἐτέθην

note: Its noun τόκος 'offspring' also meant 'interest', money bred by money; Aristotle condemned usury as the most unnatural way to get rich, and Modern Greek τόκος still means interest.
In an Athenian trial the convicted man proposed his own penalty (τιμᾶσθαι); Socrates proposed free meals in the Prytaneum.
cite: τιμάω, τιμήσω, ἐτίμησα, τετίμηκα, τετίμημαι, ἐτιμήθην

note: Honour and price are one word: what you are 'worth'. A Greek price tag today still says τιμή.

ex.t: ἡ τιμὴ τοῦ σίτου μεγάλη ἐστίν.
ex.en: The price of grain is high.

note: Modern τίμιος means 'honest'; the old sense survives in ο Τίμιος Σταυρός 'the Precious Cross' and τιμαλφή 'valuables'.

cite: τιμωρέω, τιμωρήσω, ἐτιμώρησα, τετιμώρηκα, τετιμώρημαι, ἐτιμωρήθην

note: The interrogative always keeps its acute accent, even before another word; that distinguishes it from the enclitic indefinite τις. Greek τ, Latin qu and English wh all continue Indo-European *kʷ.
cite: τίς, τί; gen. τίνος / τοῦ, dat. τίνι / τῷ, acc. τίνα, τί; pl. τίνες, τίνων, τίσι(ν), τίνας, τίνα
forms: τί; gen. τίνος / τοῦ, dat. τίνι / τῷ, acc. τίνα, τί; pl. τίνες, τίνων, τίσι(ν), τίνας, τίνα

note: Enclitic: same forms as τίς but no accent of its own, so it throws one onto the word before: ἄνθρωπός τις 'a certain man'.

ex.t: ἦν τις ἀνὴρ ἐν τῇ πόλει.
ex.en: There was a certain man in the city.

cite: τις, τι; gen. τινός / του, dat. τινί / τῳ, acc. τινά, τι; pl. τινές, τινῶν, τισί(ν), τινάς, τινά
forms: τι; gen. τινός / του, dat. τινί / τῳ, acc. τινά, τι; pl. τινές, τινῶν, τισί(ν), τινάς, τινά

en: Tissaphernes (d. 395 BC), Persian satrap of Lydia and Caria
note: Cyrus' enemy: he denounced him to Artaxerxes and after Cunaxa treacherously seized the Greek generals. The accusative Τισσαφέρνην follows the 1st declension, like Σωκράτην.

ex.en: He said things of that kind.

note: The wall of a house, against τεῖχος, the wall of a city: the same root in two ablaut grades.
The root *telh₂- 'bear, endure' also gives Latin tolerō and tulī, and Greek Ἄτλας 'the one who bears' the sky.
cite: τολμάω, τολμήσω, ἐτόλμησα, τετόλμηκα, τετόλμημαι, ἐτολμήθην

note: τοξικὸν φάρμακον was 'bow poison' for smearing on arrows; Latin kept only the poison, and English toxic followed.
Thomas More coined Utopia from οὐ + τόπος 'no-place'. Topic comes from Aristotle's Τοπικά, a handbook of argumentative 'places'.
Literally 'goat-song' (τράγος + ᾠδή), for reasons already debated in antiquity. Byzantine τραγῳδέω came to mean simply 'sing', hence Modern Greek τραγούδι 'song'.
Probably from *τετρά-πεζα 'four-footed'. The banker sat at his table, so the τραπεζίτης was a banker, just as Italian banco 'bench' gave bank.
The windpipe was 'the rough artery', named for its rings of cartilage.

cite: τρεῖς, τρία; gen. τριῶν, dat. τρισί(ν)

en: put to flight (mid. τρέπομαι: turn and flee)
note: Where the enemy turned (τροπή) the victors set up a τρόπαιον, a trophy of captured arms.
cite: τρέπω, τρέψω, ἔτρεψα, τέτροφα, τέτραμμαι, ἐτράπην

note: The root is θρεφ-: when φ loses its aspiration in ψ (θρέψω, ἔθρεψα) the θ reappears; when φ stays, the θ becomes τ (Grassmann's law).
cite: τρέφω, θρέψω, ἔθρεψα, τέτροφα, τέθραμμαι, ἐτράφην

note: Suppletive: future and aorist come from δραμ-, which also gives δρόμος 'running, race-course' and Modern Greek δρόμος 'road, street'.
Ionic τριηκόσιοι: Leonidas' Three Hundred at Thermopylae.
διατριβή, a 'wearing away' of time, came to mean a pastime, then a learned discussion; it is now an English tirade and a Modern Greek doctoral thesis.
cite: τρίβω, τρίψω, ἔτριψα, τέτριφα, τέτριμμαι, ἐτρίβην / ἐτρίφθην

en: trireme, warship with three banks of oars

note: τρι- + πούς 'foot'. Bronze tripods were prize gifts in Homer; at Delphi the Pythia prophesied seated on one.
Like δίς and Latin ter; δὶς καὶ τρίς 'twice and three times, again and again'.
From τρέμω 'tremble', cognate with Latin tremō. Sappho: τρόμος δὲ παῖσαν ἄγρει 'trembling seizes me all over'.
With a participle it marks coincidence: τυγχάνει ὤν 'he happens to be'. τύχη 'chance' is from the same root.
From τύπτω: the mark a blow leaves. Printing made it 'type', and Modern Greek ο Τύπος is 'the press'.
Originally neutral: a sole ruler who took power outside the traditional order, like Peisistratus. Sophocles' Οἰδίπους Τύραννος is 'Oedipus the King'.
Butter is βούτυρον 'cow-cheese', which reached English through Latin būtȳrum.

ex.t: τυφλὸς τά τ’ ὦτα τόν τε νοῦν τά τ’ ὄμματ’ εἶ.
ex.en: You are blind in ears and mind and eyes. (Oedipus to the blind seer Teiresias, Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus 371)
With good fortune. (formula heading Athenian decrees)

note: Herodotus uses it for a transparent stone; the diminutive ὑάλιον became Modern Greek γυαλί, the everyday 'glass'.

cite: ὑβρίζω, ὑβριῶ, ὕβρισα, ὕβρικα, ὕβρισμαι, ὑβρίσθην

note: In Athenian law ὕβρις was a crime: violence meant to humiliate. In tragedy it is the overreaching that the gods punish.

en: Hygieia, goddess of health, daughter of Asclepius
note: Personified ὑγίεια 'health', contracted to ὑγεία in later Greek; the Hippocratic Oath swears by her.
Ὑγίεια 'Health', daughter of Asclepius, gave French hygiène and English hygiene; Modern Greeks toast στην υγειά μας 'to our health'.
From ὕδωρ 'water': the three-handled jar women carried to and from the spring.
An old r/n stem (ὕδωρ, ὕδατ- < *udn̥t-), matching English water beside Old Norse vatn. Byzantine νεαρὸν ὕδωρ 'fresh water' shrank to νηρόν, Modern νερό.

ex.en: Best of all is water. (Pindar, Olympian 1.1)

note: Aristotle took the word for 'timber' as his term for matter in general; Latin translated it with māteria, which also meant timber (hence Spanish madera 'wood').
By late antiquity ὑμεῖς and ἡμεῖς were pronounced alike (both imís), so the language rebuilt them: Modern εμείς 'we' and εσείς 'you'.

ex.t: ὑμεῖς ἐστε τὸ ἅλας τῆς γῆς.
ex.en: You are the salt of the earth. (Matthew 5:13)

en: listen; answer (a knock at the door)

ex.en: Not a dream, but a true waking vision. (Odyssey 19.547)

note: τὰ ὑπάρχοντα 'what one has' meant property, as Modern Greek τα υπάρχοντα still does; υπάρχει / υπάρχουν is the standard 'there is / there are'.
cite: ὑπάρχω, ὑπάρξω, ὑπῆρξα, ὑπῆρχα, ὑπῆργμαι, ὑπήρχθην

en: (+ gen.) over, above; on behalf of, for
note: Greek ὑπέρ, Latin super and English over are cognates; hyper- and super- are therefore the same prefix in two languages.
'Showing oneself above others'. In the New Testament God resists the ὑπερήφανοι; Modern Greek είμαι υπερήφανος για σένα means 'I'm proud of you'.
