en: Hyperion: the Sun-god (Homer); the Titan father of Helios (Hesiod)
note: Probably 'he who goes on high' (ὑπέρ). Odysseus' men ate the cattle of Ὑπερίων Ἠέλιος, who took away their day of homecoming (Odyssey 1.8–9).
A poetic superlative of ὑπέρ 'above'. Sophocles calls Earth θεῶν τὰν ὑπερτάταν, 'highest of the gods'.
In the Iliad Ὕπνος and Θάνατος, Sleep and Death, are twin brothers who carry Sarpedon's body home. Latin somnus and sopor come from the same root *swep-.

ex.t: ὁ ὕπνος ἀδελφός ἐστι τοῦ θανάτου.
ex.en: Sleep is the brother of death.

en: (+ gen.) under; by (agent of a passive)
(+ dat.) under, beneath; under the power of

ex.en: He was killed by the enemy.

en: subject, plot (of a play or speech)
note: 'What is placed underneath' (ὑπό + τίθημι), calqued in Latin as suppositiō. Modern Greek uses it for any affair: είναι δική μου υπόθεση 'it's my business'.
From ὑποκρίνομαι 'answer, play a part'. When Jesus calls the Pharisees ὑποκριταί he is calling them play-actors.

cite: ὑπολαμβάνω, ὑπολήψομαι, ὑπέλαβον, ὑπείληφα, ὑπείλημμαι, ὑπελήφθην

note: From ὕποπτος 'looked at from below, suspected'; the augment falls after the prefix: ὑπώπτευε.
cite: ὑποπτεύω, ὑποπτεύσω, ὑπώπτευσα, ὑπώπτευκα, ὑπώπτευμαι, ὑπωπτεύθην

note: Sappho: λέπτον δ’ αὔτικα χρῷ πῦρ ὐπαδεδρόμηκεν 'at once a thin fire has run beneath my skin' (Aeolic ὐπα- = ὑπο-).
Masculine or feminine (ὁ/ἡ ὗς); also σῦς. Greek lost an initial s- here, as in ἑπτά vs Latin septem.

ex.en: On the next day they went away.

en: (ὁ Ὕψιστος, Septuagint and NT) the Most High, God
note: Superlative of ὑψηλός 'high' (from ὕψι 'on high').

ex.en: glory to God in the highest (Luke 2:14)

note: φαίνεται ὤν 'he is evidently' (with participle) differs from φαίνεται εἶναι 'he seems to be' (with infinitive). Modern Greek φαίνεται is the everyday 'it seems'.
cite: φαίνω, φανῶ, ἔφηνα, πέφαγκα / πέφηνα, πέφασμαι, ἐφάνθην / ἐφάνην

note: Remedy and poison are one word: Socrates drank τὸ φάρμακον, the hemlock, and Circe's magic is also a φάρμακον.
Present and imperfect only. In Attic it often stands in for φημί in the participle: φάσκων 'saying, claiming'.
Mary laid the newborn ἐν φάτνῃ, 'in a manger' (Luke 2:7); Modern Greek still calls the Christmas crib η φάτνη.
In classical Greek mainly 'second-rate'; Modern Greek has hardened it to 'wicked', as in φαύλος κύκλος 'vicious circle'.
Three unrelated stems (φερ-, οἰ-, ἐνεκ-), just as Latin ferō, tulī, lātum mixes three. Imperative φέρε 'come now!' introduces a suggestion.
cite: φέρω, οἴσω, ἤνεγκα / ἤνεγκον, ἐνήνοχα, ἐνήνεγμαι, ἠνέχθην

note: In court ὁ φεύγων is the defendant and ὁ διώκων ('pursuer') the prosecutor. Modern φεύγω is simply 'leave': φεύγω αύριο 'I'm leaving tomorrow'.
Enclitic in the present indicative except φῄς. οὔ φημι means 'I say no, I deny'; ἔφη 'he said' often follows the first words of a quotation.
The participle carries the main idea: ἔφθασαν ἀφικόμενοι 'they arrived first'. Modern φτάνω means 'arrive', and φτάνει! 'that's enough!'.

cite: φθείρω, φθερῶ, ἔφθειρα, ἔφθαρκα, ἔφθαρμαι, ἐφθάρην

note: φθινόπωρον, the 'waning of the ὀπώρα' (late summer, fruit time), is still the Greek word for autumn.

cite: φθονέω, φθονήσω, ἐφθόνησα, ἐφθόνηκα, ἐφθόνημαι, ἐφθονήθην

note: Herodotus' Solon warns Croesus that τὸ θεῖον πᾶν ἐὸν φθονερόν 'the divine is altogether envious': great prosperity invites a fall.
Among the earliest uses is Aeschylus' Prometheus, punished for his φιλάνθρωπος τρόπος, his 'man-loving ways'.

en: be wont to, tend to (+ inf.)
note: Modern Greek φιλώ means only 'kiss'; 'love' is αγαπώ. With an infinitive φιλεῖ means 'tends to': φιλεῖ γίγνεσθαι 'it usually happens'.

ex.t: ὃν οἱ θεοὶ φιλοῦσιν ἀποθνῄσκει νέος.
ex.en: Whom the gods love dies young. (Menander)

cite: φιλέω, φιλήσω, ἐφίλησα, πεφίληκα, πεφίλημαι, ἐφιλήθην

note: A pet-name formation from φίλος 'dear'; a Philinna of Larisa was one of the wives of Philip II of Macedon.
'Lover of horses' (φίλος + ἵππος). Demosthenes' speeches against Philip, the Φιλιππικοί, gave English 'philippic'.
In Homer φίλος often just marks possession: φίλον ἦτορ 'his heart'. The superlative φίλτατος is common in address: ὦ φίλτατε 'my dearest friend'.

ex.en: Friends share everything. (proverb quoted by Plato)

rel.g: generous; having a sense of honour

note: Ancient φιλοτιμία could be a vice (ambition) or the civic pride behind public benefactions; Modern Greek το φιλότιμο is a prized, hard-to-translate mix of honour, generosity and self-respect.
Socrates complains that Aristophanes' Clouds showed him 'talking a lot of nonsense' (πολλὴν φλυαρίαν φλυαροῦντα, Apology 19c).
Colloquial Modern Greek φοβερός has gone the way of English terrific: 'amazing'.
In Homer φόβος is panic flight, from the root of φέβομαι 'flee'. Φόβος and Δεῖμος, sons of Ares, name the two moons of Mars.
Herodotus calls the letters of the alphabet φοινικήια γράμματα, 'Phoenician letters', because the Greeks learned writing from them.

en: go to and fro, visit regularly
note: φοιτᾶν εἰς διδασκάλου was 'to go to school'; hence Modern Greek φοιτητής 'student'.

cite: φονεύω, φονεύσω, ἐφόνευσα, πεφόνευκα, πεφόνευμαι, ἐφονεύθην
φορέω, φορήσω, ἐφόρησα, πεφόρηκα, πεφόρημαι, ἐφορήθην
φράζω, φράσω, ἔφρασα, πέφρακα, πέφρασμαι, ἐφράσθην

note: The Indo-European word for 'brother' survives in Greek only for a 'clan brother' in a φρατρία; a blood brother is ἀδελφός 'from the same womb'.
Homer places thought and feeling in the φρένες, the midriff; φρονέω, σώφρων and ἄφρων all build on it.

ex.en: He has a high opinion of himself.

note: Aristotle's practical wisdom, knowing how to act well, as opposed to theoretical σοφία; Latin rendered it prūdentia.

ex.t: γίνεσθε οὖν φρόνιμοι ὡς οἱ ὄφεις.

en: worry about, take care of (+ gen.)

ex.en: I don't care at all about money.

note: Aristophanes' Socrates runs a φροντιστήριον, a 'thinkery'; in Modern Greek a φροντιστήριο is a cram school.

ex.en: Hippocleides doesn't care! (the suitor who danced away his bride, Herodotus 6.129)

note: From 'guarding' to 'the place where prisoners are guarded': φυλακή is the Modern Greek word for prison.

ex.en: The guards are guarding the gates.

en: (mid.) be on one's guard against (+ acc.)
cite: φυλάττω, φυλάξω, ἐφύλαξα, πεφύλαχα, πεφύλαγμαι, ἐφυλάχθην

note: Cleisthenes' reform of 508/7 BC divided the Athenians into ten new φυλαί, which then supplied the army regiments and the Council of 500.
Greek φύλλον and Latin folium (→ foglia, hoja, feuille) are cognates; English filo pastry is Modern Greek φύλλο.

ex.t: οἵη περ φύλλων γενεὴ τοίη δὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν.
ex.en: As is the generation of leaves, so is that of men. (Iliad 6.146)

note: From φύω 'grow': nature is what grows by itself. The sophists set φύσις against νόμος (convention); Latin nātūra, from nāscor 'be born', was coined to translate it.

cite: φυτεύω, φυτεύσω, ἐφύτευσα, πεφύτευκα, πεφύτευμαι, ἐφυτεύθην

en: (intr. ἔφυν, πέφυκα) be born; be by nature
note: πέφυκα means 'I am by nature': πέφυκε σοφός 'he is naturally wise'. The root *bʰuh₂- 'become' also supplies Latin fuī, futūrus and English be.

cite: φωνέω, φωνήσω, ἐφώνησα, πεφώνηκα, πεφώνημαι, ἐφωνήθην

note: Herodotus uses φωνή for a language: a people 'using the Scythian tongue'. Grammarians called vowels φωνήεντα 'sounding' letters, still φωνήεντα in Modern Greek.

ex.en: The voice of one crying in the wilderness. (Mark 1:3)
Let there be light; and there was light. (Genesis 1:3, Septuagint)

en: Chaerephon, Socrates' impetuous friend, who asked the Delphic oracle whether anyone was wiser than Socrates
note: Aristophanes mocks his sallow, half-dead look in the Clouds and calls him 'the Bat' in the Birds; in the Apology Socrates calls him σφοδρός, 'vehement in whatever he undertook'.

en: enjoy, take pleasure in (+ dat. or participle)
note: The aorist ἐχάρην is passive in form, active in meaning. Letters opened with ὁ δεῖνα τῷ δεῖνι χαίρειν 'So-and-so to So-and-so, greetings', and Modern Greeks still say χαίρω πολύ 'pleased to meet you'.

ex.en: Fine things are hard. (proverb quoted by Plato)

en: on the ground, to the ground
note: Same root as χθών 'earth' and Latin humus; the chameleon is a 'lion on the ground'.

rel.n: coined from χάος by van Helmont

note: In Hesiod's Theogony 'first of all Chaos came to be', a gaping void (related to χάσκω 'gape' and χάσμα), not disorder.
From χαράττω 'engrave': first the die that stamps a coin, then the mark itself. Theophrastus' Χαρακτῆρες sketch thirty human types.

rel.g: give away, make a present of

note: Accusative χάριν; χάριν + gen. means 'for the sake of', exactly like Latin grātiā. The Χάριτες are the Graces.
Through Latin charta came chart, card, charter, carton and cartoon; Italian and Spanish carta is simply 'paper' or 'letter'.
From χεῖμα, χειμών 'winter, storm'. Modern Greek χειμερία νάρκη 'winter sleep' is hibernation.
Stem χειρ- but dat. pl. χερσί(ν). εἰς χεῖρας ἐλθεῖν 'come to hands' means to come to blows. Modern χέρι is from the diminutive χειρίον.

ex.t: ἡ δὲ χεὶρ τὴν χεῖρα νίζει.
ex.en: One hand washes the other. (proverb, first found in Epicharmus)

note: The Athenian Assembly elected its generals by raising hands. The Church applied the word to ordination, and that is its only Modern Greek sense.
cite: χειροτονέω, χειροτονήσω, ἐχειροτόνησα, κεχειροτόνηκα, κεχειροτόνημαι, ἐχειροτονήθην

ex.t: μία γὰρ χελιδὼν ἔαρ οὐ ποιεῖ.
ex.en: One swallow does not make a spring. (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1.7)

cite: χέω, χέω, ἔχεα, κέχυκα, κέχυμαι, ἐχύθην

note: Also ἐχθές. Greek χθές, Latin herī and English yester- are all cognates.
Poetic. The Athenians prided themselves on being αὐτόχθονες, 'sprung from the land itself'. Latin humus and homō 'earthling' share the root.
Same root as χειμών 'winter' and Sanskrit hima 'snow' in Himalaya, 'abode of snow'.
Sappho, overcome by love, is 'greener than grass' (χλωροτέρα ποίας); chlorine was named for its yellow-green gas.
In humoral medicine an excess of black bile made one melancholic, of yellow bile choleric.

en: choregus: wealthy citizen who paid for a dramatic chorus
note: Funding a chorus was one of the 'liturgies' imposed on rich Athenians; Modern Greek χορηγός is a corporate sponsor.

en: chorus (of a play), band of dancers and singers

note: From χόρτος 'fodder': first used of fattening livestock, in Koine of people.

ex.t: μακάριοι οἱ πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τὴν δικαιοσύνην, ὅτι αὐτοὶ χορτασθήσονται
ex.en: blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled (Matthew 5:6)

note: The enclosed yard gave its name to what grew in it; Latin hortus and English yard, garden keep the 'enclosure'.
Contracts to η, not ᾱ: χρῆται, χρῆσθαι. Like Latin ūtor with the ablative, it takes its object in the dative.

en: it is necessary, one must, one ought (+ inf. or acc. + inf.)
note: Originally a noun 'need' with ἐστί understood; imperfect (ἐ)χρῆν, infinitive χρῆναι. It expresses moral necessity, δεῖ more practical need.
A χρῆμα is 'a thing one uses' (χράομαι); the plural χρήματα, 'goods', became 'money'.

ex.en: Money, money makes the man. (saying quoted by Pindar)

note: Delphi told Croesus that if he crossed the Halys he would destroy a great empire; it was his own (Herodotus 1.53, 1.91).
After itacism χρηστός and Χριστός sounded alike; Suetonius' 'Chrestus' may reflect the confusion.
A verbal adjective of χρίω 'anoint', translating Hebrew māšîaḥ 'Messiah'.

ex.en: Christ is risen. (the Easter greeting, unchanged in Modern Greek)

note: Modern Greek χρόνος also means 'year': χρόνια πολλά 'many years' is the birthday and name-day wish.
Epic gen. χροός, dat. χροΐ; the dative χρῷ survives in ἐν χρῷ 'close to the skin'. Sappho: λέπτον δ’ αὔτικα χρῷ πῦρ ὐπαδεδρόμηκεν 'a thin fire has run beneath my skin'.
An Athenian distinguished the ἄστυ, the town, from the χώρα, the countryside of Attica. In Modern Greek χώρα is 'country, state'.

ex.en: The enemy were ravaging the countryside.

note: From χῶρος 'space'. Modern Greek keeps the 'have room' sense: δεν χωράει 'it doesn't fit'.

ex.en: Everything moves on and nothing stays. (Heraclitus, quoted in Plato's Cratylus)

cite: χωρέω, χωρήσομαι, ἐχώρησα, κεχώρηκα, κεχώρημαι, ἐχωρήθην

note: A diminutive of χώρα; Modern Greek χωριό is 'village'.

en: pluck (a string), play the lyre or harp
song sung to the harp, psalm

note: ψευδής 'false' + λέγω 'speak'.
Modern Greek ψέμα comes from the related ψεῦσμα; 'to tell lies' is λέω ψέματα.
Since Epimenides was himself a Cretan, his line became the ancestor of the Liar paradox.

ex.en: Cretans are always liars. (Epimenides, quoted in Titus 1:12)

note: Athenian jurors voted with pebbles, and pebbles were also the counters of the abacus; so ψηφίο is a 'digit', just as Latin calculus 'pebble' gave calculate.
οἱ ψιλοί are troops without heavy armour. Byzantine grammarians named ε and υ 'plain e, plain u' to tell them from αι and οι, which sounded the same; the smooth breathing is ἡ ψιλή.
Plato's Phaedrus defines rhetoric as ψυχαγωγία τις διὰ λόγων, 'a leading of souls by words'; in Modern Greek it is just entertainment.
From ψύχω 'breathe'. In Homer the ψυχή is the breath-soul that leaves the body and flits to Hades as a shade; Plato made it the immortal, thinking self. It also means 'butterfly'.

ex.en: To take care of one's soul. (Socrates' demand in Plato's Apology)

note: From ψύχω 'blow, cool', the verb that also gives ψυχή 'breath, soul' and ψυχρός 'cold'.
Breath and cold share this root: ψυχή is the breath, ψυχρός the coolness a breath brings.
cite: ψύχω, ψύξω, ἔψυξα, —, ἔψυγμαι, ἐψύχθην / ἐψύγην

note: The diminutive ψωμίον 'little morsel' is Modern Greek ψωμί 'bread'; the ancient word for bread, ἄρτος, survives in church use and in αρτοποιείο 'bakery'.
In Attic prose almost every vocative has ὦ, and it is not solemn like English 'O': ὦ Σώκρατες is simply 'Socrates'.

ex.en: Men of Athens! (the usual opening of a speech)

en: thus, in this way, as follows

note: Contracted from ἀοιδή (verb ἀείδω / ᾄδω 'sing'); it hides in κωμῳδία, τραγῳδία, μελῳδία, παρῳδία and ῥαψῳδία.
Socrates calls himself a midwife who helps young men whose souls are in ὠδῖνες with ideas (Plato, Theaetetus).

cite: ὠθέω, ὤσω, ἔωσα, ἔωκα, ἔωσμαι, ἐώσθην

en: Ocean, the great river encircling the earth
note: For Homer, Ὠκεανός is a god and a river flowing round the flat earth, the source of all waters; later geographers made it the outer sea beyond the Pillars of Heracles.

ο ψεύτης · gen. ψεύτη · pl. ψεύτες

note: The everyday form of learned υψηλός, with the unstressed initial vowel lost. ψηλά = 'up, high up'.

ex.t: Ο αδερφός μου είναι πολύ ψηλός.

note: Figuratively 'to bring round': Τον έψησα να έρθει 'I talked him into coming'; ψήνομαι means 'I'm up for it'.
English digital counts on fingers (Latin digitus); Greek counts with pebbles — ψηφίο 'digit' is from ψῆφος 'pebble'.

ex.en: Who are you going to vote for?

note: Athenian jurors voted with pebbles — just as Latin calculus 'pebble' gave calculate. Like several ancient -ος nouns, it is feminine: η ψήφος.
cite: η ψήφος · gen. ψήφου · pl. ψήφοι

note: Grammarians named ε ψιλόν and υ ψιλόν 'plain e, plain u' to tell them apart from αι and οι; the ψιλή, the smooth breathing, is 'bare' of h.
ψύχω 'cool by blowing' also gave ψυχρός 'cold' and is traditionally linked with ψυχή 'breath, soul'.

ex.en: Put the milk in the fridge.

cite: το ψυγείο · gen. ψυγείου · pl. ψυγεία

note: A ψυχαγωγός once summoned the souls of the dead; Plato used ψυχαγωγία for the 'soul-leading' power of rhetoric. Today it is simply entertainment.

ex.t: Σ' ευχαριστώ από τα βάθη της ψυχής μου.
ex.en: I thank you from the bottom of my heart.

cite: η ψυχή · gen. ψυχής · pl. ψυχές

note: Coined in Renaissance Latin (psychologia) from Greek parts. Colloquially it also means 'mood': δεν έχω ψυχολογία 'I'm not in the mood'.

en: be in the throes of death
note: Ψυχή 'soul' + μάχομαι 'fight': the soul fighting to stay in the body.
Literally 'cold-bloodedness' — but a virtue, unlike English cold-blooded.
Everyday 'cold' is κρύος; ψυχρός belongs to set phrases like ψυχρός πόλεμος 'Cold War' and to cool behaviour.
A ψωμίον was a mere morsel — the one Jesus dips and gives to Judas in John 13:26. Ancient ἄρτος survives in church (the blessed bread) and in αρτοποιείο 'bakery'.

en: until, up to, as far as
note: Two ancient words merged here: ἕως 'until' and ὡς 'as'. μέχρι is a common synonym for 'until'.

ex.t: Το μαγαζί είναι ανοιχτό από τις εννιά ως τις πέντε.
ex.en: The shop is open from nine to five.

ex.en: Speak up, so that everyone can hear you.

note: A fusion of ως + τόσο, roughly 'for all that'.

ex.en: He was tired; nevertheless, he came.

note: Every part is plain Greek: οὖς (ὠτός) 'ear', ῥίς 'nose', λάρυγξ 'larynx', -λόγος. Greeks really use it, often shortened to ΩΡΛ.
